At least 550,000 households lost power overnight, Zelensky said, following a coordination meeting on the situation in Ukraine's regions.
Russian forces targeted energy infrastructure in 11 oblasts overnight and on the morning of Oct. 19, First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov reported. Additional power outages caused by Russian strikes and ongoing hostilities were reported in four other oblasts.
One energy worker was injured in an attack on an energy facility in Vinnytsia Oblast, Nekrasov said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity wherever security conditions allow, although prolonged air raid alerts and the threat of renewed Russian strikes are slowing restoration efforts, according to the Energy Ministry.
During the overnight attacks, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in several waves in what Zelensky described as a "targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast."
Zelensky said Ukraine had "once again" received no advance warning from its partners about the strikes.
Nekrasov said that over the past week, Russia carried out 87 targeted attacks on Ukraine's energy, oil, and gas sectors. Authorities recorded 224 incidents that caused damage to energy, oil, and gas infrastructure during that period.
The attacks come as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which are essential for defending against Russian ballistic missiles.
"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level. There are also delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also announced plans to increase production and procurement of anti-drone turrets, which he said have proven "highly effective" against Russian Shahed-type attack drones.
Russia has carried out 2,147 attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since July 16, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian published on Oct. 19, citing figures as of Oct. 17.
"Not a single day has passed without attacks on energy infrastructure," Koretskyi said.

North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:39:13 UTC
02:39:13 KST

North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.
The Unite union said on Monday that more than 160 offshore rig workers would take part in a 24-hour strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.
A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.
Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.
The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.
A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.
North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.
The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decision on the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.
A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.
The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”
Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.
Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.

Saudi Arabia trapped by miscalculations regarding Iran
The Iran newspaper argued that Saudi Arabia misjudged Iran’s broader strategy and the Axis of Resistance regarding Yemen. Riyadh imagined that military action against Yemen would weaken Iran. Instead, the conflict evolved into a strategic advantage for Tehran. Through careful management and without assuming direct control, Iran benefited from developments in Yemen.
The Ansarallah’s ability to threaten the Bab al-Mandab Strait enabled Iran to exercise influence over two major global energy chokepoints: the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. Iran also positioned itself as a responsible actor by offering mediation and linking the Yemen issue to wider diplomatic negotiations. According to the article, Saudi Arabia failed to recognize this strategic chain of events and found itself in a situation where Ansarallah’s actions ultimately benefited Iran. One of Riyadh’s key mistakes, it argues, was misunderstanding the nature of the relationship between Iran and the Ansarallah.
Ham-Mihan: Trump has already made his final decision
In an interview with international affairs analyst Hassan Hanizadeh, Ham-Mihan examined Donald Trump’s approach toward relations between Tehran and Washington. Hanizadeh said the possibility of conflict remains serious and that Trump could resort to military action in an attempt to reshape regional dynamics in favor of the United States and Israel. Such a course, he warned, could have far-reaching consequences if accompanied by miscalculations. Developments in the Strait of Hormuz and incidents involving large vessels have added further complexity to the situation. According to Hanizadeh, the US president appears to have already decided on Iran, and the possibility of military action has not disappeared. At the same time, Iran is prepared to defend its borders. Given the current sensitive environment, any military move or miscalculation by either side could widen the crisis and produce consequences extending beyond the two countries.
Sobh-e-No: Will a new war break out?
 
Sobh-e-No analyzed possible US scenarios regarding a renewed war with Iran. The paper outlined three possibilities. The first is a large-scale, comprehensive attack. The second is a limited, symbolic strike intended as a signal. The third is postponement until after the midterm congressional elections. It argues that Trump is currently managing tensions in order to get through the election period. However, this delay does not mean the danger of conflict has disappeared; it merely postpones a decision. As a result, the likelihood of a major war in the short term is considered low, though a limited attack or uncontrolled escalation remains possible. According to the article, Trump is reluctant to accept the economic costs, political risks, internal divisions, and strategic uncertainties associated with a new war. He views the conflict as a potential political vulnerability and would prefer to contain it before the election. Nevertheless, mounting pressures could still push him toward either a controlled or unintended escalation.
Javan: Control over Hormuz has significant psychological effects on foes
In an analysis of Iran’s approach toward the Strait of Hormuz, Javan argued that understanding the deeper historical and geoeconomic context is essential. The paper argued that Iran’s decision to impose new management rules over the strait and abandon passivity should not be interpreted as a temporary defensive measure. Rather, it described the move as part of a broader and proactive strategy aimed at signaling the end of American hegemony in West Asia. According to the article, Iran’s determination to maintain sovereign control over the strait has significant psychological and strategic effects on enemies. It argues that this persistence creates frustration within Washington’s decision-making process and could eventually lead US leaders to conclude that efforts to force Iran’s submission through military pressure and war are futile.
Kayhan: US concerned about Iran’s impact on mid-term elections
In an explanation, Kayhan said that the United States is increasingly concerned about Iran’s influence on the American political climate. The paper noted that Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed concern in recent weeks about Iran’s impact on the US Congressional mid-term elections. According to the article, Trump views election results as a measure of success in the war that began against Iran on February 28. It argues that over the past seven months he has repeatedly made claims suggesting that Iran’s military, economic, and political capacities have been severely weakened. However, the paper says that opinion polls in the United States indicate these claims have failed to convince the public. Kayhan contends that Trump’s repeated statements are an attempt to conceal the difficulties that the confrontation with Iran has created for Washington. The article further argues that recent surveys show growing public pessimism regarding success against Iran and increasing concern over the economic pressures associated with the conflict.

2026-10-19

02:35:17 KST

The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration.
Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views.
In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents.
The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers.
The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes.
Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.
Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”.
“I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added.
With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions.
“I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said.
“I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.”
In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.”
She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.
“We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine and access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon wrote on X. He also warned that the Administration’s policy was doomed unless it changed course.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s office declined to comment.
The publication notes that Hegseth has been seeking congressional approval for months of a record $1.5 trillion defense budget proposed by Trump. Last week, he also said the Pentagon would push for approval of a $350 billion supplemental funding package that has stalled in Congress over disagreements about how it should be funded.
The package provides funding for several of Trump’s priorities, including $17 billion for the Golden Dome homeland missile defense system, drones, and $47 billion to expand ammunition production. The Pentagon is also requesting another $36 billion for the Warrior Ethos program, which would invest in housing and infrastructure for service members.
Since Democrats are almost unanimously opposed to Trump’s war against Iran, Republican leaders will need the support of virtually every member of their House caucus to pass the package. Bacon believes the President’s soft policy toward Russia has alienated enough fellow Republicans to make it more difficult to pass defense funding and other legislative initiatives.
The agreement involving Russian diesel fuel has drawn particular criticism. Last week, a bipartisan group of lawmakers sent Trump a letter saying the deal violated, if not the letter, then the spirit of a new law imposing sanctions on Russia.
Some Republicans who spoke on condition of anonymity also criticized the President’s decision amid rising diesel prices, linking the situation to the war against Iran.
“He [Trum] needs to drop this decision. Like, A, it’s illegal. We passed a law saying there’s an energy ban on Russia. But at the same time, why did we get ourselves into a war in the Middle East to upset fuel prices? You want to lower fuel prices, figure that out,” an aide to one House Republican said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the U.S. President said that he did not want to make decisions that could push Russia away from peace talks and accused Volodymyr Zelensky of being “unwilling to end the war.”

Albania on fire: who’s behind the riots?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:33:43 UTC
02:33:43 KST

Albania on fire: who’s behind the riots?
Anti-government rioters have torched Albania’s education ministry and supreme court, as protests spread across the Balkan nation. Prime Minister Edi Rama is refusing to step down and blames the unrest on Russia. What’s really going on?
As of October 19, the Albanian capital of Tirana has been rocked by seven consecutive days and nights of rioting, while protests and clashes between demonstrators and police have been reported in the cities of Lezhe, Vlore, Elbasan, and Shkoder. A large group of rioters breached the perimeter of the education ministry in Tirana on October 14, setting the building on fire.
Running battles between demonstrators and police have broken out around the ministry on several occasions since. On October 19, hundreds of demonstrators pelted rocks at riot police, who responded with tear gas and rubber bullets. The previous night, offices of the Albanian Supreme Court were set on fire, and arson attacks on several police stations in the city were reported.
Some 500 demonstrators had been detained and 167 of them formally arrested as of October 17, according to Reuters. 295 people had been injured, including 196 police officers, as of October 19, according to Interior Minister Ervin Demo.
What do the protesters want?
The protests follow more than a year of unrest in Albania, which began when Rama banned TikTok in the runup to last March’s parliamentary elections, following similar measures inposed by the EU during every major election across the bloc since 2024. The ban was lifted in February of this year, but demonstrations broke out again in May after Rama’s government authorized the sale of protected wetlands to a development company operated by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
The protesters demanded the resignation of Rama and his entire cabinet, and the cancellation of a planned twin-phase resort project on the wetlands and on nearby Sazan Island.
The protesters’ core demand – that Rama resign – remains unchanged. However, the movement is now calling for a root-and-branch reform of the entire Albanian establishment, with demonstrators accusing both Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha of corruption. Unemployment, underfunding of schools, and declining living standards have also been cited by protesters as grievances.
What did Rama say about the protests?
Despite the repeated chants of “Rama resign” heard at the protests, Rama has claimed that the demonstrators do not oppose his government, but Albania’s “mission” of joining the EU.
“I am not being challenged,” he said in a video address on October 18. “The government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged”
“Albanians need to think very clearly,” he continued. “Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
Rama has refused to resign, and blamed the protests on “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace.” Back in June, Rama accused “the enemies of Albania and of Israel” of waging a “hybrid war” to stop the wetlands development. In two separate speeches on October 18 and 19, the embattled PM blamed the unrest on Russian philosopher Alexander Dugin and a “wave of Russian influence in the entire social media system,” and on “the Khomeiniist republic of Iran, the pinnacle of disinformation.”
Was Russia involved?
In short, no. Rama has not backed up any of his accusations, and they are being treated with skepticism and ridicule by demonstrators and opposition media. Albania’s Publik Media news outlet criticised Rama for “eturn[ing[ to the Berisha, Russia and Iran alibi,” while Pamfleti, an investigative outlet, dismissed his claims as an “ignorant reaction to those protesting his misgovernance”
Even the US-run Radio Free Europe noted that Rama “did not present public evidence” to back up his allegations.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has rejected Rama’s accusations. “No, Edi Rama,” she said on October 18, “it is the citizens of your country who have taken to the streets in protest.”
“This has all the hallmarks of the ‘highly likely’ British approach,” Serbian journalist Nebojsa Malic told RT on October 19, referring to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s failed attempts to blame the 2016 Brexit vote on Russia and a recent ‘terror plot’ at a US airbase on Iran. “We’ll just make an accusation and provide no evidence but say ‘oh it’s highly likely that Russia’s behind this’, and everybody is going to take it for granted.”
Rama is “doing this because he’s hoping it will stick,” Malic said. “He has nothing to lose. He’s seen plenty of leaders in western Europe essentially getting away scot free with covering for their malice and incompetence by blaming Russia.”
“Rama is just as opportunistic as [French President Emmanuel] Macron or any British prime minister in the last ten years,” Malic concluded. “They will say or do whatever, because they think that Russia is not able to defend itself.”
Why did Rama mention Israel?
Rama’s claim that “enemies of Albania and Israel” were behind this summer’s environmental protests stems from the involvement of Kushner in the wetlands project. A close associate of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Kushner has extensive family and financial ties to Israel. His investment firm, Affinity Partners, has funneled Emirati, Saudi, and Qatari cash into multiple Israeli businesses, including five arms manufacturers.
However, all available information suggests that the funding for Kushner’s Albanian projects comes from Albanian, American, and Qatari individuals and entities. Affinity Partners is leading the €1.4 billion Sazan Island project, while Kushner himself is a minority partner in the wetlands development.
Rama visited Israel and addressed the Knesset in January. Less than 24 hours later, Israel’s Channel 12 claimed that the Albanian PM had struck a deal with Netanyahu to accept up to 100,000 Palestinian refugees from Gaza. As speculation spread that the Palestinians would be resettled on land developed by Kushner, Rama clarified that no such deal had been, or would be, made.
Regardless, Rama’s close relations with Netanyahu are at odds with public opinion in Albania, where a 2024 poll found that 73% of the population believe that Israel should be sanctioned over its war on Gaza. Kushner is widely seen in Albania as representing Israeli interests, and Rama’s decision to amend environmental laws and grant “strategic investor” status to Affinity Partners has fueled accusations that the PM is placing Washington and West Jerusalem’s interests above Tirana’s.
Will there be an Albanian Maidan?
Some images emerging from Tirana – burning barricades, police officers set on fire with Molotov cocktails, and smouldering government buildings – are reminiscent of the scenes that played out during the 2014 ‘Maidan’ coup in Ukraine. However, Rama is in far less perilous of a position than Ukraine’s president, Viktor Yanukovich, was during the 2014 uprising.
Unlike the present unrest in Albania, the Maidan coup was planned and directed by foreign actors, namely the US State Department and the British embassy in Kiev. Rama, on the other hand, is a close partner of the EU and US, and neither Washington nor Brussels have backed the protesters. Instead, Rama has apparently been given carte blanche to squash the demonstrations, with columns of military vehicles seen entering Tirana between October 15 and 19.
The EU has condemned the use of violence by protesters, with the European Commission criticizing them for “arson, attacks on State institutions and the destruction of public and private property.” In a statement on October 18, the commission praised Rama’s progress toward EU membership and welcomed his “commitment that the right to protest will be protected.”
One week earlier, an EU delegation in Tirana said that Brussels was “aware of allegations of excessive use of force by the police against protesters and journalists,” adding that the government’s response to protests and riots “must remain within the law.”
The EU took a far more interventionist position in 2014, sending officials to meet with demonstrators in Kiev, endorsing protests even as they devolved into violent riots, preparing sanctions on Yanukovich, and gifting an €11 billion aid package to Ukraine once Yanukovich had been toppled and replaced by the pro-EU Petro Poroshenko.
The West is still firmly on Rama’s side, and he is unlikely to face any calls for resignation from abroad. However, he is still facing the most sustained public pressure campaign of his 13-year stint in power, and if the protests continue and more buildings burn, he may be left with no choice but to admit defeat and step down.

Mohajerani: Iran’s history of resistance reflects nation’s resolve to defend its sovereignty
TEHRAN – Iranian Government Spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani has praised the Iranian nation’s determination and ability to withstand external aggression, saying past wars demonstrate the country’s resolve to safeguard its independence, territorial integrity and national sovereignty.
Speaking at an event in Tehran on Monday, Mohajerani described the Sacred Defense—the term Iran uses for its 1980–1988 war with Iraq—as a lasting reminder of the nation’s resilience and ability to overcome formidable challenges despite limited resources.
Referring to Iran’s history of conflicts over the past two centuries, she said the Iranian people had achieved significant feats by relying on their determination and collective strength.
Mohajerani stressed that defending the country’s national interests and territorial integrity remained a fundamental principle, adding that Iran had not surrendered an inch of its territory in the wars following the victory of the Islamic Revolution in 1979. She described the preservation of the country’s territorial integrity as one of the Iranian nation’s greatest sources of pride.
The government spokesperson recalled that Iraq’s war against Iran began at a time when the country was grappling with internal challenges in the aftermath of the Islamic Revolution.
Despite those difficulties, she said, the Iranian people demonstrated their determination to defend the country and protect its sovereignty, refusing to compromise on their national rights.
The spokesperson also emphasized the importance of supporting the families of those killed in the war, saying the entire nation stood alongside them.
Mohajerani stressed that the capacity to withstand hardship was not limited by gender, pointing to the experiences of women who have endured profound personal losses while continuing to demonstrate strength and perseverance.

The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:30:02 UTC
02:30:02 KST

In Emmanuel Macron’s book Revolution, published ahead of the 2017 presidential election that he went on to win, he promised to restore hope to a country that was losing faith in its future. As Mr Macron’s lame-duck second term enters its last phase against a quasi-insurrectionary backdrop of torched public buildings and looted shops, the failure of that political project appears total.
The worst scenes of urban violence for years overshadowed a weekend of protest that gravely undermined what is left of the French president’s authority. As police lost control of the streets, more than 2,000 shops were ransacked. Far-left groups targeted town halls and local buildings, and engaged in pitched battles with the police, whose disastrously heavy-handed response to last week’s high school protests has succeeded only in escalating tensions.
In a statement on Sunday evening, Mr Macron rightly condemned what he described as episodes of “unbridled violence”. On the far right, Marine Le Pen is already exploiting a national sense of dismay to present herself as the law-and-order solution to the crisis. But the shocking actions of a minority should not obscure the significance of the vast, peaceful demonstrations that took place throughout France on Saturday. Calls to unite the student protests and the yellow vest movement, which disrupted Mr Macron’s first term over cost of living issues, mobilised up to 800,000 people.
The root cause of the unrest is a widespread perception that France’s social contract is broken. The young feel let down by an underfunded and unequal education system, and are fearful of the future impact of AI and the climate emergency. As is increasingly the case across Europe, they no longer trust mainstream politicians to find answers. The scale of the weekend protests showed that gen Z’s discontent has merged with that felt in the country’s neglected towns and banlieues, which have suffered repeated economic shocks since the Covid pandemic.
The obtuse and stubborn response from Mr Macron has been to double down on a cost‑cutting agenda to reduce France’s public debt, in order to appease the financial markets. But in an era where the asset-rich have continued to flourish, and the wealthiest have done best of all, to argue that that there is no alternative to spending less on schools and healthcare won’t wash. The economist Thomas Piketty pointed out during last week’s student protests that the boom in private wealth means that, despite the size of its public debt, “France has never been richer”.
Mr Macron’s reckless decision to call a snap election in 2024, which cost him his majority, left him a diminished political figure. His biggest subsequent error has been to haughtily persist with the economics of austerity, despite clear evidence of deepening political polarisation and rising popular anger. With each week that passes, the social consequences appear more ominous, ahead of presidential elections in six months’ time.
The latest polls suggest that the far right’s huge lead is widening ahead of that contest. Meanwhile, the hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to outscore progressive rivals, though the numbers suggest that he would heavily lose a runoff against Ms Le Pen. In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.

Türkiye breaks ground on massive 22-megawatt data center project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:27:51 UTC
02:27:51 KST

Zeynep Duyar and Emir Yildirim
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
A groundbreaking ceremony was held on Monday for Ankara’s data center complex, located in the Baskent Organized Industrial Zone, marking a significant milestone in Türkiye’s efforts to become a regional digital hub.
The new facility is the result of a joint venture between Ronesans Holding and global data center operator Digital Realty.
Turkish Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said at the ceremony that the initial facility will require a $450 million investment in basic infrastructure and building construction, while an additional $900 million will be allocated to cooling systems and IT infrastructure.
“Once all phases are complete, this facility will represent a fixed capital investment of $4.1 billion in the Ankara Temelli Baskent Organized Industrial Zone,” he said.
Kacir referred to data processing and cloud computing capabilities as “the oil of the 21st century,” highlighting the growing importance of technology in the modern global arena.
“The total installed capacity of data centers worldwide is expected to rise from around 103 gigawatts last year to 200 gigawatts by 2030,” he noted, adding that over one-fifth of the total value of new global investments has been made in data centers.
Kacir stated that Ankara launched the HIT-30 program to allocate $30 billion in incentives through 2030 to attract high-tech investments and support the cloud computing and technology that AI applications require.
He noted that Türkiye started a new chapter in technology development and production through its National Technology Initiative, which highlights digital sovereignty as integral to independence.
“We implemented a comprehensive support framework to develop data center and cloud computing capacity and attract global investments,” he said. “We have benefited more than 8,900 researchers to date through the Turkish Science e-Infrastructure (TRUBA), enhancing the country’s high-performance computing infrastructure with over 80,000 processor cores, 504 graphics processing units (GPUs) and 26 petabytes of data storage capacity.”
The minister mentioned that the HIT-30 program, the largest-scale incentive package in the nation’s history, includes the “HIT-Data Center Call” scheme, dedicating a $1.4 billion budget to supporting the construction of data centers of at least 30 megawatts, while the “HIT-Artificial Intelligence Call” mobilizes $1.6 billion to accelerate the establishment of domestic cloud-based infrastructure.
“And through the HIT-Quantum Call, we aim to build a quantum infrastructure of our own, the technology of the future, to further cement Türkiye’s position as a regional hub for data processing and storage,” he added.
Ankara’s broader strategy was also detailed in the 2026-2030 Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan, which aims to expand installed data center capacity, with a national goal of at least 1 gigawatt by 2030.
“We will facilitate access to high-performance chips for entrepreneurs and researchers through the ‘GPU for Everyone’ program to bring together scientists, tech startups and investors within a comprehensive AI ecosystem supported by strong infrastructure,” the minister noted.
Kacir added that Ronesans Holding and Digital Realty are expected to play a key role in reaching this goal, as the two firms plan to lead a combined investment of more than $10 billion in Ankara and Istanbul to establish a projected data center capacity of 200 megawatts, making up one-fifth of the national goal.

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim

Massive protests in France over the weekend hit European markets hard, triggering a broad sell-off across major indexes.
Germany’s DAX 40 dropped 1.36% to 25,274 points at 4 pm local time as markets responded to the growing demonstrations in neighboring France, which is seeing some of its most serious political unrest in recent years.
France’s benchmark CAC 40 traded down 1.56% at 7,832 points at the same time.
Currency markets also reflected the financial sector’s anxiety as the euro depreciated by 0.12% against the US dollar to $1.1230.
Beyond the eurozone, the UK’s FTSE 100 fell 1.29% to 10,741.51 points at the same time.
As one of the countries whose markets are highly sensitive to shifts in the European political climate, Italy saw its FTSE MIB 30 drop sharply by 1.77% to 48,970.4 points.
Government bonds came under intense pressure due to the events in France, which have also heightened political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Major financial institutions suffered, with shares of leading banks BNP Paribas, Societe Generale and Credit Agricole dropping between 2% and 2.5%.
The insurance sector was also hit as France’s largest insurance group, AXA SA, lost nearly 2% in value, dropping to €42.2 ($47.4) per share.
The wave was also felt in Spain, where upcoming snap elections next month contributed to a 1.8% drop in its IBEX 35, bringing it down to 18,978.
Defense firms and major banking institutions were among the most affected groups across the continent, as investors took a cautious stance.
All eyes turned to the earnings reports later this week from multinational corporations, including SAP, Barclays and Nokia.
Francesco Pesole, a foreign exchange strategist at ING Group, recently said the sustained protests in France will continue pressuring local corporate stocks and limit the euro’s potential rebound against the US dollar.
While the exchange rate dipped below 1.120 overnight, the euro/dollar parity showed signs of a slight recovery this morning.
Pesole noted that the euro is currently undervalued against the US dollar by 1.3%-1.5%, which aligns with France’s fiscal risks remaining firmly in the market, further reflected in the French-German 10-year government bond yield spread hovering around 140 basis points.
Investors will be on the lookout for Germany’s ZEW economic sentiment data to be released on Tuesday.

French Prime Minister calls for partial curfews after weekend riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:26:03 UTC
02:26:03 KST

France announces first curfews as government grapples with unrest
PARIS - France announced partial curfews on Oct 19 as protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris and authorities scrambled to stem discontent over living costs, after weekend demonstrations spilled into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu did not rule out imposing a state of emergency after the interior minister said police “had lost control” during the unrest, which flared six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.
With organisers calling for a new round of protests on Oct 24, Lecornu’s office said partial curfews would be enforced from 8pm to 6am local time on Oct 19 and 20 in four northern cities, including Lille, to protect businesses.
“I’m absolutely determined to restore public order”, he said.
Other European countries have also seen demonstrations over rising prices, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal.
Some half a million people turned out across France on Oct 17 to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with students demanding better conditions at high schools.
What started as peaceful demonstrations descended into violence in some places, as masked groups attacked law enforcement, broke into town halls and other public buildings, setting many of them ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters.
Listings for ‘stolen goods’
On Oct 19, France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” following the looting on Oct 17 and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay.
According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.
After the weekend scenes of chaos, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered his resignation on Oct 19, but Macron refused to accept it.
More than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
Macron acknowledged failures in the government response, despite the deployment of some 60,000 law enforcement personnel on Oct 17.
Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 per cent of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
At least 3,000 shops were affected, according to small businesses minister Serge Papin, with damage running into the hundreds of millions of euros.
In an address to the nation on Oct 18, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence.
City authorities in the southern port city of Marseille said they had banned public gatherings from noon to 8pm local time.
The European Union slammed the violence as “unacceptable” but warned that the right to peaceful protest “must be protected” in France.
Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying “further demonstrations and, in some cases, further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out”.
China has warned citizens travelling to France to be aware of risks and take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Louvre blocked
In Paris on Oct 19, about a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the iconic Louvre, the most visited museum in the world, while bewildered tourists looked on.
“We don’t want to get involved. We want to stand back and get away from them,” Pat Boland, a tourist from Australia, said of the protests.
The pensioner, 73, spoke to AFP outside barricades that had been erected at the Louvre, which was closed because a small group of protesters stood by its famed glass pyramid entrance.
Rising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40 per cent and petrol by 25 per cent since March, and where food prices have risen by 25 per cent over the past five years.
The unrest has flared before presidential elections in April and May that will see a new French president elected after a decade of centrist Macron. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, is riding high in the polls.
The government has accused ultra-left groups of stoking the violence to boost the chances of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon in the presidential polls.
Europe
During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan.
“I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself,” mayor Giuseppe Sala said.
In Belgium, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in Brussels and Liege.
In Spain, protesters have set up tents in the heart of Madrid to denounce soaring housing costs, with similar encampments going up in neighbouring Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto. AFP

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:25:53 UTC
02:25:53 KST

In the landscape of religious life in the United States, Reverend Adam Hamilton has a massive pulpit.
The organisation he founded, the Church of the Resurrection, is considered the largest United Methodist congregation in the country. It spans nine campuses and 23,000 members. Hamilton himself has authored more than 30 books.
But this November, Hamilton is eyeing an even bigger platform: the US Congress.
A mild-mannered pastor with square glasses and a receding swoop of white hair, Hamilton is hoping to achieve what many political observers once dismissed as far-fetched.
He is hoping to win a seat representing Kansas in the US Senate – as a Democrat.
Not since 1932 has a Democrat won a Senate race in the Midwestern state. Kansas is considered ruby red, with a conservative base that leans towards right-wing leaders like President Donald Trump.
But Hamilton is part of a trend in the 2026 midterm election cycle. Largely in right-leaning states, several Christian leaders have stood for election as Democrats, bucking the stereotype that religion is the domain of conservatives.
Approximately nine Democratic faith leaders, seminary students and Sunday school teachers are in the running for federal office in the November 3 election. At least a dozen were on the ballot during the primary elections earlier this year.
Many are competing in states like Iowa, Texas, Arkansas and Tennessee, which have a history of backing right-wing candidates in statewide elections.
Their campaigns have raised questions about whether appealing to Christian voters can be a path to victory for Democrats in the hotly contested midterms.
Reverend Shannon Fleck, executive director of Faithful America, a progressive Christian advocacy organisation, believes some voters have grown disenchanted with the Republican claim on religious values.
Democratic candidates, she argues, can offer an alternative.
"This is going to move the needle even more in red states because, in our homes, faith has been a part of our ecosystem for forever, but it’s also been manipulated by our leaders for forever," Fleck, an Oklahoma resident, said.
She added that faith-inspired Democratic candidates have "more opportunities for turnover" in right-leaning states, "because we are so intimately familiar with the other option".
Harnessing the evangelical bloc
More than 60 percent of Americans identify as Christian. But in the last three decades, white evangelical Protestants in particular have shifted steadily rightwards on the political spectrum.
In 2024, the Pew Research Center suggested that 85 percent of white evangelicals leaned towards the Republican Party, up from 65 percent in 1994.
Overall, 59 percent of Protestants, 52 percent of Catholics and 75 percent of Mormons identified with right-wing politics.
Experts say the Republican Party began cultivating Christian votes largely in the 1970s and 1980s. At the time, faith leaders like mega-pastor Jerry Falwell had grown disillusioned with the social policies of left-wing leaders like Jimmy Carter, himself a Sunday school teacher.
They founded groups like the Moral Majority in 1979 and the Christian Coalition of America in 1987 to support issues popular on the religious right, including restricting access to abortion and limiting the government's reach.
Trump himself has harnessed that evangelical voting bloc, pledging to protect its interests while in office. Since starting his second term, Trump has established a "religious liberty commission" and pledged to eradicate "anti-Christian bias".
But findings from the Pew Research Center have suggested Trump's hold on the white evangelical vote has started to wane.
As of January, the president's approval rating among the demographic had slipped from 78 percent in 2025 to 69 percent this year.
Only 40 percent of respondents expressed confidence that Trump has acted ethically while in office.
Democrats are hoping to capitalise on Trump's falling approval ratings in the midterm elections, which will decide which party controls the two chambers of Congress.
Deep left-wing roots
Faith leaders running as Democrats are not new. If anything, experts say the candidates are tapping into a long lineage of religious advocacy on the left.
“There have always been progressive Christians throughout American history,” said Guthrie Graves-Fitzsimmons, the vice president of programmes and strategy at the Interfaith Alliance, an advocacy organisation for religious freedom.
In his work as a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, a research nonprofit, Graves-Fitzsimmons studies the intersection of religion and politics.
He has tracked the influence of religious leaders to a range of critical moments in US history, from the civil rights movement – with figures like Reverend Martin Luther King Jr – to the push for women's rights.
Even conservative groups like the Moral Majority once participated in efforts like the environmental movement, championing a Christian responsibility to engage in the stewardship of nature.
"Every movement that we associate with the left or progressive movement in American history has been full of Christians, as well as people of other faiths and the non-religious,” Graves-Fitzsimmons explained.
Ryan Burge, a political scientist at Washington University in St Louis, traces the roots of the religious left even further back in US history, to the 19th-century fight over slavery.
"The abolitionist movement was largely a religious movement involving a lot of liberal and progressive Christians in the North,” Burge said.
Fast forward to the turn of the 20th century, and Burge said the country witnessed its "Social Gospel movement", a period in the early 1900s when theologians and pastors sought to apply Christian principles to issues like poverty and social justice.
“The best-selling book in America was A Theology for the Social Gospel for three years in a row around the turn of the century, which is a very liberal Christian book," Burge added.
But while the religious right tends to be a more homogeneous group, Burge explained that the religious left is more diverse, with faiths outside of Christianity better represented.
“On the religious right, it’s almost all Protestants and Catholics,” he said.
The religious left, meanwhile, has stronger representation among other faith groups. “You also have Muslims, who are a strong Democratic constituency, as well as Jews," Burge said, noting that African-American Christians also lean overwhelmingly left.
A shifting relationship to religion
There can be disadvantages to appealing to Christian voting blocs. Experts say Democrats have resisted being overtly religious in recent years as their coalition has grown more diverse.
Some 66 percent of Muslims identified with Democrats as of 2024. The number was 69 percent among Jewish voters.
“Candidates being overly religious is not a huge turn-on for a lot of Democrats,” Burge said. “They want strong separation of church and state. They don’t want their politicians to sound like Republicans. They don’t want to talk about Jesus.”
Burge also pointed out that the number of overtly religious voters may be shrinking.
In 2006, roughly 23 percent of Americans identified as white evangelical Christians, but that has fallen to 13 percent as of 2024, according to the Public Religion Research Institute.
The proportion of religiously unaffiliated Americans, meanwhile, has risen to 28 percent.
The shift has spurred questions about how powerful the religious voting bloc is, particularly for Democrats.
“I would even argue it’s probably the smallest it’s ever been in the last five years,” Burge said.
Still, several religious leaders have entered this year's midterm race, hoping to help the Democratic Party retake control of Congress.
They include figures like Hamilton in Kansas and Robb Ryerse in Arkansas, who founded their own churches.
Others, like Frederick Haynes III of Texas, Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, Anna Golladay of Tennessee and Lindsay James of Iowa, serve as faith leaders and pastors.
A couple – including Ben McAdams in Utah and Chaz Molder in Tennessee – have touted their work as Sunday school teachers. And then there is James Talarico, a seminary student in Texas locked in a heated race for the state's open Senate seat.
'Love thy neighbour'
Several candidates have embraced similar themes on the campaign trail in the lead-up to the November 3 vote.
Burge has noticed a heavy emphasis on values like "Love your neighbour as yourself" from the Gospels.
“There’s a lot of emphasis on the dignity of each person, in terms of income inequality as a moral issue. That filters down to things like minimum wage, workers’ rights, unions – but also to things like healthcare and health insurance,” Burge said.
The religious left, he added, "cast these issues not as economic issues but as social justice issues motivated by religion".
On the night Talarico won the Democratic nomination, the 37-year-old stood in front of a throng of supporters, some of whom waved signs emblazoned with the phrase "Love thy Neighbor".
It was a theme he reprised in his victory speech, tying the phrase to an embrace of diversity.
“My faith teaches me to love my neighbour as myself. Not just my neighbour who looks like me, not just my neighbour who prays like me, not just my neighbour who votes like me," Talarico declared to the crowd. "I am called to love all of my neighbours the way I love myself.”
Hamilton struck a similar chord when accepting his party's nod on August 4, after he won the Democratic primary for Kansas's Senate seat. He used the same biblical command to encourage civic responsibility.
“Loving your neighbour includes making sure that kids don’t go to bed hungry at night. Loving your neighbour is making sure people who are living in your midst who are marginalised, or made to feel small or belittled, are not belittled," Hamilton said.
"Loving your neighbour means making sure people don’t have to choose between making their house payment and making sure they can get healthcare.”
Religion as a battlefield
Religion has also been a springboard for attack during the midterm race, with both Democrats and Republicans pointing to Christian scripture to accuse their opponents of moral failings.
At the Iowa State Fair in August, Lindsay James, a Presbyterian minister running for Iowa's 2nd congressional district, painted her opponents as unfeeling by drawing on a biblical tale: the parable of the good Samaritan.
In the story, two religious leaders pass an injured man without stopping to help him. Finally, a Samaritan comes to his aid.
“That, to me, sounds a lot like what is happening in Washington, DC, right now,” James said. “Those who have the power and the authority to actually do something are turning a blind eye and walking away from people who are hurting and harmed.”
Republicans, for their part, have used the religious backgrounds of some Democratic candidates as a line of attack. Several have framed their opponents' beliefs as unorthodox or questioned their Christian faith.
At a conservative religious summit in July, Joe Mitchell, James's Republican rival in Iowa, even accused her of misrepresenting her credentials.
"She's also one of these people that calls herself a pastor, just like James Talarico, just like Sarah Trone Garriott," Mitchell said.
"I have a nickname for them. I call them PINOs," he added, defining the acronym as "Pastors in Name Only".
"They're not real pastors, right? They don't profess the true gospel of Jesus Christ."
Talarico has faced similar accusations in the Senate race in Texas. On a podcast, his opponent, Republican Ken Paxton, denounced the Democrat's beliefs as “antithetical to historical Christian views".
"They are literally the opposite of Christianity," Paxton said.
'Looking for authenticity'
It is unclear whether the religious backgrounds of Democrats like Talarico will resonate with voters when it comes time to cast a ballot.
Burge believes Democrats campaigning on their Christian bona fides could enjoy a boost in certain parts of the country, but not in many traditional left-wing strongholds.
“That’s not going to be a winning message in some places, like California or Massachusetts,” Burge explained. “It might work in a purplish state in the Midwest, but it’s not going to work in a deep-blue place."
Graves-Fitzsimmons, meanwhile, suggested that religion could be an avenue to build connection with voters.
“I think people are looking for authenticity right now," he said. "There’s a wide, open field for those who can speak truthfully, honestly, compassionately and from a place of faith that’s not trying to impose your faith on others.”
So far, several Democratic faith leaders on this year's midterm ballot are enjoying closer-than-expected races in their deep-red states.
Recent polling suggests candidates like Talarico and Hamilton are neck-in-neck with their Republican adversaries, even exceeding them in some measures of support.
A Marist poll this month found Talarico was leading Paxton with 47 percent support, compared with the Republican's 45 percent.
An Emerson College poll from September suggested Hamilton was also slightly ahead of his opponent, incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, by two points.
The stakes are high for Democrats, particularly in the Senate. The party needs every victory it can get to achieve a majority in the 100-seat chamber, given that only a third of the Senate's seats are on the ballot this November.
But the stakes are perhaps even higher for Hamilton, who at 62 is attempting to achieve something very few have done. Only one senator in the last 100 years has continued to pastor a church while in office, as Hamilton intends to do.
That senator is Reverend Raphael Warnock, a Democrat from another battleground state, Georgia.

Tehran theater to host reading performance of “All My Sons”

Tehran theater to host reading performance of “All My Sons”
TEHRAN- A reading performance of American writer Arthur Miller’s 1946 popular play “All My Sons” will be staged at the Neauphle-le-Chateau Theater in Tehran on October 31.
Negar Hosseini will direct the reading performance based on a Persian translation of the play by Hassan Maleki.
Javid Hashemi, Roya Rezai Mehdi Seyyedi, Nazanin Kouhestani, Sareh Asghari and Hadi Heshmati will perform the reading.
Miller wrote “All My Sons” after his first Broadway play, “The Man Who Had All the Luck”, closed after only four performances in 1944. Determined to prove himself as a successful playwright, Miller regarded his next work as a final attempt to establish his career, vowing to find another profession if it failed to attract an audience.
The play, which premiered at Broadway’s Coronet Theater on January 29, 1947, was inspired by a real industrial scandal reported in an Ohio newspaper. Miller’s then mother-in-law drew his attention to an account of the Wright Aeronautical Corporation, which had knowingly supplied defective aircraft engines to the US military between 1941 and 1943. The incident provided the basis for Miller’s exploration of corporate greed, moral responsibility and the human cost of prioritizing profit over lives.
Set in the aftermath of World War II, “All My Sons” centers on Joe Keller, a prosperous businessman who runs a machine shop with his family’s future in mind. During the war, his company supplied defective aircraft parts, resulting in the deaths of 21 military pilots. Although his business partner, Steve Deever, was imprisoned for the crime, Keller was acquitted and subsequently rebuilt his business, accumulating considerable wealth.
Years later, Keller’s carefully maintained life begins to unravel when his surviving son, Chris, announces his intention to marry Ann Deever, Steve’s daughter. Ann was previously engaged to Chris’s brother, Larry, who disappeared while serving in the war and is presumed dead. Chris and Ann’s relationship brings the unresolved past back into the Keller household, particularly because Keller’s wife, Kate, refuses to accept that Larry will never return.
The situation becomes more complicated when Ann’s brother, George, returns from the war after visiting their imprisoned father. Discovering that Keller has remained free while Steve bears the consequences of their business dealings, George challenges the version of events that the Keller family has long accepted. His arrival threatens Chris and Ann’s plans and forces the family to confront the truth about the defective parts.
As tensions rise, Chris struggles to reconcile his admiration for his father with the possibility that Keller knowingly sacrificed the lives of other men’s sons to protect his business. The revelation of Larry’s final response to his father’s actions brings the conflict to its devastating conclusion, exposing the consequences of Keller’s moral failure for his own family.
The play received the New York Drama Critics’ Circle Award for Best Play in 1947, establishing Miller as a major voice in American theater. It also won the Tony Award for Best Author.
“All My Sons” introduced themes that would remain central to Miller’s work, including the conflict between personal loyalty and social responsibility, the relationship between fathers and sons, and the ethical consequences of pursuing wealth at the expense of others. Through Keller’s downfall, Miller challenges the belief that success and family devotion can excuse wrongdoing, presenting a powerful tragedy about individual guilt and the wider obligations people have to society.

Amy Griffin’s “The Tell” comes to Iranian bookstores
TEHRAN- A Persian translation of American writer Amy Griffin’s memoir “The Tell” has been published by Milkan Publications in Tehran, with Naghmeh Hadadian translating the book into Persian.
The memoir explores the lasting effects of childhood trauma, the complexities of memory and the possibility of healing through confronting painful experiences and sharing long-hidden truths.
Originally published in 2025, “The Tell” became a New York Times bestseller and was selected for Oprah’s Book Club. The book recounts Griffin’s personal journey toward understanding a deeply buried part of her past and examines the emotional consequences of keeping traumatic experiences hidden, even from oneself.
Griffin’s life appeared successful from the outside. She grew up in Amarillo, Texas, studied at the University of Virginia as a student athlete, and later built a career in New York. She also established a family and became a successful businesswoman. Yet beneath this seemingly settled life, she was struggling with an unresolved past that she had not fully acknowledged.
A turning point came when her daughter questioned her emotional absence, asking where she was despite being physically present. The encounter prompted Griffin to begin investigating the mystery surrounding her own memories, setting her on a journey that would challenge her understanding of herself and her personal history.
Her search takes her into the field of psychedelic-assisted therapy and the limitations of the judicial system before bringing her back to the Texas Panhandle, where her story began. Through these experiences, Griffin considers how people respond to overwhelming events and how the desire to maintain control and an appearance of perfection can prevent them from confronting their vulnerabilities.
Beyond recounting her personal experiences, the memoir examines broader questions about women’s lives, including the pursuit of external validation and the pressure to meet social expectations. Griffin reflects on how these pressures shape identity and asks what freedom might become possible when people accept their experiences rather than continue to conceal them.
The book also emphasizes the importance of speaking openly about trauma, suggesting that sharing personal stories can help survivors move beyond shame and develop deeper connections with others. Its central theme is the possibility of reclaiming one’s life by acknowledging painful truths rather than allowing them to remain unspoken.

The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:25:02 UTC
02:25:02 KST

Does Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.
Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal. European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.
The Wall Street Journal laid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite most analysts saying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.
American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. More Republicans should find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from the White House. Heated denials from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, are no substitute for answers.
A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “strategically and culturally vital”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments must prepare to meet that challenge.
History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo the Three Emperors’ League that brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in 1881, the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.

Palestinian photographer’s works to be displayed in Tehran

Palestinian photographer’s works to be displayed in Tehran
TEHRAN – The photography exhibition “What Was Unseen!” featuring works by Palestinian photographer Mahmoud Abu Hamda will be launched at the Palestine Museum of Contemporary Art in Tehran on Wednesday.
Organized by the Iranian Photographers’ House, the exhibition will put on show a collection of photographs, which was exhibited in Baghdad last October, ILNA reported.
The works in this exhibition depict moments from the daily lives of children and women in the Palestinian territories; subjects whose lived experiences in the midst of war possess dimensions that go far beyond the conventional representations found in news and media.
In this collection, Abu Hamda employs a social approach to document the consequences and impacts of war, striving to capture the hidden human layers in Gaza from amidst the overwhelming imagery of bombings and destruction.
The exhibit showcases the artist's work created during the Gaza genocide, a time of great hardship and suffering for the people of Gaza, who have endured brutal Israeli aggression.
This exhibition is one of the few dedicated showcases by a Gaza-based photographer that provides a vivid and authentic image of the heart of Gaza during the Al-Aqsa storm. Its unique and documentary nature makes it rare worldwide.
Abu Hamda’s photos, with an artistic blend of technique, light, and emotion, offer an unmediated portrayal of the human impact of the crisis in Gaza. Regarding his work, he says: "My work in photography goes beyond capturing images; it is a journey to discover the secret of the hidden soul in every corner, an effort to embrace the beauty that beats in this land."
Through his powerful photographs, Abu Hamda sheds light on the human cost of conflict and the resilience of the Palestinian people. The exhibit is a testament to the enduring spirit of resistance and hope in the face of adversity.
Mahmoud Abu Hamda is a professional photographer, documentary filmmaker, and former university lecturer in photography from Gaza, Palestine. Since 2008, he has dedicated his work to capturing the spirit of Gaza, from its natural beauty, vibrant streets, and daily life before the war, to the immense destruction and human struggles of recent years.
His photography spans landscapes, cityscapes, food, and human stories, with a strong focus on resilience and memory.
His work has been featured in international exhibitions and publications, carrying Gaza’s story to the world through powerful and emotional visuals.
Earlier this month, Abu Hamda won the photography category in the prestigious Bayeux award for war correspondents for his work from Gaza.
It has been three years since Israel launched its genocide in Gaza, beginning on October 7, 2023, in response to attacks by Palestinian fighters. Over this period, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including more than 20,000 children, with thousands still trapped under rubble.
Israeli strikes have targeted hospitals and aid workers, violating international laws that protect medical facilities.
The blockade and military restrictions have also caused a severe famine. The UN officially recognized Gaza’s famine in August 2023, the first in the Middle East in recent history, with conditions expected to worsen.
Malnutrition among children has soared, with thousands suffering from severe acute malnutrition, and many infants born prematurely or underweight. The ongoing violence and blockade have created a humanitarian catastrophe for Gaza’s population.
The “What Was Unseen!” exhibition will run until November 5 at the Palestine Museum of Contemporary Art in Tehran.

Brazilian court orders Meta to prove Lula and Bolsonaro get equal treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Brazilian court orders Meta to prove Lula and Bolsonaro get equal treatment
A judge also doubled the daily fine for noncompliance with a previous court order governing political content on Meta’s platform.
Brazil’s top electoral court has doubled a daily fine for the United States-based social media company Meta, saying it failed to comply with an order about how political content is shown on its platforms.
On Monday, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) gave Meta 24 hours to show that it is not favouring one presidential candidate over the other in its content feeds.
The decision comes less than a week before Brazilians vote in a presidential run-off that pits left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
“The continued noncompliance, just a few days before the run-off election, demonstrates that the fine imposed was insufficient,” a TSE judge said in Monday’s order.
The penalty for noncompliance was also increased in the order, from 500,000 Brazilian reals ($100,000) to one million reals ($200,000).
The court order is in response to a complaint from Lula’s campaign that Meta prevented his profile from being fully promoted on Instagram and from being visible in searches.
His campaign has also argued that posts by Lula’s supporters are being disproportionately taken down by moderators, who are instead allowing content promoting his rival or questioning the integrity of elections.
Civil society groups and digital rights monitors have supported those allegations, saying Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp — three platforms run by Meta — have suppressed content from the left-leaning leader while boosting posts promoting Bolsonaro.
Meta has denied favouring either candidate on its platforms, although it admits some of Lula’s campaign ads were taken offline temporarily due to technical errors.
Lula and Bolsonaro are set to face off in a final round of voting on Sunday. Bolsonaro, the son of an imprisoned former president, performed better than many analysts expected in the first round of voting on October 4.
He garnered 47 percent of the vote, compared with Lula’s 45 percent. Neither, however, crossed the 50-percent threshold needed to avoid a run-off. Pre-election polling puts the two virtually neck-and-neck going into Sunday’s vote.
Social media bias has been a point of contention on both sides of Brazil’s political sphere.
Earlier this month, Lula’s campaign launched a website to document complaints from supporters about their activities being unfairly restricted on Meta and other social media platforms.
Several digital rights groups, such as the nonprofit CTRL+Z, have published findings that suggest Meta may have helped Bolsonaro have an outsized presence on its platforms, which many in Brazil use as their main source of news.
“Brazilian citizens have the right to know why their accounts were banned, why their posts disappeared, why their accounts lost reach, and why they are being prevented from commenting, reposting, and saving content,” CTRL+Z wrote on its website.
“Meta cannot be the invisible judge of the Brazilian electoral debate.”
On Friday, the Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported it had reviewed internal messages between Meta employees acknowledging they were aware of the inconsistent treatment of Lula and Bolsonaro’s social media presence.
Political campaigns in Brazil have dramatically increased their spending on social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram, outpacing traditional avenues like television or street advertising in recent elections, said Daniela da Silva, the executive director of CTRL+Z.
According to data collected by the Supreme Electoral Court, Facebook received more than 200 million reals ($40m) in revenue in the 2024 municipal elections, ranking at the top of advertising suppliers for that cycle.
Despite that revenue, da Silva said that Meta and other companies were not taking their responsibility towards election fairness seriously.
“These are very powerful, wealthy companies, and they do have the capacity to do much more than they are doing,” she told Al Jazeera.
More than 100 civil society groups, including Greenpeace International, Global Witness and Oxfam Brazil, have joined CTRL+Z to sign a letter calling on Brazilian authorities to enforce rules meant to rein in Meta.
They have also pushed the company itself to do a better job removing deepfakes and disinformation, and to provide clear rules on how it moderates content.
“We want transparency regarding moderation criteria, a human review channel, and timely responses to protect the election,” the group said on its website.

Kiev’s unreadiness for talks, Iran’s just cause: Lavrov’s statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:20:48 UTC
02:20:48 KST

TEHRAN, October 19. /TASS/. Iran’s struggle against the aggression unleashed upon it is a just cause, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told a joint news conference after talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi.

Funding social care is a collective responsibility | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:18:11 UTC
02:18:11 KST

Polly Toynbee asks a seemingly difficult question and discusses a knotty issue (In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?, 13 October). Her question is framed as an issue of individual choice inviting the response: “Not me if I can avoid it.”
The responsible answer is, of course, all of us – collectively. It is an uninsurable risk that can only be solved equitably and efficiently as a collective solution. By entangling the issue of funding with provision of services, moral clarity is lost. Issues of matching funding distort and influence the level of care provided and ensure that progress toward resolving the question of who determines the need for care is delayed.
The solution is to fund social care in the same way as the NHS was envisaged: as a right, free at the point of need, and funded out of general taxation as part of annually managed expenditure, like pensions and social security, as needs are presented and professionally agreed.
The Treasury has the ways and means, and nothing more needs to be discussed. The additional costs as a percentage of GDP are small and affordable by reference to other countries.
The issue of affordability is exaggerated out of all proportion by politicians who are afraid of being accused of raising taxes. In fact, because of the very high economic multiplier effect of boosting spending on low-paid workers, it is certain that it will pay for itself without impacting government deficits (unlike defence spending).
Andy Burnham knows this, and needs to overrule his cautious advisers. This is his big chance to demonstrate leadership. People don’t vote for ditherers.
 
Roger Steer
 
Sheffield
Thank you, Polly Toynbee, for your article about your visit to Liverpool with Louise Casey. Ms Casey is clearly right when she says: “If it’s public money, it should mainly be publicly run.”
I am old enough to recall the 1970s Tory privatisation of social care, and I remember sales of council facilities being forced through by rate-capping. Blatantly paying staff in the private sector less and lowering their standards and conditions of service was supposed to save money. I wasn’t aware at the time of the massive shift of public money into private establishments. The fact that the state’s bill for residential care increased more than twentyfold within seven years is scandalous, and should have been at the time.
Was the Tory government from 1979 the most ideologically driven UK government ever? Surely it is not too late to carry out an “audit” of the transfer of public assets to private individuals and companies? Until Ms Toynbee’s article, I would have suggested starting with council housing or water boards. Now I think social care is the place to start, soon.
 
Janet Dubé
 
Peebles, Scottish Borders
Polly Toynbee’s description of people with advanced dementia as having “glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape” and “that terrible human vacancy” is deeply troubling. Such language dehumanises people and reinforces the stigma surrounding dementia.
People living with dementia deserve, like everyone else, to be treated and spoken about with respect and dignity. I suggest she consult the guide to language for journalists produced by the Dementia Engagement and Empowerment Project, published in 2014 and written by people with lived experience of the impact of careless descriptors.
 
Sally Byers
 
Sheffield
