According to Klitschko, the added buses will keep residents connected to central Kyiv, including during air-raid alerts, without overcrowding Darnytsia station.
Russia widens targets to transport
The damage comes only days after Russia’s Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov confirmed to Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russian forces were deliberately striking Ukraine’s transport, particularly bridges and railway, alongside digital infrastructure.
“According to the General Staff’s plan, strikes are being carried out on bridges of strategic importance, railway transport facilities, and data centers used to support the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine,” Gerasimov said on Oct. 16, during a briefing at a command post of Russia’s Joint Group of Forces.
Since Oct. 1, Russian drones have repeatedly struck Kyiv’s South and North bridges across the Dnipro River, forcing closures that brought traffic in the capital to a standstill.
Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) Major Artem Bilyk said that Russia is using a “small cuts” approach, with repeated strikes that force bridges to close for inspections and repairs rather than destroy them outright.
Combined with so-called “double-tap” strikes – a second attack on the same location while rescuers are responding to the scene – repairs take significantly longer.
Pressure on city authorities
The repairs also come as Kyiv’s leadership faces criticism from President Volodymyr Zelensky.
On Oct. 13, he said the capital was trailing every other region in carrying out its wartime resilience plan, including those on the frontline. It was his second rebuke of Kyiv’s authorities in a week.
“And Kyivans definitely feel this,” Zelensky said, because even after a single hit by a Shahed drone, “there are power and water outages in a significant part of the capital.”
Klitschko has rejected the criticism, saying the city is working with limited time, funding and staff.

CAS ruling on disputed Senegal-Morocco AFCON final expected in late November
Unknown

Halis Sunnetci
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) announced Monday that it expects to issue its ruling at the end of November on Senegal's appeal against the decision to award Morocco the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title.
In a statement, the Lausanne-based court said a hearing concerning the Senegalese Football Federation's appeal against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation was held behind closed doors on Oct. 8.
"The Panel have begun and continue their deliberations," CAS said.
The dispute stems from the AFCON final on Jan. 18 in Rabat, where Senegal defeated hosts Morocco 1-0 after extra time following a chaotic conclusion to regular time.
With the match goalless in stoppage time, Morocco were awarded a penalty following a Video Assistant Referee review, prompting Senegal's players to temporarily leave the pitch in protest.
Play resumed after a lengthy interruption, with Morocco's Brahim Diaz subsequently having a Panenka-style penalty saved by Senegalese goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye then scored in extra time to secure a 1-0 victory for Senegal.
However, on March 17, CAF's Appeal Board overturned the result following a Moroccan appeal, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match by leaving the field without authorization.
The board awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory and the continental title, citing Articles 82 and 84 of the competition's regulations.
Senegal appealed the decision to CAS on March 25, seeking to overturn CAF's ruling and be reinstated as African champions.

Search under way for four soldiers missing after gang attack in Haiti
The UN Security Council holds a meeting on Haiti, and the attack on UN-backed forces, is expected to dominate the discussions
International forces in Haiti are working to establish contact with four Salvadoran soldiers who went missing after violent gangs attacked their armoured vehicle with explosives on Sunday.
The soldiers from the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) managed to flee the burning vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets north of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
It is the first major attack on the international force since it began operations earlier this year.
On Monday, the Armed Forces of El Salvador said the soldiers – four aviation technicians – were returning to camp when they came under attack. Helicopters were sent to “establish contact and determine the location of our military personnel”, but they were also fired at as they dispersed personnel.
“Multiple attempts to approach by land and air have been made, but the intensity of the fighting has hampered these,” said the Salvadoran statement.
The GSF said that it is assessing the situation and has advised residents to remain indoors.
The UN Security Council is scheduled to meet later on Monday about Haiti, and the attack is expected to dominate the conversation.
The GSF officially began operations on 1 June but has so far operated only in a limited capacity. A UN statement said it is expected to reach full operational capacity between now and the end of the year.
It currently has more than 1,500 troops on the ground in Haiti, including soldiers from Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack. It comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade and illustrates the power of armed gangs that control an estimated 70 per cent of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
The area where the armoured vehicle was struck is controlled by gangs, including Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent, and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and US.
“Armed gangs have overrun large parts of Port-au-Prince, the capital, employing tactics including murder, kidnapping, and sexual violence amid widespread impunity,” said a UN Security Council report last month.
Since the assassination of President Jovenel President Jovenel President Jovenel President Jovenel Moise in July 2021, Haiti has been in a multidimensional crisis characterised by extreme violence, political deadlock and dire humanitarian conditions.
Gang violence displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti in recent years. The UN says at least 5,700 people have been killed or injured from January to mid-September this year and 230 have been kidnapped.

Kenyan court convicts cult leader Paul Mackenzie of murdering 190 children, 1 adult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:39:49 UTC
01:39:49 KST

Andrew Wasike
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
A Kenyan court on Monday convicted starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and 28 other defendants of murdering 190 children and one adult in the Shakahola massacre, a tragedy linked to more than 400 deaths.
“I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 192 and one adult, contrary to Section 203 of the Penal Code,” High Court Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said while delivering the verdict.
The judge rejected the defense’s argument that the victims, most of whom were children, had willingly participated in the fatal fasting.
“I reject the defense by the accused persons that the victims, who were all below the age of 16, voluntarily fasted to death,” she said.
The court found the 29 defendants guilty under Section 203 of Kenya’s Penal Code and convicted them under Section 322 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The ruling marks a major development in a case that shocked Kenya after hundreds of bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola Forest, near the coastal town of Malindi, in 2023.
Mackenzie, the leader of the Good News International Church, was accused of encouraging his followers to undertake extreme fasting as a path to spiritual salvation.
Prosecutors argued that the deaths were not the result of voluntary religious fasting but formed part of a coordinated campaign that subjected victims, including children, to fatal deprivation.
The defendants had denied the murder charges, with the defense maintaining that the victims had chosen to fast.
Investigations into the Shakahola deaths uncovered mass graves and evidence of severe malnutrition, triggering nationwide scrutiny of religious extremism and the government’s failure to detect the group’s activities earlier.
More than 400 people died in the Shakahola tragedy, according to Kenyan authorities, making it one of the country’s deadliest cult-related disasters.
The case also prompted questions about the regulation of religious organizations, child protection and the responsibility of state institutions to intervene when vulnerable people face abuse.

Macron increasingly isolated amid unrest across France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

Saturday’s violent protests and looting across France have deepened Macron’s political isolation, raising questions over his authority.
With only months left in his presidency, Emmanuel Macron faces mounting social unrest and political criticism that could ultimately shape his legacy.
After student protests over living conditions erupted into violence last Saturday, Macron has come under fire from across the political spectrum over his handling of the security situation and his response to grievances over education, the cost of living and inflation.
The unrest comes as France grapples with record public debt, soaring fuel prices and escalating international conflicts.
The Yellow Vests movement, which has helped coordinate the protests, announced a “second act” on Monday, with further demonstrations planned for next weekend.
Addressing the nation, Macron condemned violence and announced new operational procedures for security forces.
The Paris prosecutor’s office reported 855 arrests linked to the demonstrations, with 557 people placed in police custody, 433 of whom were adults, representing 78% of those detained.
“Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” Macron said. “Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.”
The response is likely to add to the pressure on Macron, whose performance was viewed unfavourably by 82% of respondents in an Ipsos-BVA poll conducted in October.
The French president is currently on a diplomatic trip to the Gulf, which the Élysée says aims to secure energy supplies as prices rise. However, his decision to leave Paris amid the crisis has drawn criticism, with some accusing Macron of evading the situation.
Le Pen capitalises on chaos
Across the political spectrum, several potential presidential candidates have argued that Macron has lost authority and that his response came too late.
“We have the feeling that the government is collapsing under its own weight, that it is completely overwhelmed,” said Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, which is leading in polls ahead of France’s 2027 presidential election.
Speaking at a press conference at the party’s headquarters on Monday, Bardella pledged tough measures to restore order if the National Rally came to power. “France is caught in a vice between powerlessness and violence,” he said.
Polls put Marine Le Pen ahead of all her potential rivals in the 2027 presidential race. She faced Emmanuel Macron in the 2017 and 2022 run-offs, losing both times.
In the aftermath of the looting, Le Pen said France had been “ravaged” by “an alliance of criminals from the banlieues and politicised professional rioters”.
Le Pen is expected to focus her campaign on migration and law and order, issues that have traditionally resonated with far-right voters, while playing down foreign policy issues such as the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical tensions.
Macron faces criticism from former allies
Macron has also faced criticism from his former prime ministers, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both of whom are running in the 2027 presidential election.
Both are seeking to distance themselves from Macron and his political legacy.
“Like millions of French people, I would have preferred to see decisions and initiatives aimed at restoring order,” Philippe wrote on X.
Attal called on the state to employ all means "so justice is done" including AI facial recognition and deploying the army "if necessary". Macron did not announce extra security measures on Sunday, asking local authorities to coordinate with the police.
The divided French left, riven by internal tensions, accused the government of failing to protect citizens.
“This is unprecedented in its gravity,” Raphaël Glucksmann, a French MEP and social-democratic contender in the 2027 presidential election, told RTL radio. “I had the feeling that France was dissolving, that the Republic was disintegrating, that the state no longer existed.”
Bruno Retailleau, another presidential hopeful representing the conservative Les Républicains party, described Macron as “completely out of his depth, incapable of deploying the full force of the state against the chaos threatening the Republic”.
He cited the arson attack on Limoges town hall and vandalism at Marseille’s town hall.
Senior members of the government have also acknowledged shortcomings in the response.
Police fiasco
On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations. He offered to resign “because I felt responsible for everything that happened”, but Macron rejected his request.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin likewise acknowledged that the authorities had “undoubtedly failed” in their response, citing “shortcomings in intelligence gathering”.
Macron has found few defenders among his former allies, some of whom blame the current political turmoil on his decision to dissolve the National Assembly in June 2024. The move plunged France into political uncertainty, leaving successive governments exposed to the threat of no-confidence votes.
Beyond the immediate security crisis, commentators argue that Macron has alienated young people who helped propel him to power in 2017.
Some protesters have criticised his 2018 high school reforms, arguing that changes to the organisation of specialist subjects have led to longer school days.
In a recent opinion piece, Le Monde described Macron’s relationship with young people as a “major political failure”.
The article drew parallels with the Yellow Vests movement, which erupted in December 2018 amid widespread anger over purchasing power and the rising cost of living.
“Restoring public order is an essential prerequisite for beginning the talks promised on Sunday with all stakeholders and, in doing so, resuming a social dialogue that has been broken for far too long,” the piece concluded.

Russia has abandoned plan to outflank Donetsk Oblast via Barvinkove after Operation Vivaldi
Ukrainian forces have thwarted Russian attempts to outflank Donetsk Oblast via Dobropillia and Barvinkove as part of Operation Vivaldi. Russian forces have now abandoned these plans, while the 144th Division of Russia's 20th Army has been defeated and has effectively ceased to exist.
Source: Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, Commander of the 3rd Army Corps, at a meeting with journalists
Details: The task set before Russia's West grouping of forces, which comprises three armies – the 1st Tank Army, the 20th Combined Arms Army and the 25th Combined Arms Army – was to advance towards the city of Sviatohirsk and the settlement of Rubtsi via a bridgehead it had established on the Chornyi Zherebets River and a salient that Ukrainian forces have destroyed.
The aim was to split the Ukrainian grouping on the eastern bank of the Oskil River in two, destroy it and then continue advancing towards Barvinkove, a settlement in southern Kharkiv Oblast.
Quote: "This was Russia's strategic plan. It involved the enemy making one thrust via Sviatohirsk and the salient we eliminated, bypassing Lyman and encircling the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the north. With a second thrust via Dobropillia towards the same Barvinkove, they would complete the encirclement of Donetsk Oblast. This would fulfil the key political objective set by Russia's military and political leadership: the complete capture of Donetsk Oblast.
This was the plan for 2026. They began implementing it in 2025 and were supposed to reach Barvinkove by the end of 2026.
Now, at the end of 2026, the situation for them is as follows: following the destruction of the bridgehead and the offensive grouping, the 144th Division of the 20th Army has effectively been defeated and has ceased to exist as an organised military force."
Details: Following the defeat of the Russian offensive grouping, Russia has now abandoned its attempt to outflank Donetsk Oblast.
According to Biletskyi, Russia has two options remaining on the Donetsk front: either a direct assault on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which would be costly and bloody and would not guarantee success, or an alternative approach. Russian forces have also temporarily abandoned the latter plan.
In effect, the Russians now have only one main direction of effort: Dobropillia. They had made some gains there and have therefore not abandoned its attempt to encircle Ukrainian positions from that direction. However, Ukraine's senior military command is now actively conducting countermeasures in the area.
The 3rd Army Corps has reached the Chornyi Zherebets River, significantly shortening the front line and allowing infantry positions to be consolidated.
Ukrainian defence forces are now holding a highly advantageous defensive line along the river, which Russian troops would have to cross again if they resumed their offensive in this direction.
The operation is also significant because it thwarted Russia's strategic objectives.
Ukrainska Pravda first reported on Russia's plan to outflank Donetsk Oblast via Dobropillia and Barvinkove in the summer of 2025.
The Dobropillia salient was intended to serve as one of two pincers through which Russian forces planned to encircle virtually all of Donetsk Oblast that is under Ukrainian control.

too large to exhibit, anselm kiefer’s monumental painting gets its own pavilion by david chipperfield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:35:16 UTC
01:35:16 KST

too large to exhibit, anselm kiefer’s monumental painting gets its own pavilion by david chipperfield
designed with the artist, the textured concrete pavilion uses timber beams and natural light to frame one monumental painting.
prefer designboom on google
a permanent home for anselm kiefer’s ‘black flakes’
A monumental painting by German artist Anselm Kiefer has finally found a place large enough to exhibit it, nearly two decades after its creation. In Künzelsau, Germany, David Chipperfield Architects has completed a freestanding concrete pavilion built specifically to house Schwarze Flocken (Black Flakes), a work measuring more than eleven meters tall and seven meters wide. The museum building opened to the public on October 13th, 2026 in the sculpture garden of Museum Würth 2, and marked the painting’s first public presentation.
Created in 2007, Schwarze Flocken is the largest work by Kiefer in the Würth Collection. Its immense canvas incorporates oil, emulsion, shellac, earth, and twigs, creating a heavily textured surface characteristic of the artist’s practice.
The painting takes its name from a poem by Paul Celan, whose writing confronts the personal losses and devastation of the Holocaust. Kiefer’s work draws on this history through a bleak, layered composition, its physical material giving weight to the subject. The challenge of exhibiting something of this size became the starting point for an entirely new building.
a concrete volume on the hillside
The new pavilion stands on a gentle rise at the southwestern edge of the Carmen Würth Forum, another project by David Chipperfield Architects. Its compact, monolithic form sits among the works of the surrounding sculpture garden, with textured concrete walls that echo the larger cultural complex nearby.
The exterior has a rough, bush-hammered finish, giving the otherwise simple volume a tactile surface. A shallow portico cuts into one side of the building, providing a sheltered entrance and a brief transition from the open landscape to the tall interior.
The pavilion continues a longstanding architectural relationship between Chipperfield’s studio and the Würth Group, which developed the cultural campus alongside its company headquarters. The idea of creating a separate structure for a single artwork came from Kiefer himself, who has previously pursued similar arrangements for his work. Here, the building’s footprint and height follow the spatial requirements of the painting, and gives the artist an unusual degree of influence over the architecture from the outset.
daylight falls across the monumental canvas
Inside, Kiefer worked directly with the architects to establish the proportions of the exhibition room, including the positioning of its openings and the color of its walls. The painting occupies the central focus of the tall space, with exposed solid timber beams spanning overhead. Between the beams, skylights introduce soft daylight from above. The light shifts throughout the day and across the seasons, gradually changing how the painting’s dense surface appears.
The building also takes an unconventional approach to its internal climate. Behind the concrete exterior, a layer of brickwork is finished with clay plaster on the inside, forming a substantial wall assembly designed to respond to outdoor conditions. This construction maintains frost-free temperatures without an active climate-control system, while the skylights allow natural light to replace the tightly regulated illumination typical of museum galleries.
These decisions give the 140-square-meter pavilion a particular relationship with its surroundings, allowing changes in weather and daylight to become part of the experience of viewing the work.
architecture designed for an artwork
At this scale, the architecture offers something a typical gallery would struggle to accommodate. Visitors enter a space conceived for a single painting, where the dimensions of the room, the texture of the walls, and even the changing daylight have been developed in conversation with the artist.
After almost twenty years out of public view, Schwarze Flocken can finally be encountered at its full size.
project info:
name: Anselm Kiefer Pavilion
architect: David Chipperfield Architects | @davidchipperfieldarchitects
location: Künzelsau, Germany
artist: Anselm Kiefer
client: Würth Group
area: 140 square meters
completion: October 13th, 2026

Commander of 3rd Army Corps explains why Lyman offensive was named Vivaldi
Andrii Biletskyi, Commander of the 3rd Army Corps, has said that the offensive operation near Lyman was named Vivaldi because it was initially planned to have four stages. The idea came from two officers in the corps, one of whom was killed and the other seriously wounded.
Source: Biletskyi at a meeting with journalists
Details: Biletskyi said the name Vivaldi was proposed by assault soldiers Yuryst and Lieshyi.
Quote: "The thing is, our brother-in-arms Lieshyi was recently killed. He sustained seven wounds during assault operations and then moved to headquarters because he had an exceptionally brilliant mind.
Seven wounds. Anyone who understands knows that this is an extraordinary number. Usually, after the second or third wound, people no longer want to continue taking part in assault operations.
Our brother-in-arms Yuryst is from Mariupol. He joined the 3rd Assault Brigade at a very young age. He served as an assault trooper and also went on to develop his skills in this field.
Sadly, Yuryst is now seriously wounded and has been in hospital for a long time."
Details: Biletskyi added that the two soldiers had made a significant contribution to planning the operation.
Quote: "They were the ones who suggested the name. Why? The original plan had four stages – one for each season. The plan was later changed, and the number of stages increased to more than four.
We cultivate a taste for classical music – classical music usually plays in the corridors of the 3rd Corps headquarters. Knowing about this fondness, they came up with the name."

Lebanon: Tunnel found near Beirut sparks fresh Hezbollah tensions
The discovery of a tunnel northeast of Beirut has sparked fresh tensions in Lebanon, with opposition lawmakers demanding a security crackdown amid suspicions over possible links to Hezbollah.
Lebanese army engineers launched an investigation on Monday after a tunnel was discovered in the Fanar-Zaitariyeh area of the Metn district, prompting calls for a comprehensive security sweep and the arrest of those responsible.
The discovery comes just over a week after Lebanese security forces intercepted a shipment of explosives belonging to Hezbollah in Dahr al-Baydar, raising tensions between the group and its political opponents.
However, a Lebanese military source told The New Arab that initial investigations suggested the newly discovered tunnel was small and was not intended for military or security purposes.
"Inspections and investigations are continuing, but so far it has emerged that the tunnel is small and was not prepared for military or security use," the source said.
Fanar mayor Michel Salameh told The New Arab that a resident discovered the tunnel on Sunday evening and alerted the municipality, which subsequently contacted the security authorities.
Salameh said the tunnel was located in a remote wooded area that was difficult to access, with the excavation concealed by trees.
تواصلت صباحاً مع وزير الدفاع، وطلبت منه اجراء الجيش والقوى الأمنية مسحاً شاملاً لمنطقة الرويسات - الجديدة ومحيطها، عقب اكتشاف نفق في المنطقة. وأبدى تجاوباً مع المطلب. نفق في المتن، شحنة متفجرات في ضهر البيدر، ومواجهات مع قوى الأمن في الضاحية… مؤشرات خطيرة تفرض وضع حدّ نهائي لازدواجية السلاح والتنظيم العسكري لحزب الله على كامل الأراضي اللبنانية. استمرار عمل السلاح غير الشرعي والتنظيم العسكري والأمني لحزب الله يشكل خطر داهم، وعلى الدولة الحسم حفاظاً على لبنان.

When the vegetation was removed, a ladder, basic digging equipment and freshly excavated sand were discovered nearby.
"The tunnel is located in a wooded area in a remote spot that is difficult to reach," Salameh said, adding that the municipality had immediately informed army intelligence, which dispatched an engineering unit to inspect the site.
According to the mayor's preliminary assessment, the tunnel was approximately four metres deep, extended horizontally for two metres and then continued for another four metres.
He suggested that the excavation appeared recent, possibly dating back no more than a week, although its location made it difficult to detect.
Hezbollah accused as lawmakers demand security sweep
The discovery quickly prompted accusations against Hezbollah, which maintains influence in parts of the surrounding Zaitariyeh-Roueissat al-Jadideh area.
However, no evidence establishing Hezbollah's involvement in the tunnel's construction has been announced.
Lebanese Kataeb Party leader and MP Sami Gemayel said he had contacted Defence Minister Michel Menassa on Monday morning to demand a comprehensive security sweep of Roueissat al-Jadideh and its surroundings.
Gemayel said the minister had responded positively to his request.
"A tunnel in Metn, an explosives shipment in Dahr al-Baydar, and confrontations with security forces in the southern suburbs... dangerous indicators that require a definitive end to the duality of arms and Hezbollah's military organisation across all Lebanese territory," Gemayel said.
He warned that the continued operation of Hezbollah's military and security structures outside state authority posed a serious threat to Lebanon.
Kataeb MP Elias Hankach, who represents the area, also called for immediate army intervention.
He said he was contacting the Lebanese army command to demand searches of streets and buildings in Roueissat and neighbouring areas, the confiscation of weapons, arrests of those involved and the establishment of permanent security checkpoints and patrols.
The accusations come amid growing calls from Hezbollah's opponents for the Lebanese authorities to accelerate efforts to bring all weapons under exclusive state control.
Explosives seizure deepens political divisions
The tunnel controversy follows the seizure of a shipment of explosives in Dahr al-Baydar, on a route linking Beirut to the Bekaa Valley and Syria, more than a week ago.
Hezbollah acknowledged ownership of the explosives, insisting they were intended exclusively for use against Israel, and demanded their return along with the release of those detained.
The case has become a major point of contention between Hezbollah and the Lebanese government, with authorities pledging to pursue those involved in transporting and possessing weapons outside state control.
Further tensions erupted on Friday evening in the Galerie Semaan area at the entrance to Beirut's southern suburbs, when Hezbollah members confronted security personnel who had arrived to seal a pharmaceutical warehouse.
The incident was subsequently contained, but it fuelled criticism from Hezbollah's opponents over the group's continued security presence in areas where it holds considerable influence.
Lebanese security forces have intensified operations in recent days, including in Beirut's southern suburbs and the eastern Bekaa and Baalbek-Hermel regions, targeting wanted suspects, smuggling networks and unauthorised crossings along the Syrian border.
Hezbollah warns government over rising tensions
Hezbollah MP Ali Fayyad, a member of the Loyalty to the Resistance parliamentary bloc, warned on Monday that the Lebanese authorities bore "full responsibility for pushing the country towards dangerous internal tensions".
In a statement distributed by Hezbollah's media relations office, Fayyad accused the government of confronting a major component of Lebanese society and pursuing policies dictated by foreign powers.
He argued that the dispute had expanded beyond Hezbollah's weapons to encompass the movement's social, institutional and political presence.
"The authorities deliberately, knowingly and persistently expanded the dispute with the resistance, so that it is no longer limited to the issue of weapons," Fayyad said.
He also accused the government of compromising Lebanese sovereignty and failing to confront Israel's continued occupation and attacks.
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, meanwhile, reiterated on Sunday that lasting stability could not be achieved without extending state authority across all Lebanese territory.
"Stability will not be established in the country unless the state's authority is extended over all its territory, even gradually, exclusively through its own forces," Salam said.
The prime minister said he had contacted army commander General Rodolphe Haykal and Internal Security Forces chief Major General Raed Abdallah to commend the increased deployment of security personnel across Greater Beirut.
The measures followed overnight gatherings in the capital that had raised public concerns about security.
Salam also met Justice Minister Adel Nassar and Public Prosecutor Rami al-Hajj to review the investigation into the Dahr al-Baydar explosives shipment and ensure that everyone involved in possessing or transporting unauthorised weapons was brought before the judiciary.
He stressed that there would be no limits to the investigation beyond those imposed by law.
Salam further urged political groups to prioritise Lebanon's national interests over foreign agendas, reiterating that decisions over war and peace must remain exclusively in the hands of the state and its constitutional institutions.
His comments followed a telephone conversation last week in which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to hold those responsible for ordering, financing and directing the explosives shipment accountable.
Rubio also insisted that returning the seized explosives to Hezbollah should be ruled out entirely.
The latest incidents have heightened concerns over internal instability as Lebanon faces continued Israeli military attacks and occupation in the south.

Chechen court fines woman 150,000 rubles for protesting the disappearance of her friend Seda Suleimanova, whom police forcibly returned to Chechnya three years ago
Grozny’s Akhmatovsky District Court fined St. Petersburg resident Lena Patyayeva 150,000 rubles for holding a solo picket on the third anniversary of the disappearance of her friend Seda Suleimanova, a Chechen woman, according to a post on Chechnya’s Supreme Court website.
The post does not identify the person fined, but Mediazona reported that it was Patyayeva.
The court found her guilty of a repeat violation of protest laws under Article 20.2, Part 8 of Russia’s Code of Administrative Offenses. In November 2025, Patyayeva was sentenced to nine days in jail under the same provision for a solo picket.
Lena Patyayeva held a solo picket in Grozny on August 23, 2026. She stood at a monument to fallen journalists, holding a sign that read “I demand an investigation into the murder of Seda Suleimanova” and, in Chechen, “Where is Seda?” Patyayeva was detained shortly afterward.
Seda Suleimanova fled her relatives in 2022 because they were planning to force her into marriage. She lived in St. Petersburg. In August 2023, police officers came to her apartment and told her she was suspected of stealing jewelry worth 150,000 rubles, following a complaint from her mother. They detained her, took her back to Chechnya against her will, and handed her over to her relatives. A few days later, Chechnya’s human rights ombudsman, Mansur Soltayev, published a photograph and a video of Suleimanova. She has not been seen since.
In February 2024, the SK SOS project reported that Suleimanova might have been killed by her relatives. Shortly after a public campaign demanding that she be found, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a murder investigation. In May 2025, authorities declared Suleimanova a missing person and launched a search for her.

Second-hand clothing app Vinted purges suspected looted goods after France riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:32:33 UTC

Second-hand clothing app Vinted purges suspected looted goods after France riots
Vinted, an app for buying and selling second-hand clothing, said on Oct 19 it had increased checks on suspicious listings and removed adverts linked to looted goods following unrest in France.
Nationwide demonstrations across France over the cost of living and declining public service deteriorated into riots on Oct 17, with shops looted across the country as violent groups clashed with police in one of the worst days of violence in years.
Vinted said its teams had taken “immediate action” since the weekend to identify and remove listings suspected of being linked to looting, and had increased scrutiny of suspicious adverts.
Accounts found to have breached its rules could face permanent bans, it said.
“The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it,” a Vinted spokesperson said in a statement.
The company said it was working with law enforcement and the French authorities and would continue to adapt its processes to identify and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour.
Serge Papin, France’s small businesses minister, said on X that authorities would meet later in the day with marketplace operators and officials from the interior and justice ministries, after goods stolen during the unrest on Oct 17 were offered for sale online.
Platforms including Vinted, Amazon, eBay and TikTok were invited to the meeting on Oct 19, according to government officials.
Vinted did not say whether it had seen a similar increase in suspicious listings in Italy, where unrest also led to the looting of luxury stores.
France, the UK and Italy are Vinted’s largest markets.
Luxury groups including Louis Vuitton and Rolex, as well as make-up retail giant Sephora, have been caught up in unrest in France and Italy where some of the most violent protests seen in decades over living costs and declining public services have prompted police to fire tear gas and use water cannon as demonstrators looted shops and set fires.
Founded in Lithuania in 2008, Vinted became the Baltic state’s first “unicorn” - a startup valued at €1 billion (S$1.4 billion) - in 2019. A secondary share transaction led by Sweden’s EQT Growth valued Vinted at €8 billion earlier in 2026.
The online marketplace prohibits the sale of stolen items and relies on reports from retailers and users, among other checks, to detect suspicious listings. REUTERS

Pakistan providing Saudi Arabia &#8216;whatever support needed&#8217; amid Houthi attacks: Army spokesman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:30:33 UTC
01:30:33 KST

Pakistan is providing Saudi Arabia with “whatever support is needed” to defend the kingdom amid attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group, a Pakistani military spokesman said in an interview aired Sunday, Anadolu reports.
“It’s non-negotiable; it’s absolute as far as Pakistan is concerned,” Pakistan Army spokesman Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told Independent Arabia.
“So whatever support is needed to do that is being provided and will be provided,” he said, adding that alliances do not publicly disclose the specifics or extent of military support.
His remarks came amid Houthi attacks targeting Saudi oil and financial infrastructure, including airports, in recent weeks.
Chaudhry said Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of the two holy mosques were “paramount” for Pakistan.
He stressed that there could be no “ifs and buts” concerning the security of the holy sites.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have signed two defense agreements aimed at collective deterrence – the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement and the Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, which also includes Türkiye.
The Mecca agreement, signed Aug. 7, allows signatories to treat an attack against one member as an attack against all three.
Asked whether Pakistan’s support would remain strictly defensive if Houthi attacks continued, Chaudhry said all three alliance members were “absolutely clear that this alliance has no offensive intent. It is purely defensive.”
Citing Article 51 of the UN Charter, which addresses the right to individual and collective self-defense, he said the alliance was intended to deter threats to regional stability.
He said the mechanism “gives a very strong and clear message to those elements of instability, of chaos, in the region that if you directly or indirectly wage this war against any of these three countries, then the response will be collective.”
“If that deterrence doesn’t work, then that deterrence has to be re-established by all means that are available to the three countries,” Chaudhry said.
However, he emphasized that Islamabad’s interactions and discussions with the parties involved were focused on “dialing down the escalation.”

Trump signs order aimed at boosting women’s health research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:29:04 UTC
01:29:04 KST

United States President Donald Trump signed an executive order establishing two bodies to boost women’s health research, address gaps in medical knowledge and improve prevention, diagnosis and treatment.
President Donald J. Trump, alongside First Lady Melania Trump, signed an executive order on Monday creating a Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House Women’s Health Task Force to close research gaps and modernise women's care.
“My Administration is committed to advancing women’s health and ensuring that medical research, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment reflect the highest quality scientific evidence, with the goal of improving health outcomes in all phases of life,” Trump said.
Speaking before the signing, Melania Trump called this “a transformative moment for women in America”.
“Previous generations fought for women's rights,” she continued. “Our generation will fight to discover the cure that will ensure that women can live their lives in health and to the fullest.”
The task force, which is meeting on the day the order was signed, is led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
They are tasked with coordinating women’s health policy across federal agencies. The task force's role is to translate research into evidence-based healthcare, improve prevention and access to care throughout women's lives, and identify policy and regulatory reforms to improve health outcomes.
In the meantime, the Women's Health Division will be established within the NIH over the next 90 days.
It will coordinate and expand research into understudied women’s health conditions, improve the inclusion of women and girls in clinical trials, and accelerate the development of better diagnostics and treatments. It will also strengthen accountability for researchers to account for sex-based biological differences in their studies.
The goal, according to Melania Trump, is to improve women's health outcomes “in all phases of life,” using the advantages of new scientific discoveries, including super intelligence and advanced biotechnology and other therapies.
She outlined five priorities: directing research towards diseases that affect women “in a unique way”; using super intelligence to better understand women’s health and develop new treatments; speeding up access to new discoveries from labs to patients; ensuring access to all despite financial situation and addressing previously neglected conditions.

Egypt delays vote on possible military support for Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:27:53 UTC
01:27:53 KST

Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on authorising potential military support to help defend Saudi Arabia, rescheduling the decision for October 26 as regional security tensions rise.
The decision was taken during Monday’s parliamentary session, following a similar meeting on Sunday, according to state-run daily Akhbar el-Yom.
Sunday’s session had also been adjourned, with further deliberations deferred until Monday.
The discussions were held at the request of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el Sisi, who said on Saturday that Cairo would take all necessary measures to defend Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested assistance.
Sisi pledges support amid Houthi attacks
Saudi Arabia has recently come under attack from Yemen’s Houthi militias, raising concerns over the security of the kingdom and the potential for renewed regional escalation.
Sisi’s statement signalled Egypt’s willingness to consider support for its Gulf partner, while the parliamentary vote would address authorisation for possible military assistance.
The one-week postponement leaves the decision pending as lawmakers prepare to resume deliberations later this month.
Yemen conflict continues to shape regional security
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi militia seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in 2014.
A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
A United Nations-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022 brought a period of relative calm after years of fighting.
Recent attacks on Saudi Arabia have renewed concerns about the durability of that calm and the risk of further regional instability.
Egypt’s planned parliamentary vote comes amid broader efforts by regional governments to respond to security threats while assessing the implications of any potential military involvement.

Lebanese president says Israel violating framework agreement
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Monday that Israel has failed to comply with a U.S.-mediated framework agreement signed in June and continues daily violations in southern Lebanon, according to aa.com.tr.
Aoun made the remarks during a meeting with Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy at the presidential palace in Baabda, east of Beirut, according to a statement from the Lebanese presidency.
“The Israelis have not adhered to the framework agreement, and the south continues to face daily violations,” Aoun said.
He stressed that continued Israeli violations would not achieve their objectives but would instead strengthen the Lebanese people’s determination to defend their land and rights.
Aoun said the violations were obstructing the Lebanese state’s efforts to implement its stated objectives.
He reaffirmed Lebanon’s commitment to a diplomatic solution despite its difficulties, saying it was “far less costly than the devastating war” for which the Lebanese people, particularly residents of the south, continue to pay the price.
“It is time for Lebanon to have some peace,” he added.
The president also welcomed any efforts by the Arab League to help Lebanon overcome the difficult circumstances it faces.
For his part, Fahmy reaffirmed the Arab League’s support for the Lebanese state and its institutions, rejecting any infringement on the country’s sovereignty.
He expressed readiness to engage with Arab and Western countries to mobilize support for Lebanon and its people.
Fahmy stressed that the Arab position toward Lebanon remained united and that the organization was working to translate that support into practical measures and financial assistance.
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing and injuring thousands of people and displacing over 1.5 million residents.
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued its attacks on southern Lebanon.
Israeli forces also continue to occupy Lebanese territory, including areas held for decades and others seized during more recent wars and military operations.

Apply for Armed Forces Compensation or a War Pension
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:27:39 BST
01:27:39 KST

Apply for Armed Forces Compensation or a War Pension
Make a claim under the Armed Forces Compensation Scheme or War Pension Scheme.
For more about the Armed Forces Compensation Scheme or War Pension Scheme see our guidance.
You do not need to know which compensation scheme applies to you before making a claim.
A guidance video is available on YouTube which provides helpful information you might need if claiming for compensation under either the Armed Forces Compensation Scheme (AFCS) or the War Pension Scheme (WPS).
If this is your first claim, we would recommend watching this video. Claiming for compensation - Armed Forces Compensation Scheme and War Pensions Scheme.
Eligibility:
- you may be able to get a payment if you have an injury, illness or medical disorder caused or made worse by UK armed forces service
- claims can be made for both physical and mental health conditions
- if you want to claim for a condition related to exposure to asbestos, read the guidance on GOV.UK first
- only use this service to make a claim. If you want to ask for a review or appeal a previous decision, contact Veterans UK
- if you want to claim for bereavement or dependant’s benefits, do not use this service. See our guidance on GOV.UK
Before you start
You’ll be asked for:
- an email address if you want to claim online. If you do not have one, you should make a claim by post. Details of how to do this can be found further down this page
- details of anyone helping you make a claim, for example a charity or welfare adviser
- your own details, including your national insurance number
- your armed forces service, including dates you served, if you know them
- the illness or injury you’re claiming for and why you think they are related to your armed forces service
- your doctor’s details and, if you have them, details of any hospitals that have treated you for the medical conditions you’re claiming for
- any other compensation or benefits you receive or have received for the conditions you’re claiming for
- your bank account details
Gather any details or documents you need in advance - this will make it faster to answer the questions.
You do not need to get any new information you do not already have. Veterans UK cannot refund any costs involved if you do this.
Rules for sensitive roles
Rules for sensitive roles
If you have ever served in or supported a sensitive role, you may need an Express Prior Authority in Writing (EPAW) before you make a claim.
Sensitive roles are roles where your identity, work or activities are protected for security reasons.
For example, this may include:
- special military units
- intelligence or security work
- roles where you were told not to share details of your work
If you do not have an EPAW, or you’re unsure whether you need one, email MODComms-EPAW@mod.gov.uk before making a claim.
Making a claim online
If you have already started a claim
You will need your last name, date of birth and application number to access your part-completed claim.
Making a claim by post
You can also claim by filling in a paper claim form and sending it back to us. Ask for a paper form by calling the Veterans UK Helpline on 0808 1914 218 Mon to Fri 8am to 4pm or email veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk. The helpline will send you a form and a pre-paid envelope to return it.
Help with making a claim
You can get help with making a claim by contacting the Veterans UK helpline or Veterans Welfare Service. The welfare service can arrange an appointment to provide one to one help if needed.
You do not need a paid representative such as a solicitor or claims management company to apply. Free independent advice is available from the Veterans Welfare Service or charitable organisations.
Acknowledgement
You will receive an acknowledgment within 5 working days of your claim being received. Claims are processed in the order they are received. This stage may involve a wait.
Providing evidence to support your claim at this initial stage will help speed up processing time. Claims can take many months to complete but timescales may vary depending on your individual circumstance.
Initial Review by caseworker
A caseworker reviews your claim and supporting evidence. If additional evidence is required, you will be contacted. This stage can take several months, depending on individual circumstances.
Gathering additional evidence (if needed)
A caseworker may need to consult a Medical Advisor. You will be asked to provide further information if needed and there may be a short wait while evidence is gathered and reviewed.
To avoid delays, you should respond as soon as you can. You have three months from the date of the request to provide additional information or evidence (if needed) or your claim will be closed. We will keep you updated on progress throughout the claim stages.
Decision making
One all evidence is received; a decision is made on your claim. You will receive a decision letter detailing the outcome.
Payment
If your claim is successful, payment is arranged. Please allow up to 20 working days from notification for payment to reach your account.
Further information
Next steps will be included in your decision letter. If you disagree with the decision, you may have the right to appeal. For further information, please visit:
Appeal a War Pension or Armed Forces Compensation decision - GOV.UK.^

China to expand AI use in tourism industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:27:02 CST
01:27:02 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism on Monday said it will explore mechanisms for establishing ownership, pricing, and trading of digital cultural assets, as part of its efforts to expand the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the culture and tourism sectors.
Zhou Hanping, a ministry official, told a press conference in Beijing that the ministry plans to promote the integration of AI into cultural creation, public services, the transmission of intangible cultural heritage, tourism services and market governance.
Nine Chinese authorities, including the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, on Monday jointly issued a set of guidelines on boosting commerce through science and technology.
According to the guidelines, China will promote the combined use of AI, extended reality and other technologies to develop distinctive cultural and tourism products and smart services, and expand the supply of cultural and tourism services for consumers.
Zhou said the ministry has launched 14 pilot projects for AI applications in culture and tourism. A list of these projects, released by the ministry last week, has shown that the pilot program will cover fields such as museums, theaters, snow tourism, and inbound tourism.
The guidelines also encourage localities to develop consumption scenarios that blend digital and physical experiences in key locations such as pedestrian streets, commercial districts and tourist attractions.
"Emerging forms of culture and tourism have become important drivers of domestic demand, job creation, market vitality and consumer confidence," Zhou said, referring to new cultural and tourism products such as immersive cultural experiences, digital performances, and smart tourism services.
Zhou said the ministry will further encourage businesses nationwide to develop distinctive cultural and tourism products based on local resources, and promote joint training efforts among universities, research institutions and cultural and tourism enterprises to foster talent. ■

"new types of actors"—there are "questions that need to be
reflected upon from various perspectives."

Xinhua Headlines: China's Q3 economy picks up pace, reinforcing role as global growth engine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:26:46 CST
01:26:46 KST

* China's GDP grew 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter, higher than the second quarter's reading of 4.3 percent, supported by fast-growing new drivers and fresh policy support.
* New growth drivers continued to expand, contributing more than 40 percent to China's economic growth in the first three quarters.
* More foreign firms are embracing "China Opportunity 2.0," deepening their integration into China's industrial and innovation chains.
BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's economy picked up pace in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, supported by fast-growing new drivers and fresh policy support, staying on track to meet its annual growth target and remaining a leading engine of global growth.
China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5 percent year on year in Q3, higher than the second quarter's reading of 4.3 percent, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Monday.
The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan (about 15.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in output during the January-September period, expanding 4.6 percent year on year, according to the NBS.
"The national economy forged ahead against pressure and continued to shift toward innovation-driven, high-quality development, with growing positive changes in major indicators," the NBS said in a statement.
China has consistently contributed around 30 percent of global economic growth, with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva saying in January that this contribution is expected to stay at roughly the same level in the coming years.
GROWING RESILIENCE
Noting that the GDP growth of 4.6 percent in the first three quarters is in line with the country's annual growth target, NBS deputy head Mao Shengyong told a media conference that the economy added 5.7 trillion yuan in output during the period, the largest increase for the same period in the past five years.
In the third quarter, GDP growth picked up 0.2 percentage points from the second quarter, while some international institutions expected major economies to grow more slowly in July-September compared to the April-June period, Mao said.
There was also a notable rise in momentum on a monthly basis. In September, value-added industrial output rose 5.5 percent year on year, 0.3 percentage points faster than in August, while the services production index gained 4.8 percent, up 0.7 percentage points from the previous month.
Retail sales of consumer goods grew 1.1 percent in September, 0.7 percentage points faster than in August, and the surveyed urban unemployment rate edged down 0.1 percentage points from August to 5.2 percent.
"Growth momentum showed signs of marginal improvement in September," said Wen Bin, chief economist with China Minsheng Bank, citing faster industrial and services output, a rebound in consumption and an initial stabilization of investment.
China will step up efforts to expand domestic demand, improve supply, and make macro policies more effective to sustain the positive momentum of innovation-led and high-quality development, Mao said.
To this end, China has recently rolled out a batch of new policies, including financial and fiscal support. "With existing policies being implemented faster and incremental policies gradually taking effect, the economy is expected to continue improving in the fourth quarter," Wen said.
NEW DRIVERS AT WORK
New growth drivers continued to expand, contributing more than 40 percent to China's economic growth in the first three quarters. Value-added industrial output rose 5.3 percent year on year, with equipment manufacturing up 10.2 percent and high-tech manufacturing up 14.3 percent. Output of industrial robots, lithium-ion batteries and 3D printing equipment jumped 29.1 percent, 39.5 percent and 62.5 percent, respectively.
Monday's data also showed that the services sector expanded 5.2 percent year on year in the first three quarters, with information transmission, software and IT services up 10.4 percent, and leasing and business services up 12.3 percent.
The shift is visible in the economic structure. Manufacturing accounted for 25.7 percent of GDP in the first three quarters, up 0.6 percentage points from a year earlier, while the share of high-tech manufacturing in the value-added output of major industrial enterprises rose 1.6 percentage points. Investment in intellectual property products climbed 9.3 percent.
Traditional industries are also moving up the value chain. In Jingdezhen, a ceramics hub in east China's Jiangxi Province, local producers have embraced 3D printing in pottery making, propelling the sector's output to over 100 billion yuan. Meanwhile, some coal mining companies have implemented smart monitoring systems for underground operations, increasing efficiency by 30 percent.
Green development is creating openings as well. The penetration rate of new energy vehicles in China has stayed above 60 percent for six consecutive months, while the country's energy consumption per unit of GDP fell 3.1 percent in the first three quarters.
"The foundations of the economy remain solid, while new quality productive forces, modern services and high-tech foreign trade are steadily taking root," said Zhu Qigui, associate director of the China Academy of Financial Research.
"As long as China continues to rely on innovation, reform and its vast market, the trend of moving toward new and better development will not change," the scholar said.
SHARED OPPORTUNITIES
A major trading partner of as many as 169 countries and regions, China saw its goods trade rise 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan in the first three quarters. In September alone, trade grew 27.5 percent.
In the first nine months, exports of mechanical and electrical products climbed 23.7 percent and accounted for 64.3 percent of total exports, while intermediate goods made up more than half of all exports, reinforcing China's role as a stabilizing anchor for global industrial and supply chains.
In east China's Anhui Province, robotics manufacturer EFORT Intelligent Robot Co., Ltd. has continued to see growth in overseas orders this year, with a batch of its spraying robots set to be exported to Italy. The company's overseas revenue increased by more than 50 percent year on year in the first half of 2026.
Meanwhile, the company's client, German automobile giant Volkswagen, is shifting its strategy from "in China, for China" to "in China, beyond China," with cars produced in China already exported to the Middle East and Central Asia.
Foreign-invested enterprises in China remained active players in the January-September period, with their imports and exports rising 19 percent to 11.69 trillion yuan, a record high for the same period. Their trade in intermediate goods grew 27.4 percent to 7.9 trillion yuan, and their high-tech product exports jumped 42.1 percent.
More foreign firms are embracing "China Opportunity 2.0," deepening their integration into China's industrial and innovation chains, Mao said. ■

====================================================================================================

Europe's surging populist right reshapes establishment politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:26:26 UTC
01:26:26 KST

How Europe's surging populist right is reshaping the political establishment
London — From the upper floors of Millbank Tower, a skyscraper overlooking the River Thames in London, the U.K. Houses of Parliament are just a few hundred yards away. For decades, the building housed the headquarters of Britain's Conservative Party, one of the world's oldest political parties.
Today, it is home to Reform UK, the right-wing populist party led by Nigel Farage that is hoping to — and by some measures may already have — replace the Conservatives as the dominant force on the British right.
The change of occupants reflects a wider political upheaval sweeping some of Europe's biggest democracies. In France, Marine Le Pen's right-wing National Rally has overtaken much of the traditional right ahead of the next year's presidential election.
In Germany, the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has made historic electoral gains, challenging the center-right Christian Democrats. There are similar trends in Italy, Spain, Sweden and other corners of the continent.
While the histories and ambitions of the movements in all these countries differ, collectively, their rise is forcing many of Europe's established conservative parties to make a choice: either adopt some of the populist right's increasingly hard-line positions on immigration and national identity and cooperate with them, or risk losing voters to them altogether.
"The larger issue is the general great realignment of politics towards identity and nationalism being the main axis of debate, not the economy," Steve Baker, a former British Conservative government minister, told CBS News.
The European Commission forecasts EU economic growth of just 1.1% in 2026, down from 1.5% in 2025. Baker, who pointed to President Trump's election in the United States as evidence of the same wider trend, believes the shift reflects a deeper frustration with political and economic institutions.
"The world does not work for far too many people, and almost no one is able to explain why," he said. "In that environment ... someone gets the blame."
Increasingly, he warned, that blame is being directed at ethnic and cultural minorities.
Britain's battle for the right
In Britain, the Conservative Party is fighting for its political survival after its 14-year hold on power was brought to an end with a crushing electoral defeat in 2024.
Reform UK, led by Farage, has capitalized on and encouraged anger over immigration, accusing successive Conservative governments of breaking promises to reduce immigrant arrivals as net migration reached a record of nearly a million in the party's final years in power. A September poll found that 44% of Britons considered immigration one of the most important issues facing the nation.
But the battle for Britain's political right is increasingly about more than immigration numbers. It has become a debate over British identity, ethnicity and who can call themselves English, with research finding support for ethnicity-based definitions of citizenship increasing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, whose parents are Nigerian, has challenged those on the right who seek to define Englishness through ancestry alone, after London-born senior Reform UK politician Suella Braverman — who is of Indian descent — said she does not consider herself English, because "Englishness is an ethnicity."
"I don't want to live in a country run by people who ... debate whether my mixed-race children are English," Badenoch said at the Conservative Party conference in October. "We must not let these people take us backwards."
Baker, who represented the Wycombe constituency in southeast England as Conservative Member of Parliament, told CBS News that voter concerns about immigration and demographic change cannot simply be dismissed.
He said in some local areas of his constituency, "the minority white population remaining will often express discontent that the area in which they live now looks radically different to when they moved in, and people do object to that," he said. Census data does support his assertion that in some local areas of Wycombe, white residents have become minorities, though not in the constituency as a whole.
Baker added that he opposes the turn to ethnicity in Britain's current political debates.
"None of us were talking about ethno-nationalism a few years ago," he said. "I recoil in absolute horror to see this conversation going mainstream."
After polling at around 28% in May, Reform U.K.'s support has recently fallen to 22% in some surveys as the party deals with internal controversies and financial scandals.
Farage and Reform are also facing pressure from parties further to the right.
Restore Britain, led by former Reform lawmaker Rupert Lowe and publicly backed by billionaire Elon Musk, is targeting voters who believe Farage's party isn't pushing hard enough on immigration, Islam and national identity.
One poll put Restore's support as high as 9%, suggesting the battle for Britain's conservative hearts and minds is far from settled.
Germany's political firewall under pressure
In Germany, the direction of right wing political movements is especially fraught given its history as the birthplace of the Nazi party. Since World War II, all of Germany's established parties have maintained what's become known as a political firewall against far-right extremists, refusing to enter governing coalitions with any party associated with nationalist, anti-democratic rhetoric or with links to extremist movements.
That firewall, or brandmauer in German, has stood against the AfD, which has been designated an extremist group by some regional authorities due to the associations and rhetoric of figures within the party.
The AfD openly uses the term and espouses "remigration," a notion anti-hate groups say has been employed by extreme right-wing activists to advocate the expulsion of all immigrants and, in some cases, non-white European citizens.
The party insists its own definition is different, describing remigration as "all measures and incentives for the lawful and legally compliant return of foreigners who are required to leave the country to their homeland."
The AfD explicitly rejects the removal of German citizens on the basis of their ancestry, stating "all Germans are part of our nation, regardless of origin, ancestry, worldview, or religious affiliation.".
But German security authorities have documented links between AfD figures and extremist activists who advocate for a broader, ethnicity-defined concept of remigration.
The AfD's recent gains in local and regional elections is putting the firewall under pressure.
In September, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its support from the previous election. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which had previously led the state government, finished a distant second with 17.2% of the vote.
The AfD has built its strongest base in eastern Germany, seizing on lingering resentment over the unification of the country's Cold War-era East and West, economic inequality and a widespread distrust of political institutions. But its support now extends well beyond those traditional strongholds.
The AfD's rise has also been fueled by dissatisfaction with Germany's handling of the 2015–2016 European migration crisis. The country, under former Chancellor Angela Merkel and amid broad sympathy for people being displaced by Syria's civil war, welcomed about 890,000 asylum seekers in 2015 alone, more than any other European nation.
A decade later, in the 2025 federal election, the AfD won approximately 32% of the vote in eastern states and 18% in western Germany, becoming the country's second-largest party nationally.
AfD politician Tomasz Froelich told CBS News the party has attracted voters from across the political spectrum, especially "working-class voters, skilled workers in industrial occupations who fear for their economic future, and small business owners who are not financially secure."
Froelich predicted the major parties that have led Germany for decades would eventually fail to maintain the firewall keeping his own out of power.
"If the AfD continues to rise towards 35% nationally ... and comes to represent more than one third of voters, this approach will sooner or later become impossible to sustain," he said.
While electoral popularity alone may not compel other parties to cooperate with a movement they consider a threat to Germany's constitutional order, the AfD argues it has already forced its mainstream rivals to change their own policies.
"Calls for rigorous border controls, a cap on migration or a stronger emphasis on national interests were long portrayed as politically unacceptable," Mary Khan, another AfD politician, told CBS News. "Today, many of these positions are being openly discussed even within the CDU, and far beyond."
In January 2025, Merz, then the leader of the opposition Christian Democrats and now the German chancellor, faced a major backlash after backing a parliamentary motion calling for tougher immigration controls that passed with the support of AfD lawmakers. The vote prompted nationwide protests and criticism from former chancellor Merkel. A subsequent attempt to pass an immigration bill into law failed, with 12 conservative lawmakers declining to back it.
The AfD stands out in Europe as its positions have alienated some of its potential allies on Europe's nationalist right. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has cited fundamental differences with the AfD over Russia's war on Ukraine, while France's National Rally broke with the German party in 2024 after a leading AfD candidate made remarks appearing to downplay the crimes of the Nazis' notorious SS paramilitary force.
From political outsider to presidential contender
Few European politicians illustrate the transformation of the continent's right wing more clearly than France's Marine Le Pen. An early October survey found Le Pen would likely garner between 31% and 36% of first-round votes in a national election, leading her nearest rival by at least 11 percentage points. France's next presidential election will be held in April.
For years, Le Pen has worked to distance her National Rally (RN) party, formerly the National Front, from the extremist reputation it held from the time of its inception at the hands of her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen.
His antisemitic statements made the National Front politically toxic to much of the French electorate. His daughter has changed the party's name, moderated some of its positions and sought to persuade voters it is capable of governing France. The strategy, known as dédiabolisation (de-demonization), has helped National Rally shed its political outsider skin and become one of the country's most powerful electoral forces.
It has consigned France's traditional conservative party, Les Républicains, to near irrelevance, with national support around only 9% according to recent polling.
Stéphane Azihari, a French essayist who writes for the newspaper Le Figaro, said Le Pen has succeeded by appealing to voters who feel abandoned by both the traditional right and left.
"She has simultaneously filled the void left by a right wing that's greatly disappointed voters on immigration and security, while also capturing working-class voters from the left," he told CBS News. "The primary driver of RN voting remains, of course, the fear of non-European immigration, and Muslim immigration in particular."
France has a long tradition of democratic secularism, but political debate in the country has increasingly focused on perceptions of immigration and Islam as threats.
A 2024 poll found that 77% of National Rally voters considered immigration an important factor in their voting, while research published by the Brookings Institution in 2020 found that 73% believed Islam was incompatible with French society.
Around 10% of adults in France between the ages of 18 and 59 identify as Muslim, according to official statistics, the highest proportion in western Europe.
Azihari argued that concerns about Islamist terrorism, particularly following the deadly 2015 attacks on the Charlie Hebdo newspaper and the Bataclan concert hall in Paris, have helped normalize National Rally's positions on immigration and security.
"The center's inability to effectively address security and immigration concerns explains much of the National Rally's progression," he said.
President Emmanuel Macron, who cannot seek a third consecutive term in 2027, has also backed more restrictive immigration measures during his presidency. But adopting tougher positions has not necessarily diminished the National Rally's appeal.
Across Europe, established parties face a similar dilemma: Embrace tougher positions on immigration and national identity and cooperate with populist rivals, or risk losing more voters.
According to one survey of party support across 31 European nations from earlier this year, almost a quarter of voters say they now support far-right parties.
Even if those populist parties fail to win control of governments on the continent, their influence is already being felt, and the question now is how far to the right they will pull other parties that have long rejected their legitimacy.
