====================================================================================================

How to Sell a Genocide: The Media’s Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:26:06 UTC
01:26:06 KST

The dispute over whether Israel’s assault on Gaza amounts to genocide has largely been settled. Amnesty International, a UN commission of inquiry and the International Association of Genocide Scholars have all reached that conclusion, as have many leading scholars of genocide. The question that remains is how the greatest political crime of our time was allowed to happen. Adam H. Johnson’s How to Sell a Genocide goes a long way to explaining it.
Published by Pluto Press with a foreword by the Palestinian American human rights lawyer Noura Erakat, the book covers the crucial period from October 2023 to October 2024, when Western audiences were primed for genocide. Johnson shows that the mainstream American media did much of the priming. These outlets dehumanised Palestinians, treated the life of an Israeli as having more worth than the life of a Palestinian and supplied ready-made justifications for violence against the population of Gaza. Together, he argues, they formed a media ecosystem that was essential to Israel’s campaign to destroy the Palestinians of Gaza, in whole or in part.
None of this, in Johnson’s view, was inevitable. It took “deliberate choices by deliberate moral actors” – the editors, reporters, bookers, producers and TV presenters who decided in the first weeks that protecting the powerful mattered more than the truth. Rather than report honestly on Israel’s US-backed assault on Gaza, they spun a comforting fiction for Western liberal audiences to justify the horror.
The Complicit Lens: US Media Coverage of Israel’s Genocide in Gaza
Setting out to prove, “beyond a reasonable doubt, that the genocide in Gaza was enabled, facilitated, and cheerled by establishment US media providing cover for months of a nihilistic campaign of starvation, bombing, arbitrary detention, shooting, and sexual violence,” Johnson cites hard data rather than relying on polemic or cherry-picked examples. The author draws on more than 12,000 articles and 5,000 TV clips from nine major outlets, testimony from journalists inside those newsrooms and comparisons with coverage of other recent conflicts.
Why leave out Fox News and the right-wing media? Because, says Johnson, outlets such as Fox, the Daily Wire and the Wall Street Journal are openly genocidal towards Palestinians and make no pretence otherwise; a book exposing them would be met by their own reporters and columnists with an “Okay, and?”
Instead, the author focuses on the outlets that Democrats read and watch. A Democratic president was in office when the genocide began, and support from Democrats in Congress, think tanks and the press was decisive in keeping it going. He concentrates on the first year, and above all the first few months, because that, he argues, is when the logic of the “war on Hamas” took hold, Americans grew used to mass death in Gaza and the genocide became a fait accompli.
With the destruction in Gaza too brutal and too visible to ignore, the media supplied excuses to ease the public conscience. Johnson calls these “Moats of Rationalization”: a scaffolding of deflection, double standards and orientalist tropes that allowed viewers and journalists alike to excuse the war crimes their own government was funding. The real job of the centre-left press, he argues, was not to convey reality but to “make their readers and viewers feel better” about their country, their leaders and themselves.
The first chapter shows how this worked by tracing how Israel weaponised the false claim that Hamas had beheaded 40 babies. The claim, which originated with Israeli military personnel and ZAKA, an organisation Johnson describes as far-right, spread from Israeli officials through CNN and other outlets to President Joe Biden within a day. It was part of an early push by media executives and pro-Israel groups to “ISIS-ify” Palestinian militants. Israel promoted the hashtag #HamasisISIS, and US Defence Secretary Lloyd Austin called the attack “worse than ISIS”. Johnson’s analysis found that in the first month, seven major print and online outlets equated Hamas with ISIS 149 times. On air, CNN did so 350 times and MSNBC 369 times.
The media also abandoned one of its most basic duties: explaining why the attack happened. Providing context for 7 October was actively discouraged. When MSNBC’s Ali Velshi and Ayman Mohyeldin explained the history behind it on the day, Johnson’s sources say Comcast, the network’s owner, intervened; one summed up the editorial line as “We don’t want context.”
Strict gatekeeping of what can and cannot be reported also helped to sell the genocide. CNN ordered that all its reporting on Israel and Palestine be “approved in advance by the Jerusalem bureau”, which operates under Israel’s military censor. A source told The Intercept that lines were routinely edited to favour Israeli narratives. Yet lurid, unsourced claims about Palestinians were aired unchallenged, while allegations against Israelis, Johnson argues, had to be “triple vetted”.
The same double standard shaped coverage of sexual violence. Within days of 7 October, the Israeli claim that systematic rape was part of Hamas’s “terror strategy” was being repeated by liberal media outlets before Israel had offered any evidence for it. Like the “beheaded babies” story, Johnson argues, it cast Hamas as an organisation “for which any political settlement or ceasefire is not only impossible but morally objectionable”.
The flawed sourcing of the New York Times report “Screams Without Words”, Johnson says, pointed to “an ideological motivation at work” and to lower standards for stories that served Israel’s agenda. Israel’s sexual abuse of Palestinian detainees, meanwhile, barely registered. In the first three months of the genocide and three months in late summer 2024, CNN and MSNBC made 502 on-air mentions of Palestinians committing mass rape and just two of Israelis raping Palestinians. The New York Times, Washington Post, Politico and Axios did the same in print: 128 mentions against nine.
An important part of selling the genocide relied on creating a two-tier moral system. In the chapter “Who is allowed to be human?”, Johnson shows how, within hours of 7 October, pundits and reporters began ranking violence and its victims on what he calls a “moral tier system”. Palestinian violence was treated as uniquely evil, driven by hatred, while Israeli violence was treated as regrettable but necessary.
Illustrating the impact of such framing, Johnson’s figures show that in the first 100 days, seven print and online outlets used “massacre” 344 times in their own reporting to describe Palestinians killing Israelis, and not once for Israelis killing Palestinians. Over the first year, the claim that Palestinians used “human shields” was aired 888 times on CNN and MSNBC, although Human Rights Watch has long rejected such a broad use of the term. Documented cases of Israeli forces using Palestinians as human shields went unmentioned. Israel’s “right to defend itself” was asserted 755 times on the two networks; Palestinians were granted the same right eight times.
Later chapters examine how US media helped the Biden administration “distance itself from the horrors of Gaza”; how it narrowed the debate to “how many Palestinians should die”; and how it covered “war crimes like earthquakes”, reporting the carnage as if it were a natural disaster and obscuring or leaving out Israel’s role entirely.
Read: Israel’s fake news factory implodes over 7 October rape story
The chapter on campus protests, which Johnson calls “‘Antisemitism’ show trials”, contains the starkest comparison in the book. In the month after Harvard president Claudine Gay testified to Congress on campus antisemitism, six major print and online outlets ran 207 stories about her. In the month after six-year-old Hind Rajab was killed by Israeli forces in Gaza, along with six relatives and the two paramedics sent to rescue her, the same outlets ran five. On air, the gap was wider still: CNN mentioned Gay 409 times and Hind 29; MSNBC mentioned Gay 210 times and Hind not once.
Johnson sees his job as that of a “prosecutor”, and the book reads like a case for the prosecution. It is packed with figures, which some readers may find heavy going, but the sheer weight of them makes the pattern of bias very hard to deny.
A book such as this asks us to consider what history has already taught us about the role of propaganda in mass atrocity. At Nuremberg, the Allies put on trial not only those who carried out mass murder but also the propagandists who primed the public to accept it. The lesson was that genocide does not begin with killing; it begins with words that teach people to see others as less than human. Johnson shows how US media treated Palestinian lives as worth less than Israeli ones, stripped Palestinians of their history and presented violence against them as necessary.
American newsrooms have yet to answer the questions this book raises about their coverage of Gaza. They reported the deaths, but they also offered endless excuses for them. Johnson has documented the choices that shaped that coverage. It is now for editors and journalists to explain why they so often showed more understanding for those doing the killing than for those being killed.

“Imperium,” a documentary by Sergei Loznitsa, won the best film award at the British Film Institute’s 70th London Film Festival.
“Imperium” consists of archival footage shot by Italian documentary filmmakers in the Soviet Union in the 1970s. Russian captain charged with stealing Ukrainian grain from occupied territories

01:23:15 KST

The captain of a Russian cargo ship has been charged in absentia in connection with illegally transporting over 54,000 metric tons of stolen grain from Ukraine's occupied territories, the Prosecutor General's Office and the Security Service (SBU) said on Oct. 19.
This marks the first time such action will be considered a war crime by Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office.
The captain was charged with violating the procedure for entering and exiting occupied territories with intent to harm the interests of the state, and violating the laws and customs of war.
According to the investigation, the vessel, "Matros Pozynich," made two shipments between 2022 and 2023, when Russian forces seized grain from Ukrainian farmers in Crimea.
Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalskyi said that "a legal framework has been established and applied in practice that allows for the captain's participation in the removal of grain – illegally seized in the occupied territory – to be classified as a war crime."
The shipments, totaling roughly 27,000 metric tons each, departed from the temporarily occupied city of Sevastopol for the port of Latakia in Syria.
According to the SBU's statement, the vessel's captain was taking orders from top Russian officials that violate parts of the Geneva Convention, specifically the prohibition of looting property from occupied territories.
read also
Safe and reliable grain export in the Black Sea has been one of the key topics of discussion, as constant Russian attacks on Ukraine's ports put around 32 million tons of agricultural products worth approximately $10 billion at risk, according to Ukraine's Agriculture Ministry.
"We are making maximum use of alternative routes — the Danube, rail, and road transport. But they cannot fully replace maritime exports. Without the restoration of stable shipping through the Black Sea, production will begin to decline in the long term," on Oct. 14 Taras Vysotskyi, Agriculture Minister, said in conversation with Turkish Ambassador to Ukraine Fatma Ceren Yazgan.

Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:21:06 UTC
01:21:06 KST

A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced.
Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades.
The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship.
The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”.
The exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs.
Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”.
Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”
He said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”.
The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said.
A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward had Boris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airport gone ahead.
Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts.

After travelling more than 20 hours by air from Australia, Anne Boland arrived to find the Louvre shut behind barricades, prompting her to offer a piece of advice to tourists planning a trip to Paris.
"Stay home!" the 73-year-old pensioner told Agence France-Presse (AFP) on Monday outside the world's most visited museum, after a weekend of unrest that rocked some of the French capital's most iconic streets and squares.
She was one of thousands of visitors scrambling to navigate the City of Light as marches, traffic delays and wafting tear gas snarl the capital's 14-billion-euro ($16-billion) tourism industry.
A small group of protesters was blocking the entrance to the Louvre's famous glass pyramid, following days of mass protests that also spilled into some of the worst street violence France has seen in recent years.
Cycling through the city the day before, expecting charming Haussmann buildings, mansard roofs and corner cafes, Peter, a Dutch tourist, found himself touring a "war zone".
"It was terrible – debris from fires everywhere, glass on the pavement," the 63-year-old, who declined to give his last name, said.
Some shrugged off the disruptions. But almost all seemed caught off guard upon arriving at the Louvre, their plans suddenly cancelled.
Turned away, many resorted to selfies and photos in front of the former palace.
Roughly half a million people turned out across France on Saturday to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of earlier protests led by high school students demanding better conditions at their schools.
The Yellow Vests movement, which organized the weekend's rallies, has called for more protests this coming Saturday, as the government mulls partial, targeted curfews.

But many in the city carried on in typical Parisian style: a video broadcast by America's CBS news showed a couple drinking on a city terrace, unfazed by a nearby fire in the road.
"We haven't seen anything concerning," said Glenda Manna, 62, a university professor in town from the U.S.
But as the protests capture the attention of news channels – and politicians – around the world, there are incessant messages from family members back home pleading with them to "tell me you're safe," added her mother, Dorothy Hill, 82.

Qatari electricity lifeline for Lebanon includes two power plants, LNG supply deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:20:01 UTC
01:20:01 KST

Qatar plans to build two power plants in Lebanon over the next three years and sign a 20-year liquefied natural gas supply deal as part of a proposal to revive the ailing Lebanese power sector, Reuters said.
Lebanon's energy sector is at the center of the country's financial and economic malaise, contributing tens of billions of dollars to the national debt since the country's 1975-1990 civil war even as it failed to deliver 24/7 power.
The state power company currently supplies just a few hours of power per day, with the rest coming from expensive private diesel generators that spew toxic exhaust often seen forming a yellow-grey layer of smog above Beirut.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani visited Lebanon last week and publicly promised to help revitalize the country's power sector. Few details were then presented to reporters.
But according to a proposal drafted with input from the Lebanese and Qatari governments, dated October 2026 and seen by Reuters, the program "covers gas-fired power generation, LNG supply and regasification, renewable energy, battery storage, and regional electricity interconnections".
Funding and guarantees remain under negotiation
"The program aims to attract private/project financing without upfront Lebanese public-budget capital expenditure; payment obligations and guarantees remain subject to negotiation," the document said.
The blueprint, named the National Integrated Energy Investment Program, still requires the approval of both governments and is subject to amendment, a person familiar with the matter said.
They set the implementation timeframe at three years if approvals come swiftly.
Qatar has long been a financial and political backer of Lebanon, stepping in multiple times over the last decades during political and economic crises.
The Qatari Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the proposed plan. Lebanon's energy minister also did not respond to a request for comment.
Proposal follows growing Qatari presence in Syria
According to the document, the plan includes two new combined-cycle plants at Deir Ammar in northern Lebanon and at Zahrani in the south, each at a capacity of 825 megawatts.
QatarEnergy would also enter a 20-year LNG supply agreement with Lebanon, using both a floating storage and regasification unit with a capacity of 3.5 million cubic meters per day, and the Arab Gas Pipeline via Syria at a capacity of 4.5 million cubic meters per day.
The proposal also includes plans for 800 MW of solar and 440 MW of wind, battery capacity, and power imports from Syria, beginning with 300 MW via two separate routes.
Numerous proposals to reform Lebanon's power sector and provide electricity through the national grid have repeatedly stalled due to political bickering and the vested interests of senior politicians in the fuel and energy sectors.
The proposal would build on Qatar's growing presence in neighboring Syria, where the Qatari conglomerate Power International Holding has secured contracts for 5,000 MW of power generation, as well as oil and gas extraction and pipelines.

Terror attacks in West Bank have declined more than 55% this year, 'Post' analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:19:57 UTC
01:19:57 KST

Terrorist attacks in the West Bank have declined over the last two years. This continues a trend from 2024 to 2025. Data from the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and the Foreign Ministry show a 70% decline in major terror attacks between 2024 and 2025 and nearly a 60% decline from 2025 to 2026. Overall, including stone throwing and other incidents, attacks fell 20% this year, according to data through August. Nevertheless, hundreds of incidents of threats and attacks still occur every month.
The Foreign Ministry noted that “nine major terror attacks took place in July. Of these, four were carried out in the West Bank and five in Israel. In July, the Shin Bet foiled a total of 532 terror attempts; of these, 528 were in the West Bank region and four in Israel.”
The Jerusalem Post compared the data that has been compiled by the Shin Bet over the last years, most of which has also been published by the Foreign Ministry. The 2026 data is documented only through August. However, comparisons can be made with similar periods in previous years.
Major attacks decreased by 71% between 2024, 2025
Based on our comparison, there were 218 major attacks in 2024 and 62 in 2025. Overall, there were 5,663 terrorist incidents in 2024, compared to 4,744 in 2025. This meant there was a 71% decrease in major attacks and a 16% decrease in overall attacks. When we compare the period January-August 2024-2026, we find similar declines.
For instance, in overall attacks in the same period, there was a 30% decline between 2024 and 2026. This represents 1,000 fewer attacks between January and July 2024 and January and July 2026.
For major attacks, the trend was even larger, with more than an 86% decrease between 2024 and 2026. Trends can change suddenly, and data can sometimes be wrong. Overall, the picture shows a decline over the past years.
The details appear to speak for themselves. In January, one major attack occurred in the West Bank. Israel’s security services foiled 89 major attacks that month, Shin Bet noted. In March, there were four attacks in the West Bank, and in April there were five.
By May, there were two, and then four in July and two recorded in August. Meanwhile, in August, there were 288 other attacks, including 254 stone-throwing incidents. Twelve Molotov cocktail attacks were also recorded.
Wave of West Bank terror began before October 7
Israel has suffered a wave of terror attacks over the last four years in the West Bank. This wave had begun before the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre.
In 2022, the IDF launched Operation Break the Wave. Forty-five Israelis had been killed between 2022 and March 2023. In July 2023, the IDF launched Operation Home and Garden in Jenin to reduce the threats.
After the Hamas attack on October 7, the IDF also began major operations in the West Bank. This has included rooting out terrorist groups in Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm, and other areas.
Recent IDF data on three years of war since October 2023 illustrate the level of operations in the West Bank. “More than 3,800 weapons were located and confiscated,” the IDF recently said.
“Approximately 45,000 wanted individuals were apprehended and detained for questioning, including: Weapons traffickers, individuals in possession of a weapon, wanted individuals who planned to carry out imminent attacks, terrorist operatives and facilitators, individuals involved in terrorist activity, and stone and Molotov cocktail throwers.”
The results of the IDF operations appear clear. In May 2025, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies noted in a brief that “The West Bank has seen a sharp decline in terrorist attacks in 2025, as the IDF’s Operation ‘Iron Wall’ continues to dismantle terror infrastructure across the territory.”
The brief added that “according to a new report from the Israeli security establishment, just 46 attacks were recorded in April 2025, only three of which were considered significant, marking the lowest monthly total in five years. By comparison, the West Bank averaged 214 terrorist attacks per month in 2023, dropping to 115 in 2024, and further declining to just 57 in 2025.”
Recent attacks bring West Bank violence back into spotlight
There has been recent focus on the West Bank due to several incidents involving Jewish rioters attacking people. Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was attacked on Friday, and diplomats were attacked near the Christian Arab village of Taybeh on Saturday. On Monday, in the early morning, a number of suspects in the attacks were detained.
Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Monday that “addressing the severe violence committed by a handful of Jewish rioters in Judea and Samaria must fall entirely under the purview of the Israel Police’s Judea and Samaria District, encompassing prevention, investigation, and prosecution. The IDF should not, and cannot, engage in civilian law enforcement; its role is to combat Palestinian terrorism and to defend the state’s borders, as well as the Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria and along the 'seam zone.'”

A Spanish court has allowed former Catalan President Puigdemont to return to the country without the threat of arrest

A Spanish court has allowed former Catalan President Puigdemont to return to the country without the threat of arrest
Kyiv • UNN
Spain’s Supreme Court upheld the cancellation of the arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont. This clears the way for his return.
Spain’s Supreme Court has upheld the decision to cancel the arrest warrant for former Catalan President Carles Puigdemont, who has been in exile for nearly a decade following an unsuccessful attempt to secure the region’s independence. This paves the way for his return to Spain. BBC reports, UNN writes.
Details
The court’s decision concerns the case involving the referendum on Catalan independence, which the regional government organized in 2017 despite Madrid’s opposition.
After the vote, the central government imposed direct rule on the region, and Puigdemont traveled to Belgium, where he has remained ever since. In 2024, he unexpectedly appeared in Barcelona, after which police began searching for him. However, he managed to flee to France before being detained.
In 2024, Spain’s socialist government introduced an amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists involved in the movement to separate the region. At the same time, the Supreme Court ruled that Puigdemont and several of his associates should not be covered by the amnesty because of allegations of possible financial crimes connected with organizing the referendum.
Earlier this month, the Constitutional Court overturned that interpretation. On Monday, the Supreme Court also rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against the cancellation of the national arrest warrants for Puigdemont and his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín.
The political situation in Catalonia
Puigdemont was elected a member of the European Parliament in 2019 and, in 2024, to the Catalan Parliament. He leads the center-right Together for Catalonia party (JxCat).
Despite remaining abroad, the politician continued to advocate the region’s independence and criticize Spain’s democratic institutions.
It is currently unknown exactly when Puigdemont may return to Spain.
As the publication notes, the issue of Catalan independence has now moved to the background of Spanish politics. The main focus is on the housing crisis and immigration.
Following the 2023 elections, parliamentary support from Puigdemont’s party played an important role in forming Spain’s left-wing government led by Pedro Sánchez. However, JxCat’s position is weakening in Catalonia itself: some of its voters are being won over by the far-right Catalan Alliance party, which also supports the region’s independence.

Gunmen then opened fire on a second vehicle, killing two more soldiers and five members of the Civilian Joint Task Force, which assists the military, the sources said, asking not to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Suspected Boko Haram attacks on Nigerian troops continue in Borno state
Six wounded soldiers were taken to Maimalari Military Hospital in Maiduguri for treatment, the sources said.
Reuters could not independently verify the casualty figures.
Last week, suspected Boko Haram fighters killed at least 10 soldiers and wounded at least 20 others in a coordinated assault on an army base in Borno state.

Austria recorded 671 antisemitic incidents in first half of 2026, majority tied to anti-Israel acts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:19:36 UTC
01:19:36 KST

A total of 671 antisemitic incidents were recorded across Austria by the Reporting Centre for Antisemitism of the Jewish Community of Vienna (IKG) during the first six months of 2026.
While the figure marks a slight decline compared to the 726 incidents logged during the same period in 2025 and 808 in the first half of 2024, the total remains more than twice as high as the 311 cases recorded prior to the October 7 massacre. On average, 3.7 antisemitic incidents per day were recorded during the reporting period, compared to 4.2 for the full year 2025.
The Reporting Centre noted that antisemitism in the country continues to be heavily influenced by geopolitical developments in the Middle East, with escalations translating directly into local incidents where Jewish people are held accountable for the actions of the State of Israel.
Israel-related incidents remain dominant manifestation of antisemitism
Israel-related antisemitism remained the dominant manifestation, appearing in 75.4 percent of all registered cases. In the vast majority of instances, this motif occurred alongside other forms of prejudice, such as antisemitic othering, Holocaust relativization, and conspiracy myths.
IKG President Oskar Deutsch said, “Since October 7, 2023, not only the boundaries of what can be said, but also of what can be done, have shifted. Antisemitic words are followed by threats and attacks against Jews. A state of emergency has become the norm.”
The overall trend throughout the six months was heavily influenced by the outbreak of war on February 28, which pitted Israel and the United States against the Iranian regime. Acting as a catalyst, the conflict drove a sharp rise in incidents immediately following its outbreak, with 79 incidents recorded in the two weeks after the war began, almost twice as many as the 40 recorded in the two weeks prior.
This surge culminated in March as the peak month of the half-year with 152 recorded cases. High numbers also persisted in May, a month that accounted for half of all physical assaults (6 of 12), nearly a third of all calls for or glorification of terror (22 of 70), and featured events such as the Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna and campaigns surrounding the Gaza flotilla.
Analyzing the shift across different offense types, IKG pointed out that while lower-level incidents such as offensive behavior and property damage decreased compared to early 2025, falling from 432 to 347 and from 78 to 68 respectively, severe misconduct moved in the opposite direction.
Physical assaults rose from 5 to 12, up from 5 in the first half of 2025 and approaching the level of 16 recorded in the first half of 2024. Among the 12 assaults, nine were classified as Muslim-motivated, two as right-wing, and one as unattributable.
Recorded threats similarly increased from 8 to 18, compared to 8 during the same period in 2025, with more than half originating from a Muslim background, alongside three left-wing, three unattributable, and two right-wing cases.
Other monitored categories included 68 incidents of property damage and desecration, where a right-wing background was most frequent with 28 cases, followed by 22 unattributable, 14 left-wing, and only 4 clearly attributable to a Muslim background.
Mass mailings totaled 226, with a Muslim background representing the largest share at 41.6 percent, followed by left-wing cases at 35.8 percent, right-wing cases at 14.6 percent, and 8 percent unattributable. Abusive behavior reached 347 incidents, most frequently categorized as ideologically unattributable at 36.6 percent, followed by 23.6 percent right-wing, 21.3 percent Muslim, and 18.4 percent left-wing.
Out of the broader dataset, 33 incidents were connected to demonstrations, and 14 occurred within the field of education. Cases involving calls for or the glorification of terror were identified 70 times, accounting for 10.4 percent of all registered incidents, with the largest shares carrying a Muslim or left-wing background.
Antisemitism incidents motivated by left-wing, right-wing, Islamist ideologies
Regarding ideological categorization across all 671 incidents, 191 were classified as Muslim-motivated, 162 as left-wing, 147 as right-wing, and 171 as unattributable.
The data also tracked the mediums through which incidents occurred, recording 376 on social media, 175 witnessed in person, 71 by email, 33 on other online channels, and 16 across letters and alternative formats.
Johannan Edelman, head of IKG, said, "What we register is only the tip of the iceberg. The statistics only include incidents that we have verified as clearly antisemitic after careful examination. At the same time, the willingness of those affected to report such incidents is low – out of resignation or fear of becoming even more targeted. But every report helps to make the true extent of the problem visible."
IKG General Secretary Benjamin Nägele stated, "Our community has relied on extensive security measures for years. The fact that we have had to get used to this must never mean that we accept antisemitism and the associated threat as normal. Those who can deny antisemitic agitators space within their sphere of influence are called upon to act, so that cohesion in our society is strengthened."

The Joint List will dedicate its political broadcast to showcasing the destruction in the Gaza Strip in the form of 48 seconds of drone footage of Gaza rubble, the party announced on Monday.
The footage, viewed by The Jerusalem Post, cuts between different vantage points of the destruction and includes a Hebrew voiceover describing Israel as "continuing as usual" despite the destruction. Hebrew and Arabic captions match the voiceover, with somber music playing in the background throughout.
"(We) behave as if everything that has happened here (in Gaza) is completely normal," the video says. "As if tens of thousands of people weren't killed here... As if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands."
The video, which further describes the deaths of Gazan children and families, states that the party "will not be silent."
"They (other parties) want more destruction," the Joint List video claims. "We offer life."
Joint List: 'Destruction, devastation' in Gaza 'largely hidden' from Israelis
The party claimed in its announcement that such footage of the "destruction and devastation in Gaza" has been "largely hidden from the Israeli public."
"We are the only ones who have firmly and consistently opposed the war of annihilation in Gaza, from its inception and throughout its entire course," the party stated. "We did not remain silent, we are not silent, and we will not remain silent."
The statement called for Israelis to "look reality in the eye" and for Israel's media to publish footage of Gaza's destruction "in its entirety."

Trump to create new NIH division, task force for women’s health

US President Donald Trump will sign an executive order alongside first lady Melania Trump on Monday creating a task force and a National Institutes of Health division focused on women’s health, the White House said.

The new Women’s Health Division at NIH will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research.
“President Donald J. Trump & First Lady Melania Trump sign an executive order creating a Women’s Health Division at the NIH & a White House Women’s Health Task Force, aiming to close research gaps & modernise care for women,” a post on X announcing the signing said.

Two presidents, two versions of peace: Trump says Zelensky doesn’t want the war to end. Zelensky says Trump wants Ukraine to give in.

Unknown Publisher

16:19:24 UTC
01:19:24 KST

Two presidents, two versions of peace: Trump says Zelensky doesn’t want the war to end. Zelensky says Trump wants Ukraine to give in.
The U.S. and Ukrainian presidents have continued their long-distance war of words. Donald Trump wrote on social media that Volodymyr Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war.”
“[W]ith all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump said on his social media platform, Truth Social.
The U.S. president said Zelensky could have “made a better deal two years ago than he can now.” “His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost,” Trump said. He also said Ukraine had lost access to seas and oceans and that its male population had shrunk — “wounded, and/or dead.”
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Zelensky “presents a false binary” by linking an end to the war with a Ukrainian victory. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement, and President Trump is working on that every day. He’s done it since he came into office,” Bessent said in an interview with NBC News.
He also urged Zelensky to “be very careful” about accusing the United States of restricting Starlink in Ukraine. Bessent said those claims were untrue.
Zelensky said Ukraine, rather than Russia, was being pressured to make concessions. “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelensky said in an interview with Bloomberg.
I’m not saying that’s what our partners are trying to achieve. I don’t want to think our American partners believe the war can end sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.
Zelensky again said the United States had deliberately slowed Starlink service in Ukraine, putting Ukrainian military operations at risk, and was also delaying deliveries of missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
“My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president tied the U.S. actions to the November midterm elections, in which Trump is trying to shore up his Republican Party. “Politics is very aggressive during election time,” he said. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue, and I believe it will be calmer.”
The war in photographs: The aftermath of a strike on Kyiv
As Trump and Zelensky trade barbs over who should make concessions to end the war, Russian forces continue to strike Kyiv every day. Ukraine receives no advance warning of the strikes.

Russia, Iran discuss cooperation between Tehran and EAEU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:18:18 UTC
01:18:18 KST

DUSHANBE, October 19. /TASS/. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref discussed cooperation between Tehran and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk said in conclusion of the Russian-Iranian talks in Dushanbe.
"The Eurasian Economic Union is currently scaling up its engagement with the countries of the Global South. As you know, we are expanding our network of free trade agreements, specifically with Iran also. Significant time was dedicated to this topic today as well because a free trade agreement allows us to largely eliminate the problems that might have existed if there was no such agreement," Overchuk said.
The parallel work in this direction is also underway with other nations, the Russian deputy prime minister said. "An interim agreement with Mongolia has come into force, as has one with the United Arab Emirates. Work is also being carried out to bring the agreement with Indonesia into force. In addition, negotiations are underway with India, and consultations have been held with Pakistan. Just last week, we met with the Prime Minister of Thailand [Anutin Charnvirakul], and he also raised the issue of a free trade zone with Thailand," Overchuk noted.
"In other words, we now see our primary goal in expanding opportunities to establish free trade between the Eurasian Economic Union and other nations, primarily, of course, on the Asian continent and in the Global South. This is the task we are currently dealing with," he added.

Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:16:23 UTC
01:16:23 KST

Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.
The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.
The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.
The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.
Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”
Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.
The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.
After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”
The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”
“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”
The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.
Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”
If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.
Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.
An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing.
Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.
The timeline for the gift is disputed.
Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.
According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.
The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.
Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.
A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.
Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.
Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”
They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.

Russian army now more innovative, adaptable — NATO commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:15:26 UTC
01:15:26 KST

WASHINGTON, October 19. /TASS/. The Russian army has become more innovative and adaptable compared with the beginning of the special military operation in 2022, French Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, said in an interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC.
"They [Russian servicemen] learn, they adapt," he said, adding that the Russian army was no longer the same as it had been in 2022.
In particular, he noted Russia’s advances in unmanned aerial vehicles. According to him, Russia’s adoption of more advanced technologies has significantly reduced the effectiveness of some Ukrainian interception methods.
Against the backdrop of Russia’s successes, the NATO commander said the alliance was falling behind and could find itself unprepared and unable to keep pace with technological innovation on the front lines.
"I disagree with the point where we have a good industrial depth," Vandier said. He also added that he often sees officials "chatting, delaying some important decisions, not committing the money, using some <…> old-fashioned process," which reportedly keeps him up at night.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that Russia allegedly plans to attack NATO countries. Russian President Vladimir Putin has described such statements by Western politicians as attempts to intimidate their own populations and justify increased military spending. Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, in turn, has said that the alliance is pursuing a policy of "rampant militarization" and that portraying Russia as a "threat" is being used to justify a decision to raise NATO member states’ defense spending to 5% of gross domestic product.

‘Concerning issues’ found at GB power grid by inquiry into cover-up claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:14:47 UTC
01:14:47 KST

Independent investigators have found significant and concerning “cultural issues” at Great Britain’s grid operator after control room staff accused senior executives of covering up the extent of blackout risks in the UK during the June heatwave.
An external legal firm tasked with investigating a series of whistleblower allegations against the National Energy System Operator (Neso) raised concerns over how high levels stress among control room engineers was handled by the company.
The three-month investigation began after whistleblowers accused Neso of a cover-up over the growing risk of blackouts. They claimed the grid was becoming increasingly unmanageable, and that control room decisions were subject to “interference” by the company’s corporate affairs team to protect the reputation of the government-owned operator.
The unprecedented control room revolt included multiple internal complaints, the leak of internal documents to the press, and accusations of whistleblower intimidation.
Neso was forced to abandon plans for an internal investigation into the claims in favour of an independent investigation by the law firm Evershed Sutherlands, whose findings were published on Monday.
The law firm said that while it found “no evidence” of inappropriate influence over operational decisions, or that control room engineers were warned against leaving a paper trail of their efforts to stabilise the grid, the investigation found “cultural, governance and control issues” that were “significant findings in their own right”.
The allegations against Neso emerged after the June heatwave caused grid frequency levels to fall below normal operating limits on a number of occasions and required emergency assistance from neighbouring countries to keep the lights on.
The grid woes were caused by near-record temperatures that caused demand for electricity to run air-conditioning systems to surge while a high pressure heat dome slowed wind turbines and prompted unplanned outages at gas and nuclear plants across Europe.
Tim Jarvis, the chief executive of the regulator Ofgem, said that although the investigation did not uphold the whistleblower’s specific allegations, it raised “important and concerning issues about working culture and practices at Neso”.
The investigation found there were “high levels of stress and concern” within the control room over how staff would be able to keep the power system balanced as renewable energy replaces legacy fossil fuel power plants in line with the government’s net zero ambitions.
It said there was a view that senior Neso executives did not fully appreciate or understand the pressures faced by the control room engineers who were responsible for keeping the lights on “on the frontline”.
In addition, staff felt that their concerns or complaints went “largely unheard” because of the need to keep external stakeholders including the government and the regulators happy, according to the law firm’s report.
Fintan Slye, Neso’s chief executive, said the report was “constructive” in identifying areas in which the grid operator could improve how staff could raise concerns and how to respond to them.
“I want all colleagues at Neso to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make,” he said.
A separate Ofgem investigation, which is ongoing, will look into whether the cultural issues identified by Eversheds played a role in the operational decision-making, system security or raising energy costs for consumers.
“We will not prejudge that assessment,” Jarvis said, “But nor will we shy away from its conclusions. Our job is to establish the facts, identify the lessons and ensure action is taken.”
The Ofgem findings, which will be published no later than 31 March 2027, could lead to an enforcement investigation by the regulator if it believes Neso has not complied with obligations under market rules.
Michael Shanks, the minister for energy, said the government expected “significant action without delay” and would “keep progress under close review”.

Uzbekistan, U.S. sign Artemis Accords
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:14:02 UTC
01:14:02 KST

Uzbekistan, U.S. sign Artemis Accords
Following bilateral talks in Samarkand, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Uzbekistan, Bakhtiyor Saidov, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed the Artemis Accord, Qazinform News Agency learned from UzA.
The document sets principles for international cooperation in the peaceful exploration and use of the Moon, Mars, comets, and asteroids.
The signing opens up new opportunities for Uzbekistan to expand cooperation with NASA and the space agencies of other participating countries, train national specialists, and facilitate the transfer of space technologies.
Uzbekistan became the 77th country to sign the Artemis Accords.
Bakhtiyor Saidov and Marco Rubio also visited the exhibition Uzbekistan and the United States: A Shared History Across Centuries and Continents, organized as part of the C5+1 ministerial meeting.

Starvation cult leader found guilty of murder of 190 children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:13:31 UTC
01:13:31 KST

Starvation cult leader found guilty of murder of 190 children, 1 adult in Kenya
A self-proclaimed Kenyan preacher and his associates were found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in an infamous starvation cult by a Mombasa court on Monday.
"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," the judge said.
Hundreds of bodies have been discovered since 2023 at the cult base inland from the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi, in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."
Paul Mackenzie is alleged to have incited his acolytes to starve to death in order to "meet Jesus."
Mackenzie and his associates pleaded not guilty to 191 counts of murder in 2024. He has also denied charges of manslaughter and terrorism in separate cases.
In the three years since the grisly discovery, more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400.
Mackenzie looked impassive as he arrived at Mombasa Law Courts on Monday with 29 other accused, who descended from a barred-window bus handcuffed in pairs.
Relatives of the victims were also in court, many making their way to Mombasa from rural communities along the coast.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, in Shakahola.
"This day, to me, is a very, very important day," he told AFP before the session started.
"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he said, expressing anger over the initial government inaction.
There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.
The prosecution alleges that Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women and then men.
The children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said, based on postmortems and police reports.
Mackenzie's lawyers said the case was "largely founded on circumstantial evidence, hearsay accounts and inconclusive forensic findings."
Case exposed
Mackenzie was arrested in April 2023, after a rights group tipped off authorities and some followers were rescued.
The subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of shallow graves, with a soaring death toll that required a pause in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.
The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights said in 2024 that the death toll was 429. Some victims are still unidentified.
In January, Mackenzie was charged over another 52 bodies found at a nearby village.
The self-styled pastor has a history of extremism and evaded law enforcement for years.
He established the Good News International Church in 2003, and set up branches in Nairobi and along Kenya's coast that attracted thousands of devotees, though he claimed it closed in 2019.
Followers have told their families and officials they believed Mackenzie when he preached that starvation was the path to salvation. He allegedly split members into smaller groups assigned biblical names. It's believed these smaller groups died together and were buried together in mass graves.
State pathologists have said many of the exhumed victims died of starvation, but some showed signs of strangulation.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2017 over charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.
Investigators have said Mackenzie was a taxi driver in the early 2000s, before he created the Good News International Ministry. Locals have said he quickly drew followers with fiery sermons at his church on the coast in Malindi, then from across Kenya with his online presence.
Several surviving members of the group have told family members that what he preached would often come true, citing as an example his prediction that "a great virus" would come, just before COVID-19 hit the country. As people struggled during the pandemic, financially and medically, Mackenzie preached about leaving the difficulties of life behind and "turning to salvation."

The Korean War, the return of the DMZ, and prices in Ukraine — what to expect from the release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4
Kyiv • UNN
The new game from Infinity Ward will tell the story of the Korean War and the return of Captain Price. It will be released on October 23 for PC and consoles.
Already this Friday, October 23, the long-awaited release of the shooter Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 will take place on PC and consoles. The game was developed by the American company Infinity Ward and published by Activision. The new installment in the series will plunge players into a large-scale conflict on the Korean Peninsula, where, alongside the legendary Captain Price and a new hero, they will have to fight through fierce trench warfare, reports UNN.
Modern Warfare 4 storyline: conflict on the Korean Peninsula
War erupts on the Korean Peninsula as a result of a full-scale invasion by North Korea, threatening to destabilize the world in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
The Modern Warfare 4 campaign focuses on the war between North and South Korea. Following the events of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III (2023), the Korean People's Army's invasion of the Korean Peninsula threatens to destabilize the peace.
The story centers on two main characters: Private Pak (Young Mazino), a South Korean recruit who fights side by side with his squad to defend his homeland, and Captain John Price (Barry Sloane), the former commander of Task Force 141, who is on the run after killing U.S. General Hershel Shepherd.
Modern Warfare 4 takes the series into darker and more dangerous territory, where the escalation and its consequences bring long-running storylines to a powerful and emotional turning point.
The campaign plunges players into trench warfare in Korea, close-quarters combat in New York, fierce chases through Paris, nighttime SAS raids in Mumbai, and assaults on entire cities aimed at reclaiming occupied territories.
The return of DMZ and multiplayer innovations
At launch, the multiplayer mode will include 12 core 6v6 maps, as well as game modes from previous installments, such as "Gunfight," with a dedicated set of maps, and "Ground War," featuring large-scale maps and heavy vehicles.
The updated "DMZ" mode has become more dynamic compared with Modern Warfare II: it now features a weather-change system and mobile military objectives, while AI enemies will patrol the map along different routes. Players will be able to go on excursions either solo or in squads. New modes for the series, Hijack, Inflation, and Counter Attack, will also be introduced.
It should be noted that DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a PvPvE mode with elements of an Extraction Shooter. A significant part of the local gameplay involves searching for items in a wide variety of locations, crafting, and evacuating from the match to obtain additional rewards, along with correspondingly severe penalties for the character's death.
Why the game is not in Game Pass and how much it costs
The project was announced on May 28, 2026, and the game's release, as already mentioned, is expected on Friday, October 23.
Unlike Black Ops 6 and Black Ops 7, which appeared in the Xbox Game Pass subscription on day one, Modern Warfare 4 will join the service's library at least a year after its worldwide premiere.
On Steam, the game costs from 2,449 hryvnias to 3,724 hryvnias, depending on the edition. On PlayStation 5, the game costs from 3,399 hryvnias, while on Xbox S | X it costs from 3,590 hryvnias to 4,299 hryvnias.
Game crack
Hackers have also become involved with the game. Five days before release, a hacker using the nickname r4v3n announced an "offline fix" for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 that would allow the campaign to be launched without an internet connection. He clarified that he was "not returning" to hacking activities and "simply wanted to share a quick fix for the single-player game, since it is easy to do."
r4v3n himself does not plan to hack the multiplayer or other modes of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, but assumes that other hacker groups may take on the task.
However, judging by the first reviews from buyers on Steam, this year's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 campaign turned out to be surprisingly good. Some members of the piracy community admit that they are interested specifically in the campaign and would be willing to buy a standalone single-player mode for, say, $15–20, but are not willing to pay $70 for the full game—they are not interested in multiplayer or the other content.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered regional authorities Monday to introduce localized curfews following a weekend of widespread rioting, looting and violent clashes with police across the country, as the government struggled to restore order after mass demonstrations over rising living costs and education funding.
Speaking after an emergency government meeting, Lecornu said the restrictions would be targeted at specific neighborhoods rather than entire cities, particularly in areas where businesses and public buildings had come under attack. He did not rule out declaring a state of emergency if the unrest continued, but said limited curfews were more appropriate for the time being.
In the northern town of Denain, authorities introduced a nighttime curfew following disturbances involving vandalism, burning garbage containers and attacks on police. Initially imposed between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m. for all residents, the restrictions were subsequently eased Monday to apply only to minors in designated areas between 10:30 p.m. and 6 a.m. Curfews for minors were also introduced in Pointe-à-Pitre and Les Abymes in the French Caribbean territory of Guadeloupe, following violence in which three police officers were wounded by gunfire.
The situation in Lille remained less clear. Although a government source indicated that a curfew had been ordered, Mayor Arnaud Deslandes publicly opposed introducing a municipal restriction, arguing that a nighttime curfew would have little impact because violent groups had already gathered during the early evening. Lille was among the cities affected by serious disturbances over the weekend, including vandalism and attacks on public property.
The unrest erupted Saturday during nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living, high energy prices and deteriorating conditions in public schools. Hundreds of thousands took part in protests, most of them peaceful, but violent groups clashed with police in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux and other cities. Storefronts were smashed, businesses looted and vehicles set ablaze.
Among the most dramatic incidents was the destruction of much of the historic city hall in Limoges, where a fire swept through the building following clashes. More than 2,000 people were arrested nationwide during the unrest, while government officials estimated that at least 3,000 businesses had been damaged or looted.
Lecornu accused extremist groups and opportunistic rioters of exploiting legitimate grievances to provoke violence. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation over failures in the security response, but President Emmanuel Macron rejected it. The government also announced emergency financial assistance for affected businesses and a tougher judicial response to those responsible for the destruction.
The crisis has intensified pressure on Macron's government ahead of the 2027 presidential election. With protest organizers already calling for another round of demonstrations next Saturday, authorities face a growing challenge: preventing further violence without restricting the right to peaceful protest.

Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:08:14 UTC
01:08:14 KST

A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
Prosecutors say Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the court rejected that argument.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.
Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, one of the co-accused.
He was silent, staring into space before the ruling was handed down.
Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high court.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.
Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.
People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told police that his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police arrested him again in April 2023 and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.
Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Israel’s invisible hand in the war on Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:08:13 UTC
01:08:13 KST

Israel’s invisible hand in the war on Yemen
TEHRAN – The Israeli strategy in Yemen centers on exploiting the war between Saudi Arabia and the Sanaa government to establish a new reality.
This strategy has taken on added significance following U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks that Israel had been very helpful to Saudi Arabia against Ansarallah. Separately, reports cited officials as saying Saudi Arabia held CENTCOM-mediated talks with Israelis to receive the regime’s intelligence against Ansarullah. Trump also indicated that the possibility of a Saudi-Israeli normalization agreement was once again under discussion.
Taken together, these developments have raised a broader issue: Is Israeli-Saudi security cooperation being used to revive the stalled normalization process and lay the groundwork for new regional arrangements that primarily serve Israeli interests?
Analysts have pointed to four key factors that underline the Israeli regime’s position:
The security dimension
The regime views the war as a testing ground for its security assessments. Rather than treating Iran and Yemen as separate fronts, it sees them as parts of a single, interconnected theater of confrontation. From this perspective, the conflict provides a real-world test of Ansarallah’s military capabilities, particularly their latest missile arsenals, drone systems, and other military assets.
The strategic dimension
Israeli strategic calculations are based on the premise that the Yemeni and Iranian fronts cannot be treated separately. It views the ongoing war as an integral part of its broader effort to dismantle the Axis of Resistance.
From this perspective, the regime has a strong interest in weakening Ansarallah politically and militarily. Israelis regard Ansarallah as a significant component of the Axis of Resistance because of its military capabilities and its ability to threaten security in the Red Sea against Yemen’s foes. The Sanaa government has also demonstrated its capacity to strike targets deep inside Israel while supporting Gaza during the U.S.-backed genocide in the Strip.
Conversely, if Ansarallah emerges with strategic gains, the outcome would directly undermine Israeli efforts to weaken the Axis of Resistance. It could also reinforce the perception that the Israeli military can be challenged and that new strategic realities can be imposed across the region.
Israel’s regional positioning
The Zionist regime sees the war between Ansarallah and Saudi Arabia as an opportunity to strengthen its geopolitical position in the region.
Israeli public statements about Saudi security, reports that Prime Minister Netanyahu proposed providing the kingdom with military and security assistance, and Trump’s subsequent remarks on the matter are particularly significant. Together, they point to the regime’s efforts to establish itself as a security partner capable of providing intelligence and helping Saudi Arabia counter shared regional threats.
The regime also views these developments as a potential opening to revive its stalled normalization process with Saudi Arabia and create the political and security conditions for a broader regional coalition against Iran.
The significance of Yemen in Israel’s strategic calculations extends well beyond the immediate military confrontation. Tel Aviv may also seek to capitalize on the conflict to reshape regional relationships and alliances, establishing a new political reality in which it plays a more prominent role in regional security arrangements aimed at containing Iran.
Role of the United States
The U.S. dimension highlights Washington’s influence over the course of the war on Yemen. It also raises questions about whether the U.S. will intervene directly or limit its involvement to providing political, military, and intelligence support.
Any reduction in direct U.S. involvement could push the Israelis to strengthen their military, security, strategic, and political autonomy, expanding their ability to influence regional conflicts without relying entirely on the American security umbrella.
This would allow the regime to test its capacity to operate more independently, develop direct security relationships with regional actors, and increase its influence over developments involving Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
Such a shift would not signal a weakening of the Zionist-American alliance. Rather, it could reflect a redistribution of responsibilities, with the U.S. retaining its central role in providing political and military support to the regime while it assumes greater responsibility for managing regional wars and threats.
Another possible outcome, given Saudi Arabia’s publicly stated position on Palestine, is that intelligence cooperation could continue and even expand without developing into a comprehensive political and military alliance or leading to full normalization.
Under this scenario, the prospects for normalization would depend on what Riyadh is willing to concede in exchange for the intelligence assistance it receives in confronting Ansarallah, particularly if the war escalates.
The limits of Israeli strategy
The Zionist regime’s approach to Yemen goes beyond confronting Ansarallah’s military capabilities. Its broader objective is to weaken staunch regional Iranian allies. This goal is hardly concealed: Tel Aviv ultimately seeks to reshape regional alliances in ways that serve its own interests.
Yet this strategy confronts two fundamental realities. Yemen is not a peripheral component of the Axis of Resistance but an important front within it. And Iran is not a country that can easily be brought to its knees simply by increasing pressure on Yemen.
Ansarallah’s strategic geographical position and military capabilities allow it to pose significant challenges to the Zionist regime’s calculations. Iran, meanwhile, remains a major regional power with substantial strategic influence and multiple options at its disposal, as demonstrated by its ability to withstand war and sustained pressure, including sanctions and other forms of coercion.
Consequently, even if the regime succeeds in weakening one of the fronts within the Axis of Resistance, that alone will not guarantee that it achieves its broader strategic objectives.
Israel’s attempts to neutralize or weaken the Yemeni front as a prelude to containing Iran could instead become a strategic liability. Military power can destroy infrastructure and inflict significant damage, but it cannot guarantee the achievement of political objectives. Nor does attacking resistance movements necessarily mean they will be dismantled. These groups can reorganize and rebuild their capabilities, which is part of their broader strategic doctrine.
Ultimately, it has been demonstrated that Ansarallah’s ability to withstand pressure, combined with Iran’s capacity to manage the confrontation and endure despite the scale of the challenges it faces, is crucial to preventing the imposition of a regional order that serves Zionists at the expense of the region’s peoples and their causes.
The situation in Yemen illustrates that the real test is not the extent of intelligence cooperation between Tel Aviv and Riyadh, nor the scale of the airstrikes against Yemen. It is whether the pressure exerted on the ground can be translated into tangible political gains. This is where the Zionist regime has failed on every front it has launched direct military aggression.
