When diplomacy arrived in Jakarta and justice did not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:14:18 UTC
23:14:18 KST

The paradox has acquired a second dimension, and it is written in the ruins of Gaza. Indonesia, a nation that presents itself to the world as a rising democratic power and an indispensable partner for global stability, now positions itself as a moral voice for Palestine while presiding over a domestic order in which liberty is conditional, and dissent is reframed as betrayal.
Under President Prabowo Subianto, this is not a story of isolated abuses. It is the architecture of a state that has learned to speak the language of international responsibility while hollowing out the rights it claims to protect—at home and, increasingly, in its diplomatic conduct abroad. The same logic that shields Jakarta from scrutiny over West Papua now shapes its response to Gaza: a performance of solidarity that stops precisely where material power would be required.
Consider the diplomats’ dilemma. When the United Nations Secretary-General visited Jakarta in October 2026, the official readouts focused on peacekeeping, Palestine, and the reform of the multilateral system. They did not speak of the more than one hundred thousand Indigenous Papuans displaced by military operations, nor of the schools and clinics occupied by security forces, nor of the journalists and activists arrested for documenting the consequences of national development projects.
This silence is not accidental. It is the product of a calculated exchange: Indonesia’s contribution of over fifty thousand peacekeepers to UN missions—including the more than 2,700 currently deployed across eight operations, from UNIFIL in Lebanon to MINUSCA in the Central African Republic—buys it a measure of immunity from scrutiny at home. The moral economy of international institutions rewards what states contribute abroad, not how they treat their own citizens. And Jakarta has learned to spend that credit wisely.
The same exchange now structures the global response to Gaza.
Since October 2023, the United States has used its veto in the Security Council five times to block resolutions demanding a ceasefire, even as the officially confirmed death toll has climbed beyond 56,000, with civilians comprising more than 70 per cent of the dead.
The General Assembly has voted overwhelmingly—164 states in favour, eight against—to affirm the Palestinian right to self-determination and to demand an end to the unlawful occupation.
But the General Assembly cannot enforce its will. Only the Security Council can authorise binding sanctions, deploy peacekeepers, or impose embargoes, and the veto has rendered it structurally incapable of doing so. The International Court of Justice concluded in July 2024 that Israel’s continued presence in the occupied territory is unlawful. The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant in November 2024.
Neither ruling has been enforced. The law exists. The enforcement does not. This is the structural paralysis that defines the multilateral order, and it is the backdrop against which Indonesia’s Palestine diplomacy must be assessed.
Jakarta’s rhetorical commitment is genuine and historically grounded. The deployment of the hospital ship KRI dr. Radjiman Wedyodiningrat to El Arish, the dispatch of more than one hundred medical personnel, the airdrops coordinated with the Jordanian Air Force, the offer to evacuate one thousand wounded Palestinians—these are tangible humanitarian contributions, and they deserve recognition.
But they treat the symptoms of the conflict, not its causes. They do not challenge the arms flows that sustain the military campaign, the diplomatic cover that shields it, or the economic relationships that underwrite it. They are politically safe precisely because they leave the structure of impunity intact.
The reason is not mysterious. Indonesia’s economic model depends on Western capital, technology transfers, and access to global markets to fund the nickel downstreaming, infrastructure, and food-estate projects that anchor the Prabowo administration’s developmental vision. To impose unilateral sanctions, to sever commercial ties with states supporting the military campaign, or to take disruptive action outside the parameters of conventional UN diplomacy would risk the investment flows on which that vision depends.
READ: Indonesia slams Israel for discriminating against one of its pilots
And so Jakarta calibrates. It speaks forcefully in the General Assembly, where resolutions are non-binding and symbolic. It sends hospital ships and medical teams, where the gesture is humanitarian, and the political cost is low. It does not weaponise trade, does not lead a sanctions coalition, and does not convert its moral authority into material leverage. The performance is real. The teeth are not.
This calibration is reinforced by a strategic objective that shapes every diplomatic calculation: Indonesia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for the 2029–2030 term. To secure the votes of a diverse UN membership, Jakarta must maintain functional relationships across geopolitical blocs. Radical or unpredictable positions—precisely the kind that might give its Palestine advocacy enforceable weight—would alienate key voting partners.
The administration therefore prefers the safety of multilateral consensus to the risk of unilateral conviction. The seat is the prize, and the price of the prize is moderation.
The broader Middle East has moved in the same direction. The Abraham Accords, signed in 2020, normalised relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco, and they have proven unexpectedly resilient even amid the war in Gaza. Regional powers that once framed themselves as guardians of Palestinian rights now prioritise economic modernisation, security partnerships, and supply-chain integration.
The Palestinian cause remains a matter of public rhetoric and domestic legitimacy, but it is increasingly detached from the practical architecture of regional order. Palestine is caught in the gap between the high-level statements that affirm its rights and the material interests that determine its fate.
This is the same gap that defines Indonesia’s domestic order, and it is why the credibility of Jakarta’s Palestine diplomacy cannot be separated from the credibility of its human rights record at home. In West Papua, the machinery of extraction and the machinery of repression are not separate systems; they are the same system.
The legal architecture that prosecutes Indigenous leaders and environmental defenders who contest land grabs is the same architecture that criminalises insult to the president and expands police discretion over digital speech. The state that speaks of Palestinian self-determination while denying it to Papuans is not engaged in hypocrisy for its own sake. It is engaged in a coherent practice of sovereign selectivity: rights are affirmed where they cost nothing and denied where they cost something.
The international community’s willingness to compartmentalise these domains is the condition of Jakarta’s moral voice. Withdraw that willingness, and the voice loses its resonance.
For the international community, the implication is uncomfortable but clear. The implication is uncomfortable but clear. Indonesia cannot be engaged as a credible moral voice on Palestine without confronting the domestic order that sustains its international posture. The shield it has built—of peacekeepers, of non-alignment, of Global South leadership, of humanitarian gestures in Gaza—is not impenetrable.
It depends on the continued willingness of external actors to compartmentalise. That willingness should be withdrawn. Access to West Papua must be a condition of diplomatic partnership, not a concession to be negotiated.
The enforcement of international law in Palestine must be reconnected to the material levers—arms embargoes, trade measures, targeted sanctions—that give law its meaning.
And the reform of the Security Council’s veto must move from aspiration to agenda, because a law that cannot be enforced is not law. It is theatre.
The choice is not between stability and rights. It is between a stability built on silence and a stability built on consent. The ruins of Gaza, the skies over Southeast Asia, and the forests of West Papua suggest that the cost of not choosing is already being paid—by those who have no voice in the capitals where the choice is made.
OPINION: Why Ethiopia and Eritrea’s march to war demands global attention

The Utrecht Conference is a series of Polish–Dutch meetings organised since 1999. Their aim is to strengthen cooperation between Poland and the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the political, economic, and social domains.

Making a speech on Saturday, Hegseth, who served as a Minnesota Army National Guard instructor in Afghanistan, said that when he would go to the coalition base in Kabul, “there would be 50 flags at the headquarters”.
He went on: “And it was a beautiful thing to see, 50 different countries contributing to the Nato alliance and the Isaf [International Security Assistance Force] mission there. “In fact, the patch ‘Isaf’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting’. Which is sort of a joke but it’s demoralising when you feel like it’s not burden-sharing, it’s actually a burden.”
While almost 2,500 US forces died in Afghanistan, two-thirds of the total death toll, personnel from more than 30 nations died on duty there, including 457 from the UK.
Asked about Hegseth’s comments, Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Frankly, the facts speak for themselves when it comes to the UK’s and Nato’s contribution to Afghanistan.
“Thousands of British and allied families made huge sacrifices to play their significant part in that war and uphold our values, and more than 450 British personnel never returned.
“Their sacrifice and that of other Nato forces was made in the service of collective security and in response to an attack on our ally. We are incredibly proud of our armed forces, and their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten. And it is wrong to diminish their role.”
The remarks echo an even more direct rebuke to Trump by Keir Starmer in January, when the then PM said the president should apologise for “insulting and frankly appalling” remarks claiming that Nato troops had stayed “a little back, a little off the frontlines” in Afghanistan.

The spokesperson added: “Our support for Ukraine is unwavering, and I think you saw that in the prime minister’s meeting with President Zelenskyy last week.”

The appeal follows pressure from the Visegrad Group — Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Poland — on EU leaders at their 15-16 October summit to reconsider measures to lower electricity bills in the region.
Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the bloc’s carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and delaying its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.
Energy Commissioner Jørgensen acknowledged the “serious” situation facing people in Central Europe and reiterated the need for “targeted and temporary measures” that would not undermine the bloc’s goal of reducing its reliance on imported fossil fuels.
“We used to be dependent on Russia. We’re moving out of that. Now, that is good. But the current situation shows that we are now dependent on the global market, and events in the Middle East can affect citizens here in Bratislava,” Jørgensen said.
The four EU countries, traditionally more reliant on fossil fuels, argue that high energy prices make it difficult for their industries to commit to investments in electrification. Prices have been driven higher by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Central European consumers are facing a significantly heavier financial burden, with wholesale electricity futures more than 60% above pre-crisis levels, according to energy think tank Ember.
Ditching Russian energy is raising economic concerns in both countries.
Bratislava and Budapest argue that they face particular challenges in meeting the EU’s diversification requirements and want funding to expand oil and gas infrastructure in the region.
The Visegrad Group has access to several alternative energy sources and supply routes that bypass Russia, albeit at higher cost, with varying levels of integration across the four countries.
“From 2027, we will not be able to import gas from Russia and would like to sign new diversification contracts. Diversification and energy security mean that we have to have prepared rules for the supplies of oil and gas for the V4 region,” Saková added.
Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Hungary challenged the EU’s plan to phase out Russian energy imports, taking the case to an EU court.
Slovakia backed Budapest’s legal challenge, arguing that phasing out Russian energy would put its industrial competitiveness at a significant disadvantage compared with most other EU countries. A first ruling is expected to take months.

'It's significant': Ukraine fears US is withholding allied-funded air defense supplies to pressure Kyiv

U.S. President Donald Trump (L) speaks as U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (R) looks on during a meeting in the Cabinet Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., on Dec. 2, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images)
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine, Ukrainian officials and military officers told the Kyiv Independent, raising suspicions in Kyiv that Washington is deliberately withholding the weapons to pressure Ukraine.

"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," he added.

"Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
The official added that the missiles had already been paid for by Ukraine's allies.
The delay comes as Russia launches near-daily ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, leaving Kyiv dependent on its limited supplies of interceptors.
"Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them."
It also builds on the latest strain in relations between Ukraine and the Trump administration, which the U.S. president criticizing Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries.

American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to “bad weather conditions,” while U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio has cited a software malfunction.
Ukaine has also experienced disruptions to Starshield and Starlink services, which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones.
Ukrainian officials described the alleged delay as another example of political pressure that could put civilian lives at risk.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept. Any delay could seriously undermine Ukraine's defense of its cities and critical infrastructure.
A significant batch of missiles
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, one senior Ukrainian military official said. One of the main mechanisms is NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the U.S.
Zelensky said the U.S. delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine each month.
Kyiv also seeks missiles directly from countries that may have them in stock. Ukrainian embassies contact governments to identify available supplies.
Ukrainian officials declined to disclose the country's current interceptor stocks, citing operational security.
"(Ukraine) never discloses the quantity of weapons we have on hand so that the enemy remains unaware of the situation," one Ukrainian defense official said.

"It's hard to call this a 'monthly supply,' because there's no set amount of how much you need for a month," the official said. "But it's significant."
The status of the broader supply program remains less clear. A NATO official said PURL deliveries were continuing, including shipments of air defense equipment.
"Support to Ukraine through PURL continues to flow. This includes air defense," the official said.

"It looks like this is a political refusal to sign," one Ukrainian official said.

As of the morning of Oct. 19, a Ukrainian defense official said there had been no change in the supply situation, and Hegseth had still not approved the transfer.
A wider dispute over Russian oil
The dispute over Patriot interceptors comes amid mounting tensions over Ukraine's campaign against Russian energy infrastructure.
Trump has criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as his administration seeks to address rising global fuel prices, driven by his war in Iran.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to U.S. and international markets despite sanctions imposed over Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing additional supplies to reach foreign markets.
With fuel prices putting pressure on U.S. consumers, Trump has increasingly blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, while denying responsibility for the situation at the gas pumps.
One senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the administration's approach was driven by domestic politics.
"He can't admit he was wrong about the war in Iran, so — purely for campaign purposes — he's fallen back on the old narrative of accusations against Ukraine," the official said.

Russia Launches 16 Ballistic Missiles at Kyiv Without Advance Allied Warning, FT Reports

Russia Launches 16 Ballistic Missiles at Kyiv Without Advance Allied Warning, FT Reports
Ukraine received no advance warning from its Western partners before the first wave of Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv overnight on October 19, although intelligence arrived ahead of a second wave.
The Financial Times reported on October 19 that Ukraine received only partial intelligence about the Russian missile launches, raising concerns over the reliability of early-warning information shared by its allies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed that Russian forces launched two waves of ballistic missiles, at approximately 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. While no warning arrived from Ukraine's partners before the first wave, intelligence was received ahead of the second.
Ihnat explained that Ukrainian forces continued monitoring potential missile launches through their own intelligence sources and radar systems. However, the absence of advance information from partners reduced the time available to warn civilians.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the disruption in a Telegram statement on October 19, emphasizing that the latest attack was not an isolated incident.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no advance warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote.
According to the Ukrainian president, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles in a coordinated attack targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russian forces also deployed more than 200 drones of various types, including jet-powered Shahed drones, against targets across Ukraine, from the Kharkiv and Dnipro regions to Volyn, Rivne, and Odesa.
The overnight strikes targeted energy infrastructure across 11 Ukrainian regions, including Vinnytsia, Volyn, Kirovohrad, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Kharkiv, Ternopil, Odesa, and Rivne.
Zelenskyy confirmed that more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, leaving at least 550,000 households without electricity.
The strikes also damaged a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and residential buildings. Casualties were reported, while emergency and repair crews worked to restore essential services.
The Ukrainian president linked the attacks to what he described as insufficient pressure on Moscow, criticizing restrictions on air defense missile deliveries and sanctions relief granted to Russia.
"When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defense is blocked, while Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality by partners," Zelenskyy stated.
He also emphasized that Ukraine had responded positively to every proposal for a ceasefire, while the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, continued rejecting measures aimed at de-escalation.
The gap in allied early-warning intelligence had already surfaced days earlier, when five Russian ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv on October 13 without any advance notice from partners.
That attack was part of a barrage of more than 100 aerial weapons that also destroyed an apartment building in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring 41 others. Advance intelligence on ballistic launches is critical because the missiles' short flight time leaves civilians and air defense crews only minutes to react.

Ukrainian Engineers Develop Drone Detector That Reveals What Russian Drones See
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:11:59 UTC
23:11:59 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukrainian Engineers Develop Drone Detector That Reveals What Russian Drones See
A Ukrainian team has developed an SDR-based drone detector that can identify radio signals from unmanned aircraft and convert intercepted transmissions into video that an operator can view.
DOU reported on October 17 that the system, called D·Vision SDR, was developed by Kyiv-based communications equipment company CODE380. The company was founded about three months ago, while development of the detector itself began roughly a year and a half earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to DOU, the device scans radio frequencies from 500 to 8,700 MHz for signals characteristic of drones. Unlike conventional detectors that rely on analog receivers to receive video transmissions, D·Vision SDR uses Software-Defined Radio technology to analyze the radio spectrum in software.
The developers told DOU that the detector can identify a drone signal and convert it into a video feed, allowing an operator to view imagery transmitted by the aircraft. The team also claimed the system scans its entire stated frequency range without "blind spots" and offers greater sensitivity than competing detectors.
DOU noted that four people worked directly on the project, while CODE380 currently has eight employees and involves another six specialists in testing and design. The detector's lead developer previously worked on similar systems and used that experience to build the new SDR-based platform.
The system has undergone field testing with Ukrainian military personnel during combat missions, according to DOU. Feedback from those trials was used to refine the device, while the developers continue releasing software updates approximately twice a month.
Software-defined detection systems offer a different approach to fixed analog receivers because signal processing can be adjusted via software as drone communication and operating frequencies change.
Ukrainian-developed detection technology is also drawing interest beyond the front line.
In early October, Lithuania announced it was deploying the SkyFortress system, which identifies low-flying drones and cruise missiles by their acoustic or electromagnetic signatures and uses artificial intelligence to track them in real time.
The deployment came weeks after NATO fighter jets shot down an unidentified drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus.

Russian Captain Faces First-of-Its-Kind War Crime Case Over Stolen Ukrainian Grain Shipped to Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:11:55 UTC
23:11:55 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Captain Faces First-of-Its-Kind War Crime Case Over Stolen Ukrainian Grain Shipped to Syria
Ukrainian authorities have for the first time classified a Russian ship captain’s involvement in transporting stolen Ukrainian grain from occupied territories as a war crime, following an investigation into the illegal shipment of more than 54,000 tons of wheat.
The development was announced by Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalskyi on October 19.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to investigators, the Russian captain of the cargo vessel MATROS POZYNICH transported more than 54,000 tons of Ukrainian wheat that Russian forces had stolen from temporarily occupied territories during the early stages of the full-scale invasion.
The suspect, a Russian citizen, transported the grain from temporarily occupied Sevastopol in Crimea to the Syrian port of Latakia in November 2022 and January 2023, falsely presenting the shipments as Russian agricultural products.
To conceal the vessel’s movements, the captain reportedly disabled its Automatic Identification System (AIS), which transmits a ship’s location and identification data, and provided false information about its whereabouts.
Kovalskyi emphasized that the case marks the first time Ukrainian authorities have applied a legal approach treating a ship captain’s participation in transporting grain illegally seized from occupied territory as a war crime.
“This case goes far beyond a single criminal suspicion. For the first time in Ukraine, a legal approach has been developed and put into practice that makes it possible to classify a ship captain’s involvement in transporting grain illegally seized from occupied territory as a war crime,” the acting prosecutor general said.
He stressed that military occupation does not grant an aggressor state the right to appropriate Ukrainian property or natural resources.
According to Kovalskyi, establishing criminal responsibility requires investigators to determine the grain’s origin, document how it was stolen and transported, and identify those involved in the operation.
The captain of MATROS POZYNICH has now been formally notified of suspicion in absentia, including on charges of violating the laws and customs of war.
Ukraine has long been one of the world’s leading grain exporters, accounting for approximately 10% of global wheat exports and 12% of corn and barley exports before Russia’s full-scale invasion. However, Russian forces have since disrupted agricultural production by attacking grain storage facilities, damaging export infrastructure, mining farmland, and seizing Ukrainian grain from temporarily occupied territories.
The disruption has had consequences for global food security, particularly in countries across Africa and the Middle East that rely on Ukrainian agricultural supplies. In July 2022, Ukraine, Russia, and Turkey signed the UN-backed Black Sea Grain Initiative to facilitate agricultural exports, but Russia struck the port of Odesa less than a day after the agreement was signed.
Russia subsequently withdrew from the initiative in July 2023, triggering an 8% increase in global grain prices within a day. Experts accused Moscow of using restrictions on Ukrainian exports to exert pressure on international food markets, while Russian grain exports reached record levels during the second half of 2023.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly accused Russia of using hunger as a weapon, warning that disruptions to Ukrainian grain exports could threaten food supplies in Africa and Asia. The United Nations World Food Programme previously estimated that Ukraine’s agricultural land could produce enough food to feed approximately 400 million people in the absence of the full-scale war.
The case comes amid broader concerns over Russia’s interference with Ukrainian agricultural exports and its potential consequences for global food security.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia’s restrictions on maritime shipping could lead to food shortages in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East within one to two months, potentially triggering a wider global food crisis.

Ukraine Has 7 Different Drone Hunters in the Sky—and 22 Teams Racing to Build the Next Ones
Unknown

- Category

Ukraine Has 7 Different Drone Hunters in the Sky—and 22 Teams Racing to Build the Next Ones
Ukrainian forces are already using seven different types of interceptor drones against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type UAVs, Brave1 defense cluster head Andrii Hrytseniuk said, according to Oboronka on October 15.
Hrytseniuk said Ukraine began preparing specifically for jet-powered Russian drones in summer 2025, after interceptor UAVs had become increasingly effective against conventional propeller-driven Shaheds.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Back in the summer of 2025, after interceptor drones were able to close the skies to conventional ‘Shaheds,’ we began analyzing where to direct our efforts. That was when funding began for teams working on solutions against jet-powered drones. We are talking not only about high-speed interceptors, but also anti-aircraft missiles and turrets,” Hrytseniuk said.
Today, 22 Ukrainian development teams are working on high-speed interceptors designed to defeat Russia’s jet-powered Geran drones. Twelve of those teams have received state funding through Brave1.
The approaches vary widely. Some projects use miniature turbojet engines, while others rely on high-performance electric motors and propellers. Developers are also exploring ducted-fan systems, which resemble small jet engines in layout but are powered electrically.
“These are drone projects with miniature turbojet engines, as well as electric models with propellers. Another promising direction is drones with ducted-fan propulsion, which structurally resembles a turbojet but is powered by an electric battery,” Hrytseniuk explained.
Ukraine’s government has already contracted new interceptors in quantities that have “long since exceeded a thousand,” he said, although manufacturers are still working to scale production to the levels required for sustained nationwide defense.
“We will definitely catch up with Russian drone production. But this will not happen instantly. We can remember the period when conventional ‘Shaheds’ were used—scaling interceptor production took six months. Now we are doing everything possible to accelerate the process, but it will not happen in days or weeks,” Hrytseniuk said.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine is preparing for a massive expansion of its jet-powered drone and missile programs, with demand for just one type of jet engine potentially reaching 10,000 units every month by 2027.

French Nuclear Submarine Rubis Prepared for Launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:10:29 UTC
23:10:29 KST

In France, the nuclear submarine Rubis, the fifth in the Suffren class, was moved from the construction hall to a special launch site.
The French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) reported this.
This stage took place on October 16 at the Naval Group shipyard in Cherbourg. The submarine is scheduled to be launched in 2027.
After its launch, the submarine will undergo sea trials before joining the French Navy. The Rubis is scheduled to be handed over to the fleet in 2028.
The Rubis is part of the Barracuda program, which calls for the construction of six Suffren-class nuclear-powered attack submarines.
They are intended to replace the previous-generation Rubis-class submarines, which the French Navy began receiving in the 1980s.
The French nuclear-powered submarine Rubis was ordered on May 7, 2018, as part of the Barracuda program, which calls for the construction of six Suffren-class nuclear-powered attack submarines for the French Navy.
At the same time, Naval Group is developing a separate Orka project for the Netherlands based on the Barracuda family, which also includes the French Suffren-class submarines.
On September 30, 2024, the Netherlands signed a contract with the French company to deliver four Orka submarines. They are intended to replace the previous-generation Walrus-class submarines, which the Dutch Navy has been operating since the 1990s.
Unlike the nuclear-powered Suffren-class submarines, the Dutch submarines will not have a nuclear propulsion system. The project calls for modern battery systems.
Dutch industry will also be involved in the program. Local companies will supply hull structures, living quarters modules, hydraulic systems, and other equipment. The Dutch side has allocated approximately 1 billion euros in orders for its own companies.
Under the plan, the Dutch Navy is set to receive the first submarine in 2033 and the last by 2037.
Specifications:
Displacement: 4,700 metric tons on the surface and 5,300 metric tons submerged.
Length: 99 m.
Hull diameter: 8.8 m.
Maximum speed: approximately 25 knots (46 km/h) submerged.
Maximum diving depth: over 300 m.
Endurance: approximately 70 days.
Crew: 65 sailors; the submarine can also carry special operations forces.
Propulsion system: YASU, K15 reactor.
Armament:
Torpedo armament: F21 heavy torpedoes for engaging submarines and surface ships.
Anti-ship armament: Exocet SM39 missiles.
Strike armament: MdCN sea-launched cruise missiles for engaging land targets at long range.
Additional armament: sea mines.
Torpedo tubes: four 533-mm torpedo tubes.

As France picks up the pieces from a weekend that saw violent riots amid wider mass protests over education and the cost of living, reactions in Russia have ranged from outright glee and xenophobia to more muted schadenfreude and patronizing finger-wagging toward its Western adversary.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Europe was facing a “major crisis.”
“It’s hard to say whether [this] is a systemic or non-systemic crisis, but it’s clear that it’s a major crisis. These are disturbances that are, in fact, already bordering on chaos,” Peskov told reporters. “There is, of course, a clear sign of a crisis here, but, in any case, this is an internal matter for these countries.”
He dismissed accusations that Russia was involved in the protests, saying: “No one anywhere takes such absurd accusations seriously anymore. Not even in Europe itself.”
Elsewhere, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Sunday lambasted Europe’s “double standard” when it comes to dealing with protests.
Zakharova quoted Macron as saying that he would be “unyielding” in dealing with rioters who resorted to violence before asking where “human rights” and “freedom of expression” figured in the equation.
“In other words, when the French are ransacking Paris, it calls for uncompromising condemnation and tough measures, but when protesters in other countries are ransacking cities, we’re supposed to watch silently, re-reading the Élysée Palace’s angry press releases about the unacceptability of suppressing protests,” she wrote on Telegram.

The spokesperson said that an official statement will be made “at the appropriate time,” but those under TPS are safe to remain in the country.
Under TPS, Ukrainians are allowed to legally stay in the U.S., apply for an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) and enroll in educational institutions, including higher education programs.
TPS for Sudanese refugees will also be extended, CNN reported. Two other countries retaining their Temporary Protected Status are El Salvador and Lebanon.
TPS was granted to Ukraine’s citizens on March 3, 2022, just over a week after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine.
It is usually granted to countries for anywhere from six to eighteen months. Previously, Ukraine’s status was renewed on Jan. 17, 2025 and came into effect in April that year for another 18 months.
However, U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has terminated the status for multiple countries since March 2025, affecting about one million people across 13 countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti, and Syria.
The pending review from the U.S. comes at a time when President Volodymyr Zelensky and Trump’s relationship has been rather rocky following an unexpected announcement of a diesel deal between Washington and Moscow.
On Oct. 16, the U.S. also waived sanctions against Russia envisaged by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
"He (Zelensky) could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!,” Trump wrote on Oct. 18 on his social media platform, Truth Social.
In response, Zelensky has called such easing of sanctions “wrong” and told British host Piers Morgan in an interview on Oct. 14 that he laments the recent course of events.
"It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side," he added.

Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:06:53 BST
23:06:53 KST

Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
- Published
Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.
Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.
In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.
The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.
- Ex-Catalan leader ‘eludes police manhunt and flees Spain’ 
  - Published9 August 2024
- Catalonia's bid for independence from Spain explained 
  - Published18 October 2019
- Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests 
  - Published5 October
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.
Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.
The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

Aleksandr Babakov, a member of Russia’s State Duma and deputy chairman of the Russian parliament, continues to successfully evade Western sanctions by using a network of European intermediaries who are not subject to sanctions.
This is stated in a CYBINT investigation by the international intelligence community InformNapalm, based on the #BabakovLeaks data leak by the 256 Cyber Assault Division.
Having retained his seat following Russia’s so-called parliamentary elections, Aleksandr Babakov remains one of the Kremlin’s key figures in conducting hybrid operations and maintaining influence networks abroad. Western countries have known him since 2014 as the organizer of a €9.4 million loan to Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Front party through a bank in Prague.
Despite the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the European Union, and their allies imposing strict sanctions on Babakov and his son Mikhail, regulators have not fully blocked their activities abroad. The influential Russian official exploited his family’s longstanding roots and property holdings in France.
A key link in the sanctions evasion scheme was French citizen Geoffroy Marie Gonzague Doly, who has been part of the Russian politician’s inner circle for more than a decade. He became involved in Babakov’s network through a Moscow-based front organization, the Autonomous Nonprofit Organization “Institute for Research on Issues of International Integration.”
According to the leaked documents, in April 2015, the organization asked the Russian Embassy in Vienna to issue a visa to the 20-year-old Frenchman as a “research intern.” Babakov later personally contacted Russia’s ambassador to France, Aleksey Meshkov, requesting a three-year multiple-entry visa for Doly.
Over the course of a decade, the French “researcher” became an integral part of Babakov and his son Mikhail’s inner circle. Official documents list him as a “consultant,” while the parliamentary secretariat of the deputy chairman of Russia’s State Duma handled his affairs directly.
Doly’s joint trips and diplomatic missions have taken him to dozens of countries. In February 2023, for example, Russia’s ambassador to Dakar, Dmitry Kurakov, officially requested entry visas for Mikhail Babakov and the French consultant to join a Russian parliamentary delegation to The Gambia led by Nikolai Novichkov.
Beyond diplomatic logistics, Doly acts as a business and financial intermediary for the Babakov family. To facilitate travel and asset management, he obtained Serbian citizenship in 2021 and later signed employment contracts with the Belgrade-based consulting firm BLK-SKY d.o.o., headed by Babakov associate Pavel Polikarpov.
In Russia, the French citizen holds stakes in civilian companies, including a 10% share in Altacap LLC, co-owned with Babakov associate Sergey Mozhayev. Corporate records also link him to business projects in Chengdu, China.
Passenger manifests for 2023 show that Doly regularly traveled with Mikhail Babakov through major international hubs in Moscow, Cairo, Addis Ababa, Istanbul, Delhi, and Shanghai. A single Moscow-based travel agency arranged all these trips, along with the deputy’s aides Pavel Polikarpov and Evgeny Zobnin.
InformNapalm analysts emphasize that Geoffroy Doly’s case exposes a serious “blind spot” in the West’s sanctions monitoring system. Holding an EU passport, these administrative intermediaries allow sanctioned Russian elites to easily manage assets and exert influence in Europe beyond regulators’ reach.

A man has been sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment, with an additional 15 years’ supervision, for the manslaughter of four-year-old Dean Verberckmoes in 2022. This is the maximum possible sentence for manslaughter. Dave De Kock will only be eligible to apply for parole after 25 years. The court in Ghent found no mitigating circumstances.
30-year prison sentence for man who killed 4-year-old Dean
Dean, from East Flanders, went missing while staying with De Kock and his girlfriend, Romy W. The couple were friends of Dean’s mother and often looked after Dean and his younger sister.
On the evening of Friday 14 January 2022, De Kock went out alone with the toddler. Investigators were able to largely reconstruct his movements using ANPR cameras, mobile phone data, CCTV footage and bank transactions. He drove around Flanders, crossed the border into the Netherlands and spent the night at various locations in Zeeland.
On 17 January, Dutch police found the boy’s body on Neeltje Jans, an island in Zeeland. De Kock had been arrested earlier that day. He gave various accounts throughout the investigation but ultimately admitted being responsible for Dean’s death. The post-mortem indicated that Dean had been subjected to severe violence, including to his head and abdomen.
Romy W was acquitted of abduction, the main charge against her. She was found guilty of possessing and distributing images of child sexual abuse. She took screenshots of a video depicting child abuse that she had found on De Kock’s phone and forwarded them to her own phone in order to confront him.
She has spent several years in pre-trial detention and was given no custodial sentence. The conditions of her release include undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction.
De Kock is “unpredictable, untrustworthy and dangerous” and has caused “immeasurable human suffering”, the presiding judge stated. “It is a tragedy that his mother and his loved ones will never see Dean grow up to become a man.”
In 2010, De Kock was convicted of inhuman treatment resulting in the death of two-year-old Miguel, the son of his new partner. He was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment.

Ukrainian forces evacuate injured soldier from front-line position by drone in 'first-of-its-kind' mission, video shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:05:18 UTC
23:05:18 KST

Ukrainian forces evacuate injured soldier from front-line position by drone in 'first-of-its-kind' mission, video shows
Ukrainian forces have carried out what they describe as a "first-of-its-kind" aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier directly from a front-line position by drone, the Ukrainian military and defense company Gurzuf Defense announced on Oct. 19.
The operation involved Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, and 10th Army Corps, along with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Gurzuf Defense.
The Ukrainian military did not disclose the date of the operation or the section of the front line where it took place.
The wounded soldier, serving with the 30th Brigade, had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position "under constant threat of death." His fellow soldiers maintained contact with him and delivered food, water, ammunition, and medicine by drone, Gurzuf Defense said.
After the soldier suffered a severe injury, evacuating him by ground became impossible because of Russian drone activity in the area and mined terrain. Attempting to reach him on foot or with a ground robotic vehicle, the usual way of evacuating the wounded, would have put the rescue team at risk.
Ukrainian troops used a heavy-lift hexacopter drone, the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6.
The team first delivered special equipment with carabiners to the wounded soldier, then sent the drone equipped with a winch. Guided remotely by fellow soldiers who remained in contact with him, the soldier secured himself to the evacuation system, Gurzuf Defense said, calling the operation an "unprecedented mission."
The drone then transported him to a safer position, where other soldiers met him and arranged further evacuation to a hospital. The mission lasted 1 hour, 14 minutes, and 36 seconds, covering a distance of 62 kilometers (39 miles).
Drone operator of the 30th Mechanized Brigade, callsign "Chornyi" ("Black" in Ukrainian), said he is "very pleased" that everything went well.
The company said the operation required close monitoring of the airspace and electronic warfare protection throughout the flight. The soldier is now receiving treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger, according to the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade.
"An extremely complex operation, but a successful one. This is a historic event," "Napalm," a 92nd Brigade programmer who was involved in preparing the operation, said.
"It marks the next stage in the evacuation of the wounded, which we will all eventually reach. Now the serious, systematic work begins to ensure that such missions take place on a regular basis," Napalm added.
Gurzuf Defense co-founder Pavlo Feldblium warned that aerial evacuation should not be treated as a routine practice, citing the risks to wounded soldiers during flight. Each mission would need to be planned individually for the specific circumstances and location, he said.
"Air rescue is a last resort when there is no other way to save a person," Feldblium said.
According to the Ukrainian outlet Ukrainka Pravda, the hexacopter Heavy Shot Ayudag-6's platform has a flight range of up to 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) and an operational altitude of 150–300 meters (500 to 1,000 feet), while the aircraft itself weighs about 98 kilograms (215 pounds) and can carry 70–90 kilograms (150 to 200 pounds).
It is named after its six motors and Mount Ayudag near Gurzuf, a resort town in Russian-occupied Crimea.
Heavy drones have primarily been used to deliver ammunition and other supplies to front-line positions.

Brain connectivity patterns map onto sensory processing styles in autistic youth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:00:56 UTC
23:00:56 KST

A new study reveals that the wide variety of sensory experiences reported by autistic individuals corresponds to distinct patterns of information exchange in the brain. Researchers found that specific functional connections between cortical and subcortical brain regions can predict an autistic child’s sensory profile. The findings were published in Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging.
Differences in sensory processing represent a defining feature for up to 87 percent of autistic individuals. These differences mean that sights, sounds, textures, smells, or tastes might be perceived with unusually high or low intensity. Some individuals actively seek out certain types of sensory input, while others go to great lengths to avoid everyday stimuli. These variations affect how people navigate their environments and can influence cognitive development and daily functioning.
While these sensory variations can seem highly individualized, previous research has shown that they tend to cluster into specific behavioral categories. In a prior large-scale study, scientists identified five distinct sensory phenotypes among autistic youth. The first phenotype is “sensory adaptive,” describing children who show minimal sensory differences from neurotypical peers. The second is “generalized sensory differences,” which involves severe sensitivities across nearly all sensory domains.
The remaining three phenotypes involve more specialized sensory responses. One group is characterized primarily by selective sensitivities to taste and smell. Another group features children who are generally underresponsive to their environment but actively seek out intense sensations. The final group is defined by movement difficulties combined with low physical energy. Until now, it was unknown exactly how these five behavioral profiles mapped onto the brain’s internal wiring.
Western University researcher Matthew Kolisnyk and senior author Ryan Stevenson led a team to investigate whether these sensory profiles arise from specific patterns of brain activity. They designed an analysis to determine if different sensory behaviors correspond to unique functional connectivity configurations in the brain. Uncovering these neural foundations could help explain the immense biological diversity seen across the autism spectrum.
To test this idea, the research team analyzed data from 146 autistic children and adolescents between the ages of three and twenty-one. The participants’ caregivers filled out a standardized clinical questionnaire detailing the children’s daily responses to various sensory stimuli. Based on the scores from these questionnaires, the researchers sorted each participant into one of the five previously established sensory phenotypes.
The participants then underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. This brain scanning technique tracks blood oxygen levels to measure brain activity while a person rests quietly without performing a specific task. By observing which areas of the brain activate and deactivate in sync over time, researchers can map out the brain’s functional connectivity. This connectivity represents how different neural regions communicate and share information.
The researchers divided the brain scans into 200 distinct sections of the cerebral cortex and 32 subcortical regions located deep within the brain. They then applied a mathematical framework known as graph theory to quantify how information moves through this sprawling biological network. Graph theory provides specific metrics, such as how strongly regions are connected to one another and how efficiently they pass information to local neighbors.
The team also used graph theory to calculate betweenness centrality, a metric that identifies whether certain brain regions act as central hubs for long-distance communication. Another metric, called the clustering coefficient, measured how highly interconnected a region’s immediate neighbors are with one another. Together, these mathematical calculations generated hundreds of individual data points describing each participant’s unique brain network.
Finally, the team fed all these graph theory measurements into a machine learning algorithm. Machine learning involves training a computer model to recognize hidden patterns within massive datasets. The researchers tested whether the model could learn the connectivity data well enough to correctly identify which sensory phenotype a child belonged to, running comparisons between all ten possible pairs of the five groups.
The algorithm successfully differentiated between seven of the ten pairs of sensory phenotypes based purely on their brain connectivity metrics. The model performed best when comparing the two most extreme behavioral profiles. It most accurately distinguished the sensory adaptive group from the group with generalized sensory differences.
Specific brain networks emerged as strong predictors of a child’s sensory profile. Children in the sensory adaptive group showed stronger global connections in the prefrontal cortex, a region primarily involved in decision making and executive function. They also showed high connectivity in the orbitofrontal cortex, an area just above the eyes that helps integrate sensory information with emotional rewards.
Conversely, children with generalized sensory differences exhibited stronger local connections within the somatomotor network, which directly handles touch and voluntary physical movement. Their primary sensory processing regions appeared highly interconnected on a local level but lacked strong communication links to the prefrontal cortex. This pattern points to a potential difference in how higher-level executive brain regions modulate incoming sensory signals from the outside world.
The analysis also identified distinct connectivity signatures for the more specialized sensory profiles. Children characterized by isolated taste and smell sensitivities consistently showed altered hub activity in the posterior parietal cortex, a region important for spatial reasoning and directing attention. Differences in broad attentional networks and the default mode network, a system active during internal thought and daydreaming, also helped the algorithm separate several phenotypes.
Subcortical regions proved highly relevant for distinguishing specific sensory groups. These deep brain structures, which include areas like the thalamus and the nucleus accumbens, often act as the initial gatekeepers for sensory information before it reaches the cerebral cortex. The study found that subcortical connectivity patterns were particularly distinct in the generalized sensory differences group and the taste and smell sensitivity group.
The study carries several caveats regarding its interpretation. The machine learning model failed to produce statistically significant distinctions between three of the phenotype pairs, such as the underresponsive group and the movement difficulty group. This lack of differentiation suggests that some sensory profiles might share overlapping neural mechanisms, or that a larger sample size is needed to detect subtler brain differences.
The analysis relied heavily on caregiver reports to categorize the children’s sensory behaviors. While these questionnaires are standard clinical tools, they introduce a degree of subjectivity that might not perfectly capture the internal experiences of the autistic participants. The study also did not account for variations in overall autism symptom severity, intelligence quotient, or co-occurring conditions, which might independently influence brain connectivity patterns.
Small head movements during brain scans can artificially alter functional connectivity measurements. While the researchers removed data with excessive motion and applied mathematical corrections, systematic differences in how well children from different sensory groups tolerate the scanner environment remain a potential factor. Future research will need to test these predictive models on separate groups of autistic individuals to verify that the patterns hold true across broader populations.
The study, “Decoding the Neural Basis of Sensory Phenotypes in Autism,” was authored by Matthew Kolisnyk, Kathleen Lyons, Eun Jung Choi, Marlee M. Vandewouw, Bobby Stojanoski, Evdokia Anagnostou, Azadeh Kushki, Rob Nicolson, Elizabeth Kelley, Stelios Georgiades, Jason Lerch, Jennifer Crosbie, Russell Schachar, Muhammad Ayub, Jessica Jones, Paul Arnold, Xudong Liu, and Ryan Stevenson.

A separate drone attack Monday in the capital Khartoum killed four, including three children.
A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching trucks home, a medical source and a witness told AFP on Monday.
The strike in the town of Al-Dibab in West Kordofan state Sunday evening left "50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed", Ahmed Abakar Wadi told AFP, using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout.
Read moreUN warns drone attacks have become leading cause of civilian death in Sudan
He said 47 others were transported to the nearest town, Al-Mujlad, where 30 of them died from injuries, a medical source told AFP.
"A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on Al-Dibab, and another drone strike on Al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated," the medic said, requesting anonymity for his safety.
The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
Read moreAt least 82 killed in gold mine collapse in remote area of Sudan, paramilitary RSF say
The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out the strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.

A separate drone strike near the capital's airport killed three children aged two to six, according to a medical source.
"Four bodies arrived at the morgue -- three children, aged between two and six, and one man -- due to a drone strike this morning on a house in the Nasser Extension neighbourhood" just east of the airport, he said from the morgue.
There is no definite toll from the conflict as a whole, but aid workers estimate it has killed more than 200,000 people, besides creating the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis.

The conference will open with two panels titled “Mediation in a Changing World: Reclaiming the Space for Diplomacy” and “Partnerships and New Perspectives for Peace: Shaping the Future of Mediation.” The sessions will explore how the international community can create greater space for diplomacy and how mediation can play a more effective role in preventing conflicts.

China on path to meet annual economic growth target in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:57:00 UTC
22:57:00 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
China’s better-than-expected growth has eased expectations for broad stimulus measures and fueled optimism that Beijing’s annual growth target will be met this year.
The Chinese economy grew 1.2% on a quarterly basis and 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, exceeding expectations, following growth of 5% in the first quarter and 4.3% in the second.
China’s economic growth for the first nine months of the year reached 4.6%, aligning with Beijing’s target range of 4.5-5% for this year.
Last year, China’s gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5% in the fourth quarter, while the economy expanded 5% for the year as a whole, prompting Beijing to revise down its 5% target for the previous three years to a range of 4.5-5%.
Arjen van Dijkhuizen, a senior economist at ABN AMRO, told Anadolu that the bank maintains its growth forecast at 4.6% for this year and 4.5% for next year.
“This would imply that annual GDP growth would still come in at the lower end of Beijing’s growth target range (4.5-5.0%) for this year,” he said.
He attributed the Chinese economy’s growth to strong exports led by the artificial intelligence (AI) and tech sectors, saying export strength offset the negative impact on growth from the Middle East conflict and continued weak domestic demand.
“Our forecasts are partly based on the fact that the authorities are adding some targeted support, while refraining from large-scale macro stimulus,” he noted.
Dijkhuizen said recently released Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) data showed a slight recovery in economic growth during the summer months.
“In line with strong annual export/import growth for September published data last week (on the back of the ongoing global tech/AI boom), industrial production accelerated further, to 5.5% y/y (consensus: 5.5%, August: 5.2%) and 0.6% m/m (August: 0.5%). Retail sales growth came in stronger than expected at 1.1% y/y (consensus: 0.5%, August: 0.4%) and 0.4% m/m (August: -0.2%),” he added.

U.S. lauds Israel for arresting 10 over West Bank settler violence as more attacks on Palestinians reported
Tel Aviv — Israeli police announced on Monday the arrest of 10 people suspected to have taken part in recent violent attacks on Palestinians, an American photojournalist and European diplomats in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
The arrests come amid an avalanche of criticism, including from some senior U.S. officials, directed at Israel over repeated violent attacks by groups of mostly young Israeli settlers targeting Palestinians and others in the West Bank.
The announcement of the arrests came as more violence against Palestinians in the occupied territory was reported Monday.
Israeli police said officers working in conjunction with the Shin Bet domestic security and intelligence agency conducted a pre-dawn raid in the West Bank to locate individuals suspected of involvement in the violence and of violating a military commander's order declaring a closed military zone.
The arrests, dubbed Operation Olive Leaf by the police, came in the wake of multiple reported attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians as they worked on the annual olive harvest.
"Items linking the suspects to the alleged offenses were seized, and several vehicles were confiscated," the police said in a statement after the arrests.
On Friday, several Palestinians and Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine were injured when a group of masked Israeli men attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eyewitnesses and Palestinian authorities.
On Saturday, European officials and the Israeli military said a diplomatic convoy with representatives from France, Belgium and Poland was assaulted by masked individuals near the Palestinian village of Taybeh.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, in a social media post on Monday, called the arrests "a very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine an unarmed journalist."
Over the weekend, Huckabee called the attack on Levine an "act of terror carried out by masked cowards."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also condemned the attack on Levine Saturday, saying President Trump didn't want to see a crisis in the West Bank.
"We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office, in a statement on Saturday, urged people to exercise caution before drawing conclusions about the reported attacks on the European diplomats.
Netanyahu's office noted that video published online of the incident appeared to show masked individuals confronting a diplomatic vehicle and others showed a smashed car window and someone lying on the ground, but it said those images alone did "not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility."
Israel's military said the diplomatic convoy was not coordinated with the defense forces, and that such coordination would've provided more safety, but it did not deny that the convoy came under attack by settlers.
On Monday, new attacks on Palestinians by Israel settlers were reported by WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority, which governs most Palestinians in the West Bank but has limited control over security in the occupied territory.
Two Palestinians were injured in the villages of Turmus Ayya and Deir Abu Mash'al, northwest of Ramallah, amid attempts by individuals to set homes on fire by torching vehicles in front of the buildings, WAFA reported.
On Sunday night, Israel's military said several Israeli civilians entered the Palestinian village of Wadi a-Rahim in the West Bank, sprayed graffiti and set fire to a storage shed. The military said it had begun dismantling an illegal Israeli settler outpost in the area.
Violence by Israeli settlers targeting Palestinians in the West Bank has surged in recent years.
Statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office show that it started ramping up after Netanyahu took office in 2022 at the head of Israel's most far-right-wing coalition government in modern history in late 2022.
The attacks have intensified in the wake of the war in Gaza, and amid strong support from some members of Netanyahu's cabinet for settlement expansion, and even for the West Bank to be completely annexed by Israel.

Europe Weighs More Ukraine Support as Trump Waives Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:54:04 UTC
22:54:04 KST

Ukraine reported receiving no advance warning before Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday, Oct. 19, after President Volodymyr Zelensky said US intelligence sharing had resumed.
The latest attacks damaged more than 10 energy facilities and left at least 550,000 households without electricity, Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
For European governments promising to maintain support for Ukraine, the attack sharpened an immediate problem: funding and weapons pledges must translate into protection while Washington eases economic pressure on Moscow and Kyiv reports delays in American missile deliveries.
Europe has outlined several responses, including further sanctions, accelerated British air-defense supplies, and Belgian fighter-jet deliveries. But Ukraine’s request for another €70 billion ($78 billion) in 2027 remains unresolved.
Intelligence resumes, but missile deliveries remain disputed
Zelensky told NBC’s Meet the Press in an interview published Sunday, Oct. 18 that US intelligence cooperation was working again after an interruption.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio disputed that account on Monday, saying Washington had not paused intelligence sharing. The competing statements leave uncertainty over which information was interrupted and why Ukraine received no warning before the latest attack.
Intelligence is only one part of Ukraine’s defense against ballistic missiles as its crews also need sufficient interceptor missiles to engage incoming threats.
Trump’s Policies Upping the Pressure on Zelensky
In a separate Bloomberg interview on Sunday, Oct. 18, Zelensky said Washington was delaying approval of some Patriot interceptors already paid for through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (or PURL).
“The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue,” he said.
Zelensky clarified that Ukraine was receiving 12 Patriot interceptors a month, approximately one-quarter of the monthly supply under the Biden administration. His account identifies an obstacle European funding alone cannot remove: allies can finance purchases, but American approval and delivery remain necessary.
Europe rejects sanctions relief and prepares further restrictions
The dispute over military support accompanies a widening disagreement over sanctions.
Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order waived major new sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act before the Oct. 18 implementation deadline. However, existing restrictions imposed under earlier executive orders remained in place.
The legislation gave Trump substantial powers to waive additional penalties, meaning its passage did not guarantee that Moscow would face the full measures Congress authorized.
European leaders had already criticized his earlier Russian diesel agreement and pledged to maintain their own sanctions. Their Oct. 15-16 summit conclusions expressed regret over the temporary lifting of US diesel restrictions and called for stronger measures against Russian energy revenues and sanctions evasion.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Friday, Oct. 16 that work was underway on a further sanctions package.
“We will not lift any sanctions until Russia ends the war,” she said, according to LaPresse. The package’s full contents and adoption date were not specified in those remarks.
Missiles and aircraft are pledged, while larger funding remains open
Britain has announced practical steps alongside its criticism of Moscow.
An Oct. 13 government statement outlined £45 million ($60 million) in surface-to-air missile deliveries, with £10 million ($13 million) accelerated to meet urgent winter needs. Ministers were also instructed to prepare further sanctions, military assistance, and financial measures.
The missiles include Lightweight Multirole Missiles used against drones. These can strengthen Ukraine’s defenses, but the announcement does not resolve the separate shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic threats.
Belgium has also pledged 10 F-16 fighter jets by the end of 2026, following Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s meeting with Zelensky in Brussels.
The Ukrainian president has urged Belgium to accelerate deliveries, saying F-16s were proving particularly effective against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones.
On financing, the European Commission transferred €2.86 billion ($3.2 billion) for military procurement on Wednesday, Oct. 14 through the existing €90 billion ($101 billion) Ukraine Support Loan.
The larger question is what follows. European leaders have asked the Commission to develop proposals to bridge Ukraine’s €70 billion ($78 billion) funding gap for 2027. That instruction opens negotiations over additional support. It does not constitute an agreed funding package.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico subsequently said Slovakia and Hungary would not participate in the initiative, underlining the political obstacles to securing the money.
AfD uses Trump’s Russia deals to challenge Europe’s position
European governments also face domestic opponents invoking Trump’s approach as a model.
Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany has argued that Berlin should pursue its own Russian energy agreements rather than maintain the existing policy.
In an Oct. 15 statement, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called for the undamaged Nord Stream pipeline to return to operation and questioned why Trump alone should be allowed to make deals with Russia during an energy crisis.
AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance also sought a joint vote in Saxony-Anhalt backing renewed Russian energy supplies, Frankfurter Rundschau reported.
Such a regional vote cannot overturn national or EU sanctions, but it demonstrates how Washington’s decisions are being used to challenge them politically.
Europe’s response now depends on adopting further restrictions, supplying promised weapons, and agreeing how to finance another year of Ukrainian resistance.
Monday’s attack exposed the urgency of those decisions, particularly where European money still depends on American authorization to become usable military support.
