Saudi Arabia turned down Israel’s offer to help fight Ansar Allah, but that could change soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Even autocracies have to be concerned about angering their population too much.
That principle was on display earlier this week, when Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman (MBS) declined Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s offer of help in fighting Ansar Allah (also referred to as the Houthis), which has been launching devastating attacks on Saudi Arabia and has also been fighting Saudi and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces for control of Yemen’s coast along the Red Sea.
MBS cited concerns about how the Saudi public would react to Israel openly coming to the aid of Saudi Arabia, and he was right to do so. A poll conducted in 2025 by the Arab Center, DC showed that only 4% of Saudis supported the idea of normalizing relations with Israel. There will be scant support for Israel fighting alongside Saudi soldiers.
For years, it’s been clear that one faction in the Saudi royal family, led by MBS, was interested in finding a way to normalize relations with Israel, while others were staunchly opposed to this until the Palestinians have a state of their own or were otherwise freed from Israeli occupation.
The genocide in Gaza put the matter on hold entirely. Even MBS understood that he could not ignore an Israeli crime of that scale. His refusal to allow Israel to attack Ansar Allah demonstrates how much MBS still believes that he can’t draw closer to Israel without angering the Saudi population.
But how long will that last?
Ansar Allah attacks are certainly generating concern in the kingdom, and their escalation to attacking Saudi Aramco sites—the largest oil production corporation in the kingdom— poses a real threat to the Saudi economy.
That economy is already reeling thanks to the war on Iran, and the ongoing fighting with Yemen. Saudi visions of modernizing and diversifying their economy have been set back by years, possibly decades. Once seen as a safe place for investment, for global sporting events, and for tourism, the outlook for all of these sectors has taken a severe hit.
Does Saudi Arabia have anywhere else to turn? And if not, how will Israel try to leverage Saudi concerns for its own gains?
The regional balance
While it would not be true to say that either Saudi Arabia or Ansar Allah are fighting this war completely on their own, both sides are finding that key allies have to careful about their involvement.
Ansar Allah has the support of Shi’a militias in Iraq, and they have been effective in some instances. But they are only able to carry out limited attacks and are otherwise too small to offer much help to Ansar Allah.
Hezbollah in Lebanon has often lent support to Ansar Allah, but they are limited by geography and their need to focus on the Israeli invasion of Lebanon.
Iran has to walk a careful path. Though Tehran makes no secret of its support for Ansar Allah, it is reluctant to engage in combat with Saudi Arabia. Tehran and Riyadh have reached a temporary truce based on neither party attacking the other or helping their enemies attack them. Saudi refusal to allow its airspace to be used for American attacks on Iran since early in the war has been a key advantage for Tehran, while Riyadh has suffered far less damage from Iran than some of the other Gulf states, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
Iran is certainly not unhappy about the Saudis getting hit by Ansar Allah, but they want no part of that fight. They have enough on their hands with the United States, and Iranian eyes have remained fixed on the reality that they will need to eventually work out an accommodation with Riyadh.
Ansar Allah has proven that they are not a mere ragtag militia, nor are they simply pawns in Iran’s chess game. They are independent actors, well trained, armed with far more sophisticated weapons than other regional militias, and quite capable of advanced strategic planning and meticulous tactical execution.
Iran does play a key role, however, in a deterrent capacity. Other countries are reluctant to get involved in this conflict to some degree because they do not want to end up in conflict with Iran, or to see their relationship with Iran suffer.
That is a significant consideration for Saudi Arabia’s partners in the recently-signed defense pact, called the Mecca Agreement. Both of the other countries involved in that deal—Türkiye and Pakistan—also have ties with Iran. Pakistan in particular does a considerable amount of business with Iran, and would not want to see that relationship rupture, even if it has significant ideological and strategic alignment with Saudi Arabia. They will help Riyadh, but are going to stop short of engaging Ansar Allah, much like France has done.
Then there is the United States, which has been unable to decide whether or not to come to Saudi Arabia’s rescue.
Strategically, there is little reason for U.S. President Donald Trump to attack Ansar Allah. The Yemeni group has been as good as its word and refrained from attacking American and other shipping, aside from Saudi ships, in the Red Sea. The last thing the American military needs now is another front in a war that has been a humiliating and disastrous defeat, with major political repercussions for Trump’s Republican party that are likely to be felt in the midterm elections.
But MBS does have a major card to play that, at least it seems, he has not yet laid on the table.
Trump and his family have made a considerable number of high-priced deals with Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has also pledged a tremendous amount of investment in the United States.
While Saudi Arabia would never be able to find an arms merchant that can offer the quantity, and much of the quality, of American weaponry, they can invest in other industries located in countries other than the United States. They can also find investors from other places for much of their industry, or do business with Americans other than Trump if they choose.
For a president as corrupt as Trump, this would be a significant threat. There is no indication that MBS has tried it yet, but if he does, it could push Trump into action.
Yet, even if Trump does feel enough pressure to try again to fight Ansar Allah, he may wait until after the midterms, which might be longer than MBS thinks he has.
Netanyahu waiting in the wings
This is what Netanyahu sensed when he offered to join Saudi Arabia in the fight against Ansar Allah.
And there may come a point, if MBS feels sufficiently vulnerable or the kingdom is facing significant enough losses, that Saudi desperation might overcome their concerns about working with Israel.
The opportunity to strike Ansar Allah is important to Netanyahu and to Israeli strategy. They have been largely sidelined in the war on Iran and the war in Lebanon has been frozen in place by Washington.
Israel continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza on a daily basis, and it continues to use settlers to assault Palestinians in the West Bank. But these are double edged political swords for Netanyahu.
While the ongoing killing of Palestinians fits with Israel’s program of genocide and ethnic cleansing, the incremental killings and displacements have not progressed into tangible gains for the state in the public eye, while they have brought significant costs in terms of sanctions and isolation.
None of this serves Netanyahu in his effort to hold on to power. He is seeking an opportunity not only to show Israeli voters that he is still “Mr. Security” despite his many failings, but also to make it more enticing for some of the most hawkish parties in the opposition to consider joining his coalition after the election.
Israelis have not forgotten that Ansar Allah took some of the most decisive action in support of the Palestinians at the start of the Gaza genocide, and that they did so with very little possibility of tangible gain for themselves. To Palestinians, that was an act of generosity. Israelis see it as proof that Ansar Allah hates them so much, they will use any pretext to attack “the Jews.”
Israelis across the political spectrum also very much want to see normalization with Saudi Arabia.
All of this comes together to make the idea of attacking Ansar Allah very attractive for Netanyahu, even though the prospects for real success are not particularly good. Ansar Allah withstood Israeli and American attacks before, as well as years of an American-backed Saudi onslaught. There is little reason to think what failed before will work now, especially considering that Ansar Allah is stronger now.
But that doesn’t really worry Netanyahu. Ultimate victory is a secondary concern for him. What is most important in his calculations is a short-term victory that can elevate his status in the eyes of the Israeli public and open options for his efforts to build a governing coalition after the election.
Netanyahu cannot attack Ansar Allah in support of Saudi Arabia counter to the wishes of MBS unless Ansar Allah attacks Israel first. But it wouldn’t be difficult for Israel to manufacture an excuse to attack Ansar Allah independent of Riyadh, claiming it was their own security needs that drove them to do so. MBS could then object and get himself off the hook, and by the time any concerns about a real normalization process arose, the incident would no longer be important.
It is likely that American and Israeli planners are considering something along these lines, because it will be very dangerous for Trump to escalate against Iran while Saudi Arabia is as vulnerable to Ansar Allah as it appears to be at the moment. An Israeli attack on Yemen might not trigger the kinds of regional retaliation against energy and civilian infrastructure that worries Trump so much.
For Netanyahu, however, this is just another opportunity to destabilize the region, stoke the flames of war with Iran, and, he hopes, gather support for continuing his seemingly endless time in control of Israel. He knows that both Ansar Allah and Iran are capable of hitting Israel with missiles, especially now that American regional defenses are dramatically weakened.
Saudi Arabia may want the U.S. to intervene on its behalf, but the sort of massive bombing campaign that would result is certain to bring retaliation against Saudi territory that will dwarf what it has experienced in this past week. And it is quite possible that Iran, which may well want to preempt what seems likely to be the looming American escalation by escalating themselves, will seize upon such attacks to launch retaliatory strikes at American, Israeli, and Gulf sites.
Like the U.S. with Iran, the best course for MBS is to cut losses and try to work out a ceasefire. But that is a path neither country is prepared to pursue. And, as always, Israel’s agenda is to sow as much instability as possible.

Japan’s sample return mission to Phobos may also collect some Mars dust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

For decades, scientists have dreamed of getting Martian rocks into Earth’s laboratories — a Herculean feat that would revolutionize our knowledge of the Red Planet. An audacious mission from the Japanese space agency might offer the next best thing: rocks from Mars’ larger moon, Phobos.
That’s the task confronting the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft, due to launch October 19 at 3:41 p.m. EDT. The mission aims to crack the long-standing mystery of how Mars got its two odd moons by delivering a sample of Phobos to Earth in 2031. These rocks are no substitute for true Martian material — but given that NASA’s plans to fetch the Perseverance rover’s prized samples are in limbo, scientists are eager for even an indirect glimpse of Mars.
“It’s a chance to get a totally different sample and view of Martian materials,” says planetary scientist Briony Horgan of Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., who is not involved in the MMX mission. “It’ll be a great contribution to our sample collection back here on Earth.”
Focus on Phobos
If it’s successful, MMX will be the first mission to reach Phobos. Three previous spacecraft from Russia failed.
The MMX itinerary is action-packed: After launch, the spacecraft will spend about one year cruising out to Mars, then slip into orbit around Mars alongside Phobos for about three years. During its stay, the spacecraft will deploy a small rover named Idefix to scout the moon for good sampling sites. The main spacecraft will then make two landings to grab 10 grams of sample, about the weight of four U.S. pennies. It will use two different devices to snag the sample: One will drill two centimeters down into the rock, while the other will blow pressurized gas at the surface to collect loose material.
Once loaded up, MMX will zip past the smaller moon Deimos before making the one-year trek home to drop its cargo in Australia’s outback, just as Japan’s two previous asteroid sample-return missions have done. After the Japanese space agency JAXA sorts and catalogs the samples, it will share portions of them with other institutions.
Such a small handful of rock may not sound impressive, but it’s enough to thrill researchers. “A few grams of sample are going to be a real bonanza for scientists,” says planetary scientist Michael Zolensky of NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where 15 percent of the sample will eventually end up.
MMX is designed to reveal the enigmatic origins of Phobos and Deimos — the only moons in the inner solar system besides our own. “The Martian moons are so different from [the] terrestrial moon: They are two, very small [and] very dark,” says planetary scientist Tomoki Nakamura of Tohoku University in Sendai, Japan.
The strange objects look like rocks that wandered in from the outer asteroid belt and got trapped around Mars. But their tidy circular orbits suggest they coalesced after a massive collision tore material off the Red Planet. Or perhaps they came about some other way that scientists simply haven’t imagined, says planetary scientist Kiyoshi Kuramoto of Hokkaido University in Sapporo, Japan. “The natural world often reveals aspects that exceed our expectations,” he says.
Studying the features and composition of Phobos’ surface could solve the mystery. But although MMX carries sophisticated instruments to explore Phobos, those observations may not suffice. Hence bringing rock back to Earth’s labs, where scientists can enlist equipment far too large or delicate to ever send to space.
Martian mysteries under the microscope
Although sample analysis will focus on understanding Phobos, researchers will also be able to use the rocks to fine-tune our understanding of Mars. For example, pinpointing the material’s age will allow scientists to calibrate the chronology of cosmic collisions in the neighborhood of Mars. Currently, scientists estimate ages on Mars based on a timeline based on our moon, which may not apply at the Red Planet.
Scientists even have reason to hope that stray grains from Mars will be hidden amid the MMX treasure. This material could be ancient relics of the two bodies mixing during a moon-forming process, potentially including grains that hail from deeper in the Martian crust than scientists have seen so far in rare meteorites the cosmos has delivered us. No matter how Phobos formed, the material could also include fresher debris flung off the Red Planet by cosmic collisions.
The biggest challenge may be positively identifying which grains came from Mars. Such lucky samples would lack valuable geologic context and be far from pristine. “They’re material that’s been blasted off Mars from some unknown location, micron-sized things, sitting on the airless body Phobos, getting irradiated by space,” says planetary scientist Nancy Chabot of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md. Nonetheless, scientists are prepared to get creative and use the latest technology to tease out every secret they can manage in any sample they can snag.
MMX offers a very different type of sample return than what NASA has initiated with the Perseverance rover, which has spent years squirreling away fresh material drilled from the most interesting outcrops it can find. That’s all in hopes of a future mission ferrying the rock to Earth for scientists to hunt for signs of ancient microbes. But the U.S. Congress has axed funding for that successor due to spiraling costs and concerns about feasibility — particularly of accomplishing the first ever launch from Mars.
Even if MMX can’t give scientists the satisfaction of an ultimate Mars sample return, there’s still plenty to learn, says planetary scientist Vicky Hamilton of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colo., who is not involved in the mission. “It’s always a happy day when we’re getting a sample from another object in space and bringing it back to Earth to study,” she says.

Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:57:02 UTC
21:57:02 KST

Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Columbia University Irving Medical Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.
- Share:
Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.
Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a new path toward Alzheimer's treatments.
The discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.
Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.
That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?
A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.
"This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.
"We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection."
How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier
The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.
When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.
To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.
Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.
Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.
In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.
Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage
One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.
The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.
Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.
These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.
"The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved."
The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.
They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.
These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.
When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.
"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling."
Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection
Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.
Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.
Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.
Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.
"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.
A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire New Alzheimer's Treatments
The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.
Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal new opportunities for prevention and treatment.
The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.
One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.
Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.
However, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.
By identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.
"By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify."
Although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising new direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

Lithuania aims to have integrated airspace detection system partially operational by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Lithuania expects to have at least part of an integrated airspace detection system operational by the end of 2027, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Monday, following a drone incursion that ended with an explosion in the country’s north.
“Once everything is integrated into a single system, I hope that by late 2027 we will have at least a partial, seamless system,” Kaunas said. He cautioned that progress would depend on how quickly companies could develop the necessary software and connect existing equipment.
The remarks followed Sunday’s incident, when a drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland and crashed in the village of Juodžioniai in the Pasvalys district. An explosion damaged a civilian car, but no injuries were reported. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said the drone was Ukrainian and carried explosives.
Sinkevičius said in August that he hoped a fully integrated detection system would be in place by 2030. Kaunas said the government was working to accelerate that timeline, although equipment deliveries could take one to two years because of demand from other countries.
A state procurement tender has been launched to develop software that would connect different systems used to detect airborne objects. Nineteen Lithuanian companies have submitted proposals, Kaunas said, adding that authorities would analyse them in the coming days and select those best suited to the country’s needs.
The system is expected to combine radar data with information from acoustic sensors deployed along the border, as well as cameras operated by residents and border guards.
Kaunas said the main problem was that existing detection tools operated separately, limiting the ability to interpret potential threats.
“Everything needs to be merged into one system,” he said, explaining that radar can identify an object’s speed, altitude and direction but does not provide other information needed to assess the situation.
Reports from residents who hear unusual sounds could also help identify potential threats, he added.
The Defence Ministry said in September that developing a short-range air defence system was one of Lithuania’s key ongoing projects, with an estimated cost of up to 1 billion euros. The three Baltic states would need about 2 billion euros combined, the ministry said.
Lithuania plans to allocate 2.03 billion euros between 2026 and 2030 to develop airspace surveillance, air defence and electronic warfare capabilities.
The Baltic states have also asked the European Commission for additional European Union funding to address urgent air defence needs.

Benny Gantz quits Israel's election race eight days before vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

21:53:45 KST

Former Defense Minister Benny Gantz announced Monday that he would not run in the October 27 election, abruptly reversing his pledge to remain in the race until the end as polls consistently showed his Blue and White party failing to secure enough votes to enter parliament. The announcement came just eight days before the election and a day before voting begins for soldiers, raising the prospect of a last-minute shift in support within the political bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"I will not run in the upcoming election," Gantz said in a statement ahead of a news conference scheduled for 8 p.m. Monday. "I will continue fighting for unity. This is the only solution that will prevent another disaster and protect Israel against all the challenges it faces at home and abroad." Gantz is expected to answer reporters' questions at the news conference, where he will explain his decision to withdraw.
The former military chief had spent weeks weighing whether to leave the race. Members of his professional team had encouraged him to remain, presenting internal polling that they believed showed his message could gain traction if he continued campaigning. However, surveys published by major news outlets consistently placed Blue and White below the 3.25% electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset, Israel's parliament.
His candidacy also triggered disagreements within his own party over whether remaining in the race could damage the wider opposition bloc by drawing votes away from parties with a realistic chance of winning seats. Blue and White lawmaker Alon Schuster was among those who opposed continuing the campaign at any cost. "We must not simply burn votes," he said in private conversations.
A source close to Gantz said the timing of the decision was directly linked to voting among military personnel, which is scheduled to begin Tuesday. "The decision was made today because soldiers start voting tomorrow, and he did not want to needlessly waste the votes of soldiers who wanted to support him," the source said. "Ultimately, he made the necessary decision because he understood that, under the current circumstances, there was no point in running."
The announcement drew immediate praise from other opposition leaders, including former Gantz ally Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party. "I thank my friend, Lt. Gen. (res.) Benny Gantz, for his correct and responsible decision to withdraw from the most consequential elections since the establishment of the state," Eisenkot said. "I thank him for his many years of service to Israel's security and am confident he will continue contributing to Israeli society in the future."
Yair Golan, chairman of the Democrats party, also welcomed the decision, framing it as an important step toward defeating Netanyahu. "Gantz made a responsible and correct decision," Golan said. "At a decisive moment for Israel's future, our shared responsibility is to ensure victory for the bloc seeking change." He added that his party was committed to genuine political reform and to building a Jewish, democratic, liberal, strong and secure Israel.
The withdrawal marks a striking reversal from Gantz's remarks just a week earlier at the "People of the State" conference organized by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, where he insisted he would remain in the race regardless of the polls. "No matter what happens, I'm in because we need to save the country," he said at the time. "I'm running all the way. We are facing the greatest challenges imaginable, and there is no way to solve them with a narrow government."
Gantz also defended his previous decisions to join governments led by Netanyahu, a move that had damaged his standing among parts of the opposition. "The two times I joined Netanyahu, it was despite the fact that he was there, not because of him," he said. "Politicians are in politics for their seats and their own interests. I care about the country."
In recent weeks, criticism of Gantz had intensified within the opposition, where some accused him of allowing personal political grievances to outweigh the objective of replacing Netanyahu. "He apparently wants to take us down with him to prevent the possibility of replacing Netanyahu," one opposition figure said, referring to Gantz's insistence on remaining in the race. A senior member of the Beyachad party went further, suggesting Gantz would ultimately prefer Netanyahu to other potential prime ministers from the opposition. "If you ask Gantz which government he would prefer, one led by Eisenkot, Bennett or Lieberman, he would answer that he prefers a government led by Netanyahu," the official claimed.
Gantz's decision now removes one potential source of lost votes for the anti-Netanyahu bloc, although it remains unclear where his remaining supporters will shift their allegiance in the final eight days of campaigning. For Gantz, who only days ago vowed to fight until the final vote, the announcement brings his latest election campaign to an abrupt end.

Ebola: Kenya confirms eighth case as DRC outbreak reaches new province
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:52:22 UTC
21:52:22 KST

Kenya has confirmed an eighth Ebola case, while the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to spread to new areas.
Kenyan authorities have detected an eighth case of Ebola in the country after another person tested positive while in quarantine, a health ministry official said on Sunday.
The latest case is a 49-year-old man who had attended to the first Ebola patient. He showed symptoms including fever, high temperature, headaches and muscle pain and had been quarantined after probable exposure to the virus.
"Today we tested 38 persons; one turned positive," said Health Ministry chief Patrick Amoth, adding that the man had been in quarantine since 9 October.
Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola death on 5 October when a man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) died after returning to Kenya.
The other seven cases are relatives of the first patient or health workers who treated him; Amoth said they were in a stable condition.
The ministry said 128 contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine.
The country remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, as advised by the World Health Organization (WHO). However, the country is stepping up work on Ebola surveillance and community awareness.
The neighbouring Tanzania has tightened border screening and introduced mandatory health declarations and 21-day monitoring for travellers arriving from high-risk countries.
The outbreak reaches eighth province in Congo
Meanwhile, the outbreak continues to grow in the DRC and has reached an eighth province. Two new cases, including one death, have been reported over the last weekend in previously unaffected Nord-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic.
Nord-Ubangi lies between Sud-Ubangi and Bas-Uele, the last two provinces the disease had reached, where recurring armed violence has forced thousands to flee and seek refuge in nearby Congolese communities.
Authorities have reported 9,455 cases and 4,561 deaths so far in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
“We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it’s spreading out,” WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told The Associated Press.
Janabi said one of the biggest challenges has been persuading infected people to seek medical care, adding that some deaths occur in communities outside health centres.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccines or specific treatments are available, although trials are under way in the DRC.

Witnesses are being located and questioned, and operations are ongoing to also seize the illegal arms in the area," he said.
People displaced after 15 houses torched in Kamjong
At least 15 houses belonging to the Kuki community were torched in Chassad village in Kamjong district late on Saturday night, officials said on Sunday. Suspected militants allegedly set the houses on fire, forcing several civilians to flee to forest areas and a nearby Army camp.PTI reported that a Kuki civilian was killed and four others sustained bullet injuries when suspected militants attacked the village earlier on Sunday.Deputy chief minister Nemcha Kipgen condemned the violence in Chassad, expressed grief over the death and concern for the injured village leaders and displaced families. Lhatoo said security agencies were coordinating to maintain law and order and prevent further escalation."Manipur Police, in close coordination with the CRPF, BSF, Army, Assam Rifles and other sister security agencies, is working continuously to maintain law and order and prevent further escalation," he said.He added that senior police officials were coordinating with stakeholders to restore normalcy and protect residents."All necessary legal and operational measures will be pursued in the strictest manner to identify those responsible and to bring them to justice," he said.The ADGP appealed to residents to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information."We appeal to the public to remain calm, exercise restraint, and not take the law into their own hands. At least 18 killed in Houthi attack on military camp in Yemen’s Shabwa

Houthi attack on Yemen army camp in Shabwa kills at least 53: reports
Houthis launch ballistic missiles at camp in southern governorate during training exercise, government forces spokesman says.
A Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen has killed at least 53 people, according to local authorities.
The Iranian-backed armed group launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for Yemeni government forces said.
Officials for the internationally recognised government and medical sources initially said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded when the strike hit the facility, where new security recruits were undergoing training.
Those numbers increased dramatically later on Monday, when the local authority in Shabwa said 53 people had been killed and 200 injured, news agencies reported.
‘Hostile threat’
The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war between the Saudi-backed government and Houthis had eased after a 2022 truce, but the regional impact of this year’s US-Israel war on Iran reignited hostilities.
Fighting escalated rapidly when the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God – seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Aramco.
On Monday, Saudi authorities sent alerts to residents of the capital Riyadh warning of “a hostile aerial threat”.
New recruits
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed in Shabwa were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.
“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.
“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”
Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.

What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:50:59 UTC
21:50:59 KST

What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
CAIRO, Oct 19 - Egypt's parliament is expected to vote next week on whether to authorise the armed forces to help defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen's Houthis if Riyadh requests its support.
The move would bring the Arab world's most populous country closer to direct military involvement in the widening conflicts unleashed by the US-Israeli air assault on Iran in February.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested the approval in a speech on Saturday, saying Egypt would "never, never forget our brothers in the Gulf" and telling Saudi Arabia's leaders that Cairo would "take any measure to protect you".
Like the Gulf states that have come under attack from Tehran in the Iran war, Egypt is a longstanding partner in the US-led security order that is being tested by the conflict.
WHAT IS EGYPT'S STANCE ON THE IRAN WAR?
Sisi's comments marked a clear escalation from the more measured tone authorities have tended to adopt since the Iran war started. Though Egypt has repeatedly voiced strong support for its Gulf allies, Cairo has stopped short of publicly committing itself to a direct combat role in the conflict.
In May, the presence of Egyptian Rafale fighter jets in the United Arab Emirates was disclosed in Emirati state media coverage of an official visit by Sisi. Egyptian coverage of the visit did not mention the deployment. When Saudi Arabia signed a joint defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, Egypt did not join, though it said it was considering it.
The tone started to shift after the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi oil and other infrastructure. Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman last month visited Egypt, where he discussed the need to ensure freedom and security of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, on which both countries have long coastlines.
WHAT'S AT STAKE FOR EGYPT?
Egypt's economic stability has long been tied up with the oil-producing Gulf. Remittances from Egyptian expatriate workers there are an important source of foreign currency and income for families back home at a time of double-digit inflation worsened by surging food and fuel prices.
Saudi Arabia, the UAE and other Gulf countries have been among Sisi's key financial backers, providing tens of billions of dollars of aid, central bank deposits and investments since the army overthrew President Mohamed Morsi, a senior Muslim Brotherhood figure, in 2013.
"We can never forget how our brothers in the Gulf states stood by Egypt during that period," Sisi said in his speech.
Saudi Arabia has a $5.3 billion deposit at Egypt's central bank due this month along with $267 million in interest, central bank data shows.
WHAT ABOUT SECURITY?
Growing security concerns have also pushed Cairo towards a more active stance, analysts say. A drone strike on two gas vessels at the Mediterranean port city of Damietta in July underscored that Egypt could not expect to keep itself fully isolated from the conflict.
"I think they realise that they can't be on the sidelines about this indefinitely," said H. A. Hellyer, a scholar at the Royal United Services Institute think tank.
For the authorities, the economic and security concerns were "one and the same," he said.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt also have a shared interest in securing shipping through the Red Sea, an outlet for Saudi oil blocked from leaving the Strait of Hormuz. Egypt earns billions of dollars a year from fees on Suez Canal traffic. These overlapping concerns mean "Saudi Arabia's security constitutes a dimension of Egyptian national security," said Sherif Aref, an Egyptian political researcher and journalist.
WHAT SORT OF MILITARY DOES EGYPT BRING TO THE TABLE?
Egypt has one of the Arab world's largest armed forces, with hundreds of thousands of active personnel and large air, land and naval inventories, according to military analysts. Egypt sources equipment from a range of countries, and its air force operates US-made F-16s, French Rafales and Russian-made MiG-29s.
Egypt receives about $1.3 billion a year in US military aid, which helps fund its purchases of American military equipment. Washington waived human rights conditions on a tranche of the funds this year after what it called Cairo's "helpful role" since the Iran war began.
In the years after the 2011 uprising that ousted President Hosni Mubarak, the armed forces fought a counterinsurgency campaign against Islamist militants in the Sinai Peninsula. Egypt also contributed air and naval forces to the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015, and conducted airstrikes against Islamic State targets in Libya during that country’s civil war.
Egypt has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War, when its troops joined the US-led coalition to drive Iraqi forces from Kuwait. Nearly three decades earlier, President Gamal Abdel Nasser had sent Egyptian forces into Yemen in a costly intervention later compared to the US involvement in the Vietnam War.
WHAT SORT OF SUPPORT IS LIKELY?
Sisi's speech and subsequent statements have not specified what sort of military forces, if any, Egypt would ultimately intend to send. A deployment of Egyptian troops inside Yemen itself is unlikely, military analysts say.
More likely interventions might include air defence and naval support, said Samir Ragheb, a retired Egyptian military officer who heads the Arab Foundation for Development and Strategic Studies think tank.
"The threats, missiles and drones, require air defence and air forces," he said, adding that the navy could be used for protecting ships, naval operations against piracy and protecting the Saudi coastline.
Still, the entry of another large conventional Arab military would not "suddenly solve the Houthi problem", said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London.
"The Houthis are difficult precisely because they generate disproportionate effect through missiles, drones, dispersed forces and geography. Egypt cannot bomb that problem away," he said.
"What Cairo can do is strengthen Saudi resilience, improve Red Sea control, share the defensive burden and increase the political cost of continued attacks." REUTERS

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia’s Kalashnikov Group has delivered a batch of 9M333 anti-aircraft missiles to the customer earlier than planned, the company told TASS.
"The Kalashnikov Group has successfully delivered another batch of 9M333 anti-aircraft missiles to the customer. As part of meeting its 2026 obligations, the products are being supplied ahead of schedule. It is important to note that these products remain in consistently high demand due to their effective performance in the special military operation zone," the company said in a statement.
The anti-aircraft missile is deployed by the Strela-10 air defense missile system and its versions. Over the past few years, the 9M333 has demonstrated its effectiveness in combat operations.
The missile is designed to hit aerial targets at any time of day under conditions involving the use of dropped, parachuted and modulated organized optical countermeasures, including remotely piloted aircraft and cruise missiles. The missile’s homing head has three operating modes: photo-contrast, infrared, and jam-resistant, giving it a key advantage over other products in this class. The missile’s average speed is 550 m/s, and it can strike targets at altitudes ranging from 10 to 3,500 meters. The munition operates on a fire-and-forget principle.

Roche acquires Chinese antibody-drug conjugate rights for $500m
The Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche has acquired the rights to a portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) developed by its Chinese competitor Hansoh Pharma, for $510 million (CHF420 million).
The transaction consists of an initial instalment of $400 million, to be paid upon signing the contract, and a second instalment of $110 million, to be paid one year later.
The contract also provides for funding of $15 billion, subject to the achievement of development, regulatory or even commercial milestones, as well as commissions of an unspecified amount on any revenue, the Shanghai-based group stated in a press release issued today.
ADCs, or antibody-drug conjugates, are preparations that combine, amongst other things, an antibody and a chemotherapeutic molecule. Their purpose is to combat tumours.
More
Personalised cancer vaccines take a leap forward – can Swiss pharma catch up?
Hansoh will retain control over the early stages of development, up to the completion of the first clinical phase. Roche will then take over on a global basis, with the exception of mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan.
Roche first entered Hansoh’s business exactly one year ago, acquiring the rights to the drug HS-20110 for an initial payment of $80 million, which at the time was the subject of a Phase I clinical trial in China and the United States for colorectal cancer and other cancers.

Kazakhstan fits snow leopard with satellite collar for first time in Southern Altai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan fits snow leopard with satellite collar for first time in Southern Altai
A snow leopard named Altai has become the first in Kazakhstan's Southern Altai to be fitted with a satellite tracking collar. The animal, listed in Kazakhstan's Red Book of endangered species, was fitted with the device at Katon-Karagay National Park, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
The satellite collar will allow researchers to track the snow leopard's movements, study its travel routes, and identify key areas of its habitat.
The data collected will provide valuable insights into the behavior of snow leopards in the Southern Altai and help improve conservation efforts.
Snow leopards typically inhabit remote, mountainous areas, making them difficult to observe in the wild. Satellite tracking will enable scientists to monitor Altai's movements without having to remain physically close to the animal.
According to conservation specialists, satellite monitoring plays a crucial role in studying rare wildlife, helping researchers identify habitat areas and gather scientific data needed to protect endangered populations.
On October 16, speaking at the COP17 summit in Yerevan, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced that Kazakhstan's snow leopard population had reached approximately 190 individuals. He also highlighted the progress made through conservation efforts and scientific monitoring.
The collar was fitted with the participation of Katon-Karagay National Park employees E. Kassymov and Zh. Amanbayev, alongside researchers A. Grachev, M. Bespalov, S. Bespalov, and S. Saparbayev from the Institute of Zoology.
The project is supported by Pernod Ricard Kazakhstan.
Satellite data will be used to map Altai's movements and habitat, helping researchers better understand snow leopard ecology in the Southern Altai and develop more effective conservation measures for this rare predator.
Qazinform previously reported that rare animal populations in Kazakhstan are rising.

French President Emmanuel Macron has begun a Gulf tour to seek additional oil and diesel supplies and help ease soaring fuel costs, following a weekend of violent protests over the cost of living that saw more than 2,500 arrests, according to the supplied report.
Macron arrived on Monday in Kuwait, where he was welcomed by Emir Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, hours after condemning what he called “unbridled” violence in an address to the nation on Sunday.
The visit will also take him to the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar by Wednesday.
Paris says the trip is intended to strengthen economic and defence partnerships, secure energy supplies and improve the safety of maritime routes disrupted by the US-Iran war.
Fuel supplies and defence deals on the agenda
Macron said before departing that the trip was necessary to “secure our supplies”, pointing to fuel prices as one of the concerns raised by protesters.
In Kuwait, discussions included plans to deliver pre-positioned stocks of kerosene and diesel from Oman to the French overseas territories of Reunion and Mayotte, according to the French presidency.
French armed forces minister Catherine Vautrin also signed a letter of intent on defence cooperation with her Kuwaiti counterpart. Talks included potential arms sales, according to a member of the French delegation.
Airbus separately signed a letter of intent to support the renewal of Kuwait Airways’ fleet and cooperate on maintenance and training.
Macron is accompanied by senior executives from France’s two largest energy groups, TotalEnergies and Engie, as his government seeks concrete commitments on oil and diesel volumes.
Hormuz disruption drives search for alternative routes
The tour comes amid a major disruption to energy shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for Gulf oil exports, during the war between the United States and Iran.
The French presidency said Macron would discuss ways to secure maritime shipments and establish “alternative and bypass routes” for energy exports with Gulf leaders, including the UAE president and Qatar’s emir.
The G7 countries, under France’s chairmanship this year, agreed in early October to release 100 million barrels of oil through a coordinated effort to ease pressure on energy markets.
France and Britain have also assembled an international mission to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz, mainly through demining operations, once Washington and Tehran agree on the waterway.
Energy expert Francis Perrin of the French Institute for International and Strategic Relations cautioned that the Gulf tour was unlikely to have an immediate impact on fuel prices, saying exporters may struggle to make firm commitments while regional instability persists.
Macron faces criticism over unrest at home
The overseas trip comes as Macron faces mounting scrutiny over the government’s handling of France’s worst unrest in years. More than 2,500 people were arrested during clashes and looting, with shops and town halls reportedly damaged or set on fire.
Macron acknowledged security and intelligence failures but refused to accept the resignation of his interior minister.
Constitutional expert Benjamin Morel warned that the Gulf tour could project an image of normality but also risk making the president appear disconnected from events at home and suggest a “kind of power vacuum”.
The government now faces the twin challenge of addressing public anger over living costs while pursuing energy commitments abroad that may not translate quickly into lower prices at the pump.

Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams.
Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty.
Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP

The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation.
The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.
Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures.
Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies.
“The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.”
The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation.
Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland.

World will face a serious energy crisis if US launches another war against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
