Marco Rubio visits India this week, with a visit to the world's largest oil refinery topping the agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:31:00 UTC
21:31:00 KST

India's Russian oil in focus as Rubio visits major Reliance refinery
October 19, 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.
Rubio's business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India's purchases of Russian oil.
Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it's a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India's energy relationship with Russia.
In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.
US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.
An elusive US-India trade deal
Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India's continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.
In February 2026, Trump announced a "trade deal" that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.
While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India's deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India's top supplier of crude oil.
In mid-September, Trump signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act," imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.
Rubio: Trade deal 'very close'
Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the "C5+1" diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.
"We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries," he said.
"We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that," Rubio added.
In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.
Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
He said Jamnagar is an "important node in global trade" because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.
Although Trump's sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.
Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio's decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.
"The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar," she told DW. "The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.
Shankar pointed to Reliance's proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is "one of the states in play" in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
"Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome," she said.
Trump eroding trust in Delhi?
The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology and energy.
Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.
"Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values," he said.
The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.
Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.
On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.
The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.
Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump's own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.
"Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians," Pant told DW.
Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump's presidency.
"The sense that America is unreliable, that America can't be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse," he said.
The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.
"If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals "will have consequences."

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Iran Monday for his first visit since the start of the Middle East war, as Moscow attempts to mediate, according to Russian media.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Sunday the trip would focus on "regional and international developments."
Lavrov will meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry.
Lavrov said Moscow's efforts "aim to prevent a return to large-scale war." Talks between Tehran and Washington have stalled.
His visit follows Russian President Vladimir Putin telling Pezeshkian in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Russia and Iran, two of the world's most heavily sanctioned nations, maintain close ties. Their military and economic cooperation increased since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said discussions during Lavrov's visit would focus on "ways to resolve the acute international crisis triggered by the unlawful aggression of the U.S. and Israel against Iran."
The ministry said the war was a blow to stability and security "not only in the Near and Middle East, but also globally."
Despite a cease-fire in April and a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, hostilities in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue.
In a separate development Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway.
"An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room," Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying.
The tanker was traveling in the strait's "unauthorized southern route" and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said.
It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines.
The Guards' naval commander Adm. Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered "hostile."
Iran claims control of the strategic waterway – through which one-fifth of the world's hydrocarbons pass in peacetime – and regularly targets vessels crossing without its authorization. In response, Washington maintains a naval counterblockade on Iranian ports.

The night watch: Palestinians protecting their homes from settler pogroms
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are organising to protect themselves from settler attacks.
The life of 32-year-old Abdul Rahman Jabr changed more than a year ago when his home in the village of al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank was targeted by Israeli settlers. After the attack, he put up barbed wire in an attempt to fend off future settler pogroms.
The house, built by Abdul Rahman in early 2023 before his marriage, is located on the outskirts of the village in an area with a long history of settler violence. He now lives there with his wife and their two-year-old daughter, but settler attacks on his home and his neighbours have intensified over the past year.
His vehicle was set on fire by settlers in April 2024, and his home’s windows were smashed with stones. He cannot count the number of times his home has been targeted. In the past week alone, settlers reached his property seven times, which forced him to miss work to stay at home to protect his wife and child.
“I thought about my wife and child. How could I protect them from the settlers when there is no protection for us? I began surrounding the house with barbed wire and an iron fence. This isn’t a sufficient measure, but it’s the only thing I can do on my own,” he told Al Jazeera.
“All the neighbouring households have had to install these fences to protect themselves. We’ve made countless appeals, but no one listens, so we had to take this step. At the very least, it has helped keep their livestock away from our yards.”
Night guard
Abdul Rahman’s experiences are not unique. They are part of a rapid rise in settler activity across the West Bank since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Settlers carried out 14,742 attacks against Palestinians, their land or properties from October 7, 2023, to October 4, 2026, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, which is part of the PLO.
In the first seven months of 2026 alone, the commission recorded 4,113 attacks, ranging from assaults on people to vandalism of orchards. This was a 63 percent increase compared with the same period in 2025, and this month saw a spate of attacks on Palestinian farmers as they harvested olives.
Palestinians are now beginning to organise to protect their families and homes from settler attacks.
In the town of Sinjil, north of Ramallah, a group of young Palestinian men have repelled several settler attacks in recent months. Basel Awad, a pseudonym used for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that the village’s guard committee, which he is a member of, is unofficial and intended to protect the homes of residents.
Each night, 20 to 30 unarmed people gather at key locations that settlers have used as staging posts for their raids into Sinjil.
They have paid a high price for their efforts. The Israeli army has arrested six members of the guard and at least 10 have been injured in an apparent bid by Israel to dismantle this neighbourhood watch.
“We had set up a tent in the Jabal al-Batin area, which is frequently targeted by attacks. Soldiers arrived last winter and fired tear gas canisters inside. We all suffered from suffocation, and then they demolished the tent and confiscated it,” Basel told Al Jazeera.
Protecting communities
Despite the dangers, Palestinians are refusing to leave their homes and have their land seized by settlers.
Nasr Radwan, 53, is one of the landowners in the village of Beitillu, west of Ramallah, whose property is frequently raided by settlers. The land owned by Nasr, his brothers and their relatives spans 1,500 dunums (1,000sq metres or a quarter of an acre) and contains more than 100 springs.
He has been beaten by settlers on several occasions, but he and his brothers insist on being present on the land every single day.
In June, settlers established an outpost near his land, which is being used as a base to attack his crops and assault his family, he said.
“The most recent attack took place last Saturday. We were on our land harvesting olives when settlers attacked us, smashed the windows of our vehicles and beat my brother. Even so, we continue to go there every day,” he added.
For the past three years, settlers have tried to seize the family’s land, blocking an access road to prevent Nasr and his relatives from reaching it by car. Family members persist, travelling 5km (3 miles) on foot to reach their land.
“We know that being on our land means facing constant attacks. It could even cost us our lives. But we also know that if we abandon it, it will be lost forever,” he said.
“This is not just land or a source of livelihood; it is our soul, our memory and our very life.”
Violation of international law
With the settler raids sanctioned by Israeli authorities, Palestinian residents have no real protection or recourse for legal action when they are attacked. This has left West Bank villages exposed to continual assault with no penalties for settlers who destroy, assault or sometimes kill.
Human Rights Watch in August reported that Israeli authorities have failed to prosecute settlers for acts of violence committed against Palestinians. By the end of 2025, the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din reported that out of hundreds of cases it has documented since 2005, only 3 percent have resulted in convictions. The village watch scheme is an attempt by Palestinians to mitigate these risks.
Omar Rahhal, director of the Ramallah-based SHAMS Center for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that the fact that Palestinians resort to self-protection measures against settler attacks doesn’t absolve Israel as an occupying power of its legal responsibility under the Fourth Geneva Convention to protect civilians.
He said such measures are merely a stopgap solution to the settler dilemma for Palestinians, who are faced with a profound power imbalance. An illustration of this is the presence of Israeli soldiers as settlers attack their families and raze their lands.
“Impunity, the arming of settlers, the allocation of funds to settlements and policies adopted by ministers in the Israeli government are factors that contribute to the continuation of attacks and the resulting increase in the number of victims,” he said.

Al Jazeera investigation challenges Israeli account of Heidi Levine attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:28:27 UTC
21:28:27 KST

Al Jazeera investigation challenges Israeli account of Heidi Levine attack
The investigation has exposed how Israeli forces present at the site of the attack chose not to intervene, and instead fired tear gas at Palestinian youth who had helped save Levine.
An Al Jazeera investigation has challenged official Israeli narratives regarding an attack by settlers on Palestinian olive harvesters and an American photojournalist on Friday in Khirbet Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.
The investigation by Al Jazeera’s Data Journalism Unit used open-source verification and analysis of visual and geographic evidence.
Official Israeli accounts of what happened differ: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has questioned whether Israeli settlers were to blame at all, while the Israeli army has suggested that the military was engaged in addressing a confrontation between Palestinians and settlers at the time.
But verified footage and mapped coordinates reveal a coordinated attack by masked settlers, with Israeli military vehicles passing by shortly before the incident, without intervening.
The October 16 pogrom left veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, with a broken rib, four fractured vertebrae, and wounds requiring hand surgery, despite wearing a clearly marked press vest.
To establish the facts, the Data Journalism Unit monitored and analysed more than 20 videos and photos taken by journalists and witnesses on the ground. The team independently verified the footage, arranged it chronologically, communicated with local journalists, and mapped key locations.
Geography of attack
Geospatial analysis pinpoints the settler outpost where the attackers originated, the harvesting land, and the location of the assault on Levine.
The attack on Levine was mapped at the coordinates 32°01’13.5″N 35°18’40.7″E. This site is approximately 455 metres southwest of an outpost on a hill near the Misholash settlement, and just 120 metres north of the land where Palestinians were picking olives.
The unit also identified rooms traditionally used by Palestinians to store fertiliser and agricultural tools, and where farmers occasionally spend the night. These rooms are near the outpost, 430 and 500 metres northeast of the attack site. A local journalist, speaking on condition of anonymity due to security concerns, said that Palestinian owners can no longer enter these rooms, where settlers now stay and gather.
The journalist explained that the outpost is located in Area B under the Oslo Accords, where the Palestinian Authority (PA) manages civil affairs and Israel retains security control. While only a few settlers typically reside in the outpost to “prove” their presence, during any incident, 50 to 100 settlers from other outposts gather there before descending on the fields.
He noted that other settler tents on the adjacent mountain overlooking the village serve as additional gathering points to attack anyone harvesting olives.
Chronological evidence
Tracking the footage chronologically reveals a gradual escalation leading up to the attack.
Movements began around 8am when a 4×4 vehicle carrying settlers headed towards the site, followed by six motorcycles moving towards the area opposite the harvesters. In a video posted shortly after 9am, about 30 settlers are seen gathering near the farmers.
Al Jazeera correspondent Tharwat Shaqra, who was at the scene, said that Israeli military vehicles passed through the area, and after their passage, settlers headed towards the journalists and farmers, “as if it were a green light.” Independent Israeli journalist Oren Ziv noted that military jeeps made no attempt to stop the masked men.
The settlers then set fire to the olive trees and advanced towards the harvesters, prompting village youths to respond by throwing stones.
Footage subsequently documents the assault on Levine after she was knocked down. Her colleagues could only reach her after young Palestinians pushed the settlers back by throwing stones in their direction.
American journalist Jasper Nathaniel, who helped pull her away, wrote on X: “The only reason I was able to get to Heidi is because Palestinian youth provided cover with stones facing settlers and soldiers with machine guns and tear gas.” He added that the army pursued the young Palestinians after the attack, not the settlers.
During the same period, a video captured the sound of four gunshots followed by two more, which Tharwat Shaqra confirmed originated from the settlers.
Israeli forces only appeared to be deployed at the attack site in later footage, with their vehicles stationed in the settlers’ area. Soldiers then shot local council member Abdel Jaber Obeid and intercepted the ambulance before his transfer to hospital, as the army continued firing tear gas at the olive harvesters.
Conflicting Israeli claims
The timeline and geographical data contradict the official Israeli narratives.
The Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said that “the facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation”. It cited reports indicating “some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths”.
However, footage and testimonies show that the settlers gathered, descended, and burned trees before the youths responded, and the assault on Levine is documented on video.
Conversely, the army did not question the assault, acknowledging the injury of a foreign journalist. The Israeli military stated that forces were dispatched “following a report of a violent confrontation” and broke it up using “riot dispersal means”. It said soldiers “fired warning shots into the air and then fired toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object,” making no mention of the settlers or their gunfire.
The Israeli military’s international spokesperson Ariella Mazor told The Washington Post that soldiers in the area were trying to disperse a large, violent crowd and did not see the assault on Levine.
But evidence from videos and other testimony suggests that military vehicles in the area passed by the settlers without intervening and that Israeli forces eventually directed tear gas at Palestinians after the attack.
Widespread condemnation
The attack prompted widespread condemnation. United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee demanded that “those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison”.
He said that “attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”.

Ecological Imbalance Is Driving Bear Encounters in Mongolia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:28:00 UTC
21:28:00 KST

In recent months, Mongolia has experienced rare bear sightings in its northern provinces. Local authorities have so far been successful in capturing the bears alive and placing the animals back into their natural habitat. The sudden movement of such a large number of bears indicates a deeper ecological imbalance not only in Mongolia but also Russia and Japan.
As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns. Solo bears, bears with cubs, and lost cubs have been sighted. More alarmingly, bears have encountered nomadic herders, killing one person and injuring several others. People from remote towns and herding communities have reported attacks on livestock. Most of these bears encounters have been reported in Khuvgsul, Bulgan, Darkhan-Uul, and Tuv provinces – all Mongolia’s northern provinces with robust habitat for bears, wolves, elk, deer, and wild boars.
The sudden surge and the possible migration of bears clearly demonstrate the changing environment in their natural habitat. Khuvsgul, Bulgan, and Darkhan Uul provinces are 51 percent forest and considered a perfect habitat for bears. Mongolia’s boreal forests, known as taiga, offer cedar and pine nuts, types of berries, and water access for bears. In the fall, particularly in the months of August, September, and October, bears forage throughout the taiga with their cubs in preparation for hibernation.
The increased movement of these bear populations points to several issues in Mongolia’s ecological system. One of the speculated causes is a shortage of food. Mongolia’s extreme weather fluctuations, including shorter summers with amplified heatwaves, can impact vegetation and dry out grasslands. Particularly in Khuvsgul and Bulgan, given the short summer, there is a risk of shortage of berries and nuts.
In addition, Khuvsgul and Selenge provinces hold one of Mongolia’s critical river basins, which is crucial to the forestry and its natural habitat. One of the remaining questions concerning bear movements is whether these river basins and other water sources are experiencing a fish shortage, caused by climate change and mining activities.
Given the pristine nature of Northern Mongolia, these provinces are subject to strict environmental scrutiny and protection. Still, mining does occur. Bulgan Province, in particular, is known for its extractive industries, including gold and polymetallic mining (although in comparison to other notable extractive sites, the scale of mining in Bulgan is relatively moderate).
According to the World Resources Institute, Mongolia’s gold rush has become one of the leading sources of water contamination. Gold extraction sites particularly are a major issue for the local environment. “Lead, arsenic and other toxic chemicals released during gold extraction processes have leached into Mongolia’s groundwater and flowed untreated into rivers,” the WRI found.
Thus Mongolia’s bear sightings may be related to the country’s mining activities, along with extreme weather aggravated by climate change-caused food shortages. In response, the government and conservation groups are taking a humane approach. Local authorities and the population continue to capture bears and place them back into the wild.
In comparison, Russia and Japan, both experiencing a similar bear issue, are handling it very differently.
In Russia’s Far East, in the Siberian forests, the bear population thrives. This October, local authorities in Siberia (Krasnoyarsk), Tuva, and Buryatia reported a surge of bears entering local towns and villages. In Buryatia, the local authority has deployed 24 specialized teams to kill bears. With Russian authorities allowing an “open season,” bear killings will likely increase.
In 2025, the Environmental Ministry of Japan reported a historic surge in bear sightings and attacks, during which more than 14,600 bears were killed. The ministry believed that “climate change and poor tree-nut harvests have reduced natural food supplies in the mountains.” The ministry also highlighted that around 12,000 brown bears in Hokkaido and Asiatic black bears elsewhere have expanded their roaming range.
While Northeast Asia faces a shared ecological challenge in conserving bear populations and managing their movements, Mongolia, Russia, and Japan have adopted vastly different approaches. Mongolia emphasizes strict legal protections and non-lethal management whereas Russia and Japan both have implemented aggressive population control methods.
According to Rebecca Watters, founder and director of the Mongolian Wolverine Project and a biologist, bears are attracted to any kind of predictable food source. Once they associate people with food – in the form of garbage, livestock, gardens, birdfeeders, etc. – they will continue to seek out human settlements.
In Mongolia’s case specifically, she added, “I wonder too whether some of the increase in sightings and conflict is due to population shifts, in both people and the bears. Paradoxically, some of these issues might also be related to conservation successes and more bears cubs surviving.”

Ukraine Claims World’s First Frontline Air Evacuation Using Heavy Drone to Save Soldier, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:27:55 UTC
21:27:55 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Claims World’s First Frontline Air Evacuation Using Heavy Drone to Save Soldier, Video
Ukraine’s 92nd Assault Brigade announced on October 19 that Ukrainian forces had evacuated a wounded soldier from the front line using a heavy aerial drone, calling it the world’s first such operation.
The brigade’s Unmanned Ground Systems Company reported the mission on its official Telegram channel the same day. The evacuation involved personnel from the 92nd Assault Brigade, 30th Mechanized Brigade, 14th Mechanized Brigade, 10th Army Corps, and Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“This is a historic event, at least for our unit,” stated Napalm, a squad commander and programmer with the 92nd Brigade’s unmanned ground systems company.
The wounded infantryman from the 30th Mechanized Brigade was unable to leave his position using conventional unmanned ground vehicles. The unit attributed this to intense Russian drone activity and heavily mined terrain.
The soldiers instead adapted a Ukrainian-made Gurzuf Defence heavy hexacopter, originally configured as a bomber, to carry the wounded serviceman. Gurzuf Defence provided the drone free of charge for the operation.
Specialists from the 92nd Brigade worked with the manufacturer to modify the aircraft and maintain stability while carrying a person. They also conducted preliminary tests at Gurzuf Defence facilities before planning the mission with other participating units.
A drone operator from the 30th Mechanized Brigade piloted the aircraft during the evacuation. The mission succeeded, and the wounded serviceman is now undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, with his life no longer in danger, according to the unit.
The evacuation highlights a broader Ukrainian effort to use unmanned systems for missions traditionally performed by personnel and ground vehicles. Such platforms can reduce exposure when mines, artillery, and persistent drone surveillance make conventional casualty evacuation especially dangerous.
The rescue came days after Ukraine began front-line testing of StarGate, a purpose-built aerial evacuation drone developed by defense company SkyFall at the request of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment.
The aircraft carries up to 150 kilograms on a medical-grade stretcher and has a one-way range of 15 kilometers, enough to reach troops inside drone-saturated kill zones. Each system is expected to cost at least $50,000, with production targeted at up to 1,000 units per month by the end of 2026.
Ground robots have so far handled much of this work, with machines operated by the Third Army Corps evacuating more than 600 wounded soldiers during their first year of operations.

Ukraine Exposes Foreign-Made Components Behind Russia’s Anti-Jamming Tech Used in Missiles and Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:27:52 UTC
21:27:52 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Exposes Foreign-Made Components Behind Russia’s Anti-Jamming Tech Used in Missiles and Drones
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has identified foreign-made components used in the production of Russia’s Kometa anti-jamming navigation modules, which are installed in Russian missiles, attack drones, and guided aerial bombs.
According to HUR from Ukraine’s military intelligence, the modules are designed to protect onboard navigation systems against electronic warfare interference, allowing Russian weapons to maintain navigation capabilities in contested environments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Kometa system uses controlled reception pattern antennas, which can suppress interference by adjusting the antenna’s reception pattern and applying signal-processing algorithms.
According to HUR, a standard Kometa module used in modern Russian missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and guided aerial bombs consists of two main components: an antenna array containing a specified number of patch antennas and a signal-processing module based on a programmable logic device.
The system’s resistance to electronic interference depends on the number and arrangement of its patch antennas, as well as the algorithms used to process incoming signals.
By combining signals received through multiple antennas, the module can determine the direction of incoming interference and reduce its impact on the navigation system.
Ukrainian intelligence reported that Russian forces are already widely deploying Kometa modules equipped with 16 patch antennas, while efforts are underway to establish serial production of more advanced 20-element antenna arrays.
HUR also identified the Russian company VNIIR-Progress as the developer and primary manufacturer of various Kometa modifications. The enterprise belongs to the ABS Electro group of companies, which Ukrainian intelligence linked to sanctioned Serbian pro-Russian politician Nenad Popović.
According to the intelligence agency, another company within the same group is responsible for procuring components needed to manufacture the navigation modules. The supply network includes Chinese distributors and sellers of microelectronics, as well as Russian intermediaries involved in obtaining foreign-made electronic components.
To fulfill orders from Russia’s defense industry, VNIIR-Progress uses both its own manufacturing facilities and the production capacities of other companies within the ABS Electro group. HUR also identified the principal customers for Kometa modules as Russian manufacturers of cruise and ballistic missiles, attack drones, guided aerial bombs, and glide munitions.
In a separate investigation published on October 14, The Insider reported that Chinese technology company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology was prepared to supply mesh communication modems to a Russian drone manufacturing facility despite being informed that the equipment was intended for military use.
The investigation found that the company was willing to deliver communication systems to a drone production facility in Alabuga, Russia, where the equipment could be used to support long-range drone attacks against Ukraine.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) pledged Monday to distribute resources more evenly across the city's 29 districts if elected, CNA reported.
Speaking during a visit to Taipei Zhenbei Temple in Banqiao District, Su said every district should benefit from the city's growth. She said her goal is to improve local communities and give residents a stronger sense of pride in where they live.
Su credited cooperation between the central government and New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih's (侯友宜) administration for improvements in the city's infrastructure. Drawing on more than a decade of experience representing New Taipei as a legislator, she said she would build on that progress, per Liberty Times.
Her priorities include expanding transportation networks, developing technology parks, and helping small businesses modernize. Su said these measures would create jobs and business opportunities across the city, per UDN.
To narrow development gaps between districts, Su proposed two regional initiatives targeting coastal and mountain communities. The plans aim to improve local infrastructure, attract visitors, and support regional economies, per FTV News.
The New Crown Plan focuses on eight coastal districts through fishing port upgrades, better transportation, and tourism development. The Diamond Mountain City Plan targets mountain communities by improving hiking trails, restoring former mining sites, and promoting tea culture and tourism.
Su said she wants to make New Taipei a better place to live and work while strengthening residents' connection to their communities. She also hopes to make the city a destination that international visitors would want to experience at least once in their lives.

EU to fund permanent magnet production line in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

EU to fund permanent magnet production line in Estonia
A new permanent magnet production line will be built in Estonia after the European Commission agreed to fund a project from Neo Performance Materials, which owns the Silmet plant and a magnet plant in Ida-Viru County.
On Monday, the European Commission selected 77 European net-zero technology projects to receive a total of €3.4 billion in funding from the Innovation Fund call for applications launched in December 2025.
Among the funding recipients is Canadian-registered Neo Performance Materials, which owns the Silmet plant in Sillamäe and the permanent magnet factory in Narva, both located in eastern Estonia.
The Silmet plant, owned by Neo Materials, is dependent on raw materials from Russia but has pledged to phase them out. The plant has come under scrutiny after Estonia requested that its supplier be exempted from European sanctions.
"The project will establish a rare-earth permanent magnet production line in Estonia, covering separation, metallization and magnet manufacturing. The line will be capable of producing up to 3,000 tons of permanent magnets annually, one-third of which will be supplied to EU offshore wind farms," the project description states.
According to plans, the project will prevent the emission of more than 3.4 million tons of CO2 equivalent during its first 10 years of operation.
The funding will come from the Innovation Fund, using revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).
The final terms of the grant agreements will be made public in the first quarter of 2027.
The Innovation Fund aims to channel an estimated €40 billion in revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System between 2020 and 2030 into investments in cutting-edge low-carbon and net-zero technologies to support Europe's transition to climate neutrality.
A methanol plant planned for Pärnu has previously received funding from the same program in Estonia.

What the Greens Misunderstand About the Ukraine Conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

At the end of September, the Australian Greens elected David Shoebridge their new leader. Shoebridge had previously been the party’s spokesperson for foreign affairs and defense, and he retained those responsibilities. While he has always been a combative politician, he immediately created controversy by stating it would be the Greens’ policy to oppose providing further military assistance to Ukraine. Extraordinarily, in a meeting with a number of Ukrainian-Australian community groups this week he left a further sour taste by informing them to not “burn any bridges” by criticizing the Greens.
Shoebridge has said that the party is one of “peace and non-violence,” but within this perspective comes a number of often naïve assumptions about international relations and how states manage conflict. It leads to an odd scenario whereby in proclaiming to be advocates of peace and nonviolence the Greens end up supporting belligerents over victims.
There are some common traits that “pacifist” parties exhibit that are worth analyzing to understand the Greens’ position.
The first is that they see violence as a self-perpetuating system. War creates a cycle of fear, militarization, and retaliation. The participants become trapped in an escalating security dilemma – each interpreting the other’s actions as a threat. Therefore peace requires breaking this cycle through restraint, negotiation, and disarmament. This may seem rational on the surface, but it doesn’t account for bad faith actors who believe solely in domination and cannot be trusted to honor any negotiated deal. This is the type of state Ukraine is facing with Russia.
Alongside this, there is a distrust of the distinction between offensive and defensive power. There is a belief that all military power is essentially used for offensive purposes to varying degrees. Based on that assumption, states which arm themselves in defense – or become a part of an alliance system – are creating the conditions for aggressive actions to occur. Yet this assumes that larger states will naturally respect the sovereignty of their smaller neighbors if they are not armed. This, again, is a misunderstanding of Russia, which views weakness, not strength, as an incentive to escalate.
What pacifists often believe is that nonviolent resistance is an underutilized alternative to military resistance. There have, of course, been instances where nonviolent resistance has proved incredibly effective, in India during British rule, for example. But nonviolent resistance relies on two factors – when an occupying force requires the assistance of the invaded population, and when this force has enough of a moral compass to be able form some empathy for those it has invaded. Russia simply does not believe that Ukraine is a legitimate nation-state. A disarmed Ukraine is a nonexistent Ukraine.
For some pacifists the priority is to stop conflict, even if the resulting settlement leaves the aggressor state with territorial or political gains. A ceasefire can be argued as saving lives. Yet any settlement that rewards aggression may be an encouragement for further aggression. Russia not only sees Ukraine as an illegitimate state, but also Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Georgia, and Moldova. Rewarding Russia for its invasion of Ukraine sends a signal that it can make military gains in these states too.
The concept of deterrence is built on the assumption that there will always be belligerence in the world and that peace requires demonstrating and communicating clearly through credible military power that this belligerence will not succeed. For parties like the Greens this is a difficult assumption to swallow. Their belief is that peace can be secured through diplomacy and “good vibes” alone.
The danger within this pacifism is that it becomes an inflexible political doctrine that treats a refusal to use force as a self-perceived moral victory, and overlooks the actual victims of violence. It confuses the insisted innocence of their own actions with the justice of a real world outcome.
As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one, but as a political position it is self-defeating. Support for military assistance to Ukraine is a popular position in Australia, and many people believe that Australia should be doing more to help.
Support for the Greens themselves has plateaued at around 12 percent of the Australian public. The party’s approach is mostly to cultivate its status within this 12 percent and they seem disinclined to try to speak to anyone else. Therefore, the party’s position on military assistance to Ukraine probably has less to do with Ukraine itself, and was simply devised as a form of internal moral posturing with little comprehension how peace and security are actually achieved.

US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches

Unknown Publisher

US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not confirm reports that Ukraine received no advance warning before Russia's ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 19, citing a lack of information, as he spoke to reporters during a visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu asked Rubio during a press briefing to comment on Kyiv's statements that it had received no advance warning of Russian missile launches.
"I don't know. I mean, where did it happen last night? I don't know exactly," Rubio told reporters on Oct. 19.
In the Oct. 19 attack on Kyiv, at least one person was killed, and eight others were injured as Russian missiles struck Kyiv in multiple waves overnight. Explosions were reported shortly before 11 p.m., followed by further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m. local time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X on Oct. 19 that Ukraine had not received early warning from its partner countries, including the U.S., ahead of the attack. He added that Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region as the primary targets.
Later in the day, Ukraine's Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on national television that Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners before the first wave of ballistic missile attacks at around 11 p.m., but that information about the second wave, at around 3 a.m., was provided.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes overnight on Oct. 19, though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that "a few nights ago" there was a software problem involving the Ukrainian early warning system.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back. I can't comment on what happened last night," he said.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first overnight wave followed a similar pattern.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened," the official said. "They're up to something again."
It can be common for Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles to hit with very little advance warning.
The attack came just hours after Zelensky said the U.S. had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine about Russian missile launches.
The president's announcement came as a relief after Kyiv endured "massive explosions" on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack came after the U.S. threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries, sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials have previously explained that satellite surveillance of launch sites can be vulnerable to transmission delays. Bad weather may also cause interference with the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellites, a surveillance network U.S. forces use to monitor Russian launch sites.
But the senior official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said although bad weather had affected warnings before, this number of strikes with little to no warning "has never happened before."
"Now we're seeing 'bad weather' three times in a row," the official said. "When nothing comes through on any channel... well, we get it."

Dozens killed in Houthi missile attack on Yemeni government military camp
More than 30 soldiers for the internationally recognised Yemeni government were reportedly killed and dozens wounded on Monday after Houthi forces launched a ballistic missile attack on a military camp in Yemen's southern Shabwa province, according to military and medical sources.
The attack targeted Al-Alam military camp near the city of Ataq while soldiers were taking part in a training course.
Yemeni armed forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said the Houthis had fired three ballistic missiles at the camp.
The Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, have not yet commented on the attack.
The camp belongs to Shabwa's emergency forces and was hosting recruits from a newly formed military brigade at the time of the strike.
A source at a government hospital told The New Arab that the number of casualties was high, while other sources reported that Houthi drones had been flying over the area on Sunday evening, hours before the attack.
A Yemeni military source told Germany's DPA news agency that more than 30 soldiers had been killed and dozens of others wounded.
Social media users also circulated footage purportedly showing dead and wounded soldiers scattered across the military camp following the strikes. The New Arab could not independently verify the footage.
The attack comes amid an escalation in Yemen's conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, accompanied by increasingly hostile rhetoric and threats from the warring sides.
Fighting intensifies in Taiz
On Sunday evening, warplanes belonging to the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government carried out airstrikes on Houthi positions in the Dhi al-Birah and Najd Qasim areas of Al-Misrakh district, south of Taiz province.
Two additional strikes targeted Al-Wazi'iyah district in western Taiz.
The airstrikes coincided with an escalation in fighting around Jabal Sabir, where government forces and local resistance fighters have been attempting to repel Houthi attacks and infiltration attempts.
Sources told The New Arab that local resistance fighters from the village of Al-Rahn were engaged in fierce clashes with Houthi groups attempting to advance from the villages of Khurayshah and Al-Ma'yanah towards Al-Najjadah and neighbouring communities.
The sources said the Houthis were seeking to reach the summit of Jabal al-Arus and cut off a road connecting several villages and districts across the Sabir mountain area.
The clashes coincided with heavy Houthi attacks on the Al-Sina'a position on the opposite side of the front, following the group's reported loss of several positions in Al-Sanamat, Al-Sarari and Ambiyan.
Elsewhere in Taiz, an 11-year-old Yemeni girl was wounded by shrapnel to the head on Sunday evening after Houthi shelling struck the village of Al-Shaqab in Sabir al-Mawadim district, south of the province.
The latest violence comes as Yemen's long-running war continues to intensify, with renewed clashes and missile attacks threatening to deepen the country's humanitarian and security crisis.

ARMA head selection commission softens criteria for passing legislation knowledge test
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:23:47 EEST
21:23:47 KST

The competition commission for selecting the head of the National Agency of Ukraine for Detection, Tracing and Management of Assets (ARMA) unanimously approved a new version of the competition procedure and the assessment criteria and methodology at a meeting on Monday.
Under the new rules, the legislation knowledge test will be considered passed for every candidate who appeared for testing and completed it within the allotted time, regardless of the number of points scored. The participant then automatically moves on to the next stage, the cognitive abilities test.
Candidates who score 55 or more points on the cognitive skills test will be entered in the subsequent ranking list based on the results of the two tests. The "weight" of the cognitive test in the overall ranking will be 40%, and of the legislation knowledge test 60%.
In addition, the commission unanimously approved an updated version of its own rules of procedure, which included technical amendments concerning the modification of calendar working days and the handling of materials with restricted access.
The composition of the competition commission remained unchanged after the first attempt to hold the competition. All six members took part in the meeting: head of the economic crimes investigation department of the Wuppertal prosecutor's office, Federal Republic of Germany, expert of the German Foundation for International Legal Cooperation Wolf-Tilman Baumert; chairman of the board of Prozorro.Sales JSC Serhiy But; academic secretary of the V.M. Koretsky Institute of State and Law of the National Academy of Sciences Anzhelika Krusian; chief researcher of the research laboratory on problems of state-building and law enforcement of the educational and research institute of law and psychology of the National Academy of Internal Affairs Valentyna Lukianets-Shakhova; deputy executive director for legal affairs of the Transparency International Ukraine NGO Kateryna Ryzhenko; prosecutor (Portuguese Republic), international expert in financial crimes, corruption, money laundering and asset recovery, senior asset recovery (policy) specialist at the Basel Institute on Governance (ICAR) Rita Simoes.
As reported, the commission also announced the dates for submitting documents to participate in the competition: they can be submitted from Oct 26 to Nov 26.

The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine calls on the president to veto the law on workplace safety due to the narrowing of workers’ rights
Kyiv • UNN
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine believes that the law was adopted without proper consultation with the social partners and proposes that it be revised.
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine is asking President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to veto the law on the safety and health protection of employees at work and return it to parliament for revision with the participation of the social partners. This decision was made at a meeting with the FPU’s member organizations in Kyiv on October 19, reports UNN.
Details
The meeting participants discussed the challenges related to the adoption by the Verkhovna Rada of Law No. 10147, "On the Safety and Health Protection of Employees at Work," which, according to the FPU, significantly narrows existing workers’ rights, benefits, guarantees, and level of protection compared with current legislation, in particular the Labor Code and the Law of Ukraine "On Labor Protection."
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine emphasized that the law was adopted without proper coordination with the social partners, which constitutes a violation of the principles of social dialogue and European integration requirements.
"The discussion held demonstrated the FPU’s, as well as the all-Ukrainian trade unions’ and territorial organizations’ rejection of the adopted draft law. The heads of the member organizations expressed a common view: to return the law to parliament for revision with the participation of the social partners within the framework of the National Tripartite Social and Economic Council and to appeal to the President of Ukraine with a request to veto this document," the FPU said.
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine proposes using the opportunities of the interparliamentary parliamentary group "Trade Unions of Ukraine" and appealing to global trade unions for international support.
In addition, further steps include holding a number of events in support of the trade unions’ demands, including mass informational appeals from local areas to the President of Ukraine concerning the veto of the said Law, a flash mob, and other informational events.
As noted, the all-Ukrainian trade unions and territorial trade union associations supported the draft Appeal of the Joint Representative Body of Trade Unions regarding the application of the veto power to the Law of Ukraine "On the Safety and Health Protection of Employees at Work."
Let us recall
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in the second reading draft law No. 10147, "On the Safety and Health of Employees at Work."
However, the head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, Serhii Byzov, reported that the draft law passed by parliament contains provisions that could weaken worker protection. According to him, this concerns risks to workplace safety, compensation for victims, and social guarantees for people working in difficult and hazardous conditions.
The Federation of Trade Unions’ reservations regarding certain provisions of the law "On the Safety and Health of Employees at Work" were also supported by the inter-factional parliamentary association "Trade Unions of Ukraine." Member of Parliament and head of the association Andrii Klochko stated that the law is not perfect, as it could narrow social guarantees for workers employed in difficult and hazardous conditions.

====================================================================================================

Stop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:20:08 UTC
21:20:08 KST

The environment watchdog is being urged to intervene in “cash to trash” planning rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in the Norfolk Broads despite the damage to one of the UK’s most environmentally protected areas.
Labour’s flagship planning reforms allow damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked if developers pay into a central nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date. These environmental delivery plans (EDPs) have been called “cash to trash” by critics, who say they roll back decades of environmental law and are a “licence to kill nature”.
The Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected biodiversity hotspot that is home to more than a quarter of the UK’s rarest plants and animals, is the guinea pig for the first EDP. Developers will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – and in return get permission to build 15,780 new homes in the Broads.
The government’s nature adviser, Natural England, which created the plan, states the development will cause environmental harm in the form of physical, chemical, hydrological and biological damage to the habitats and rare species from increased nitrogen and phosphorus pollution. The Broads are already in ecological decline and require cuts of 91-97% in nutrient pollution to recover.
Chris Hinchliff, the Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, is calling on the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP) to intervene and stop the approval of the plan. He said the first EDP – which will be used as a blueprint for others – is in breach of the requirements of the government’s Planning and Infrastructure Act, is not based on the best available science and does not address pollution. In a letter to Natalie Prosser, the chief executive of the OEP, he said: “Unless the OEP acts now, those failures will be locked into the first plan of its kind and repeated in every future EDP that follows.
“On Natural England’s own figures, the conservation measures it funds would leave about 83% of the extra nitrogen and up to 61% of the extra phosphorus going into the water, every year and permanently. These are protected sites that the plan itself says need pollution inputs cut by up to 97% to recover,” he said.
Hinchliff said measures that would have reduced nutrient pollution from the new homes, such as upgrading septic tanks, using small-scale underground treatment plants for homes not connected to the mains sewers and planting riverside buffer strips, were not included in Natural England’s EDP.
“In their place, the plan relies on indirect measures: fen cutting, deer control, catch-dyke works, removing one weir and restoring one kilometre of river,” he said.
“A plan that leaves most of the pollution unaddressed, that ‘locks in’ ecological degraded status, does not ‘address’ the harm in any ordinary sense of the word,” he added.
Ministers say the EDPs are needed to unblock growth as they pursue a target to build 1.5m new homes by the end of this parliament and are a “win-win” for nature and economic growth. The nature restoration fund, they say, will deliver coordinated, larger-scale conservation measures rather than piecemeal offsets.
Broadcaster Chris Packham, who is supporting the campaign against the Norfolk EDP by the charity WildFish, said environmental laws fought for over decades would be cancelled at the stroke of a pen.
“The Norfolk Broads are among Europe’s most precious wetlands: swallowtails and fen orchids, bitterns booming in the reeds and lamprey and bullhead in the gravels of the Wensum, one of England’s finest chalk rivers,” said Packham.
“But … they are drowning in pollution and the government has devised a cunning scheme to pour in a whole lot more.”
The push for growth comes as the UK is in a nature crisis: wild bird populations have fallen to their lowest level since records began, with nearly half of species in decline, hedgehog numbers have plummeted by 66% and sewage, agricultural runoff and chemicals have left rivers suffering with a toxic cocktail of pollution.
The Norfolk Broads EDP is out to consultation, which ends on 27 October. The Wildlife Trusts said the EDP would allow phosphorus from new homes to increase existing pollution levels on the rivers Yare, Bure and Wensum – a delicate chalk stream – without sufficient action from developers to mitigate for the impact.
“Even minor increases could be enough to tip the health of these rivers over the edge, with calamitous consequences for the Norfolk Broads,” said Matthew Browne, the head of public affairs at the Wildlife Trusts.
Bradley Tooze, the nature restoration fund director at Natural England, said: “The environment delivery plan aims to deliver better outcomes to protect the precious habitats of the Norfolk Broads while enabling sustainable development, including through river restoration measures and wetland habitat creation.
“We welcome all views on our proposals and encourage stakeholders to share their expertise to help shape this new approach to nature restoration.”
A government spokesperson said: “The aim of this environmental delivery plan is to protect and boost the natural environment. It’s based on the latest evidence and has been scrutinised by a scientific panel including independent experts. We welcome contributions to the ongoing consultation where people or organisations have views about how best to secure the aims we all share – protecting and restoring nature at a scale the status quo isn’t delivering.”

It was followed by ship, yacht and services exports, which grew 35 percent to $2 billion, mining products with a 20% increase to $5.4 billion, hazelnuts and hazelnut products with a 19% rise to $1.9 billion, and the defense and aerospace industry, where exports advanced 16% to $6.9 billion.
The number of sectors posting declines in exports during the January-September period stood at eight.
Exports of olives and olive oil fell 28 percent to $274 million. The sector was followed by dried fruits and products, down 8 percent, processed fruit and vegetable products, down 4 percent; ready-to-wear apparel and garments, down 3 percent and cereals, pulses, oil seeds and related products down 2 percent.
Exports of leather and leather products declined 1 percent to $1.1 billion, while furniture, paper and forestry products fell 1 percent to $5.8 billion. Ornamental plants and related products also slipped 1% to $121 million.

Lammert described acts of violence, arson, looting and attacks on people or public buildings as "unacceptable."
He said the EU supported French authorities' efforts to protect people, property and public institutions while fully respecting fundamental rights.
Lammert emphasized that national authorities were responsible for law enforcement, noting that investigations into the incidents were ongoing at the national level.

He added that the commission remained in close contact with French authorities and the country's Digital Services Coordinator.
Regnier said another meeting with French officials was scheduled for later Monday.
The remarks followed nationwide demonstrations Saturday that were marred by violence and looting in several French cities.

From 'Werwulf' to a 1930s Batman: Key takeways from Robert Eggers masterclass at Lumière
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:15:25 UTC
21:15:25 KST

A world exclusive for 'Werwulf', talk of Lily-Rose Depp's eyes, and the enduring horror of Ridley Scott's 'Alien'... Director Robert Eggers treats audiences at Lyon's Lumière Film Festival.
A guest of honour at this year’s Lumière Film Festival was American director Robert Eggers, the mastermind behind gothic folklore horror gems like The VVitch, The Lighthouse and Nosferatu.
Prior to the upcoming release of his new film, Werwulf, a werewolf horror film set in 14th-century England starring Nosferatu alum Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp and Willem Dafoe, the director sat down with the Lyon audience to discuss the dark and instantly recognisable worlds he has created on screen.
Sadly, there was no time for any questions on the director’s upcoming project - an adaptation of Shakespeare's "Romeo And Juliet" – and very little space given to the audience so they could ask questions. This is a recurring issue at the Lumière Festival and a shame, since the only two questions afforded to the attendees of Eggers’ masterclass were excellent.
Still, the Lumière audience was treated to nothing short of a world exclusive: the first screening of the beginning of Werwulf, which was prefaced by Eggers saying that the grading process is complex and that he was still working out some of the kinks in the lab.
Warning: Mild spoilers for the opening scenes of Werwulf.
The film starts with a howl in the dark, followed by the first (and not last, as Eggers confirmed) transformation. There’s vomit, there’s screaming, there’s writhing, there’s bone crunching. Safe to say that this is Eggers – as is his custom - taking mythical authenticity seriously and delivering something that goes beyond the sudden eruption of face fur... It’s significantly more visceral than any other body horror transformation we’ve seen in previous werewolf movies.
The audience barely got to glimpse the creature’s final form, but did witness the consequences. In this case, a lot of dead livestock. This was followed by a bloodied figure (Taylor-Johnson), back in human form, who knocks on a door and is greeted by a disfigured woman (Depp) in a... shall we say unique way, which suggests that Eggers will be tackling the knotty interspace where violence, animality and sexuality co-exist.
Take it from us: we’re in for a treat once Eggers' latest horror film is released and if you liked Nosferatu, chances are you'll get a kick out of this. Werwulf comes out next year, on 1 January in the UK and the following week in mainland Europe.
Before we get more nightmares under a full moon, here are the key takeaways from Robert Eggers’ masterclass.
On what he’s watching...
“All my favourite directors are dead and I rewatch films often – I watch Jack Clayton’s The Innocents once a year, and there are a lot of films I often revisit. In fact, I have a hard time keeping up with what’s in cinemas sometimes, because I’m always chipping away at a list of old films which generally have to do with research for what I’m currently working on.”
On the importance of silent cinema...
“I love silent cinema. Everybody knows the story that when sound cinema began, there was a dip in people using images to tell stories and it became all about dialogue. Of course, there are exceptions to the rule. Fritz Lang immediately knew how to do it. I think that I’ve succeeded in Werwulf in making a film where you can turn off the sound and still understand the story. The images are telling the story. Werwulf is also in Middle English, archaic English, but for English speaking audiences who don’t have the benefit of subtitles, you don’t really need to understand anything anyone says to understand the story. I was watching 12 Angry Men last night and it’s great – it's a dialogue-driven film and it’s cinema. But I’m more interested in telling stories with images.”
On the recurring image of women’s eyes in his films...
“Eyes are the window to the soul... And Anya (Taylor-Joy – The VVitch) and Lily-Rose (Depp – Nosferatu) have big eyes, so that helps! It can be a frustrating discipline for the actors at times... In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan shoots with IMAX cameras, which are so big that actors can’t see each other, and they devised a mirror system so that actors can see each other. But I always put a little piece of tape near the lense, so actors often have to look at the camera... I always like tight eyelines... Watch Elem Klimov’s Come And See, and you realise why it’s a good idea to do that!
On why the past is such an inspiration compared to the modern world...
“I get enough of the kitchen sink in my own kitchen! It’s always a mirror to society but if the mirror is too close, I feel like the film can be working too hard to say something. By trying to make a film that is timeless and of the time... It’s impossible. Of course, I don’t live in a vacuum, and if I was making a period movie for purely a period audience, or a Viking movie for a Viking audience, that would be a problem! But in endeavouring to go into not only the verisimilitude of the physical world of the period but also the interior world of the period, I think we may be able to more easily see who are today and where we’re going.”
On the use of specific languages...
“Language is always very specific in all of my films and I like the way language informs how you think. Language isn’t perfect and it can’t really express everything. When you learn other languages, you learn different ways to think. ‘Oh, in Germany, they have a word for that concept I struggle to describe...’.”
On the common setting of night in his films...
“I hate night shoots! The older I get, the more it’s difficult! But if you’re making a vampire movie or a werewolf movie, you don’t have a choice. You know, I don’t like the end of Nosferatu, because it doesn’t really work. The monster, the actual vampire, has power in the darkness. But also, when you don’t see the monster, the monster has power. Like in Ridley Scott’s Alien. When you shine a bright light on the monster, it’s killing the illusion – because then you’re seeing Bill Skarsgård in makeup.”
On what a Batman film directed by Robert Eggers would look like...
“There’s an internet rumour that I was doing a black-and-white, 1930s Batman as a detective movie... There are only so many movies you can make in a lifetime, so I wouldn’t make a comic book movie. But if I could make an infinite amount, that sounds like it could be fun! A 1930s Rolls Royce Batmobile, anyone?”
On creating a new monster from scratch, one which isn’t inspired by past myth or folklore...
“I’m not very creative! I read something that I haven’t seen and I do that! There is a part of me that feels this connection with the past and the urge to preserve it. For example, witches becoming hares is something common in British and Celtic folklore, but in America that idea was totally lost.”
On defining what a monster is...
“It’s always a reflection of us. (...) What is the trauma that doesn’t die? (...) There are many modern horror directors that I admire, but the touchstone for a creature is still for me Alien, 1979. The (H.R.) Giger design – it’s a phallus with a vagina... It’s us. And also, it has no eyes, and this gives it power. This is often the problem with werewolf movies – it's that the eyes of the werewolf aren’t right and you understand that it’s someone in a suit. With Alien, the creature is cold, which gives it more threat.”
Werwulf is out on 25 December in the US and Canada, and early January 2027 in European cinemas.

What a Somali-British MP reveals about Europe&#8217;s hijab obsession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:15:10 UTC
21:15:10 KST

What would George Orwell make of today’s debates over identity, integration, and the Muslim veil in Europe?
It is an impossible question, of course. Orwell has been dead for more than seventy years. Yet one of literature’s great privileges is that it allows us to bring the dead back into contemporary arguments, if only as witnesses against our assumptions.
To imagine Orwell’s answer, it is worth returning to his lesser-known observations from Morocco in 1938. His notes were never intended as a comprehensive study of Moroccan society, nor should they be treated as one today. Yet they remain striking precisely because they were written by an Englishman who arrived with inherited assumptions and left with a more complicated picture than he expected.
Among the things that caught Orwell’s attention was the everyday visibility of women wearing traditional veils in public life. They moved through markets and streets without appearing socially segregated from the communities around them. He also noted that relations between men and women seemed less burdened by the anxieties that many Europeans associated with Muslim societies. Ordinary social encounters, including casual interaction between the sexes, appeared far more unremarkable than prevailing Western stereotypes suggested.
Reading those observations today, another scene comes to mind on the opposite side of the Mediterranean.
Recently, Sagal Abdi-Wali entered the British Parliament as a Labour MP, wearing a traditional hijab and Somali dress without feeling compelled to downplay her origins or dilute the cultural markers associated with them.
At first glance, there seems little connection between Orwell’s Morocco and contemporary Britain. Yet an invisible thread links the two.
The connection is not the hijab itself. It is the fragility of the assumptions surrounding it.
What Orwell encountered in Morocco challenged the image he carried with him. Likewise, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s presence in the House of Commons challenges assumptions that continue to shape parts of the Western debate about integration and national belonging. In both cases, the problem lies less in reality than in the stories people tell themselves about reality.
Sagal Abdi-Wali did not enter Parliament as a softened version of her identity. She entered as a fully British politician whose Somali heritage remains visible rather than concealed. Her election illustrates a principle that often gets lost in political arguments: integration is not the same as assimilation. Citizenship does not require the erasure of memory, culture, or origin.
The significance of her presence has less to do with what she wears than with what her presence represents. Confident societies do not need their citizens to look identical in order to belong. The strength of democratic institutions is measured not by the uniformity they produce but by the diversity they can accommodate.
At first glance, Orwell’s remarks may seem little more than the observations of a curious traveler. Their deeper value lies elsewhere. They show an outsider confronting the limits of his own assumptions. Orwell arrived with ideas shaped by an imperial era that often imagined the Muslim world as uniquely restrictive, socially rigid, and defined by separations between communities and between men and women. What he found was a reality more nuanced than the caricature.
That history raises an uncomfortable question today: what happened to both sides of the Mediterranean?
READ: UK police take no further action against security adviser’s wife over Palestine Action post
Parts of the Arab world have undoubtedly become more conservative since the 1970s in matters of dress, gender relations, and public morality. Yet parts of Europe have travelled their own ideological distance. In several countries, the hijab is no longer discussed primarily as an issue of personal freedom or religious expression. Increasingly, it is treated as evidence of failed integration or as a symbol of social separation.
The irony is difficult to ignore. The debate is no longer about whether a woman should have the right to wear a hijab or reject it. Instead, it often revolves around who gets to make that decision on her behalf. Some voices in the Muslim world wish to impose the veil in the name of virtue. Some voices in the West seek to restrict it in the name of liberation. Between these competing certainties, the principle of individual freedom becomes the first casualty.
If Orwell were alive today, the garment itself might not be what surprised him most. What might astonish him is the obsession surrounding it.
In the Morocco he visited, he saw veiled women participating in public life and did not regard their presence as a contradiction requiring explanation.
Today, the same piece of cloth has become an ideological battleground. For some, it functions as a measure of religious virtue. For others, it serves as proof of cultural incompatibility. Lost between these opposing interpretations is the individual human being, whose right to define her own life should be the starting point of any liberal society.
None of this means that the past was a golden age of tolerance. Orwell saw only a fragment of Morocco, and he observed it through the lens of a British visitor in a country under French colonial rule. His account cannot stand as a definitive judgment on Arab societies. Its value lies instead in its ability to disturb easy certainties and expose the weakness of stereotypes that often survive long after the realities that produced them have changed.
That is why Sagal Abdi-Wali’s story matters beyond the boundaries of British politics. It demonstrates that national identity and cultural difference are not mutually exclusive. A democratic society does not become weaker when citizens bring multiple histories and traditions into public life. It becomes stronger when it possesses the confidence to accommodate them.
If Orwell were to walk today between Casablanca and London, he might discover that the central struggle is no longer one between East and West, as many in his generation imagined. It is increasingly a struggle between those who believe individuals should be free to define their own identities and those who insist on defining those identities for them.
He might conclude that tolerance belongs to no single civilization and that intolerance is not the monopoly of any culture. The real danger begins when symbols become more important than people, when identity becomes more important than citizenship, and when abstract arguments about belonging eclipse the freedom of the individuals whose lives are being debated.
That may be the enduring lesson connecting Orwell’s Morocco with a hijab-wearing British MP in Westminster. Progress is not measured by the number of laws, skyscrapers, or technologies a society produces. It is measured by its ability to live comfortably with people who are not exactly like itself.
Empires rise and fall. Ideologies come and go. Yet the temptation to tell others how they should live remains one of history’s most persistent habits.

However, Egyptian lawmaker Mostafa Bakry offered more details in a statement Sunday, explaining that parliament would discuss the president's decision, in his capacity as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, to send military forces to Saudi Arabia on a defensive mission.
Bakry said Egypt's National Defense Council, chaired by el-Sissi, had already approved the proposed deployment and its assigned mission before parliamentary deliberations began. The council's public statement pledged support for Saudi Arabia but did not specify the deployment of troops.
"Egypt has never abandoned its pan-Arab role or its responsibility to safeguard Arab national security," Bakry said. "For us, Saudi Arabia is an integral part of Egypt's own national security, and any threat to its security and stability is also a threat to us."
The parliamentary discussions were extended after additional lawmakers requested an opportunity to speak. Bakry subsequently indicated that a vote could take place Tuesday.

Egyptian military sources cited by the newspaper claimed that the decision to publicly announce the move and seek parliamentary approval was prompted by rapid developments on the ground requiring additional forces, alongside consideration of supplying Riyadh with defensive weapons.
