Saudi Arabia's request for Egyptian assistance comes after weeks of significant casualties and damage caused by Houthi missile and drone attacks. The rebels say the attacks are retaliation for the Saudi air blockade of Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen and for military operations against them by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized government, which Riyadh supports.
The deadliest recent attack on Saudi Arabia occurred when a Houthi missile struck Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and injuring more than 300.
The continuing attacks are also damaging Saudi Arabia's economy and threatening Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030, an ambitious program aimed at diversifying the kingdom's economy and reducing its dependence on traditional sources of revenue.
Egypt's parliamentary discussions come just over a month after Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 and met with el-Sissi.
Following that meeting, the Egyptian presidency said the two leaders had reaffirmed their commitment to ensuring freedom of navigation and maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Houthis have recently tightened their control over nearby areas and shipping routes.
El-Sissi stressed Egypt's opposition to any attack targeting Saudi Arabia or threatening freedom of navigation along international shipping routes. The statement said both leaders agreed that the current circumstances required greater solidarity and coordination between their countries.
Egypt is among the countries most vulnerable to security developments around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although the Houthis are currently concentrating their attacks on Saudi Arabia, Egypt, farther north, depends heavily on revenue from the Suez Canal, which is reached through the strait and the Red Sea.
Any escalation in the area can therefore cause substantial economic damage to Cairo.
For that reason, although Egypt is generally reluctant to enter military alliances and prefers to maintain a neutral position as a regional mediator, it has a clear interest in ending the confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis as quickly as possible.
The Houthis, who are closely following developments in Egypt, have already begun issuing warnings to Cairo.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi political bureau, told Qatar's Al-Araby television that the Egyptian military carries bitter memories of its involvement in Yemen between 1962 and 1968, and said he could not imagine it repeating that experience.
Al-Bukhaiti was referring to the events following a military coup in Yemen in September 1962, when Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser decided to support the republicans fighting royalist forces and sent some of Egypt's most elite military units into the country.
Egypt paid a heavy price for that intervention. Over the course of the conflict, it deployed approximately 70,000 soldiers to defend the new government and became trapped in a prolonged war fought under difficult conditions, with mountainous terrain and few roads.
The campaign, which ultimately forced Egyptian troops to withdraw, is still sometimes referred to as "Egypt's Vietnam."
In his interview with Al-Araby, al-Bukhaiti also mocked Saudi Arabia's leadership, claiming that el-Sissi's remarks exposed the depth of the kingdom's humiliation.
The Saudi leadership, he said, had reached a point where it was begging other countries to defend and protect it, even though, in the Houthis' view, Saudi Arabia itself was the aggressor. "We do not expect Egypt to become involved in aggression against Yemen. Egypt is bigger than that," he said. He added that such an intervention would place Egypt in the same camp as the United States and Israel.
Meanwhile, Al-Akhbar reported Monday that Houthi intelligence was monitoring movements by foreign forces that had allegedly arrived in Jizan, in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border. According to the newspaper, the area has become a staging ground for planning attacks against Yemen.
The report claimed that Pakistani forces were also present, following a defense alliance recently signed by Pakistan and Turkey with Saudi Arabia. It further alleged that Ukrainian personnel had arrived in the area several days earlier aboard a military transport aircraft. Those reports have not been independently verified.
The Houthis have threatened to target foreign forces involved in military operations against them, raising the possibility that Egyptian, Pakistani or Ukrainian personnel could come under attack if they participate in the campaign.
Fighting inside Yemen is also continuing between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
On Monday, reports from Yemen described a major Houthi attack on the al-Alam military base in Shabwa province, allegedly carried out during a training exercise. Dozens of Yemeni government troops were reportedly killed or wounded.
Houthi missile and drone launches toward Saudi Arabia have also continued. Early Monday morning, an alert was issued in Jizan following reports of another launch.

20:13:50 CST
21:13:50 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government announced on Monday that an additional 1,400 hectares of wetlands in the southeastern state of Victoria will receive international recognition and stronger environmental protections to safeguard threatened migratory shorebirds.
The expansion will increase the size of the Port Phillip Bay (Western Shoreline) and Bellarine Peninsula Ramsar Site to 24,110 hectares, according to a joint statement by federal Environment and Water Minister Murray Watt and Michaela Settle, Victorian minister for water.
The newly included areas comprise the Moolap Wetlands, parts of the Edwards Point Swan Bay Wildlife Reserve and Coastal Reserve, Lake Connewarre Complex Conservation Reserve, and Point Cook Cheetham Coastal Park and Marine Sanctuary.
The wetlands provide important saltmarsh and seagrass habitats for migratory shorebirds travelling thousands of kilometers along the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, including the critically endangered curlew sandpiper and Far Eastern curlew.
The expansion will also provide greater protection for threatened plants, including spiny peppercress, which will be included within the Ramsar site for the first time.
Watt said the expansion would help protect internationally significant wetlands and safeguard wildlife and biodiversity for future generations.
The statement said the expanded listing would strengthen conservation efforts, support habitat restoration and improve the wetlands' resilience to climate change.
The extension will be submitted to the Convention on Wetlands Secretariat for adoption.
Australia currently has 67 wetlands recognized as internationally important under the Ramsar Convention, covering more than 8.3 million hectares, an area larger than the island state of Tasmania. ■

China's retail sales strengthen in first three quarters as consumption upgrading continues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:13:01 CST
21:13:01 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's retail sales strengthened in the first three quarters of 2026, with retail sales of services growing faster than sales of goods and new forms of consumption continuing to emerge, official data showed on Monday.
The country's total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of consumption spending, rose 2.6 percent year on year in the January-September period, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
In September, total retail sales of consumer goods, which cover sales of physical goods and revenue from catering services, grew at the fastest pace in six months, rising 1.1 percent year on year and 0.7 percentage points faster than in August, the data showed.
Final consumption expenditure contributed 46.7 percent of overall economic growth in the first three quarters, up 0.7 percentage points from the first half of the year.
Consumption is a key driver of economic growth and a tangible reflection of people's pursuit of a better life, said Wang Guanhua, an NBS spokesperson, noting that with consumption-boosting policies implemented this year, consumption has effectively played its foundational role in economic growth.
Spending on services has become an increasingly important driver of consumption growth, Wang said. Retail sales of services grew 5 percent year on year in the first three quarters, 4 percentage points faster than sales of goods.
In terms of services consumption, the categories of communication and information services, tourism consulting and leasing services, and cultural, sports and leisure services posted rapid growth, the NBS data showed.
Cultural and tourism activities such as study tours, intangible cultural heritage experiences, and exhibitions and sporting events flourished, while immersive and experiential consumption gained popularity, Wang said.
Goods consumption is shifting toward newer, higher-quality and greener products, she said. In the first three quarters, retail sales of energy-efficient home appliances grew more than 20 percent, and retail sales of new energy passenger vehicles topped 7.7 million units.
Online retail sales of goods and services exceeded 15.1 trillion yuan, up 4.4 percent year on year. Of the total, online sales of goods rose 3.8 percent, while online sales of services increased 5.3 percent.
Wang said online shopping formats were expanding and online supply was becoming more diverse, with instant retail maintaining double-digit growth and brick-and-mortar retail shifting toward one-stop, experiential and high-quality formats.
As rural supermarkets and logistics improve, consumption potential in county-level markets continues to be unlocked, Wang said. Retail sales of consumer goods in urban areas rose 0.9 percent in the first three quarters, compared with a 2.3 percent increase in rural areas.
Inbound consumption is also expanding as travel to China becomes more convenient, Wang said. In the first eight months, visa-free foreign arrivals rose 26.8 percent year on year, while departure tax refund applications and refund amounts grew rapidly in many places.
In July, China released its first five-year plan dedicated exclusively to expanding consumption. The plan aims to unlock the full potential of the country's super-large market, optimize the consumption structure, and improve people's livelihoods through targeted measures.
Looking ahead, Wang said China's consumer market is expected to further unlock its potential, supported by sustained economic development, rising living standards, improved supply of goods and services, and the emergence of new business forms and consumption scenarios. ■

Services for children in parts of England are in a “state of emergency”, according to a report that identifies what it claims to be the hardest places in the country for young people to grow up in.
The children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, said in some local authorities individual service failures or systemic problems meant “no child could reasonably be expected to thrive and those that do thrive do so against the odds”.
She said she had spoken to children on recent visits to schools, youth clubs and young offender institutions around the country and some of the things she had heard and seen had “utterly disgusted” her.
On a recent visit to Middlesbrough, a 14-year-old-girl had informed her of the crime statistics in her area. “Children should not have to know those statistics,” De Souza said.
She added: “Their parents should not have to talk about them over dinner to explain why children cannot play outside. Schools should not have administrative staff dealing with drug overdoses and racist thugs. Nowhere in England should ‘a chase from the police’ be a primary source of entertainment.”
De Souza said she wanted to shine a light on areas where childhood was hardest. “We cannot shy away from the fact that indicators such as poor education outcomes, long health waiting lists or simply feeling unsafe converge in particular places,” she said.
“In some communities, these challenges amount to nothing less than a state of emergency. Not for every child. Not everywhere. But what we see here is a litany of failure. In so many areas of the country, children are being radically failed.”
Her analysis is based on official data covering more than 160 measures, including child poverty, educational outcomes, community safety, NHS waiting times and access to playgrounds.
It names a clutch of relatively deprived areas – Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway as the hardest places in which to grow up in England.
By contrast, a series of relatively wealthy areas – Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham – are identified as the least challenging places in which to be a child.
“What children across the country feel to be true is in fact true. That it simply is harder to be a child in Middlesbrough than it is in Cheshire … the outcomes are shocking … an unacceptable failure,” the report says.
It adds: “When areas are unsafe, that is not a point on a dashboard, it is children being the subject of racist abuse and violence on the way to school. When local services fail, it is not a failure to hit KPIs [key performance indicators], it is a child on the phone to their school with their parents dead in the other room.”
The report, called The Childhood Lottery, says a north-south divide exists, with authorities in the south more likely to score higher across the metrics, and those in the north more likely to score lower, with the Midlands in between.
De Souza said children should be a priority in the government’s devolution agenda and she urged the government to draw up a series of minimum standards for education, policing, health and youth services. A national fund should be created to invest in areas that fail to hit the benchmarks.
She recommended that every strategic authority should have a deputy mayor for children, accountable for delivering on a “children’s test” ensuring that local policies bring benefits and improvements to young people’s services.
The Department for Education said it was working to improve childcare support and school standards, and it was giving more power to “local leaders” to shape the future of their education.

====================================================================================================

Exchange card, registration, a contract with a doctor: what maternity hospitals can actually require from a pregnant woman
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:11:13 EEST
21:11:13 KST

Exchange card, registration, a contract with a doctor: what maternity hospitals can actually require from a pregnant woman
Kyiv • UNN
Pregnant women can register at a facility with an NHSU contract without a referral. Giving birth is permitted at any maternity hospital regardless of registration.
From the moment a woman learns she is pregnant, she follows a certain path through the healthcare system, formalized by clinical protocols and medical guarantee packages. Women often have questions about whether an antenatal record is mandatory or whether they must give birth at the maternity hospital where they are registered. UNN tried to clarify these and other issues.
First consultation and registration
Let us imagine that a woman has learned she is pregnant after receiving a positive test result and has decided to see a gynecologist at a hospital that has a contract with the NHSU. Importantly, such a consultation does not require a referral from a family doctor. However, it is still worth signing a contract with a family doctor if you do not have one yet, as this will make it easier to receive free medical services in the future.
It is generally considered best to have the first examination during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. During this visit, the doctor will confirm the pregnancy, determine its term, take a medical history, and identify possible risks. The following tests are also mandatory: blood type and Rh factor, complete blood count, urinalysis, testing for infections (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis), and others as indicated. If you visit a hospital that has a contract with the NHSU, all these services are provided free of charge under the medical guarantee package for pregnancy monitoring.
During the visit, the gynecologist enters information about the patient into the Electronic Healthcare System. It will also contain the results of tests, screenings, and other examinations. This provides a degree of autonomy: if you want to change doctors, for example, because the security situation in your region has deteriorated, you will not need to carry paper documentation with you—the new doctor will be able to obtain all the necessary information from the electronic records.
First trimester
The first trimester of pregnancy lasts 13 weeks. During this period, the expectant mother usually undergoes the first prenatal screening, which includes an ultrasound examination, a blood test for hormones, and an assessment of the risk of chromosomal abnormalities.
Detection of a high risk of abnormalities or other deviations in the health of the pregnant woman or fetus is grounds for additional examinations—the vast majority of them are free of charge under the medical guarantee package. Even if it is impossible to obtain a consultation at your hospital, from a geneticist, for example, you will be referred to the nearest hospital where this option is available.
Second trimester
The second trimester of pregnancy lasts from week 14 through week 27 inclusive. Even if the pregnancy is progressing normally, visits to the doctor should be regular.
An anatomical ultrasound examination is performed at approximately 18–22 weeks, during which the development of the baby's organs is examined in detail. Also important during the second and early third trimesters is a glucose tolerance test, which makes it possible not to miss the development of gestational diabetes. Monitoring antibodies is also important for Rh-negative women.
Third trimester
The final, third trimester begins at week 28. Doctor visits become more frequent, and at approximately 30 weeks, a medical conclusion necessary for arranging maternity leave is prepared. As for medical procedures, at around 35–37 weeks of pregnancy, the woman should be tested for group B streptococcus. The fetus's position is also assessed, and the method of delivery is planned: vaginal birth or cesarean section when indicated.
Choosing a maternity hospital and doctor
A woman may give birth at any maternity hospital that has a contract with the NHSU, regardless of her place of registration or actual residence. At the same time, under the medical guarantee package, she may choose only the facility, not the specific doctor she wants to deliver the baby. As for choosing a specific doctor, most facilities officially provide this as an additional paid service.
"If you have not signed a contract with the doctor of your choice, the on-duty team will deliver the baby free of charge," explains Dmytro Hovsyeiev, director of the Kyiv Perinatal Center.
No additional agreement with a doctor is required to give birth at any particular maternity hospital. Likewise, your official place of registration makes no difference. An exchange card is not mandatory either.
However, if you give birth prematurely or develop complications, you will likely be referred to the nearest Perinatal Center (either during pregnancy or once labor has begun). Such centers are level III medical facilities—everything necessary to provide emergency care to both the woman and the child is available here: intensive care, equipment for nursing premature infants, a surgery department, and experienced staff. Under the medical guarantees package, this care is also provided free of charge.
If everything goes according to plan, you can prepare a birth plan: choose pain relief, decide whether the birth will involve a partner, and determine the conditions for the first contact with the baby. This is also covered by the medical guarantees package. However, a separate upgraded room is an additional service that can officially be paid for at most public or municipal maternity hospitals.

Europe does not care what happens to Ukraine — expert
Unknown

12:09:32 UTC
21:09:32 KST

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Europeans have little sympathy for Ukraine and are largely indifferent to the country’s future, Andrey Sushentsov, dean of the School of International Relations at MGIMO University, told TASS.
Unlike Russia and the United States, Europe lacks "full strategic autonomy and is not truly capable of collective action based on a unified position," he argued.
"Every major decision requires a consensus among nearly 30 countries," said Sushentsov, a member of the Scientific and Expert Council under the Russian Security Council. "There is no unified army. Europe falls far short of even the loosest form of a confederation. It would carry strategic weight if it could act as a single entity, but there is no sign of that happening."
According to the expert, Europeans "dread the prospect of being directly drawn into a military crisis with Russia like the plague." As a result, any discussion of deploying troops to Ukraine comes with the caveat that such a move could take place only after a stable peace has been established and a ceasefire is in force.
"To some extent, their enthusiasm is fueled by the perception that supporting Ukraine - and this proxy confrontation - comes at a relatively low cost," Sushentsov said. "They do not feel sorry for Ukraine. They are indifferent to what happens to the country, its borders or its population."
Astronomical sums spent to no avail
Sushentsov argued that Europe’s willingness to support Ukraine and sustain what he described as a proxy conflict is partly driven by the perception that doing so is relatively inexpensive. He noted that the European Commission has a limited budget of its own and relies primarily on the financial resources of individual member states.
"Despite sharing a common currency, each country calculates its debt separately," he explained. "The instrument available to them is debt financing - essentially, lending to Ukraine - and the total has approached $500 billion."
Although the sum is "astronomical," Sushentsov argued, it has failed to deliver the desired strategic results. Instead, he said, the support has further weakened Europe’s own position, with the money effectively "going up in smoke."
Loud voices, permanently on the sidelines
Against this backdrop, Sushentsov believes Europe’s options are limited to issuing forceful statements and staging high-profile diplomatic gatherings.
"All Europe can do in the current situation is express rhetorical outrage, convene summits, pose for ‘family photos’ and issue categorical statements," he said.
"In essence, however, this is nothing more than a gathering of spectators who are not actually taking part in the military crisis itself," he concluded.

The multiple sclerosis gap Europe cannot afford to ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:08:45 UTC
21:08:45 KST

The multiple sclerosis gap Europe cannot afford to ignore
Providing the right support and treatment starts with measurement. Current tools do not reflect the lived reality of MS patients and miss early signs of progression.
As Europe plans its response to the neurological disease burden, a fundamental measurement gap is being overlooked — and the cost of ignoring it is being felt.
A briefing requested earlier this year by the European Parliament’s Committee on Public Health (SANT) put it plainly: neurological diseases are one of Europe’s most urgent and rapidly expanding health, social and economic challenges. Published in February 2026, it calls for a coordinated European plan linking prevention, early diagnosis, research and innovation.1 But before Europe considers what that plan should look like, a foundational question demands attention: are we measuring the right things?
Multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic, progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts communication between the brain and the body, offers a revealing case study. Consider a woman in her mid-30s, working, raising a family, managing what her neurologist calls “stable” MS. She has not slept properly in years, her memory has been slipping and she is cutting her hours at work. Her last clinical note reads: “No change.” On paper, she is stable, but in reality she is anything but.
Her story is not unusual. According to research commissioned by Sanofi*, the gap between what health systems measure and what people with MS experience may be costing individuals, families and economies more than we realize.3
The stakes for Europe
Over 3 million people globally live with MS and Europe has the highest prevalence, at 133 per 100,000 people.2,3 The condition strikes primarily during prime working years, meaning hundreds of thousands of people are navigating a progressive, unpredictable disease at precisely the point when inadequate support is felt most acutely.3
That support begins with measurement. And right now, the tools used to assess MS in clinical practice do not fully capture what people with the disease experience.3
The consequences extend far beyond the clinic: 82 percent of people with severe MS rely on unpaid family caregiving, yet this burden rarely appears in standard health data or policy design.3 When the full impact of disease is not measured, health systems can underestimate need, delay support, and overlook the wider effects on work, welfare and family life.3
The measurement gap
The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), the primary tool used to measure MS disability, was developed in 1983 to assess walking ability. We now know that MS affects far more than mobility. Fatigue affects 94 percent of people with MS, while 75 percent report cognitive difficulties, but both are absent in the EDSS assessment.3 In a field where clinical consensus is rare, seven in ten neurologists agree: a more comprehensive approach is needed.3
Growing recognition of smouldering neuroinflammation has made the need for new methods of quantifying MS progression increasingly urgent. This slow, chronic disease activity can persist even when a patient appears clinically stable, with effects that are subtle, cumulative and easy to miss until significant damage has already occurred.4
This is why Sanofi initiated the development of the Smouldering Associated Worsening (SAW) Index+. The SAW Index Study — led by an international steering committee of leading MS clinicians, researchers and patient advocates — is due to complete in 2027. Based on hundreds of hours of in-depth qualitative research with people with MS, the goal of the SAW Index is to provide neurologists with a comprehensive measurement framework that bridges the gap between lived experience and what clinical tools are currently able to detect.
According to the European Multiple Sclerosis Platform, people with MS experience an average of 14 symptoms within the first five years of diagnosis, with fatigue, sensory problems, sleep disturbances, cognitive impairment and balance problems among the most common.5 These are precisely the experiences the SAW Index is designed to surface, replacing static labels like “moderately affected” with measurement metrics grounded in the experience and words of people with MS.
The cost of this gap
These aspects of MS can be challenging to quantify and are associated with substantial societal and economic burdens. Lifetime productivity loss per person with MS ranges from €394,000 in France to €668,000 in Germany.3 The cost profile shifts significantly as the disease progresses: in mild MS, direct healthcare costs dominate; in severe MS, indirect costs become the primary driver.3 Indeed, lost wages, absenteeism, early retirement, disability payments and the growing burden on unpaid carers outweigh medical costs in many countries, placing growing long-term pressure on social insurance and disability systems.3
Early identification of progression could change that trajectory, extending years of employment, preserving household income, and reducing long-term dependence on disability and social benefits.3,6 That is a cost-avoidance opportunity current measurement frameworks are missing.
Progress in motion
There is no single fix, but there is momentum.
MS care has advanced significantly in recent decades: diagnosis is happening earlier, treatment options have expanded and the focus is shifting from relapse control alone to slowing long-term disability progression.7 Furthermore, there is growing recognition of the importance of cognition, mental health, rehabilitation and the day-to-day realities that shape whether people living with MS can remain independent and active.8
The challenge now is to ensure policy keeps pace with that progress, and better measurement is part of the answer. If Europe wants health spending to deliver lasting value, it should see these improvements not as costs to be managed, but as investments in independence, participation, productivity and more sustainable health systems.
Time to act
The European Parliament’s SANT Committee has called for a fully funded European neurological health plan — one with the scale and ambition of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, aligning health, research and societal action in a unified framework.1 MS offers a clear and immediate test case for what that ambition looks like in practice.
But ambitious plans require accurate data. If Europe is serious about a coordinated response to neurological disease, getting measurement right is not a secondary concern; it is the foundation on which everything else depends.
The people living with MS across the continent cannot wait for the tools that measure their disease to catch up with the science that understands it. Neither should policymakers.
*Research commissioned by Sanofi. All editorial control retained by Economist Impact. +Sanofi initiated and funds the SAW Index Study.

A secondhand store chain has repaid the state UAH 51.5 mln in unpaid taxes following an investigation into a scheme involving sole proprietors, the Office of the Prosecutor General has reported.
“Under the procedural guidance of Office of the Prosecutor General prosecutors, over UAH 51.5 mln in value-added tax unpaid by a chain of used goods stores has been returned to the state budget,” the agency said on its Telegram channel on Monday.
According to the investigation, in 2023-2025 officials of the secondhand chain used a scheme of artificially splitting the business to reduce tax liabilities.
“To do this, sales of used clothing, footwear and other goods in the chain’s stores were registered in the names of controlled sole proprietors who were on the simplified taxation system,” the report says.
According to prosecutors, formally the retail outlets and sales operations belonged to individual entrepreneurs, but in fact the stores were run by chain employees who organized trade and controlled the movement of funds.
“In this way the company understated the volume of transactions subject to VAT. According to an analytical study, the amount of unpaid tax exceeded UAH 51.5 mln,” the agency stressed.
The company’s officials fully compensated the damage caused to the state during the pre-trial investigation. Because the tax liabilities were paid, prosecutors asked the court to release the individuals from criminal liability under Part 4 of Article 212 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Ukraine has accumulated a substantial strategic reserve of such equipment.
"Our repair crews, electricians, and energy technicians have demonstrated the capability to perform restorations in the tightest possible timelines. Then another strike hits, and then restoration follows again. And this cycle has been continuing for many, many months," the prime minister said.
He noted that as winter approaches, the intensity of strikes has grown substantially, but the action plan remains unchanged: continue protecting facilities, build distributed backup generation capacity, and maintain a constant supply of equipment. This reserve is continuously replenished alongside international partners to enable the replacement of entire power units, transformers, or their components whenever necessary.
In the prime minister's view, the fact that a vast volume of attacks has not led to a total power system collapse or prolonged blackouts demonstrates that a significant portion of the infrastructure is effectively protected.
"And for what is destroyed by such an incredible number of attacks, our energy workers. Heartfelt gratitude to them, it will never be enough to say 'thank you.' Restore it as quickly and high-qualitatively as possible," Koretsky said.

====================================================================================================

Saudi Arabia’s offensive against the Houthis aims to secure Bab el-Mandeb - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:07:24 UTC
21:07:24 KST

Early in September, the Houthis launched a rapid and unexpected offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. They captured the strategically important port of Mocha and pushed south toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, gaining roughly 150 km. of coastline and threatening the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The offensive turned Bab el-Mandeb into a second maritime pressure point in Iran’s conflict with the United States. Before it, US naval and military resources could concentrate on the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s principal economic lever.
The Houthi advance put the Red Sea route into play as well, giving Iran potential leverage over both of the region’s main oil-shipping corridors.
Oil prices are determined at the margin, so even when actual lost production is relatively small, the mere threat of disruption can produce a large price increase. That is exactly what happened in September.
Brent crude, the principal international benchmark price for crude oil, had averaged about $89 per barrel for most of 2026. After the seizure of Mocha, despite there not yet being an equivalent actual loss of global oil production, it went above $110. It now sits just below $110.
The Houthi assault was too vitally significant to go unanswered. On October 4, the internationally recognized Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, launched a major counter-offensive. With substantial Saudi air and naval support, government forces attacked the areas recently gained by the Houthis.
In its public statements, the Yemeni government has emphasized that its long-term aim is national reunification. Accordingly, when Rashad al-Alimi, president of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced the operation on October 5, he described it as an effort to restore state institutions, retake Sanaa, and defeat the Houthi movement. Probably more in hope than expectation, he dubbed it “Operation Dawn of Yemen.”
Reuters suggested that Saudi Arabia’s more immediate strategic requirement is to recover the Bab el-Mandeb area and remove the leverage the Houthis acquired in September.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Michael Ratney, put that narrower objective succinctly: “Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic.”
The coalition’s military effort is considerable. Its spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said that 100 fighter aircraft participated in the opening phase, and that 324 “high-value targets” had been destroyed.
The coalition also announced round-the-clock support for Yemeni ground forces and air cover over Bab el-Mandeb, while naval operations have extended north to Hodeidah governorate.
The coalition said it struck weapons depots and facilities storing explosive-laden boats and naval mines, and thwarted a planned attack on southern Red Sea waterways.
The Houthis origins
Who are these Houthis, who call their movement Ansar Allah and are perhaps the most blatantly antisemitic of all jihadist groups? They brandish a flag inscribed with the words: “A curse on the Jews”, in addition to such slogans as “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
They emerged in the late 1980s from within Yemen’s Zaydi Shi’ite communities in the northern Saada region. The current conflict stems back to the sadly misnamed “Arab spring” uprisings of 2011. Inside Yemen, they resulted in mass protests against the long dictatorial rule of its president, Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Saleh was forced to step down in favor of his vice-president, Abed Rabbo Mansour Hadi. In 2015, Hadi tried to sponsor a revised constitution for Yemen that envisaged a federal system split between northerners and southerners. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels rejected it.
Although the Houthis are fundamentalist Shi’ites, Yemen’s ex-president Saleh, a Sunni Muslim, decided to collaborate with them in a bid to return to power.
It was through Saleh that the Houthis were able to gain control of most of the Yemeni military, including its air force. As a result, and supported with military hardware from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, they overran large tracts of the country and in September 2014 captured Yemen’s capital city, Sanaa. Subsequently, they expanded their control across much of northwestern Yemen.
Saudi Arabia, alarmed at the prospect of Iran gaining a foothold on the Arabian peninsula, formed a coalition to support Hadi’s government, and intervened in March 2015 to beat back the Houthis. The internal struggle for power has continued ever since, and despite years of coalition air operations and ground fighting, the Houthis have retained their north-western power base.
A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 substantially reduced the fighting. Although it formally expired in October that year, the UN acknowledges that relative restraint had continued until the present escalation.
The Houthis’ conflict with Saudi Arabia has been both religious and political. Zaydis opposed the spread of Saudis’ Sunni Wahhabi influence on religious grounds. It was the Saudis’ political and military influence in Yemen that the Houthis resisted.
From 2022, Riyadh cut back substantially on its own military activity, attempting a policy of support for the PLC by way of diplomacy. Even so, it continued to fund and arm anti-Houthi forces. In the past year, it has increasingly reasserted direct military involvement, culminating in its current support for the offensive against the Houthis.
Although the ground fighting is being conducted primarily by Saudi-backed Yemeni forces rather than Saudi troops, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has been a significant driver of the counter-offensive.
Following the Houthi advance toward Mocha and Bab el-Mandeb in September, he personally pressed US President Donald Trump to strike them. Trump declined direct US participation, but Washington subsequently provided intelligence and targeting support.
MBS’s likely strategic objectives are to restore the Red Sea security buffer by pushing the Houthis away from Bab el-Mandeb and the Saudi-facing Red Sea coast. He is probably not at one with the PLC in seeing the conflict as another attempt to win the Yemeni civil war.
The rapid Houthi gains were a serious setback to the Saudi-backed Yemeni order. Reversing them, even partially, demonstrates that Saudi Arabia can still defend the security of its southern frontier.
MBS’s immediate strategic calculation is probably to deny the Houthis – and by extension Iran – a durable position at Bab el-Mandeb, protect Saudi maritime and energy interests, restore Saudi leverage, and enter any eventual negotiation from a position of strength, backed now by the offer of Egyptian support.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com

Foreign journalists still cannot enter Gaza without military escort, Israel tells High Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:07:17 UTC
21:07:17 KST

The state has told the High Court of Justice that journalists should still be barred from entering Gaza without military escort, citing continuing security risks in response to the Foreign Press Association’s renewed push for independent access.
The response, dated Sunday, maintains the restrictions a year after the October 2025 ceasefire agreement and more than two years after the association filed its petition.
The dispute centers on whether journalists can enter Gaza and report independently, rather than through visits organized and escorted by the IDF. The state points to escorted visits allowed at various stages of the war, while the association argues that those visits cannot substitute for reporters choosing where to go, whom to interview and what to investigate.
In its September 27 request, the association argued that conditions had changed substantially, including through arrangements allowing international aid workers to enter and move within Gaza. It said those arrangements undermined the justification for continuing to bar independent journalists' access.
The association asked the court to allow entry while the case remained pending, require the state to formally justify the restrictions, or alternatively hold an urgent hearing. It also argued that repeated delays were causing lasting harm: the opportunity to report on events as they happen cannot be recovered through access granted months later.
Latest response doesn't allow journalists to enter without military escort
The state’s latest response, submitted after an instruction from Deputy Supreme Court President Noam Sohlberg, says the current security assessment still does not allow journalists to enter without a military escort. It opposes the requested orders and offers to provide another classified explanation to the judges.
The proceedings have continued through several rounds of updates and extensions, including a review the state promised after the ceasefire agreement.
In its June 19, 2025 response, the state relied on the court’s January 2024 rejection of an earlier petition. That ruling found no automatic right to enter Gaza and no grounds to intervene in the restrictions under the circumstances at the time. It nevertheless left the association free to approach the authorities again, and return to court if necessary, should conditions change.
On October 9, 2025, the government approved the hostage-release framework that included the ceasefire arrangements. At a hearing two weeks later, the state said it would reconsider its policy in light of the agreement.
In its October 26 decision, the court gave the state time to complete that review and set November 23 as the deadline for an update. It also recorded the state’s intention to resume escorted journalist visits to areas up to the Yellow Line within days.
Following extensions, the state submitted its response on January 4, 2026. It acknowledged changes on the ground but maintained that continuing threats and security incidents prevented independent entry. At that time, it also cited the continued captivity of the remains of hostage Ran Gvili.
At a January 26 hearing, state representatives presented classified security information to the judges without the petitioners present. The court subsequently ordered another update by March 31, without issuing the order sought by the association requiring the state to formally justify its policy.
Following two extensions, the state filed that update on June 3, again maintaining its position. At Sohlberg’s instruction, it then provided a classified explanation on June 15, after a short extension. According to the latest state response, no further decision followed on that material.
Allowing temporary entry grants main request without final ruling
The state now argues that allowing independent entry temporarily would effectively grant the main request in the petition before the court had reached a final ruling.
It said it could prepare another classified submission within approximately 20 days if the court requested one. An affidavit supporting its current security assessment would also be submitted in the coming days, it said.
The court’s response will determine the next steps in the case.
The state submitted the affidavit on Monday. As of the time of writing, the court had not issued a decision on its response, which, when issued, will determine the next steps in the case.

Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.
The TV personality sat still and upright in the dock on Monday as the woman’s pre-recorded police interview was played to jurors at Southwark crown court.
She told officers she found Brand funny on Big Brother spin-off shows on Channel 4, but that he sexually assaulted her within a minute of meeting her at the bar.
She said: “He literally just grabbed my boobs, out of nowhere, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs.
“I was completely in shock and was like: ‘What the hell are you doing? I’ve literally just met you.’ Then literally he grabbed my arm and dragged me into the toilets.”
She broke down in tears as she recounted how, within seconds, Brand allegedly orally raped her in a locked, flooded toilet as she told him: “What are you doing? I don’t want to do this.”
She said: “I pushed him away and he said: ‘Come on, come on, don’t be a spoilsport.’ He kept pushing my head down and wouldn’t let me go. I just froze. I didn’t know what to do.”
She said she closed her eyes during the alleged attack and remembered a man knocking on the toilet door saying: “Are you OK?” before she walked out in a daze.
“I remember this really, really clearly – he [Brand] turned to me and went: ‘Oh, I guess we should swap numbers now’, like it was just all normal, like he hadn’t just forced me to do that,” she recalled.
When she was asked to go over the alleged attack in more detail, the woman described how Brand had a “big grin … like a clown” and a “weird look” in his eye after he assaulted her at the bar. “There was no sexual flirting, it was just a normal conversation about him being on Big Brother,” she said.
The woman alleged she then recalled being “steered” into Brand’s car before the comedian’s driver ferried them to a different bar in Camden.
“I was in disbelief and shock and I felt this nudge and I looked around and he [Brand] had his penis out again in the car and he was going ‘come on, come on, suck it’ and I was just like ‘no’. He took ‘no’ for an answer then.”
She did not report the alleged sexual assault and rape to police until 2023, when media reports about Brand’s alleged misconduct were published.
“I just felt this shame that I allowed him to do that to me,” she told officers in her interview. “I just didn’t want to admit it to myself, not to anyone.”
She did tell a friend and colleague that Brand had “tried to” assault her and that he was a “sexual predator”.
Giving evidence from behind a screen on Monday afternoon, the woman said she was “terrified” to report the attack at the time because of the “lad culture” of the 2000s. She said: “He was a celebrity and it would be his words against mine. I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends.
“I just thought the odds weren’t in my favour and I didn’t want to have to go through a court where somebody is tearing down my character.”
In cross-examination, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why the woman had not reported the alleged attack during the #MeToo movement and suggested she had “willingly” gone into the toilet with Brand for “a kiss and a cuddle”.
She denied that was the case, and the barrister’s suggestion that she had been excited and charmed to meet Brand.
She said: “I was not charmed in the slightest. I’d met this person for a minute before I was sexually assaulted.”

Parliamentary commission identifies two suspects for David Rossi's death
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:02:17 CEST
21:02:17 KST

Gianluca Vinci, the chairman of the Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the death of former Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) Bank Communications Chief David Rossi, said Monday that two people suspected of involvement in his case have been identified as a result of the commission's work. 
The 51-year-old's lifeless body was found 13 years ago - on 6 March 2013 - under a window of his office in the courtyard of Palazzo Salimbeni, the MPS HQ in the Tuscan city. 
The death was initially ruled a suicide, but suspicions remained that Rossi was the victim of foul play and parliament opened a commission of inquiry into the case in 2021. 
Vinci said the two suspects have been identified thanks to information obtained from two prison inmates. 
He named them as former MPS president Giuseppe Mussari, "the instigator of an act of intimidation that was not initially intended to result in David Rossi's death", and Gabriele Ceccherelli, "the individual who allegedly organized and selected the persons—who have not yet been identified—to be involved in the execution phase, while he himself remained outside Palazzo Salimbeni. 
"We will send all the documentation to the prosecutor's office," Vinci told a press conference. 
"The judicial authorities will know how to proceed." Mussari said he would take legal action after being implicated in the case. 
Ceccherelli, a former Calcio Storico Fiorentino player, said he was innocent.
"I know nothing about this; I don't know anyone involved in this case," he said. 
"The only time I've ever been to Siena was to buy a pair of shoes; I have nothing to do with this case". 
A series of expert reports commissioned by the parliamentary commission have backed the assertion that Rossi was killed. 
A new report presented last month said Rossi was attacked by at least two "large" people and was conscious before falling out of the window. 
It said he most likely tried to defend himself and, once he fell out of the window, he attempted to cling to the ledge and was held by his attackers—perhaps in an attempt to intimidate him—but then their grip slipped and Rossi fell. 
The report was presented by the Carabinieri police's RIS unit, which conducted simulations at a gym in Rome with a police officer acting out how the experts think Rossi responded to the attack. 
A previous expert report on facial injuries sustained by Rossi said they were not caused by his fall from his office window but instead by pressure on his face and head exerted by third parties against the safety bar or the wooden frame of the window. 
Another report on injuries to his wrist found that Rossi had been held by third parties outside the window before the fall. 
MPS is Italy's third-biggest bank, and the oldest in the world.

Modi ‘more likely’ to visit Russia next year – Kremlin
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is likely to visit Russia next year for his annual summit with President Vladimir Putin, the Kremlin said on Monday, after preparing for a visit this year.
”More likely next year,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS when asked whether Modi would visit before the end of the year.

Moscow, however, raised the possibility of a 2027 visit last month. A visit this year is possible if Modi’s schedule permits, but Russia will otherwise arrange the meeting in the first half of next year, Kremlin presidential aide Yury Ushakov said.
The two countries are working toward an annual trade target of $100 billion by 2030, with energy, investment, and industrial cooperation central to their economic relationship. Bilateral trade reached $38 billion in the first six months of 2026, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar said at a business forum in Kazan last week.
Cooperation has also advanced on workforce mobility. Putin signed an agreement on the temporary employment of Indian and Russian nationals last week.
India remains a natural partner for Russia as Moscow strengthens its relations with Asian countries, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said last week. Maintaining strong ties serves the interests of both nations and the world, he added.

Authorities have received nearly 20,000 reports about property damage as a result of the torrential rainfall and the resulting floods, Governor Davut Gül said.
The toll from flooding in and around Istanbul last week rose to eight on Monday as rescuers found more bodies after Turkey's largest city was battered by the heaviest rainfall in over 80 years, officials said.
Six died in Istanbul, while the bodies of two more people from a neighbouring province were washed up on the southeastern outskirts of the megacity, Istanbul governor Davut Gül told reporters.
Wednesday's historic rainfall, which officials said was the heaviest since records began in 1942, caused chaos and flash flooding, with footage showing cars and people being dragged away by the fast-flowing waters.
By Thursday, Gül said three people had died and another five were missing as huge efforts were under way to drain the floodwaters and clear up the damage and destruction caused by the torrential rainfall.
One was a 14-year-old boy who was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle. A fourth body was found on Friday and a fifth on Sunday in the Golden Horn estuary, state media Anadolu said. Both were men.
On Monday, Gül's office said the body of another man was found near Ayvansaray ferry pier on the Golden Horn who had been reported missing.
"In Istanbul, a total of six people have died and one person is missing," Gül told reporters, saying another two people had died outside of Istanbul in the neighbouring province of Kocaeli.
"Two people who died in Kocaeli and were swept away as far as Pendik were found dead by our search and rescue teams. Therefore, a total of eight bodies have been found," he said, adding that search efforts were continuing for one more missing person.
So far, authorities have received nearly 20,000 reports about property damage as a result of the torrential rainfall and the resulting floods, Gül said.
"We experienced a disaster that generated around 19,300 reports, each with different types of problems. At this point, it has been determined that around 2,000 homes and about 900 businesses...have suffered serious damage," he said.
On Friday, authorities paid out 10,000 Turkish lira (€180) to 5,200 affected residents and will pay out the same amount to another 2,500 people on Monday, he said.

====================================================================================================

Women’s attention to beauty isn’t limited to the sex they’re attracted to, eye-tracking study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:17 UTC
21:00:17 KST

When viewing pairs of faces, men tend to linger selectively on attractive faces that match their sexual orientation, whereas women spend more time looking at attractive faces regardless of the person’s sex. A new eye-tracking study published in Evolution and Human Behavior suggests that this preference occurs during deliberate, sustained viewing rather than in the first split-second of automatic attention. The findings also indicate that being in a committed relationship does not necessarily stop people from looking longer at attractive faces.
In psychology, attentional bias refers to the tendency for our visual system to prioritize certain types of information over others in our environment. Facial attractiveness, which is the subjective judgment of how aesthetically pleasing a face is, acts as a strong magnet for human gaze. From an evolutionary perspective, physical beauty is often thought to serve as a signal of health and fertility, which may explain why human cognition is tuned to notice desirable potential mates.
How this visual pull operates depends heavily on both who is looking and who is being looked at. In a 2003 study of young adults, researchers outlined several competing possibilities for how gender and mating motives guide our eyes. One possibility is that people focus mainly on attractive members of their preferred sex to find mates, while another suggests that both men and women look longer at attractive women: men to evaluate potential partners, and women to assess potential romantic rivals. A third proposed that men in particular would show a strong pull toward attractive faces of their preferred sex, because physical attractiveness tends to weigh more heavily in men’s mate preferences.
Subsequent research has complicated this picture by examining how relationship status and different stages of mental processing shape our gaze. For instance, a 2018 eye-tracking study indicated that single people exhibit a stronger visual pull toward attractive faces than people in committed relationships, who may dial down their attention to protect their existing bond. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that when viewing faces matching their sexual preference, people’s brains initially react strongly to both very attractive and very unattractive faces before settling into sustained neural activity specifically for the attractive ones.
Psychologists separate visual attention into two distinct stages: immediate attention and volitional attention. Immediate attention is a rapid, automatic reflex that pulls our eyes toward a stimulus before we consciously think about it. Volitional attention is the slower, deliberate process of choosing where to keep looking to gather more information.
Separating these two stages matters for attractiveness research. A 2023 study of speed-daters, led by Tom S. Roth, the senior author of the new study, found that people’s personal ratings of facial attractiveness predicted where both men and women directed their deliberate gaze, while results for quicker, more automatic glances were mixed across the sexes. However, almost all prior eye-tracking studies on facial attractiveness have relied on college undergraduates, whose casual dating habits may not reflect how older adults in long-term relationships view attractive strangers.
To address this, lead author Johanna M. Bellue and her colleagues, including Roth, an assistant professor at Utrecht University, set out to test how immediate and deliberate attention to attractive faces varies by sex, sexual preference, age, and relationship status in the general public.
“Previous studies on attractiveness bias have mostly been performed with heterosexual undergraduate students as a sample,” Roth told PsyPost. “However, to understand this phenomenon it is more interesting to see whether similar effects are present in a broader sample, containing people of different ages, relationship statuses, and sexual orientations.”
The researchers recruited 105 adults attending the Betweter Festival, an annual public science festival held at a music venue in Utrecht, the Netherlands. After excluding three non-binary participants, who all reported being pansexual and so had no “non-preferred” faces to compare, the final sample included 65 women and 37 men. The participants had an average age of 38, and most (87 of the 102) were heterosexual, while the 63 participants in exclusive relationships had been with their partners for an average of about 12.6 years.
Each participant sat in a booth about 60 centimeters away from a computer monitor equipped with an infrared eye-tracker that recorded their eye movements 300 times per second. To prevent participants from consciously altering their behavior, the researchers told them only that the study examined general face perception, without mentioning attractiveness. Across 36 main trials, participants viewed pairs of same-sex portrait photos, either two men or two women, with neutral expressions.
Each pair featured one conventionally attractive face and one less attractive face, selected from established academic photo databases based on pre-existing consensus ratings. All of the faces were of white adults, mostly in their twenties and thirties. The face pairs remained on the screen for three seconds while participants looked wherever they wanted. Afterward, participants completed a paper questionnaire detailing their age, sex, sexual orientation, relationship status, relationship length, and how many alcoholic drinks they had consumed at the festival that evening.
The authors matched each participant’s stated sexual orientation with the sex of the faces shown on screen to categorize every trial as either “preferred” or “non-preferred.” For example, female faces were coded as preferred for heterosexual men and homosexual women, while all faces were coded as preferred for bisexual participants. In their statistical models, the team controlled for alcohol consumption, which photo database the images came from, and whether the attractive face appeared on the left or right side of the screen.
When looking at immediate attention, measured by which of the two faces a participant’s eyes landed on first within half a second of the images appearing, facial attractiveness had no noticeable effect. Women looked at the attractive face first about 50.0% of the time for their preferred sex and 50.7% of the time for their non-preferred sex, which is essentially a coin toss. Men looked at the attractive face first in 53.9% of preferred-sex trials and 49.9% of non-preferred-sex trials, a difference that was not statistically robust.
Instead of beauty, the first automatic glance was heavily dictated by screen position. Participants looked at the left image first in roughly 78% of the trials, regardless of how attractive the person was. This strong leftward habit is a well-known quirk of how the human brain’s hemispheres process visual space, and it may have masked any immediate pull toward attractive faces, as could the noisy festival setting. The null result also contrasts with some earlier reaction-time studies that found a rapid pull toward attractive faces, which the authors suggest may reflect differences in the type of attention each method captures.
A different pattern emerged when the researchers examined volitional attention, which was measured by the proportion of total viewing time spent looking at the attractive face over the full three seconds. Women demonstrated a general appreciation for facial beauty, spending 55.4% of their viewing time on the attractive face when looking at their preferred sex and 54.7% when looking at their non-preferred sex. Both figures were statistically above the 50% mark that would indicate equal viewing.
Men, by contrast, were more selective with their deliberate gaze. They spent 54.9% of their viewing time on the attractive face when the pair matched their sexual preference, but only 52.0% when viewing their non-preferred sex, a figure that did not reliably differ from chance. Men’s bias toward attractive faces of their preferred sex was no stronger than women’s, and a statistical test comparing the two sexes’ patterns directly fell just short of the study’s threshold, partly because women also looked slightly longer at attractive faces of their preferred sex.
The authors note that the pattern parallels earlier research suggesting that men’s visual and physical sexual responses tend to be specific to their preferred sex, whereas women’s tend to be less specific.
“We find that men and women differ in their attractiveness bias,” Roth explained. “Men are specifically interested in attractive faces that align with their sexual orientation, while women have a general bias toward attractive faces of both sexes. This is in line with previous research. We don’t find that men have a stronger bias toward attractiveness in their preferred sex, as has been suggested by some evolutionary hypotheses.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that more attractive faces drew more direct eye movements but did not speed reactions on a task measuring attention shifts that happen without moving the eyes. Although the two studies used different tasks, both suggest that attractiveness influences where people choose to look more than it captures attention automatically.
The researchers also ran statistical simulations to predict how a newly recruited individual would behave, rather than just looking at group averages. They found that a new female participant would have about an 80% probability of looking longer at attractive faces of either sex, while a new male participant would have a 76% probability for attractive faces of his preferred sex, but only about 62% for his non-preferred sex. This wider uncertainty at the individual level suggests that while the group trend is reliable, personal viewing habits vary considerably from one person to the next.
“While humans do seem to have an attractiveness bias of some kind, we also found that there is quite some variation between participants,” Roth noted. “While the majority of individuals indeed have a bias, others do not. This shows that it is at least not a fixed trait that generalizes to everyone.”
Contrary to expectations and some prior university-based studies, relationship status did not meaningfully alter how long people looked at attractive faces of their preferred sex. Participants in exclusive relationships spent just as much time looking at attractive faces as participants who were single or in open relationships. In addition, an exploratory check of participant age showed only weak, inconclusive tendencies, with attractiveness bias slightly increasing with age in men and slightly decreasing in women.
“We were also interested in effects of relationship status, but we did not find any,” Roth said. “We had expected that people might look less at attractive faces that aligned with their preference when they were in a relationship, as they want to ‘protect’ their relationship. However, our sample mostly contained data from participants who were already in very established relationships with a long duration. Maybe our expected effect would apply more to new relationships specifically.”
The authors noted that this difference in relationship maturity may help explain why their festival sample behaved differently from student populations. In the early stages of dating, which are common among college students, people may actively avoid looking at attractive strangers to protect a fragile new bond and build trust. Once a relationship has lasted over a decade, partners may feel secure enough that they no longer need to unconsciously police where their eyes wander during a casual viewing task. It is also possible that relationship status only dampens attention when people are first primed to think about romance or their partner, a step used in several earlier studies that this experiment omitted.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. “One important caveat is that we measured where people looked, not whom they wanted to date or felt sexually attracted to,” Roth added. “Women looking longer at attractive faces of both sexes should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of sexual interest in both sexes.”
Because the experiment took place at a bustling public festival, the researchers had to keep the procedure brief and relied on pre-existing average ratings to define which faces were attractive. People have diverse personal tastes, meaning a participant might not have personally found the designated “attractive” face appealing, which could dilute the measured gaze patterns.
The festival setting also meant that the researchers recruited whoever volunteered rather than sampling to balance groups, resulting in noticeably more women and coupled people than men and singles. The photo databases featured only white faces, mostly of young adults in their twenties and thirties, which may have skewed how older participants responded to the images. Future studies could test larger, evenly balanced groups using faces of many different ages, while also asking participants to rate the faces themselves and answer detailed questions about their relationship satisfaction and jealousy.
“Although our science-festival sample covered a broader age range than a typical student sample, it still overrepresents highly educated people from urban settings, and most participants were heterosexual,” Roth said. “Recruiting people from a wider range of backgrounds and sexual orientations would help us establish how broadly these patterns apply. We would also like to account more directly for individual preferences: the faces that are attractive on average are not necessarily the ones that every individual finds attractive.”
The study, “Sexual preference modulates attentional bias towards attractive faces in men, but not women,” was authored by Johanna M. Bellue, David Terburg, Mirre E. Balke, Tessa W. Coster, Jorg J.M. Massen, and Tom S. Roth.

Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

These warmly spiced fritters are inspired by the tikki-chaat carts found all over India, which sizzle fresh chickpea, potato or lentil patties on hot-plates until crisp, then slather them with chutneys. The coconut sambol ushers forth the flavours of south India – coconut, mustard seeds and lime; add a teaspoon of tamarind paste to increase the tartness, if you like. A good dollop of yoghurt is a must, and a fried egg or avocado on the side turns these fritters into a satisfying supper.
Masala chickpea and parsnip fritters with coconut sambol
Prep 10 min
 
Cook 30 min
 
Serves 2-3
60g red chillies (about 4 large ones)
 
5 tbsp vegetable oil, plus extra for frying
 
4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
 
65g desiccated coconut
  
2 tsp black mustard seeds
  
1½ tsp fine sea salt
  
2 tbsp brown sugar
 
2 tbsp tomato puree
  
Juice and grated zest of 1 large lime, plus 1 lime extra, cut into wedges, to serve
  
400g tin 
 chickpeas, drained
 
2 large parsnips, peeled and grated
 
2 tsp garam masala
  
2 tsp coriander seeds, crushed
 
100g ricotta
  
3 
 tbsp plain flour
  
1 tbsp baking powder
  
15g fresh coriander, finely chopped, plus extra to serve
 
Yoghurt, to serve
  
Fried egg or avocado
 , to serve (optional)
In a small blender, blitz the chillies, four tablespoons of vegetable oil and two crushed garlic cloves to make a smooth paste.
Toast the coconut and mustard seeds in a small frying pan over a medium heat for one to two minutes, until they take on a little colour. Pour in the chilli paste with 100ml water, then cook for four to five minutes, until much of the water has evaporated and the paste begins to darken. Add a teaspoon of fine salt, the brown sugar, tomato puree, lime juice and zest, then cook for another two minutes, until you have a thick sambol. Empty into a bowl and leave to cool.
Blitz the chickpeas and the remaining tablespoon of vegetable oil to a coarse paste in a blender or food processor. Put this in a large bowl with the grated parsnips, the remaining two crushed garlic cloves, the garam masala, crushed coriander seeds, ricotta, plain flour, baking powder, fresh coriander and a half-teaspoon of salt. Mix together using your hands until fully combined, then shape into six large patties, about 4-5cm wide and 1½cm thick.
Heat a little vegetable oil in a nonstick frying pan, then cook the fritters in batches over medium heat for seven to eight minutes, flipping occasionally, until golden brown on both sides. Serve warm with a dollop of yoghurt, a generous spoon of coconut sambol and a fried egg or avocado, if you like. Garnish with fresh coriander and a wedge of lime.

Third Ebola case in Kenya highlights US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.
It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.
The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.
“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.
Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.
“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.
“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.
The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”
The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”
Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.
The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.
A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.
Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of infections in the country was eight.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.
“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.
In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.
Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.
Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.
“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.
Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.
Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”
