====================================================================================================

Israel’s AI propaganda was built to silence Palestinians. Now it targets voters at home.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:36:46 UTC
20:36:46 KST

Israel’s first election advertisement to be banned for undisclosed use of artificial intelligence presented a scene of peace. In the fabricated video, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot embraces Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas.
The footage was produced by Bezalel Smotrich’s far-right Religious Zionism party to frighten voters with the suggestion that Eisenkot might reconcile with the Palestinians.
The irony is difficult to miss. A synthetic image of coexistence was deployed as a political threat by a movement whose ministers have openly advocated annexation, displacement and the destruction of Palestinian life.
Yet the fake video is only the visible edge of a much larger system.
As Israel approaches crucial national elections, AI is not simply being used to invent images. It is being used to manufacture voters, infiltrate private conversations, harvest personal information, and quietly shape what people believe is public opinion.
The Economist reports that Israeli technology companies have developed swarms of bots that masquerade as human voters, influence online conversations and distort informal polls.
More sophisticated AI avatars can have telephone numbers and even credit cards, letting them join WhatsApp groups and act like real people.
Political campaigns can combine information gathered through chatbots with commercial data on purchases, searches, viewing habits, and location, then tailor advertisements, messages, and lifelike robocalls to individual voters.
This should alarm anyone concerned with democracy. But there is a danger in telling the story as though Israel has suddenly discovered a menacing technology on the eve of its own election.
The machinery did not appear from nowhere. It was developed, funded and normalised through years of information warfare directed at Palestinians, Arabs and Western publics. What is new is not the weapon. It is the identity of some of its targets.
Money poured into Hasbara
Since October 2023, Israel has treated public opinion as another front in its genocidal war on Gaza.
Its government has poured extraordinary sums into hasbara, the state’s public diplomacy and influence apparatus.
Its 2025 allocation of roughly $150 million was already a dramatic expansion.
The 2026 budget reportedly raised that figure to about $730 million. An investigation by the Quincy Institute concluded that direct Israeli government spending on public diplomacy since October 2023 had exceeded $1 billion.
That money does more than purchase conventional advertising.
In 2024, OpenAI exposed an Israel-based influence operation it called ‘Zero Zeno’. The network, operated by the Israeli political marketing firm STOIC, used AI to generate articles, comments and fabricated online personas across Facebook, Instagram, X, YouTube and websites posing as independent organisations.
Its material attacked UNRWA, portrayed pro-Palestinian university protesters as “supporters of terrorism” and targeted audiences in the United States, Canada and elsewhere. Reporting at the time linked the wider campaign to Israel’s Ministry of Diaspora Affairs, which denied involvement.
The ambition has since become even more brazen. A 2026 investigation revealed that an apparently fictitious American think tank, the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, had published more than 560,000 words in nine days.
Its reports were dressed as neutral, sourced research on questions such as whether Israel was committing genocide, starving Palestinians or torturing prisoners.
The site was part of an Israeli-government-funded campaign designed to influence what AI chatbots tell users. One contract explicitly referred to delivering ‘GPT framing results’ in chatbot conversations.
This is more insidious than a clumsy deepfake. A false video can be identified, labelled and removed. But when thousands of synthetic accounts, pseudo-academic reports and engineered search results flood the information environment, propaganda begins to resemble consensus.
A user asking an apparently neutral chatbot about Gaza may never know that some of the material shaping its answer was created by a foreign government seeking to obscure its own conduct.
A manipulation apparatus
For Palestinians, this is not an abstract debate about technological ethics. The manipulation of information accompanies the destruction of lives.
While Palestinians document children killed, hospitals attacked, families starved and entire neighbourhoods erased, an immensely funded apparatus works to dispute the evidence, smear the witnesses and recast demands for accountability as “extremism” or “anti-Semitism”.
AI allows that apparatus to operate at a scale no team of human propagandists could match.
It also helps explain a familiar distortion in Western debate.
Palestinian voices are routinely treated as interested, emotional or unreliable, while Israeli state claims are repeated as the default account even when they later collapse under scrutiny.
Digital influence operations exploit that imbalance. They do not need to convince everyone. They only need to create enough noise, doubt, and artificial agreement to delay political action while facts on the ground become irreversible.
Now the same culture of manipulation is turning inward. Netanyahu and his allies have spent years building databases and election technology, while opposition-linked figures in Israel’s powerful tech sector are reportedly preparing to fight with similar tools.
The problem therefore cannot be reduced to one party or one politician. Once covert persuasion becomes an accepted instrument of statecraft, it does not remain neatly confined to foreign audiences.
A system designed to impersonate citizens abroad will eventually impersonate citizens at home.
There is another bitter contradiction.
Israeli institutions are now discussing safeguards to protect Israeli voters from AI-generated deception, yet there has been little comparable concern for the millions of people abroad whose politics have already been targeted—or for Palestinians whose reality these campaigns were built to erase.
Democracy cannot mean defending Israeli citizens from manipulation while accepting the covert manipulation of Americans, Europeans and Arabs as legitimate public diplomacy.
Nor should governments in London, Washington or Brussels treat this solely as an Israeli election story.
Foreign interference does not become benign because it comes from an ally. If Russia, China or Iran financed fake American organisations, synthetic citizens and campaigns intended to alter what chatbots tell voters, Western officials would describe it as a threat to national security.
Israel should not receive an exemption from standards applied to everyone else.
‘Profiled, targeted and manipulated’
The lesson is larger than Netanyahu. Governments must require full disclosure of state-funded digital campaigns, enforce foreign-agent and data-protection laws, compel technology companies to expose coordinated inauthentic networks and create transparency around efforts to manipulate AI training and retrieval systems.
Political parties should be prohibited from deploying synthetic identities or using covertly harvested personal data to suppress or redirect voters.
But regulation alone will not answer the moral question. Israel’s influence machine exists because its leaders believe the problem is not what the state has done to Palestinians, but that the world has seen too much of it.
No algorithm can make mass killing humane, occupation democratic or starvation defensible. The more public opinion turns against these policies, the more money and technology are spent trying to correct the public rather than the policy.
Israel’s AI propaganda apparatus is now coming home. The danger to Israeli voters is real, but Palestinians have lived for years with the consequences of the worldview that produced it: that people can be profiled, targeted and manipulated; that inconvenient truths can be buried beneath manufactured narratives; and that technology can solve a political crisis created by domination.
A weapon does not become objectionable only when those who built it discover that it can be aimed at them.

On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:35:52 UTC
20:35:52 KST

On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahu
In the rest of the world, the Israeli PM is often blamed for the Iran war. His opponents say he hasn’t been tough enough with Tehran.
When Israel launched a sweeping military assault on Iran with the United States in February, the Israeli government enjoyed overwhelming support from the Jewish Israeli public.
Opposition parties lent their support to the army and backed the audacious step. Enmity towards the government in Iran is an issue mainstream Zionist parties agree on.
Then in June, Israel’s role in the confrontation halted abruptly with an announcement from US President Donald Trump, who said Iran and Israel had agreed to stop attacking each other.
That announcement – and Netanyahu’s decision to abide by it at the time – were unpopular in Israel. According to the Israel Democracy Institute, 65 to 70 percent of Jewish Israelis believe that stopping the war did not serve Israel’s national security interests.
As Israelis prepare to vote in national elections on October 27, Iran remains an important election issue for many. Opposition parties present Iran as an example of what they say are Netanyahu’s many failures. They promise to reset security and foreign policy if they’re elected.
The frontrunner, Gadi Eisenkot, says the conflict is unfinished. While saying that a change in Iran’s government was an unrealistic goal, Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of doing little to dismantle Iran’s nuclear programme. In September at the inauguration of his new party, Yashar, Eisenkot told supporters: “Ultimately, it must end in the destruction or dismantling of the Iranian nuclear programme, a goal not yet achieved with 440kg [970lb] of highly enriched uranium already there, which could quickly be turned into several nuclear devices.”
Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, who is now the head of the opposition in the Knesset, accuses Netanyahu of a strategic failure. He recently told the Atlantic Council that toppling the administration in Tehran is a realistic objective that requires a military escalation: “What Israel should do or the alliance should do is bomb all the energy facilities, especially on Kharg Island, but other places as well in order to make sure that the Iranian economy is demolished. And the reason is that it’s the only thing that will overturn the regime.”
Bombing this civilian infrastructure was actually something Netanyahu had lobbied for himself. An international outcry about such bombings likely constituting war crimes and Trump’s refusal to offer backing put the brakes on the plan.
Naftali Bennett, another former prime minister, says Israel must ensure its military dominance over the entire region. For Bennett, toppling the government in Iran and crushing it is a must. But he says that is not enough. The right-wing politician calls Qatar an “enemy” and says Turkiye is “the new Iran”, going as far as saying that military confrontation with the NATO member was inevitable.
“We will build an alliance of moderate forces in the region against the Islamist forces, against Iran, against Qatar, Turkiye and all the radical forces. We will take proactive actions to shape the region,” Bennett recently told supporters.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders do not rule out renewed confrontations. They focus on their confidence in the military and security establishment in assessing the dangers and dealing with them appropriately.
But opposition leaders have voiced concern that Netanyahu might resort to military escalation before the elections to tilt the balance in his favour or even disrupt them altogether – even though the prime minister said last week that he did not plan to attack Iran before the vote.
Those fears were elevated after Netanyahu posted a video from the Tel Nof Airbase warning that Israel’s enemies might attack before the elections. Other news reports said Netanyahu has shared intelligence on new threats from Iran with the US president.
Netanyahu was quickly rebuked by opposition leaders, who accused him of “political fearmongering”.
Lapid openly questioned Netanyahu’s motives. Lapid also accused him of using the Israeli military and bases as “backdrops” for election campaign videos.
Ultimately, most Israeli opposition parties and leaders aren’t opposed to war with Iran, and many are in fact even more hawkish in their approach towards Tehran than Netanyahu. They just don’t want a new military escalation before the elections.

Israel to Supply PULS Systems and EXTRA-MR Missiles to Unnamed European Country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:35:24 UTC
20:35:24 KST

Israeli company Elbit Systems has signed a contract worth approximately $235 million to supply EXTRA-MR missiles and PULS multiple launch rocket systems to a European country.
The developer’s press service reported the deal.
The contract is scheduled to be completed over three years.
Under the agreement, Elbit Systems will supply EXTRA-MR medium-range missiles, PULS launchers, associated artillery platforms, and a logistics support package.
EXTRA-MR is a precision-guided missile designed to effectively engage high-value targets at ranges of up to 80 km. It is fully integrated with PULS launchers and existing C4I systems.
The development of the PULS (Precise & Universal Launching System) began with the Lynx rocket artillery system, developed by Israel Military Industries, which was later acquired by Elbit Systems. Israeli engineers sought to create a universal, modular platform that could launch a wide range of munitions without extensive technical modifications.
The system’s key conceptual feature is its use of a container-based design. PULS is equipped with two standardized transport-launch containers, each loaded with a specific missile type based on mission requirements, ranging from unguided rockets to precision-guided ballistic and cruise missiles.
The artillery system can employ AccuLAR-122 rockets (18 rockets per launch pod, with a range of up to 35 km), AccuLAR-160 rockets (10 rockets, with a range of up to 40 km), EXTRA missiles (4 missiles, with a range of up to 150 km), as well as Predator Hawk ballistic missiles (2 missiles, with a range of up to 300 km).
The EXTRA (Extended Range Artillery) missile has a 306 mm caliber, a length of about 4.7 meters, and a total weight of nearly 450 kg. It carries either a high-explosive fragmentation warhead or a penetrating warhead weighing up to 120 kg.
The high accuracy of the EXTRA and EXTRA-MR missiles is achieved through a combined guidance system that integrates GPS satellite navigation with an inertial navigation system, providing a circular error probable of less than 10 meters at maximum firing range.
The PULS launcher can be mounted on a variety of wheeled chassis with a payload capacity of 10 tonnes or more, including those manufactured by Tatra, MAN, and Scania. The system can transition from march configuration to combat-ready position in less than three minutes.
PULS’s versatility and advanced technical capabilities have made it highly sought after on the international market. In addition to the Israel Defense Forces, where it is in service under the designation Lahav, the system and its variants have been selected by the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany (MARS 3), and several other NATO and Middle Eastern countries.

Hundreds of people missed their flights and thousands more faced long delays at Schiphol on Sunday after all 78 of the airport’s automatic passport gates went down at around 6am.
The Royal Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border checks, said the outage was caused by an IT malfunction and that there was “no indication whatsoever” of a cyberattack.
The exact cause is still being investigated, but the results will not be made public, Marechaussee head of press, Major Mike Hofman, told Dutch News.
“For operational reasons, we do not comment regarding the further configuration, operation and technical details of our systems,” he said.
With the e-gates down, everyone flying to or from a country outside the Schengen area had to be checked manually by hand, including passengers in transit. The Marechaussee opened every desk and carried out less thorough checks to keep the queues moving.
Passengers waited an hour on average, and some waited up to an hour and a half, Schiphol officials said. The gates were working again by around 3pm.
KLM held departures where possible, and Transavia said it would be flexible with rebookings. A claims specialist told the Telegraaf the number of people affected in some way could run into the tens of thousands.
Few are likely to receive compensation, experts told the paper, because the outage will probably count as force majeure since the e-gates are run by the Marechaussee, not the airlines. The Marechaussee said travellers who missed their flights should contact their airline.
The outage happened during one of the busiest weekends of the autumn, as the one-week October school holiday began in the middle and south of the country and ended in the north. The Amsterdam marathon on Sunday also attracted thousands of runners to the city from all over the world.

The third President of Ukraine, Viktor Yushchenko, emphasized that history and language form the core foundation of Ukraine's state agency and sovereignty.
"One of the Institute's key missions is that we must understand our enemy... For 300 years we were taught to be confused about who he really is," he said at a forum celebrating the 20th anniversary of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP) in Kyiv on Monday.
He stressed that national memory work constitutes a grand national endeavor.
"Lina Kostenko wrote: 'Nations do not die of a heart attack; they do not get sick from it. Nations die when their language is taken away from them.' I add a comma. What if a nation's culture is taken away, does it not die? It dies. And if its memory is taken away, does it die? It dies," he added.
Yushchenko noted that history and language are fundamental components of Ukraine's national subjectivity and identity.

Women’s wheelchair basketball beat Cambodia at Asian Para Games
TEHRAN - Iran’s women’s wheelchair basketball team got off the mark at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games on Monday, beating Cambodia 52-39 in their third match of the tournament.
After back-to-back defeats to Japan and Thailand, Iran needed a response, and they delivered. It was a tight opening half, with the Iranians edging ahead 24-23 at the break.
The second half was a different story. Iran stepped up in brilliant fashion, pulling away from Cambodia to seal a comfortable 13-point win.
It is the team’s first victory of the 2026 Para Asian Games.
Iran still have China and Laos to face. The women’s wheelchair basketball event at the fifth edition of the Games is a round-robin featuring six teams: Iran, Japan, Thailand, China, Laos and Cambodia.

Georgia exported record-breaking 948.4 tons of figs to Russia in September 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:31:40 UTC
20:31:40 KST

TBILISI, October 19. /TASS/. Georgian fig deliveries to Russia stood at 948.4 metric tons in September 2026, marking a record-breaking monthly high, according to data from the Georgian national statistical service reviewed by TASS.
According to the authority, exports of fresh or dried figs from Georgia to Russia in September reached 948.4 metric tons valued at $1.3 mln, which is 1.7 times higher than the figure of September of last year. The previous record for fig shipments to Russia was set in August 2025 and amounted to 916.6 metric tons.
In total, since July, the start of the fig ripening season, Georgia has exported 1,800 metric tons to Russia valued at $2.4 mln. Apart from Russia, this commodity was purchased from Georgia in minor quantities by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan (18 metric tons each), and Armenia (2.5 metric tons).

UK may sanction firms bidding on Israel’s E1 settlement tender, Miliband warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:30:24 UTC
20:30:24 KST

British foreign minister Ed Miliband on Monday urged companies and individuals not to proceed with bids for the E1 West Bank settlement project, warning those involved in the construction of settlements could face sanctions.
"We urge businesses and individuals not to proceed with bids for E1 construction tenders," Miliband said in a statement. "They should be aware of legal and reputational consequences, including the risk of involving themselves in serious breaches of international law."
E1 is a largely undeveloped area between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim. Its location has made it one of the most disputed construction projects in the West Bank.
Many Western states and campaign groups have opposed the project over concerns that it could undermine a future peace deal with the Palestinians.
Contractors warned on deadline to submit bids for E1 tender
Last month, the Jerusalem District Court allowed a tender for 1,234 homes in the E1 area to move forward, but did not decide whether the underlying construction plans are legal.
Contractors have until the end of the day on Monday to submit bids for the project. Their proposals must then be examined, winners selected, and building permits obtained before work can begin.
Sa'ar responds to Miliband: "Israel will not be intimidated by threats"
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar strongly condemned Miliband's remarks, defending Israel's historical claims to the West Bank and insisting that Israel would no longer tolerate threats or attempts to dictate its policies.
"The days when Israel would quietly accept threats, sanctions and attempts to dictate its policies are over," Sa'ar said.
"Judea and Samaria are not foreign lands to the Jewish people. Our historical rights are not subject to approval from London," he continued.
Sa'ar then turned his criticism toward the British Labour government, arguing that it should focus on the challenges facing the UK rather than targeting Israel.
"The British Labour Government would do better to address the serious challenges facing its own country rather than pursue its relentless campaign against the Jewish state," Sa'ar said.
"Israel will not be intimidated by threats. We will defend our rights and our national interests," he concluded.
Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

Nathan Fielder’s Surprise Call From Elizabeth Holmes: ‘I Trust You’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

A few months ago, Nathan Fielder’s publicist sent me an unexpected email: Would WIRED be interested in Fielder for a fall cover of our magazine?
The answer, before we even got a reason, was yes. The reason, it turned out, was that Fielder would soon release a project that was so top-secret, I’d need to sign an NDA to even hear about what it was—let alone watch it. I signed, I heard, and then I saw, counting myself among the few dozen people who’d screened You Can See Everything before the film debuted in the first days of September as a secret addition to the Telluride Film Festival.
If you’re a human being with internet access, you know that the buzz following Telluride was nothing short of an online thermonuclear event: Reddit forums exploded; best-in-class memes were born overnight; every journalist on planet Earth, including the staff at WIRED (who had no idea their boss was NDA’d to hell, and seemed confused when I ordered them repeatedly not to contact Nathan Fielder’s publicist), pined, pleaded, and jockeyed for access to the film. Or, even better, for access to Fielder himself. The notoriously inscrutable performer, after all, has become a cult hero for his ability to turn human discomfort into high art. He built a coffee shop called Dumb Starbucks, creating an international news event in the process. He built an entire fake bar so that one man could practice having a difficult conversation with a friend. He trained to be a commercial airline pilot—lunacy!—and flew a 737 filled with passengers (the Miracle over the Mojave), in what can only be described as the most transcendent moment of television I’ve ever seen. For a certain genre of viewer, Nathan Fielder is a comedic god among us mere mortals.
He’s also, not surprisingly, rather particular. Fielder was going to do the cover of WIRED; then maybe he wasn’t. A week went by. Our features director and I didn’t sleep. Then we were a “go.” Great! For a few days, at least, until things got dicey again. This kind of back-and-forth is a normal part of booking celebrities. But given the secrecy, the buzz, the Nathan of it all—the stakes for WIRED were high. I told several people in my life that I hated Nathan Fielder. Then we were on again. I told several people in my life that I loved Nathan Fielder.
You might be wondering: If I found Fielder’s pre-interview agita so stressful, why didn’t we just scrap the cover entirely? Maybe see if Aaron Sorkin was still available, or some other guy involved in some other tech-adjacent fall movie. There are plenty.
The thing is, You Can See Everything is a singularly astonishing film. I’d go so far as to say that it’s among the best I’ve ever seen. Codirected by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it begins as a strange, captivating, occasionally hilarious 34-day psychological dance between Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes, and her partner Billy Evans before Holmes’ incarceration, and subsequently morphs into something so beguiling and brilliant that it’s futile to try to describe. After screening You Can See Everything in early September, I thought about the movie every single day until I saw it again a few weeks later. I’m still rolling it around in my brain. When a small handful of WIRED staffers screened the film before Fielder’s cover shoot, we spent hours afterward debating facial expressions, relationships, and even the meaning of single sentences. We agreed on very little, other than that Fielder—notorious for his meticulous building of worlds—seemed to have finally stumbled into one much stranger than anything he could have conjured.
When I ultimately sat down with Fielder for a conversation in late September, any lingering irritation at his pre-interview jitters instantly fell away: For all of his overthinking, lines in the sand, and apparent ambivalence to press, Fielder presented as considerate and genuine. Over nearly an hour and a half, Fielder—in trademark New Balance sneakers and nondescript men’s apparel, a Summit Ice windbreaker in tow—slumped casually on a sofa, seemed to mull my questions earnestly and in good faith, and did the best he possibly could to answer them. Verbal communication, Fielder repeated several times in our conversation, isn’t always easy for him. It’s a quality that’s often put to good use in his work, and his blunt demeanor makes Fielder particularly effective in the role of truth-seeker vis-à-vis Holmes and Evans. The same can’t be said for a sit-down interview, which made my conversation with Fielder all the more endearing in the moment; at least, I told myself, the man was really trying.
Our time together concluded at 2:17 pm; I’d been warned beforehand that Fielder had a Zoom meeting at 2:15 pm sharp. “I’m trusting you,” his publicist told me before leaving us alone to talk. I took the entreaty seriously, practically shoving Fielder out of the room as soon as I realized he was running late. This lovely, thoughtful man has a meeting! Days later, a thought gnawed at me: 2:15 pm is an odd time to start a meeting. On a Sunday, no less.
I couldn’t shake it. Had the publicist looked me in the eyes and lied? Had Nathan? I considered asking them outright. I’ve never been one for ambiguity, and a journalist craves nothing more than to know what’s real. Then again, people make things up all the time. They present different versions of themselves to different people, obfuscate and perform, and they do it in little ways and sometimes bigger ones. Did it really matter if he’d left for a real meeting or the excuse of one? And hadn’t I spent enough time letting Nathan Fielder make me feel crazy?
In the end, I decided that this time it was better not to know. It was better just to trust. And after a second talk with Fielder a few weeks after our first conversation, I learned that Elizabeth Holmes might feel the same way.
The interview has been edited for clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: I have a lot of anxiety about recording interviews.
NATHAN FIELDER: Why? About losing the recording?
Yeah.
OK. You have a backup too.
I have two.
I would do the same thing.
Do you?
What?
Double-record things?
No, but if I had your job, I would.
OK. Before we get into it, I just want you to know that I know how important it is for you to preserve the experience of the film.
Yes. But you know, some people enjoy knowing what happens. I read this thing where they told people the end of a story, and then they had another group that didn’t know, and then the group that knew the ending said they enjoyed it more.
So it could just be a me thing. Maybe it is. But I love being surprised. I love the experience of just sort of not knowing.
When this interview comes out, the film will be just out in theaters. But it was a secret for three years, right?
Yeah.
My understanding is that only a few dozen people knew it was happening.
We kept it really small.
Secrecy has been a feature of your work before. What made you decide to keep it so under wraps? Why was that important to you?
I think, firstly, it was a concern on the subjects’ part. No one knew where they were at first. But while we were shooting there, paparazzi started surrounding the location and all that. So one of the understandings was, we needed to keep it secret because it could affect things with them, and we didn’t want to do anything where our involvement would be a news story or change things with them.
In addition to that, I think when stuff comes out about a thing, then the narrative is out there, and it may affect our ability to make the project. We didn’t know who we wanted to talk to or get on camera. We didn’t have a plan when we went in, so we were just like, “It’s best to operate in a place where no one knows it exists.” We thought it would be a net benefit.
How many people did you have to lie to about this?
I didn’t lie as much as say, “Oh, I can’t talk about this thing I’m working on, but I really want you to see it when it’s out.” People knew I was working on something. My family knew, people I’m close with that are trusted friends and collaborators.
And now there’s a teaser out. There’s a trailer. That’s about it. How did you think about the lead-up to the film? Was that strategic in terms of deciding what to put out there and what not to?
Is this strategic? I don’t know. I think everyone didn’t really know how to handle this.
Even people at A24 didn’t know we were making this for a bit, because we just went and started doing it, and so it wasn’t really on their radar in terms of what it’s gonna look like. Then, they’re the pros on how to release a movie. I think they saw an opportunity in doing it all at once at Telluride. I was like, "Will that be enough time?" Because they normally have a long lead time when they first do these movie things. It was gonna give us five weeks until it was released.
Oh, wow.
They felt confident in their plan. And then it was a question of what we put out there. We got the sense pretty early on that she’s a very toxic figure to people everywhere, so I understood that we were dealing with material that people were gonna project a lot onto. I think everyone thought that maybe the audience will meet us halfway with some of the stuff we put out.
Have you been reading the speculation? Are you reading—
Speculation about what?
About the film, from everyone who hasn’t seen it.
What are people speculating? I haven’t seen.
Theories that she’s naked, that you’re naked, that—
Oh that.
—that you dress up as Elizabeth Holmes, that you become her. I saw an image someone made of you with a blonde wig on.
I haven’t seen a lot of that stuff. When this all came out and we did the Telluride Film Festival, my phone was off for that whole night, and then I started looking at some stuff the next day, but there was a lot, and it was a little overwhelming. I couldn’t really engage with everything. I definitely understand that people would project stuff onto a new project that feels like stuff I’ve done in the past. But this is a totally unique thing. It feels, to me, so different than what I’ve done before in the way it came together, in the way it functions, and what we’re able to explore in it.
I’ve never done something like this before, but the process was fascinating, and I really enjoyed shooting this way. It was a real freeing and fascinating experience.
What was freeing about it?
Well, for example, I think a lot of projects usually have to be generated by you. You have a concept, and you go and pitch that concept, and then you have to present a plan to get the money to make it, and then you go and execute it. Things can change while you’re doing it, but usually if they green-light a project, you have to deliver something.
Ideally.
Yes. You can’t—
You seem like someone who plans quite a bit.
I mean, I try to. I try to plan, and then I’m always met with the absurdity of me trying to plan too much. I experienced that when I did Nathan for You. I was trying to be like, “OK, we can know where things would go.” But then the best moments were when we’re just totally surprised by something we didn’t expect, and then we end up going in that direction. And the aftermath of that was like, “Why did I think I could predict or control that?”
That was part of the inspiration for The Rehearsal—that tendency that I have to want to, like, plan. There is a pressure sometimes of, “you have to deliver something,” so you want to think things through. You can’t just go into something.
But with this, because I came into this feeling like the story’s been told about her, I was very interested in meeting her, but I did not see what a film about her or a project about her could be.
You and Lance reached out to her initially, right?
It was a bit of a both thing, because she and Billy [Evans] had approached A24 with the desire to have their life documented in some way. But no one was attached. It’s just them approaching A24. And I guess the negotiations fell apart because there was nothing to it, really.
Months later, I heard that that had happened. So I called A24 and said, “Well, could I meet her?” That was the start of it all.
Why her for you? Why did she seem interesting?
It’s a good question. Sometimes I don’t know why I’m drawn to something. But I had read Bad Blood.
Yeah.
I was really interested in that book when it came out, and I thought her relationship to the media was interesting too, because she sort of went silent and didn’t talk to anyone about anything in the aftermath. I was just personally curious. Like, “I wonder what this person’s like.”
And also, why now? Why is she wanting to speak and have her life documented and do it in this way? And even after I met her, if I didn’t know what I knew, I would just think I was talking with a very affable, soft-spoken, kind person. But then I kept having this thing where I was tracking my thoughts about how honest she was being, or if I was being manipulated in some way.
The feeling is so odd. It felt like watching a magician. I talk about it a little in the film, but when me and Lance were first talking about her, we happened to be at the Magic Castle. I’m a member, and it just came up that way. It was sort of poetic. I told A24, “I don’t really know what the angle is, but there is something tickling in my brain.”
She was about to go to prison, so we didn’t know what was gonna happen. I was like, “If you guys want, I’m down to go down and start filming and see what emerges. But we need the ability to deliver nothing to you guys if it doesn’t work out.” And they said sure.
So was that freeing?
Yes. It really meant I didn’t have to hold back with her or with them. Making a film or making any project is very stressful. So if we had to pull the plug because it didn’t work out, it would sort of be a relief to me. It’s a very nice zone to operate in. Lance and I both thought, “Well, at the very least, this will be an interesting week or two that we’ll have as a story.”
I’ve seen it a few times. As I was watching it recently, I found myself trying to figure out: What did Elizabeth and Billy think they were bringing you in to tell? What was the story that they thought had not been told?
Yeah. Right?
Do you know? Do you feel like you know why they wanted you in their home, in their life?
This is a question that we are still debating to this day. Me and my editor, Adam Locke-Norton, who has worked with me on The Rehearsal and for years—we were debating exactly this.
Because it keeps changing. The difficult thing about this whole thing is there are so many pieces, and some of them are contradictory. You have to have a mindset of someone playing 7D chess with you, and they are so far ahead to make sense of all this stuff that it almost seems implausible sometimes.
Did you worry that they were ahead of you?
I didn’t worry, because I’m there, and I’m just trying to experience it and let my curiosity drive me. The first couple days, we were trying to figure out how to capture this and what they were gonna give us and what they were trying to do. We didn’t really know. We didn’t know if we would sit in there and they’d bring out papers and lay out a whole thing or they’d just be like, “We’re just gonna live our life.” They weren’t immediately coming to us with some sort of narrative they were trying to push. So we realized it was this game of figuring this out in a way.
We ended up having this plan where we would come in every morning. We started with two cameras, and we eventually got to three cameras, and we had one that was on a 12-millimeter-wide lens that could get the whole main area of the house. And then we had two other cameras that were on 25- to 250 [millimeter] zoom lenses, so they could go wide, but they could also go really tight. And we’d place them in the far ends of the house. We found these angles where if anything happened at any point in the house, we could not only have it in our wide shot, but then we could get it in close-ups eventually.
We only had two camera operators. Lance wouldn’t always be in there. He would sometimes be outside with the monitor. So sometimes there were only three people, and our sound guy who’d sometimes be outside. I could definitely sense that she felt the stakes were high for her, and that can cause people to be unnatural in ways that they may not be in real life.
That’s a part of the work I make. I like to show how the cameras can affect how people are, a little bit. That feels the most honest way to do things. With this project as well, we were really trying to show how she is, even when the cameras aren’t there.
When did you realize that you needed to be in it?
That’s another thing. I started this thing being like, “I’m definitely not gonna be on camera in this.” The situation was very intense. She was going to prison. And that’s another thing about having the ability to pull the plug on the project with no consequences, why it was really nice for me, because I could also say to both of them—if I did sense there was tension or stress about this whole thing—I was very aware this is the final month that she’s gonna have for a decade with her kids and her family.
I said almost every day, "If ever you’re regretting this decision, just tell me and we’ll go. Like, no problem." I’d usually bring it up if there was tension, because sometimes we’d be trying to do shoots, and Billy would be trying to stop it or just be like, “That’s enough time.”
So I was like, “We don’t have to be here at all, but if we’re gonna be here, we just wanna be able to do this.” They never once said, “OK, we don’t want you here anymore” or seemed to be like, “OK, let me think about if we wanna change our minds.” That was confusing for me too. Because it didn’t make sense to me. I definitely would not want a camera crew following me for the last month of freedom that I would have.
Not only would I not want a camera crew, I don’t know that I would want you there.
Are you feeling that because of the conversation we’ve had so far?
No, but I would—
You’re saying I’m worse than the average person.
No, I would’ve seen your earlier work and the way you observe people and behavior, and I’d be very stressed out at the prospect of Nathan Fielder being in my house.
Yeah. This is part of the mystery that, like, doesn’t make sense to me.
No offense, but why you? You know what I mean?
Yeah. I asked her that on, I think, one of the first days we shot. I still don’t fully understand it. That really messed with my head. Also, I got the sense very early that she hadn’t seen a lot, but she had seen some of what I did, and she had talked to people who had seen what I did. Billy had seen more. I think she found the clip that she said she saw funny.
But you know, her relationship to that … to what’s funny? I don’t even know. She said her favorite movie is Elf, the Will Ferrell movie. You have the tattoo—
It’s actually my daughter’s initials, but I get that a lot.
Do you love that movie?
I like that movie well enough.
OK. So you and her there.
I like it well enough.
What areas do you feel like you’re similar to her, besides liking Elf? Or in what ways?
To Elizabeth Holmes?
Yeah.
I don’t like where this interview is going. But we’re both convicted felons, with a long track record of fraudulent behavior. We both had children to avoid prison time. We have that in common.
Do you feel those things about her?
Everything I just said?
Well, I guess you said various things. Some things are obviously true.
We both have blue eyes. I believe that her eye color is real.
Here’s a question. How do people view her? I’m assuming WIRED is very in with the tech world—
Yeah.
How did people view that, at the time, in that world? And how do people view it now, and is it the same, or has that changed?
There’s this broader culture of Silicon Valley that she operated within, where everyone’s a liar. You start a company, you lie, you fake it till you make it, and VCs expect it, and it is part and parcel of launching a business. Elon Musk is an incredible liar—lies to the public, lies to regulators, lies to lawmakers, investors, shareholders. That’s part of the game. And she, to me, in many ways, played that same game.
She did it to the nth degree; she took it very far. But what she was doing at the time was very much in keeping with what startup founders do. They go out, they raise money, they talk a big game, they get magazine covers. I think today, if you ask any journalist, whether they’re a tech journalist or not, they’d say she’s a convicted felon. She’s a fraud. And I think the first time I saw the film—now I’m going on a bit of a tangent, and I’m going to have to start asking you questions again soon, but—
No, I’m really curious, though. I hadn’t thought about Theranos in a long time, right?
Yeah, I think a lot of people coming into this haven’t thought about Elizabeth Holmes in five, six, seven years.
Yeah.
I have a 9-year-old daughter, and watching Holmes with her kids in the first half of the film, I felt tremendous empathy for this woman. I was asking myself a lot of questions about her romantic relationships and wondering whether that was at the root of it all along. I wondered if there was something wrong with her. Cognitively wrong with her.
And then I was getting ready to do this interview, and so I read back about everything she had done, about the timing of when she had kids. I went to screen the movie a second time and felt like such a fucking dupe for being close to tears watching her with her little kids. I still feel sad for the kids, but I felt much less empathy for her. I would say, broadly within the journalism community, Bad Blood was the definitive reported account of what she did.
Mm.
But I think watching the movie brings a lot to the surface for the viewer and raises a lot of questions about her and her character and what’s influencing her and what motivates her. What was I asking you? How rude of you to distract me.
It’s interesting for me, I think, because I couldn’t really talk to people about this fully while I was making it, besides the people that we were there with.
How did you process on a daily basis what you were experiencing?
In a way, we processed it with each other. One of the reasons early on that we felt this could actually be a project was because of what came out of those processing sessions. At the end of the day, I would have in my head what I thought was a very clear idea of what was happening, and Lance or our camera guy, Jonathan Mitchell, or our DP, David Bolen, or our sound guy, Richard Carlos, they would all have a different take on what actually happened.
I was like, how is this possible? We’re all in this room experiencing this thing. We’re all witnessing something and having a different idea of what’s going on. And I thought that was a basic premise to explore and chase.
At Telluride, you said that you still don’t know what you experienced. You want audiences to help you understand. What specifically do you want to hear from people after this comes out?
I generally don’t see myself as having a great framework for understanding all the variables of things and people. In a lot of the work I do, because it’s shorter or television sometimes, you have to take a human that’s very complex, obviously, with a lot of nuance in a lot of different areas, and you’re generally trying to simplify. You have to be like, “OK, well, this is the essence of the situation or the person, or this is an interesting flavor of them, and that’s what we’re gonna show.”
But with this, we’re really trying to give the viewer everything. We’re trying to focus on these moments that we couldn’t really make sense of fully. Like I was saying, still to this day, I’m debating. Why are me and my editor talking, two days ago, about trying to understand certain things? I’ve talked to people who have seen it, and they’re all bringing out new ideas that I would never even consider.
So you trust the audience.
I just think people are smart. I don’t see myself as the most knowledgeable at everything, and I love learning from the world and from people. I definitely don’t come to anything being like, “I know what the answers are” or “I know what things are.” Just in general, not with this project. When I was in grade six maybe, or grade seven, I was with a tutor, and they were like, “I think you know probably less than 200 words.” And I was like, “No, I know more than that.” I started naming them. I started trying to count, because I was insecure that I didn’t know as much as others or something. But now I think I’ve grown into being comfortable with anything I don’t know. I think it drives a lot of my curiosity, and probably why I hate you asking me questions.
You hate this right now?
I want to set this thing up so people can watch this in the right way. I want people to go and see the film, because that’s what I want to express. You know? It’s the film. So that’s why I’m more curious about your experiences—because you can think you know something, and then you start talking to a lot of people, and then you’re like, “Oh, I actually know nothing.” Anyways.

That was 20 minutes ago.

I was talking about that process of where we put the cameras, and how we did it to get to this. Because what would happen is they would be living their life and doing things, and we would try to capture these things.
But then a couple things started happening. Firstly, because I was there, they would keep engaging with me. So they would be talking to each other, but then they would be like, "Nathan, what do you think?" And I would chime in from off camera. Or if nothing was really happening, I would ask a question to see what they would say about something. But I was off camera, and it was more to prompt a discussion or something like that. Or they would start talking to me, and conversations would go on for long enough that the operators started panning over to me.
But also, they would say stuff that tickled a part of my brain that was like, “Something’s off about this.” Or I feel like this is them trying to do some sort of propaganda. So I would wanna interject to be like, “Well, actually, I read this,” or “I thought this was the case.” We realized, “Oh, someone has to push back, and we can’t just let them run whatever show they kinda wanna do.”

Do you feel like you know Elizabeth? You spent so much time with this woman. You lived in their home.
Well, I know her better than I did going in. Sure. I knew nothing about her.
How much about her had you read and watched before you showed up? Did you go in with this canon of Elizabeth Holmes reporting and filmmaking?
I’d read the book. Which I thought was the main document. And then when we started doing it, I listened to the ABC podcast they did on the trial, but I was sort of cramming it. I would go home, I would listen to more.
As we were there, I would just be like, “OK, I’m trying to digest everything I can.” But at the same time, I’m not a science journalist. This isn’t my specialty, so I was also aware that I may not be able to go into certain areas with her, but I could approach her through other means.
I felt like I knew enough to know when something didn’t feel right. I definitely had engaged enough with that, but I was digesting more and more as time went on. I don’t know. That’s such a crazy concept—knowing enough, I’m realizing. It’s like, what does that even mean?
Well, yeah. How do you know that you ever really know someone is kind of a big—
Oh, well, that … Yeah. I mean, in terms of knowing her, I’m like—
Do you feel like you know her as a real person? Like a person person, not the character of Elizabeth Holmes, the fraud that everybody has read about. Is there a different version there?
I think because she’s someone that has limited her presence—she hasn’t done a lot of interviews, and she has really limited her engagement with the media in general—I think the version that is out there of her is largely a version that people are putting together from the pieces they have. The first time I met her, I was like, “This is not how I thought she would be.”
How did you think she would be?
I guess I expected a little more outward anxiety and a desire to control.
She wasn’t controlling?
That was very jarring for me, because she did not come across as controlling. I thought the situation that she was in, there would be a lot about it. We’re in this tiny beach house. That’s a tense environment. The weird thing is that she let us come there without trying to be like, “OK, well, what’s your angle? What are you gonna do here? What is this interview gonna be about?” You know, there wasn’t that stuff, and I totally expected we would get all that.
And that, I think, messed with my head as well. Is that intentional? Or is there some design to this whole thing that I’m not aware of, and I’m in some hall of mirrors that I am not even conscious of?
It was a wild experience, but one thing I feel like I really know is her tendencies. We’re talking about spending 12 hours, 18 hours a day, with this person in all these different environments. I feel like I know how she would handle any situation or what she would act like or say in response to something. Can I say something off the record?
[Goes off the record.]

We’re back on.

A lie, a classic lie, is someone who’s like, “OK, I am saying something that I’m consciously knowing is not true in this moment.” But it’s not just the words, it’s the design of every aspect of her life that feels like a part of what is going on. What’s interesting about her to me, I think, just goes beyond that in any given moment … I can’t piece it together. How is that possible?
They were working on an appeal. There was a sense that something maybe was gonna happen that would cause her not to go.
I don’t know if I find that endearing or just so—what’s the word? Just the arrogance of it, the delusional arrogance of it.
I guess it’s a question of, what is the level you’re supposed to operate at in terms of how positively or negatively you’re supposed to think about anything in your life? When you think about future events, is it healthier to be like, “I see my future as this happy place that’s going to be great and great things are gonna happen,” or is it better to be like, “There are all these things that might be bad, and I need to be ready and I need to understand that that is a possible reality”? What is the balance?
I’m going into zones that are not my expertise. You should talk to a psychologist about this stuff.
I think if I was going to prison in two weeks, I would understand and accept that I was going to prison in two weeks.
Her prison date shifted at one point, so I don’t know if it puts these things in your head where it’s a possibility. But with everyone, there’s a gap between what they think the future will be and what it really is, the actual odds. How often is anyone aligned with the actual odds of, like, a future thing happening? But people who are positive, people who are optimistic generally, don’t stew in the negatives, right?
She can come across as a very positive person. She focuses on those positive things. The idea of, “Maybe I’m not going to prison.”
You mentioned a few minutes ago that you did not find her to be controlling.
Just to correct, she didn’t appear to be controlling.
She didn’t appear to be.
That was my sense. But then—yeah, go ahead.

Oh, I don’t know about [marriage]. They even muddy the waters with that. Like, he’ll call her his wife.
How did you come to understand that relationship?
That came to be a big part of trying to understand her. But I could say certain things right now that would definitely affect how people enter the movie. That’s interesting. It’s fascinating to watch it back and watch these moments where I am not even thinking about the production or what’s happening. I see myself fully just being in it with them. A lot of it was like, how is this possible that I’m meeting humans that are talking like this?

Well, I don’t know what their expectations were.
I don’t either, but I have to imagine that they were different than the end result.

Extremely comfortable.

The 27th.
In the last, like, three weeks.

No. Not to my knowledge. We haven’t shown it to him. I was trying to think if there was a screening that had happened. By the time this comes out, maybe? Or probably? I have no idea.
He’ll probably go on opening weekend.

Well, I can end the interview for us. I think what you were saying about human behavior, and people being complicated, that’s ultimately what it’s about, right? One thing that’s emerged that’s interesting is the way you and your coworkers are having different ideas of what’s actually happening in this movie. Each of us has our own life and our own experiences, and maybe it’s partially about what we’re bringing to it too.
That’s how it’s gonna hit differently for different people. That’s why I feel like it’s the healthy thing for me to be like, “I don’t know a lot,” or I feel more comfortable in a place where I’m … Ugh, I don’t have the words to describe what I’m feeling right now.
Close your eyes and try again.
I’m gonna give up halfway through this sentence. I think my tutor was right.

Japan’s mega-quake that never was, and the danger of false alarms
A software error triggering a false magnitude 9.9 quake in Japan sparks fears that eroding public trust could cost lives in a real quake
3-MIN READ3-MIN

Julian Ryallin Tokyo
Kanako Hosomura was working in a clothing store in Yokohama when an alert on her phone warned of an imminent magnitude 9.9 earthquake.
“We all rushed outside,” Hosomura said, recalling how people poured out of nearby shops and offices to watch tall buildings and power lines for signs of shaking.
But no earthquake came. Eight minutes after issuing the warning on Friday, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) cancelled the alert, leaving residents to wonder what had gone wrong.
“These alarms do not go off very often – only maybe a couple of times a year – so when they do sound, everyone is worried that the quake is going to be really big,” Hosomura said.

For the first time in the world, Ukrainian military personnel evacuated a wounded person from the front using an aerial drone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:26:19 EEST
20:26:19 KST

For the first time in the world, Ukrainian military personnel evacuated a wounded person from the front using an aerial drone
Kyiv • UNN
The Defense Forces evacuated a wounded infantryman from the front using an aerial drone for the first time in the world. The operation was carried out despite mines and Russian UAV activity.
The Defense Forces conducted the world's first aerial evacuation of a wounded service member from the front line using a drone. This was reported by the 92nd Ivan Sirko Separate Assault Brigade, writes UNN.
Details
Specialists from the company of unmanned ground systems of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, the Ground Forces' Drone Forces, and other units took part in the operation.
The need for an unconventional solution arose after an infantryman from the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade was wounded at a position.
Due to the high activity of Russian drones and the mined terrain, it was impossible to evacuate the service member using a ground-based robotic system.
The specialists of the 92nd Brigade then took on a task they had never performed before — evacuating a person using an aerial drone.
For this purpose, they used a heavy hexacopter manufactured by the Ukrainian company Gurzuf Defence, which provided the equipment for the operation free of charge.

The Domino Effect: How Strikes on Data Centers Paralyze Russian Businesses
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:25:58 EEST
20:25:58 KST

The Domino Effect: How Strikes on Data Centers Paralyze Russian Businesses
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian drones attacked the data centers of Yandex, Sberbank, and VK. Expert Oleksandr Hlushchenko explained that strikes on server infrastructure paralyze business processes and harm the Russian economy.
The massive attack by Ukrainian drones on St. Petersburg on the night of October 18 targeted an oil terminal, energy infrastructure, and a data center. After the strike, Russians began massively complaining about disruptions to the operation of the "VKontakte" social network. However, the consequences of further attacks on data centers could prove much more serious—from disruptions to banking payments to interference with the operation of businesses. Read about what this threatens for the Russian economy in the UNN article.
The Russians themselves effectively created the conditions under which their digital infrastructure is becoming vulnerable to such strikes. Russia spent years building a centralized digital system, moving an increasing number of services online, concentrating enormous amounts of data in large technology companies, and at the same time requiring that the personal data of Russian citizens be stored on Russian territory. In peacetime, this model makes it possible to centrally manage services, scale them, and control information flows. But during wartime, it creates serious risks. When a significant part of digital infrastructure is concentrated within a single state, and its operation depends on a limited number of large technology platforms, damage to individual elements can have consequences far beyond a single enterprise
In fact, this concerns a threat not only to social networks but also to the entire system of digital services on which Russians' daily lives depend. Data centers ensure the storage of enormous volumes of information and the operation of applications, cloud platforms, and financial and corporate services. Damage to such facilities can deprive companies of part of their computing capacity and users of access to their usual services.
Repeated strikes pose a particular danger. Large technology companies have backup data centers capable of taking over the load of damaged facilities. However, their capabilities are limited. If several complexes go offline at once, the load on the remaining ones increases, along with the risk of large-scale disruptions.
At a certain point, servers can no longer fully process all requests. Some services begin operating more slowly, others periodically become unavailable, and some operations end in errors. And the less reserve capacity remains, the harder it is for the system to withstand even ordinary technical failures
How will strikes on data centers affect the Russian economy?
The consequences of such disruptions will be felt most acutely by Russian businesses. Modern enterprises simultaneously depend on banking, cloud, logistics, and other digital services.
You may have goods, employees, and customers, but be unable to make a payment on time, process documents, or organize supplies. In other words, economic activity slows down not because the goods or enterprises themselves have disappeared, but because the mechanisms connecting them have stopped working properly
Why is it difficult for Russia to restore data centers?
Another problem for Russia is replacing damaged equipment. Data centers require not only servers but also complex information-storage systems, networking equipment, power-supply and cooling systems. Due to technological sanctions, purchasing the necessary components may turn into a lengthy and expensive process.
A data center cannot be restored simply because a company has enough money in its account. Servers, storage devices, network switches, optical equipment, power-supply systems, cooling systems, and other components are required
According to the expert's assessment, the additional costs of restoring the infrastructure may ultimately also be felt by Russians themselves. Technology companies will be forced to spend more money on equipment, reserve capacity, and maintenance. This creates the conditions for services to become more expensive for end consumers.
At the same time, several damaged data centers do not mean the immediate collapse of the Russian internet. Large companies have backup systems, but their capabilities are not unlimited.
This does not necessarily mean an immediate collapse, but it may mean a gradual degradation in the quality of digital services
Therefore, if the attacks continue, Russia’s main problem may no longer be the temporary unavailability of individual websites, but the gradual depletion of digital infrastructure, the increasingly costly restoration of that infrastructure, and growing risks for the entire economy.

Belgian Queen, Crown Princess targeted in AI-generated nude images

Unknown Publisher

20:25:30 KST

Melike Pala
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Queen Mathilde of Belgium, her daughter Crown Princess Elisabeth and several other prominent Belgian women have become targets of sexually explicit images generated by artificial intelligence (AI), renewing concerns over the growing spread of non-consensual deepfake pornography.
The fabricated images, which depict the women naked, have been circulating on social media platforms in recent days, the Belgian newspaper Le Soir reported on Monday.
The victims reportedly also include wives of politicians and government officials, as well as prominent female politicians.
According to an investigation by several Belgian news outlets, Flemish Vice-Minister-President Melissa Depraetere and former Belgian Defense Minister Ludivine Dedonder were among those targeted.
"As disgusting as it is, very little surprises me anymore," Depraetere said, adding that people needed to understand that the creation and distribution of such images was unacceptable and could destroy lives.
Dedonder announced that she intended to file a legal complaint over the fabricated images.
The Belgian Royal Palace also confirmed that action had been taken to have the images depicting the queen and the crown princess removed from the internet.
The controversy has once again drawn attention to AI-generated or manipulated images that make real people appear naked or engaged in sexual activity without their consent.
Civil society organisations and digital rights advocates have repeatedly warned that AI-generated sexual abuse disproportionately affects women and girls, with consequences extending beyond individual privacy violations.
The European Union prepares to introduce stricter measures against AI applications that generate non-consensual intimate images.
Under amendments to the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, AI systems designed to generate or manipulate realistic intimate images of identifiable people without their explicit consent are set to be prohibited.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has also become a prominent example of the risks posed by manipulated images and videos.
In 2024, Meloni sought 100,000 euros in damages in a case involving two men accused of producing and distributing pornographic deepfake videos featuring her face.
She also initiated a process to trademark her voice through the European Union Intellectual Property Office in an effort to protect her identity against AI-generated impersonations.

Meloni calls emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:23:36 BST
20:23:36 KST

Italy plans tougher security measures after violent protests
- Published
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is poised to approve emergency security measures, according to local media, after protests over rising costs broke out into violent clashes in Milan.
The measures include extending preventative detention to minors and restricting group gatherings, Milanese paper Corriere della Sera reported.
Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers over the weekend. More than 250 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Italian police said.
The expected crackdown comes after Meloni chaired an emergency security meeting on Monday afternoon. No official announcements have been made.
More than 5,000 people gathered in Milan over the weekend. As well as clashes between police and some protesters, stores were looted and property was set on fire.
High-end shops in the city's centre closed early on Monday, with many boarding up their windows over fears of further damage.
Measures to crack down on youth gangs are expected to be approved as early as Tuesday as part of a decree law, according to Corriere della Sera.
Local media reports suggest social media was used to invite young people to Italy's squares over the weekend.
Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania, in recent weeks.
Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried this represented a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".
Speaking to Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".
Of the 271 people taken to police stations on Sunday, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.
Violence between protesters and police also spread to other cities in the north.
Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.
"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".
The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.
"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said in a post on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".
Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.
The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:23:26 UTC
20:23:26 KST

Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.
- Share:
A new study suggests that even low levels of physical activity could protect the brain from Alzheimer’s disease – but not in the way scientists expected.
The researchers tracked almost 300 older adults with early brain signs of Alzheimer’s for nine to 11 years using pedometers. They found that physical activity didn’t reduce the toxic amyloid plaques that most Alzheimer’s treatments now target.
Instead, in people who already had these plaques, physical activity reduced the accumulation of misfolded tau proteins in specific brain areas. These proteins appear later in Alzheimer’s disease and are more closely linked to cognitive and functional decline. These signs of dementia were reduced by almost half in more active participants.
Benefits appeared at just 3,000 steps – roughly half an hour of walking at a moderate pace. The optimal range was 5,000 to 7,500 steps daily, after which the effect plateaued. More steps didn’t necessarily mean greater protection, which suggests a realistic target for older, sedentary people, rather than the often-cited 10,000 steps.
The study had limitations, however. It involved a fairly small group of mostly white, well-educated people in the US, and it didn’t take other lifestyle or health factors into account. Also, there may be other protective mechanisms of walking at play. But it does support other research suggesting that being physically active may lower the risk of dementia.
A UK study of 1,139 people over 50 found that those who were moderately to vigorously active had a 34-50% reduction in dementia risk when followed over eight to ten years. Among those who developed dementia, staying active reduced their memory decline, particularly in older women.
A larger 2022 UK study tracked 78,430 people for seven years using wrist accelerometers. It found a 25% reduction in dementia risk with just 3,800 steps daily, rising to 50% at 9,800 steps.
However, people who walked more also had better cardiovascular health – lower cholesterol, better sleep and blood pressure and reduced diabetes risk. Since these heart and stroke risk factors also increase dementia risk, the picture is complex.
Healthy habits often go together. People who exercise are more likely to eat well, not smoke, look after their heart health and have fewer financial stresses. This makes it hard to know which factor is having the biggest effect. The researchers tried to account for this, but because these habits are so closely linked, it’s difficult to say that exercise alone is responsible.
However, there is a strong case for this as there are multiple ways exercise might support the brain: improving cardiovascular health, increasing blood flow and boosting chemicals that promote brain-cell connections.
One such substance is irisin, a hormone produced by muscles that acts on almost all faulty brain mechanisms associated with Alzheimer’s, including inflammation. This and other chemicals, such as BDNF, associated with exercise, provide plausible biological pathways for how physical activity might directly influence brain health beyond its cardiovascular benefits.
But the relationship might work in reverse, too. People may become less active because of early Alzheimer’s symptoms. Those with hearing problems, for instance – itself a dementia risk factor – often report barriers that make them stop being active before other dementia symptoms appear.
Vicious circle
Reduced activity then accelerates memory decline. This creates a vicious circle. Early disease symptoms – such as not hearing – can affect self-esteem and reduce engagement in physical activity, which in turn worsens cognitive decline.
Brisk walking might be particularly beneficial. A small trial of 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s who did Nordic walking (an enhanced walking technique that uses poles to work your upper body as well as your legs) maintained brain function over 24 weeks, with some functions even improving.
The 15 who received only standard care showed decline or no improvement. Though small, the trial suggests that even people already diagnosed with Alzheimer’s might benefit from increased physical activity, including brisk walking.
Getting outside, particularly in nature, may be especially beneficial for preventing dementia – possibly because it improves mood and sleep while reducing isolation – all dementia risk factors. The combination of physical movement, natural light exposure and social interaction when walking outdoors may create multiple protective effects that complement each other.
The challenge now is helping people overcome barriers to outdoor activity, such as safety concerns, fear of falling, or simply preferring the comfort of the sofa – particularly during wetter, colder months. But the evidence suggests that even a few minutes of walking could make a difference, and that modest, achievable targets – a half-hour stroll rather than a marathon training regime – may offer substantial protection against cognitive decline.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Eef Hogervorst, Professor of Biological Psychology, Loughborough University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Mariana Lenharo. Alzheimer’s decline slows with just a few thousand steps a day. Nature, 2025; DOI: 10.1038/d41586-025-03596-2

Development Road Project to contribute $55B to Türkiye's economy over 10 years: Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:23:17 UTC
20:23:17 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The Development Road Project is expected to contribute around $55 billion to Türkiye's economy over 10 years, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu said Monday.
Speaking at a conference in Ankara, Uraloglu said the project would also provide employment opportunities for an average of 70,000 people annually while strengthening Türkiye's position in global trade and supporting Iraq's economic reconstruction.
The planned corridor will connect Iraq's Grand Faw Port in the Gulf to Europe through Türkiye, integrating railways and roads with energy transmission lines, fiber-optic infrastructure, and oil and natural gas pipelines.
“For our country alone, we foresee the project contributing approximately $55 billion to our economy over a 10-year period and, through the establishment of production and logistics centers, providing employment opportunities for an average of 70,000 citizens each year,” he said.
Uraloglu said tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Russia-Ukraine war had exposed vulnerabilities in global transport networks, prompting countries to seek safer, shorter and more predictable routes.
The Development Road would offer a strategic alternative that reduces dependence on the Strait of Hormuz, particularly for cargo moving from Gulf countries to Europe, he said.
He added that the route could cut journey times to approximately 25 days, compared with 45 days via the Cape of Good Hope and 35 days along the Southern Corridor.
 
Complementary trade routes
Uraloglu said Türkiye viewed the Development Road as complementary to existing trade networks, including the Middle Corridor linking China and Central Asia to Europe through the Caspian Sea and Türkiye.
“As Türkiye, located at the heart of the Middle Corridor, managing the Turkish Straits and building the Development Road, we are clearly demonstrating both at the negotiating table and on the ground: There can be no corridor without Türkiye,” he said.
Existing, ongoing and planned Turkish railway lines connecting to the Middle Corridor total 2,156 kilometers (1,340 miles) , with completed and planned investments amounting to $47.1 billion, he said.
The minister said the Development Road Project could help Iraq diversify away from oil revenues, generate transit trade income and strengthen its role as a regional commercial hub.
He recalled agreements signed by Türkiye and Iraq on July 28 this year, saying the two countries planned to secure parliamentary approval before beginning construction.
These include a memorandum on rail and road transport through the Fishkhabur-Ovakoy border crossing and a framework agreement to develop transport infrastructure in Iraq in exchange for natural resources.
Uraloglu also pointed to a recently signed railway cooperation memorandum with Saudi Arabia, saying efforts to revive the historic Hejaz Railway would create additional connections from the Gulf through Türkiye to Europe.
“The Development Road Project has the potential to reintegrate the Middle East's fragmented geoeconomic structure, transform Iraq into one of the crossroads of regional trade and strengthen Türkiye's position in global connectivity networks,” he said.
