Becerra’s muted gubernatorial campaign comes to life in home stretch
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- After months absent from the campaign trail, Democrat Xavier Becerra has increased public appearances and began airing television ads as mail ballots reach California voters.
- Republican rival Steve Hilton has campaigned aggressively, attacking Becerra’s low profile since the primary; Becerra leads in polling and fundraising in the Nov. 3 race.
- A crowded primary, record spending and California’s outsized political influence have drawn national attention to a gubernatorial contest considered a likely Democratic lock.
While Republican Steve Hilton has spent months jackrabbiting around California during his long-shot bid for governor, Democratic front runner Xavier Becerra just recently emerged from quasi hibernation and stepped into political daylight.
Hilton has blasted Becerra as taking the state’s voters for granted, failing to hold public campaign events to explain his detailed plans to address California’s many ills. Despite pledging to participate in multiple debates, Becerra brushed aside several invitations, agreeing to just a solitary one-hour face-off against Hilton on CNN in late September.
That month, Hilton held 14 public events, a dozen more than Becerra, but the Democrat’s spokesperson said he appeared at multiple functions sponsored by other groups. Hilton wasn’t buying it.
“He is a useless nothing, a totally unaccomplished pipsqueak who is so smug, so arrogant, so entitled, that he somehow thinks he’s owed this job just because he was picked as a useful puppet by the Sacramento machine,” Hilton, a former Fox News commentator and British political strategist, said last week in West Sacramento.
On Oct. 10, Becerra, a longtime member of Congress and Biden’s secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, scoffed at his GOP rival.
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing in the race for California governor. Here’s what you need to know about the candidates.
“Uh, hello?” Becerra said sarcastically to reporters in Sacramento after being asked about his absence from the campaign trail.
“That Steve Hilton doesn’t see me on Fox News is his problem, not mine. I am gonna talk to voters,” Becerra said, rattling off a list of his recent campaign events. “I will talk to them until November the 3rd, and then I’ll be ready to talk to voters and taxpayers and the people of California when I’m the next governor.”
On Thursday, Becerra held a news conference in downtown Los Angeles with Latino leaders and famed Mexican actor Eugenio Derbez urging voters to turn out despite alleged intimidation efforts by the Trump administration.
On Monday, he held get-out-the-vote events in Santa Clarita and Glendale, shortly after he campaigned for former state Sen. Richard Pan, a congressional candidate, in Sacramento, and urged voters to cast their ballots early at an event in Santa Rosa. In September, Becerra promoted Proposition 1, a proposal on the November ballot that would allow the state to sell nearly $11.3 billion in bonds to fund affordable housing.
“We know we can get these men and women who are wearing these orange vests to work and keep them working, so they can afford to buy a house if we pass Proposition 1,” Becerra said, standing alongside union members in front of a chain-link fence encircling a vacant lot in North Long Beach.
Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson, who endorsed Becerra in April and appeared at the housing event, pushed back on the notion that Becerra is taking the election for granted after winning a top spot in the primary, positioning him to be the first Mexican American elected governor of California.
“I’ve seen firsthand the work that has taken place under the radar that may not be explicitly, openly political or openly be seen as campaigning, but it is the kind of thing you want to see,” Richardson said in an interview on Thursday, adding that he saw Becerra meeting with elected officials of both parties, the mayors of the state’s largest cities and labor leaders. “I’ve seen a very active candidate that has been making sure that real time was put into building relationships that will ultimately translate to a successful governorship, because that’s the goal. I mean, ultimately, what we want is a leader who has the relationships to lead our state.”
Becerra’s campaign said that the candidate has frequently met with voters since the primary without press coverage to hear from Californians, and that he would be a frequent public presence in the weeks before the election, when “voters really get engaged, when ballots land in their mailbox,” said spokesman Jonathan Underland.
GOP gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton faces backlash from fellow Republicans and Democrats over a provocative ad.
“People have incredibly busy lives. They are worried about affording their healthcare, putting food on the table, paying for gas to fill their tank,” Underland said. “What is at the forefront of Secretary Becerra’s mind is the very real problems that Californians are facing every day.”
In contrast, Hilton has been publicly barnstorming California since the June primary.
Becerra’s schedule is not surprising given Democratic dominance in California, where the party’s registered voters outnumber Republicans nearly 2 to 1. While appearing at parades, pancake breakfasts and in voters’ living rooms can be effective for candidates running in local campaigns, the most effective way for candidates to reach voters in a state as vast as California is through sustained advertising buys, which can cost tens of millions of dollars.
“If you’re the Democrat running in California, the operating theme of your campaign is do no harm and measure the drapes and figure out how you’re going to put an administration together and what is the tone that you’re going to set for that administration,” said Tim Rosales, a veteran GOP consultant who led businessman John Cox’s unsuccessful 2018 gubernatorial campaign and previously worked on Arnold Schwarzenegger’s successful effort to replace Gov. Gray Davis in the 2003 recall campaign.
Newsom was more active in the 2018 general election campaign against Cox than Becerra has been this year, but Rosales argued that could be because Becerra views it as the final chapter of his political career, which also may have been the case with former Gov. Jerry Brown in his 2014 reelection campaign. Newsom, however, is pondering a 2028 run for the White House.
“This is potentially more of a swan song for Xavier Becerra, the icing on the cake for a long and distinguished political career, and for Gavin Newsom, it was a stepping stone,” Rosales said.
Becerra has raised $40.5 million, as of Friday, while Hilton has raised $29 million, according to the fundraising disclosure reports filed with the state. Those figures do not include the exponential advantage that Becerra had in independent expenditure committees’ spending over Hilton in the primary.
Veteran Republican strategist Rob Stutzman, an advisor to Schwarzenegger, said that while Becerra will almost certainly be the state’s next governor, he should be cautious about his approach weeks before the November election.
“What he needs to be careful of is a big Democratic night across the United States that looks muted in California, and if that happens, the analysis will be that it’s his fault,” Stutzman said. “He should want to optimize his political capital as the clear leader of his party now in California. So he has to be a little careful of leaving some political capital on the table by not creating a stronger brand over the next three weeks.”
The last gubernatorial race that was viewed as competitive took place in 2010 between Brown and former eBay chief Meg Whitman, then a Republican who spent $144 million of her personal wealth on her campaign.
That contest drew national attention, but Brown beat Whitman by nearly 13 percentage points. Every gubernatorial election since that race has been sleepy and ignored in national politics, with Democratic candidates coasting to victory. The state has seen contentious gubernatorial primaries, notably in 2018, and this year, when the Democratic field was so crowded that party leaders urged low-polling candidates, including Becerra, to drop out.
He won the top spot in the primary after then-Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Dublin) dropped out amid rape and sexual assault allegations.
Mason Harrison, who worked for Republicans Carly Fiorina in a 2010 Senate bid and Neel Kashkari in a 2014 gubernatorial campaign, and worked with Hilton on business ventures but is not affiliated with his campaign, noted that while Brown was well-known by Californians because of decades in the public eye, Becerra is not. However, given Democrats’ edge in the state’s voter registration, as well as current headwinds against the GOP in California and across the nation, it’s unsurprising that Becerra has been less visible than Hilton. Harrison compared Becerra’s campaign to Biden’s in 2024 before the then-president bowed out of the race.
“The calculus seems to be, the more he gets out on the campaign trail, the greater the potential of him having a misstep in an interview or getting some tough question that he’s going to have to answer, and what’s the advantage of that in a year when you’re running against a party that, by historical standards, stands to lose significantly,” Harrison said. “Why make it more competitive by making yourself more vulnerable?”
Indeed, Becerra previously committed to multiple debates, but has participated in one so far and appears unlikely to agree to another. Still, he has repeatedly disputed the notion that he is taking the race for granted.
“If I were trying to coast, I’d be out on the coast right now instead of here with you all,” he told reporters one sweltering August afternoon in Little Tokyo in downtown Los Angeles, an area he represented in Congress.
While there, he met with local business and community leaders. And he bought merchandise and delicacies, including a sweet mango mochi wrapped in a thin, fluffy pancake at a 123-year-old Japanese confectionery.
Times staff writer Nicole Nixon contributed to this report from Sacramento.

Horrible, unmanly, indispensable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
27 minute listen
If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed in his 1492 postmortem inventory. Guns and gunpowder were controversial. In art and literature, they were labelled the Devil’s work, and were perceived as fundamentally unchivalrous. Yet within half a century, by the early months of 1539, Lorenzo’s descendant Duke Cosimo de’ Medici had 91 firearms in his Florentine storerooms. Somehow, in the courts of late-Renaissance Italy, the gun had become an acceptable, even valued, weapon.
Beyond the palazzi of the peninsula’s towns and cities, guns were also making inroads into more ordinary lives. There were no standing armies in the 16th-century Italian states. Their wars were fought through temporary mobilisations, and with considerable help from companies of mercenaries. Yet as the 1506 provision that established the Florentine militia made clear, ‘little hope’ could be placed ‘in foreign and hired arms’. Far better to establish a new magistracy with ‘full authority and power’ to enlist men from Florentine territory, at least 10,000 of them. One in 10 of these men were to be equipped with firearms, and 500 handguns (schioppetti) should be kept in the Palazzo della Signoria (the city hall, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio) along with ‘such money as should be necessary for the schioppetti’, presumably to purchase gunpowder and shot. Three or four companies (bandiere) entirely of schioppettieri might also be established.
This militia, most often noted for the role of Niccolò Machiavelli in its foundation, was to be organised after the fashion of the Germans, in whose cities there was a centuries-old tradition of civic defence and a duty on every male citizen to maintain suitable arms for the purpose. In fact, one of the Florentine militia’s early constables was German (a Giovanni Tedesco); another (Giliberto Spagnolo) came from Spain, a country making the running in the use of small arms on the battlefield. Giovanni Tedesco arranged target practice for his company, which from 1508 was extended more generally among the militia, with exercises taking place on a monthly basis.
Militias were not new but, by the 1490s, large-scale foreign military intervention on the Italian peninsula was giving a new impetus to their development, as was the growing importance of infantry in the military context. In Friuli, where Venetian lands bordered Ottoman territory, the militia were using handguns from the 1490s, and city guards across the Italian peninsula were soon provided with guns too. The growth of militias was the single most important factor in the proliferation of firearms in 16th-century Italy. This is too early a period for the kind of autobiographical writing that would tell us what these men made of the process, but there was certainly ample encouragement to become familiar with firearms and acquire shooting skills.
The backdrop to these developments was the decades of war in which France and Spain contended for hegemony on the Italian Peninsula. In the 1480s, while pitching his services to the duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci, highlighting his potential as a military engineer, wrote:
I have also plans of mortars most convenient and easy to carry with which to hurl small stones in the manner almost of a storm; and with the smoke of this cause great terror to the enemy and great loss and confusion.
By the turn of the century, Spanish arquebusiers – named for the long, wooden-stocked gun with which they were armed – were doing precisely that on the battlefields of Italy. As the conflicts of 1494-1559 rolled on, the rulers of the peninsula’s multiple states promoted shooting in the interests of civic defence and military preparedness and, as they did, their own use of firearms shifted too.
The Medici were not the only leading family of Renaissance Italy to take an interest in this new military technology. In 1538, the duke of another Italian city-state, Urbino, described a novel firearm as ‘very dear to me’. Such appreciation, however, ran counter to the dominant image of guns in the period’s literature. Leonhard Fronsperger, once a captain of the ducal armoury in Munich, wrote of gunpowder as ‘indispensable’, but also as ‘horrible’ and ‘unmanly’. Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem Orlando Furioso (1532) described guns as a ‘foul and pestilent discovery’, weapons through which ‘no more shall gallantry, no more shall valour prove their prowess’. Only in edgier texts, like the swashbuckling memoirs of the goldsmith and sculptor Benvenuto Cellini, did anyone hint that guns were fun. ‘Frightened’ by a plague that hit Rome in the early 1520s causing thousands of deaths, Cellini ‘began to seek relief in a sport that I found very enjoyable’. In between sketching the city’s ancient ruins, he shot pigeons. He developed his own gunpowder recipe, and boasted of his ‘really good marksmanship’, claiming to be able to shoot ‘200 yards point-blank’. This is probably exaggerated, but just as relevant is Cellini’s explanation that, by getting him out into the fresh air to go hunting, and combating his ‘naturally melancholy disposition’, his gun ‘brought me more gain than loss’.
The textual enthusiasm of both Cellini and the duke of Urbino finds a material counterpart in a growing culture of luxury weapons. The aesthetics of these high-end guns helped firearms fit into a court culture that valued beauty and craftsmanship. They were decorated with classical gods, Christian figures and mottoes, and images of the hunt, while the novelty value of combination weapons such as spears with miniature guns attached appealed to the Renaissance sense of fun.
Records of gun ownership in elite households, too, tell a different story from the literary sources. It is at court that wheellock guns – a groundbreaking technology that allowed concealed carry – first leave traces. Leonardo’s sketches of their mechanisms (probably developed in Germany) can be seen in the Codex Atlanticus. Expensive, convenient and modern, wheellocks seem to have become a status symbol. The standard military firearm of this period, the matchlock, was fired by means of a lighted cord (the match) that ignited the powder when the gun was triggered. But the wheellock was a self-lighting mechanism that avoided the need for a lighted match. It was a more complex and therefore more expensive technology, and could be unreliable (probably especially if produced on the cheap). On the other hand, wheellocks had advantages in hunting, avoiding as they did the glow and smell of the burning match cord which might alert prey to a hunter’s presence.
Designs echoed court imagery: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, biblical figures
By the start of 1539, Duke Cosimo de’ Medici owned four wheellock handguns made in the German style that he (or more likely his bodyguards) took with him when he travelled. Not a decade on, a wheellock appeared in the first portrait of a European ruler with a handgun: Titian’s equestrian portrait of the victorious Emperor Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg, in which Charles is shown ‘in the manner in which he went against the rebels’, that is, in the garb of the wheellock-toting Spanish cavalry.
The aesthetic qualities of high-end firearms helped guns blend into the wider courtly environment. Designs echoed imagery common to the court: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, or biblical figures like Judith. A wheellock pistol made in Germany and dated 1548 features a figure of the Roman heroine Lucretia along with a Christian motto and image of the Crucifixion. By this time, guns were finding new uses in Europe’s religious wars: far from the Devil’s weapon, they were a means of asserting true Christianity against the heretics.
Back at court, novelty weapons such as the match-fired combination pollaxe and gun in the Royal Armouries, or the boar-spear with two small guns attached given to Cosimo de’ Medici, engaged with a fashion for wider theatrical and festival machines aimed at provoking wonder in their audience. These firearms functioned as marketing devices, promoting their makers – and perhaps also the cities or states of their makers – as potential providers too of the thousands of weapons that might be commissioned for use in war. A striking indication of their acceptability in elite culture comes in 1553, when Mantuan officials began to make ceremonial presents of firearms to the city’s duke in place of the crossbows they had previously given. That the gun could now appear in these ritual contexts shows it had truly arrived.
In wider society, luxury decoration was out of reach, but other factors favoured an expansion of gun ownership. Florence was not the only state to establish or revive a civic militia. In the context of long-running on-off war, it made sense for rulers across Italy to mobilise citizens and equip them with up-to-date weapons. Alongside requirements for militia drill went contests to incentivise the acquisition of shooting skills. Farmers found guns useful for pest control; hunters used them too. Thus, in the 1520s and beyond, more and more Italian states formalised or expanded their militia. Giovanni Moro, a Venetian official who had previously handled military supplies, proposed in 1525 the formation of a citizen militia of 12,000 men, of whom two-thirds would use firearms; these men would receive powder and lead for practice, and a contest would be held three times a year to encourage them. This would be, said Moro, to the ‘honour and utility’ of Venice, and of ‘great benefit’ when it came to conserving Venetian territory.
Such ambitious plans didn’t always succeed, as two cases from Tuscany show. Jacopo Pessina’s detailed study of military organisation in the Republic of Siena estimates that in the last 30 years of the republic (1525-55), between 20 and 33 per cent of adult men served in the militia, with each 500-strong battalion including 150-200 arquebusiers. A report from 1543, however, suggested that the militia was not fit for purpose, lacking not only sufficient men but also the necessary firearms and helmets. The case of Florence, moreover, where the last republican government of 1527-30 fell to the Spanish-backed Medici party after a long siege, shows the limits of a city militia in the face of a foreign army. Anticipating attack, the republican government issued new ordinances for the militia, instituting training in the use of arquebuses, and shooting contests. During the siege of 1530, artisans from shoemakers to cutlers were equipped with arquebuses. They did not, however, prevail against the much better-resourced Spanish army. Still, governments across Italy continued to expand their militia, which made firearms increasingly available to men of all social ranks.
‘Every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’
If militia service provided one route to familiarity with firearms, so did the related rise of shooting contests. In 1506, Venice introduced a competition to encourage the development of handgun skills among the archers serving on its naval galleys. In 1518, the first prize was 16 arms-lengths of damask fabric, worth 32 ducats, along with 6 ducats in cash. In 1520, the Republic of Lucca instituted a thrice-yearly shooting contest in order to ensure that its citizens were prepared for defence, the founding decree urging them to prefer ‘death over the loss of dear liberty and the reduction of their fatherland to servitude’. Prizes included a silver cup worth almost 20 ducats, and six arms-lengths of damask worth 5 ducats. Soldiers’ pay could be less than 30 ducats a year, so these were generous rewards. Contests, however, were not only about financial incentives. They were also about establishing an acceptable social image for the firearm, just as the iconography of luxury weapons had done at court. The language of the Lucca decree, for example, offered a new and more positive discourse of the gun, as a weapon for the defence of liberty.
Hunting was another context in which guns became familiar not just for elites but more widely. In 1552, for example, a cowherd named Vincenzo obtained a licence from the Bologna authorities that allowed him to carry arms, including a gun for the purpose of hunting. It came with the standard caveat that the weapon must not be carried in churches, at festivals or in markets. These were busy environments where an accidental misfire had higher risks than out in the countryside, and where a generalised ban on arms-bearing (staff weapons such as pikes were also included) made policing more straightforward. Such wide access to guns, however, was a matter of concern. The anonymous author of a proposition for international gun control observed, probably in the late 1570s, that if the Italian princes did not take action soon, then ‘there will be no place nor state where people are safe, given that every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’.
As guns became more common, so did their appearance in the criminal records. By 1600, firearms had become the predominant weapon used to commit homicide in Bologna. That said, they still accounted for only a third of offences, and in interpreting the figures we should bear in mind the relative lethality of guns when compared with other weapons. In fact, across the broad range of gun crime, it was still relatively rare to come across cases where guns were directly used in planned homicide. More commonly, they were used to threaten: the ideal outcome for the highwayman who shouts: ‘Your money or your life!’ is to ride away with the money without firing a shot.
Many of the historic investigations feature possession of illegal guns and/or their use to intimidate. In a 1554 case near the northern Italian city of Brescia, Valerio Soncino and a gang of 20 men ‘armed with various weapons, including arquebuses’, scaled the walls of a property belonging to Valerio’s brother Annibale, and ‘with various threats’ forced two of his stewards to bring them carts, which they loaded up with goods, stealing in addition cattle and a horse. The robbers got only five miles, however, before they were halted by some villagers who had got wind of what was happening and sounded the alarm. In the ensuing violence, two men and a woman among the villagers were injured. Here, the primary use of the guns was to frighten people into doing as they were told, not to kill them. That is not to say, however, that the proliferation of firearms was not risky. Criminal records from Bologna describe a case in 1575 in which an elderly woman named Giovanna was killed by a man named Pierantonio Fangarezzo; Fangarezzo had been looking over an arquebus (perhaps an early variety of flintlock) to see how it worked when it accidentally went off.
In some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership
People engaged in, or considering, political violence also used firearms. The distinction between criminal and political activity was not always straightforward. The system of exile in the Italian states – in which offenders were banned from their home territory and had their property confiscated – often made banditry an attractive option (hence the overlap between the concepts in Italian, where the word bandito is also used for an exile). Civic authorities were particularly keen to police weapon ownership when it posed a risk to the regime. The early years of Medici ducal rule in Florence (formally established in 1532) saw numerous confiscations of illegal weapons: Girolamo di Filippo Bonciani and Francesco di Piero Serragli, for example, fell foul of the law after an arquebus was found under the straw of their former stable. Some of these weapons were probably planted by city officials, but opponents of the regime might reasonably have decided to arm themselves in case of an uprising (for which there were several precedents).
Dissidents in Brescia (a subject city of Venice) also obtained weapons: testimony from 1539 shows how one alleged firearm offender, Antonio Maria, was accused of saying several times that ‘he desired nothing more than that the Emperor and the King of France should make an accord against our Venetian lords, and that he hoped to come with them to sack Brescia.’ Antonio Maria was further accused of ‘continually keeping in his house exiled men of a bad sort, who go out killing on the streets’; he had in his house around 25 guns of different types. While we typically learn about these cases from regime records, by reading between the lines it becomes clear that at least in some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership.
People in northern and central Italy owned guns for several reasons: to participate in militia service, for hunting and livestock control, and for criminal activity. Some of this ownership was purely practical: a gun would more reliably than the alternatives kill the fox eating your chickens. Some of it had political motivations, whether to defend the liberty of one’s own fatherland or to oppose a tyrannical overlord. By the middle of the 16th century, a lot of people had guns. It is challenging to establish quite how many. Based on population estimates and numbers enrolled in the militia, the historians Michael Mallett and John Hale estimated that one in 15 rural households in Venetian territory would have had a firearm following the establishment of the militia in the later 1520s: ‘the government’, they observed in Military Organisation of a Renaissance State (2009), ‘was calculatedly accepting a risk to public order’. By 1540, the ruler of Modena required that one in three countryside households should have a gun. These calculations concern militia service, however, and other people may have bought guns second-hand from soldiers, or won them via gambling.
Later in the century, larger cities had shops where guns might be mended and probably also purchased. A 1559 proclamation issued in Bologna in anticipation of riots declared that ‘shopkeepers, who sell those polearms and arquebuses, must store them in their shops in such a way that they are not ready to use’. There is no reason to think that the anonymous author who complained of wheellock-toting shepherds was greatly exaggerating the extent of proliferation.
Guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership
Certain moments in wartime no doubt accelerated access to firearms. Besides the 1529-30 Siege of Florence, records of the defensive provisions in Ferrara of 1552 (when the city was likewise preparing for a possible siege) show that, out of 520 households equipped with armour, pikes, arquebuses and morions, more than half (270) had a gun. Included in this list are 18 female heads of household, of whom six had guns. This raises the question of how many women were gun-owners more generally. The answer seems to be rather few. Sieges were emergency situations in which gender norms might temporarily be suspended, such as when the women of Siena took responsibility for repairs to the city walls. Outside the wartime context, Joe Tryner’s study of court records in Bologna turned up only a single example of a woman with a firearm, and nothing in my wider survey of source material has suggested that was untypical.
In contrast, guns did come to be associated with masculinity. In The Fruit of Liberty (2013), Nicholas Scott Baker argued that the siege of 1529-30 was a particular turning point for elite identity, redefining notions of masculinity from those associated with practices of civic governance to something more ‘rugged, militaristic’. This was particularly apparent in changing clothing styles, to which the bearing of new types of arms might be added. Focusing on Florence after 1537, in Masculinity, Arms and Armour (2020), Victoria Bartels identifies guns as one factor in shifting performances of masculinity, noting that they increased the danger attached to ‘routine bouts of aggression’ that had traditionally been employed to settle disputes between men. In the context of the Italian Wars (and specific local conflicts within them), guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership. This is confirmed in the account of Benvenuto Cellini, whose self-aggrandising narrative of his participation in the Italian Wars includes a comment he made to a companion, Alessandro del Bene, to persuade him to stick around and shoot back at an invading army during the 1527 Sack of Rome: ‘Now you’ve brought me here, we must show that we’re men.’
Over the course of the 16th century, familiarity with firearms grew. It was increasingly expected that men would be able to use a gun: the expansion of militias was a key factor here alongside direct soldiering experience. The acquisition of skills in shooting was positively encouraged through civic contests with generous prizes. Rhetoric about the importance of guns for civic defence and for the maintenance of honour and liberty offered a counterweight to more negative images of gunpowder weapons as diabolical, unchivalrous or impious. Guns were useful for protection of livestock from predators as well as for hunting more generally. In turn, their ready availability also made them accessible for use by bandits, during vendettas and indeed for political violence. However, their lethality shifted the dynamics of violent encounters: so effective were guns as a threat that in some cases they may have prompted victims to give up without a fight. On the other hand, with increasing proliferation came an increased risk of both accidents and casual use in interpersonal violence. Yet not all gun ownership was enthusiastic. Some applicants for arms licences evidently felt constrained to carry guns in self-defence, and cultural ambivalence about these weapons remained long after they became common objects.
As firearms became more familiar, it was as much a decision not to be a gun owner as to acquire the new technology.

Nidal Hasan: America’s killing machine wants an audience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:59:23 UTC
18:59:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Nidal Hasan: America’s killing machine wants an audience
Donald Trump has cancelled the Pentagon’s plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution after an outcry from Republicans and Democrats alike. Yet the former US Army psychiatrist, convicted of murdering 12 soldiers and a civilian at Fort Hood in 2009, is still scheduled to face a firing squad on 3 December. If it goes ahead, it will be the US military’s first execution since 1961.
The prospect of broadcasting the killing provoked a political backlash. The decision to kill him remains intact.
Under the current Trump administration, one might think we have seen it all, that hardly anything can shock us. Yet almost every day, the US rulers seem to raise the threshold of what the ‘civilised world’ can tolerate, commit to and advocate.
I did not see the proposed return to public executions coming. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted an audience for the military’s next killing; Trump has decided that the public will not be allowed to watch.
American killing machine
As an opponent of capital punishment, I see no crime that requires transforming an execution into entertainment potentially available to millions, including children. But the removal of a camera should not be mistaken for a retreat from state violence.
While the military is preparing to resume executions after a 65-year hiatus, we must remember that the wider American killing machine never went away in the first place.
Individual jurisdictions have abolished capital punishment or suspended its use, but the machinery remains operational. In 2024, 25 people were executed and 47 in 2025, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.
Beyond execution chambers, the toll is far greater. According to Campaign Zero’s Mapping Police Violence project, US police killed at least 1,314 people in 2025, an average of 3.6 every day. Even that horrifying toll represented a 5% decline from 2024, the first annual decrease in six years.
Black people were still 2.6 times as likely as white people to be killed. These figures cover police killings in many different circumstances, rather than judicial executions. But they demolish any suggestion that lethal state violence had taken a holiday.
Then there are the deaths without execution warrants or guns. A 2023 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine associated poverty with approximately 183,000 US deaths in 2019. Another study, following people identified as homeless in the 2010 census, found that those under 65 faced 3.5 times the mortality risk of housed people after accounting for demographic and geographical differences. Researchers also estimated that more than two million deaths during the 2020 and 2021 pandemic years could have been avoided if US mortality rates had matched those in 21 other wealthy countries.
Poverty, inadequate housing and denial of healthcare are silent mass killers whose victims are unlikely to make headlines or front-page news. This is structural violence, with political responsibility resting on US elites, which is otherwise conveniently obscured.
America today
Political choices shape access to treatment, decent housing, safe work, and adequate food. The ruling US elites have repeatedly subordinated those needs to profit. By all accounts, today’s America is a social Darwinist experiment on steroids. The poor are poor because they deserve it. The sick die because they cannot afford treatment, so what?
The state must not intervene to provide protection because, God forbid, that would be socialism. The cruelty is routinely dressed up as individual responsibility and economic common sense.
Trump’s administration brings a more openly vindictive politics to this inheritance. Racism, misogyny, and xenophobia feed its vocabulary of hierarchy. Take, for example, Trump’s language about immigrants “poisoning the blood” of the country. Once people are represented as contamination, cruelty toward them becomes easier to sell as national renewal. Across the country, masked ICE agents are snatching foreigners, breaking up families, and shooting protesters in the name of the law.
Abroad, the same entitlement assumes imperial proportions. US forces seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. Trump entertained taking Greenland by force before ruling out military action at Davos. The US and Israel launched another war against Iran in February. Kidnapping a foreign president, treating another people’s territory as an acquisition, and promising salvation through bombardment revive the prerogatives of nineteenth-century colonialism.
Hegseth, who proposed the latest live-streamed execution, gives this politics a crusading aesthetic. The civilian Pentagon chief bears a Jerusalem Cross and “Deus Vult” tattoos, and has promoted conservative Christianity inside the military. His church network is associated with a patriarchal Christian nationalism. Its prominent pastor, Doug Wilson, advocates postmillennialism, envisioning Christian rule before Christ’s return. This combination of religious supremacy and military power gives the execution proposal a particularly ominous setting.
Michel Foucault helps us understand the relationship between public punishment and less visible forms of coercion. In Discipline and Punish, he argues that public execution was a ritual through which the ruling authority reasserted itself. But the retreat of the scaffold did not make punishment humane.
Power changed its methods, working through prisons, institutions and everyday routines. Live-streaming Hasan’s execution would have created a power spectacle. Does the cancellation mean a return to rationality? Not necessarily. It leaves the coercive institutions and their authority in place.
Hegseth’s supporters have presented the execution as a warning to would-be killers. The argument for deterrence, however, lacks empirical support. Existing research cannot provide any conclusions on whether capital punishment increased, decreased, or had no effect on homicide.
American rulers preside over death through several different mechanisms: execution orders, armed policing, policies that leave millions vulnerable to preventable illness and poverty, and wars waged abroad. A society cannot claim to respect human life while treating so much death as acceptable, unavoidable or even exemplary.
The self-proclaimed enlightened world should be judged by the lives it protects and the power it restrains. Trump can cancel the livestream. The machinery behind it remains.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.

Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:58:52 UTC
18:58:52 KST

Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London
Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London
A Family of Cheetahs in a Rocky Landscape, attributed to Basawan, Mughal India, circa 1575-80 (PC: ilgiornaledellarte)
Not all paintings in the world are being sold in crores. But there’s one particular painting titled A Family of Cheetahs in a Rocky Landscape that was sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London. It created a stir in the world of painting and made headlines. This is the painting attributed to Basawan, one of the most prominent painters associated with Akbar’s court.Back in 1575–80, when Mughal emperor Akbar was building one of the most influential courts in Indian history, Basawan created an extraordinary painting of a family of cheetahs. The painting which was made nearly 450 years ago has survived and has seen several empires rise and fall. It witnessed the ever-changing artistic tastes and centuries of collecting.In October 2025, the painting made headlines when it was sold at Christie’s in London for £10.245 million (₹119 crore at the time).What’s so interesting about the painting
Different view of the same painting
If you look at the painting, it doesn’t look like a grand royal portrait. The painting’s beauty lies in its remarkably detailed study of animals in their natural surroundings.
Yet this intimate glimpse into the wildlife of Mughal India became one of the most valuable paintings of its kind ever sold at auction.According to Christie’s, the sale also set a world auction record for a Classical Indian or Islamic painting. What makes the story particularly fascinating is that the artwork’s importance extends far beyond its extraordinary price, offering a glimpse into the artistic imagination. It shows the royal interests of sixteenth-century India.The painting belongs to a flourishing period of Mughal art. Akbar was an artist who supported a flourishing royal workshop where Indian and Persian artistic traditions came together. Painters working under imperial patronage developed a distinctive style and created masterpieces worth remembering.Who was Basawan?Basawan was a leading artist from the Akbar period. His work is largely associated with innovation and expressive figures. The cheetah painting, dated to approximately 1575–80, is attributed to him rather than being definitively signed by the artist.What makes this painting unique is its subject. Rather than depicting any royal figure or a scene from a religious book, it focuses on animals in their natural habitat. The composition brings together art and observation.When art became a record
The young Akbar’s court at the age of 13 (PC:The Art Institute of Chicago)
The Mughal fascination with animals was not just decorative. Hunting, falconry and the keeping of exotic animals were part of courtly life. Akbar and other Mughal emperors maintained elaborate courts in which artists recorded people, events, landscapes, plants and animals. Under Akbar’s successor Jahangir, naturalistic painting became prominent, with artists producing remarkably detailed studies of birds and animals.Against this background, a family of cheetahs is an evocative subject. The painting does not simply use an animal as a symbol of royal power; it presents a glimpse of wildlife as a subject worthy of close artistic attention.From a royal-era painting to a private collectionThe artwork went on to become part of the personal collection of Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan and Princess Catherine Aga Khan. Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan (1933–2003) was a diplomat and philanthropist who served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees from 1965 to 1977. He was also a collector of unique artwork. The couple acquired much of their collection between the 1960s and the 1980s. Many of the paintings they selected were later studied and published by scholars. They were also put you display.The collection was displayed at Château de Bellerive, their home on the shores of Lake Geneva in Switzerland. The cheetah painting was among 95 works offered at Christie’s London auction on October 28, 2025.
How a painting estimated at ₹8 crore sold for nearly ₹120 croreBefore the auction, Christie’s estimated the cheetah painting at £700,000 to £1 million. Its eventual sale price of £10,245,000, including the buyer’s premium, was approximately 14 times more than its estimate.The result was also the highlight of the wider auction, which totalled £45.76 million, six times its pre-sale estimate. Every lot sold, with bidders registered across 20 countries and four continents, according to Christie’s.

IDF reveals Hamas plan to plant bombs near Gaza displacement camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:56:57 UTC
18:56:57 KST

The IDF on Monday revealed what it said was an internal Hamas document outlining a plan to plant explosives near camps housing displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, with the aim of creating panic among civilians to help Hamas terrorists escape advancing Israeli forces.
According to the military, the document, written in April 2024 by Hamas' engineering department and disclosed for the first time, proposed placing explosive devices around displacement camps and detonating them as Israeli troops approached. The resulting chaos would serve as a distraction, allowing Hamas leaders and terrorists hiding nearby to flee.
The proposal also called for planting explosives along routes used by Gaza residents to delay the advance of Israeli troops, the IDF said. Another suggested tactic involved firing stun grenades into displacement camps to frighten civilians and create additional confusion while Hamas terrorists escaped.
According to the IDF, the document demonstrates that Hamas was prepared to knowingly endanger displaced Palestinian civilians to protect its leadership and fighters during Israeli military operations.
The military said the proposed tactics reflected Hamas' willingness to exploit the civilian population for operational purposes, despite the risk of direct harm to those sheltering in the camps.
The IDF did not specify whether the plans outlined in the document were approved or ultimately carried out.

Zamir orders Border Police reinforcements as nationalist violence and crime rise in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:56:47 UTC
18:56:47 KST

IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir has decided to deploy an additional Border Police company to the Judea and Samaria Division to combat rising settler violence in the West Bank, following a recommendation from IDF Central Command, Walla learned on Monday.
The company, which will specialize in combating nationalist crime, will operate using IDF personnel allocations. It began training in August and is expected to take on dedicated operational missions in violence hotspots beginning in late November.
A security official familiar with the training process and operational preparations said, "A Border Police company is like adding two infantry battalions when it comes to nationalist crime. The marginal output of a Border Police company is much higher."
Katz: Israel Police must take full responsibility for nationalist violence in West Bank
Defense Minister Israel Katz said that responsibility for addressing serious violence by a small group of Jewish rioters in the West Bank must rest entirely with the Israel Police's Judea and Samaria Division, including prevention, investigation, and prosecution.
"The IDF should not and cannot engage in civilian law enforcement, but must instead fight Palestinian terrorism and protect the country's borders and Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria and along the seam line," Katz said.
Katz also reiterated that he would not reinstate administrative detention orders.
"Administrative detention orders are not the solution. Only strong and effective police enforcement," he said.
Katz had already announced a proposal in August to transfer authority for handling extremist Jewish activists’ problems from the IDF to the police, which was not coordinated with the relevant authorities and may yet be blocked, The Jerusalem Post learned.
Katz did not clear the issue with a number of top relevant IDF authorities before making the announcement, to the extent that until a meeting on Monday, many of them did not even understand what he was proposing.
New IDF company will be able to respond faster to incidents in West Bank
According to IDF assessments, the new company will be able to respond quickly to incidents of nationalist crime and serve as an operational arm for intelligence gathered by the Israel Police and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), including in cases of sudden outbreaks of violence.
In August, Zamir ordered the reinforcement of Judea and Samaria with two additional battalions following a sharp increase in the number of isolated farms and new communities in the area, accompanied by growing friction between Israelis and Palestinians, violence, and property damage.
The Judea and Samaria Division currently has four battalions deployed in each of its regional brigades. In addition, a headquarters of the IDF's 98th Division operates in the area to improve oversight, supervision, command, and control, including efforts to prevent nationalist crime.
IDF criticizes police leadership over lack of resources in West Bank
Meanwhile, criticism has emerged within the IDF over the Israel Police's senior leadership, which military officials say has failed to reinforce the Judea and Samaria Police District with additional personnel and resources despite the growing severity of nationalist crime incidents.
A security official noted that the IDF, not the Israel Police, allocates all Border Police positions in Judea and Samaria.
"The Israel Police can strengthen the Judea and Samaria District with more patrol cars and more investigators," the official added.
The IDF has praised the work of Judea and Samaria District commander Moshe Pinchi and the close cooperation between the military and the district. However, military officials maintain that the resources available to the district commander are insufficient.
"This is the smallest district in the police. It is about a third the size of all the other districts in the State of Israel. Why don't they have a special patrol unit to deal with nationalist crime?"
Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Ra'am, Joint List push community for high voter turnout in hopes of boosting anti-Netanyahu bloc

18:56:32 KST

Israel's Palestinian leaders are urging the Arab community to vote in the October 27 election, hoping that a high turnout could nudge Israel's complex coalition arithmetic in favor of an anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Yashar chairperson Gadi Eisenkot.
"We can ensure the formation of a new government of change," Ra’am head Mansour Abbas told Reuters in his office in Nazareth, Israel's most populous Arab city.
Abbas and other Arab leaders face one big obstacle to their goal of playing a role in any future administration without Netanyahu. Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties that most Palestinian Israelis will vote for, citing a lack of shared values.
But Abbas thinks there will be room to maneuver, perhaps after the vote, largely because of the cold, hard realities of electoral maths.
Recent polls suggest Eisenkot's patchwork bloc of centrist, right- and left-wing parties will get the most votes, but fall short of a majority, and will need Arab support, either as coalition partners or from outside, to prop up a minority government.
"We want to replace the right-wing government... to end the wars and these policies, to stop the expansion of settlements and to address the failure to stop settler attacks," Abbas said.
"We also want a government that brings shared security and peace for Palestinians and Israelis."
For now, Eisenkot is sticking to his position.
“I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles,” Eisenkot said in a recent interview with The Jerusalem Post, citing, among other issues, their refusal to label Hamas a terrorist organization.
If no bloc forms a workable government, it could lead to a period of political deadlock and then fresh elections in 2027, with Netanyahu left in charge in the meantime.
But Netanyahu, for one, seems to take the threat of some sort of Eisenkot-Arab alliance seriously, or at least sees it as an opportunity to rile up his base. His campaign has used doctored images and AI-generated videos to depict his rivals embracing Arab leaders.
One AI-generated video, released over the summer, showed Eisenkot running through a meadow into the outstretched arms of Abbas.
Abbas' own career shows that such alliances are possible. In 2021 he became the first Arab Muslim to join an Israeli coalition as a minister, in a government led by Naftali Bennett, now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.
That government collapsed after 18 months, partly over disagreements between the two men on the West Bank.
This time round, Abbas said he could paper over those differences. To win over Jewish parties, he has taken the unprecedented step of giving the number two spot on his slate to a Jewish former police official, Yoav Segalovitz.
"It sends a message of partnership with the Jewish community and with Jewish citizens," Abbas said.
Arab's frustrated with demonization by Israeli Right, crime
The upcoming election will be Israel’s first since the October 7 massacre, and is being viewed as a referendum on the leadership of Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader.
Abbas' party is projected to win five seats, with a further eight going to the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab parties.
Ahead of the vote, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich proposed a plan to "Judaize" areas around Nazareth in the north and in southern Israel where most Arabs live, describing it as similar to settler expansionism in the West Bank.
Party organizers in Nazareth are hoping to capitalize on Arab anger with Netanyahu, Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, as well as frustration with rising crime in their communities.
Last week, canvassers with Abbas' party handed out flyers near Nazareth's massive Church of the Annunciation.
"There is a greater need this time than ever before to go out and vote in large numbers," said one of the people they approached, 74-year-old Gassan Bsoul. "The danger is greater than in the past," he added.
Arab turnout expected to be high
Israeli pollsters expect Arab voter turnout to be higher than in the 2022 and 2020 elections. The Stat-Net Research Institute, based in an Arab Druze town near Haifa, projects turnout at 63%, up from 56% in 2022.
While Abbas has tried to position his party to potentially join government, leaders of the Joint List have said they could wield just as much influence by staying in opposition.
Ahmad Tibi, a Joint List leader, said his group was ready to form "a preventive block to support [a government] from the outside."
He said the Joint List would join an Eisenkot-led government in voting "to establish an official commission of inquiry into October 7," a stated priority of the former military chief and his partners.
"We are placing as our top priority getting rid of the extreme right-wing government of Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir," Tibi said.
Keshet Neev and Shir Perets contributed to this report.

A fire at a military base in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured dozens, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday, calling it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's armed forces.
Carney announced the deaths without detailing the cause of the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright Saturday.
"Four service members have lost their lives, and their loved ones have been notified," Carney said in Ottawa, noting that dozens more were seriously injured.
"This is one of the worst tragedies the Canadian Armed Forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime," he said.
A doctor at a hospital in Edmonton, about 200 kilometers (110 miles) northwest of the base, told public broadcaster CBC that Wainwright's health care facilities were overwhelmed by patients.

The Department of National Defence said the fire broke out about 4 p.m. Saturday in the base's training area.
The Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire spread rapidly because of high winds. It later said the blaze was contained, though firefighters would continue to monitor the area.
"Military and civilian crews fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians," Carney said.
The base is one of the largest of the Canadian Armed Forces, regularly hosting training exercises with NATO personnel.
"We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery," Carney said. "And we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss; they will not carry it alone because in Canada we take care of one another."
The fire disrupted advance voting for Monday's vote on starting the process toward a referendum on Alberta's independence.
Alberta's provincial elections office said the advance voting station in Wainwright closed.

Beyond the Headlines: Dedicating Torah study and why no good deed is done alone - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:55:52 UTC
18:55:52 KST

One question in the chat caught me by surprise recently. Some 4,000 women had registered for an open class on Parashat Bereishit, organized by the “Mitchadshot” community. At the beginning of the Zoom session, I mentioned that the class was dedicated to the recovery of the students who had been injured in an explosion just hours earlier, during a trip in northern Israel.
Then someone wrote in the chat: “This is my first-ever Torah class. What does it mean to dedicate a class to someone? I’ve never heard of such an idea.”
I explained that every good deed we do in this world generates spiritual merits. Torah study and prayer have a special spiritual power. And when we do something good, we can dedicate the merit of that act to a particular purpose. For example, to the recovery of someone who was injured just hours earlier.
The Jewish people are bound together by a sense of mutual responsibility. We all affect one another through our good deeds and mitzvot - or, God forbid, through our wrongdoing. We are all part of one human fabric, and every action has an impact.
Then, just as the Zoom class was ending, almost as though it were a direct continuation of our discussion, I received a message written by Chani Leiter, the mother of Neria, who was seriously wounded in a terrorist attack several weeks ago:
Mutual responsibility, Jewish concern extends beyond the personal
“From the intensive care unit at Shaare Zedek Medical Center, we are receiving messages and videos of so many prayers, Torah study, acts of kindness, and good deeds being performed all around the world on behalf of our Neria. If only I could describe how much strength this gives us.
“We are seeing how the mutual responsibility and concern of the Jewish people extend far beyond our own personal ordeal. This is the hidden Jewish soul, now revealing itself.
“We named our son Neria - the light of God - because we wanted him to spread God's light in the world. God's ways are mysterious, but we can see with our own eyes how Neria is doing exactly that right now. All of this surrounds us with love and gives us strength.”
Wow.
A question from one woman and an answer from one mother remind us of something fundamental: No one is ever alone, and no good deed benefits only the person who performs it.
May Neria Dov ben Chana, and all those who were injured, have a complete and speedy recovery.
If Not Now, When?
When Sandy and Rosalie Goldstein were in their forties, they were both considering making Aliyah from the United States. Somehow, after a conversation with an official, they mistakenly received the impression that they were too old. They understood that Sandy would not be able to find work in Israel as an accountant at his age, and so they put the dream aside and continued building their lives in New Jersey.
Decades passed. But it is always possible to grow, to renew ourselves, to do better. And today, you can find the Goldsteins in Netanya, surrounded by grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Some members of the family had already made aliyah before them, and they themselves are just one small part of the worldwide wave of aliyah.
You look at their ID cards, and you cannot help but be inspired. Sandy has just celebrated his 105th birthday, and Rosalie will turn 101 in January. This month, they will celebrate their 79th (!) wedding anniversary.
They could have stayed in their comfort zone. They had already built careers in the United States, raised a family, worked on behalf of Soviet Jews behind the Iron Curtain, and over the years had also grown stronger in their observance of Torah and mitzvot.
They both love to quote the ancient words of Hillel the Elder: “If not now, when?”
They remind us: whatever change or improvement we have been dreaming about, whatever new beginning we have been postponing - now is the time.
5 Things About the Parashah
1. This week’s Torah portion, Lech Lecha, is the third portion in the Torah. In a sense, we are starting from the beginning for the third time. The universal, global “experiments” of the Garden of Eden, Noah’s Ark, and the Tower of Babel have all failed. The world needs nations, countries, and distinct identities. The world needs Avraham.
2. Avraham and Sarah make their first appearance on the stage of history - and, in fact, have never left it. If there were a ranking of the most influential people in human history, they would take first place. Billions of people around the world consider themselves their spiritual heirs.
3. Avraham and Sarah are the first olim, the first immigrants to the Land of Israel. “Go forth from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father’s house,” God tells Avraham - and he sets out for the Land of Israel. Millions have followed in his footsteps over the generations.
4. The first commandment Avraham fulfills is also the only commandment in this Torah portion: brit milah, circumcision. Close to 100 percent of his Jewish descendants continue to observe it to this day.
5. It’s worth remembering: In his own time, nobody called him our forefather Avraham. They probably called him Avraham the eccentric, the lunatic. The entire world worshipped idols, while he introduced us to the revolutionary ideas of monotheism, charity and kindness, faith and optimism. Today, everyone knows he was right.

UNICEF says 60,000 children in Gaza have lost one or both parents during war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:55:21 UTC
18:55:21 KST

Approximately 60,000 children in the Gaza Strip have lost one or both parents during the war, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), which warned of the lasting psychological and humanitarian consequences for children affected by the conflict.
Speaking at a press briefing at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, UNICEF communications officer and deputy spokesperson Riccardo Pires said around 800,000 children remain displaced, with most living in tents or damaged buildings considered unsafe.
Pires said nearly all displaced children require some form of mental health and psychosocial support to help them cope with the trauma of the war.
He also reported that more than 340 children have been killed and hundreds injured in Gaza since the ceasefire was declared in October 2025.
The UNICEF official warned that overcrowding in displacement areas, inadequate sanitation and deteriorating living conditions continue to expose children and their families to serious health and safety risks, particularly as winter approaches.
READ: Gaza buries remains of 75 Palestinians recovered from rubble of homes destroyed by Israel
Despite these challenges, Pires said the ceasefire had facilitated increased deliveries of humanitarian aid and commercial supplies, contributing to improvements in food security.
He also noted progress in restoring access to education, reporting that more than 560,000 children have returned to learning, including those attending classes at over 200 UNICEF-supported learning centers.
However, Pires expressed concern about the deterioration of Gaza’s sanitation infrastructure, warning that all six wastewater treatment plants remain out of service.
As a result, he said, much of the territory’s untreated sewage is being discharged directly into the sea, posing additional environmental and public health risks.
UNICEF stressed that continued displacement, damaged infrastructure and the approaching winter threaten to deepen the humanitarian crisis facing Gaza’s children, despite improvements in aid deliveries and educational access.

Alberta votes in referendum to seal fate of likely Canada secession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

Residents of the oil-rich province of Alberta vote Monday in a referendum on whether to stay in Canada or start a process toward a legally binding secession vote.
Recent polls show about 70% of residents favor remaining part of Canada, while roughly 20% favor secession and the remainder are undecided.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and both of the country's major political parties have repeatedly opposed secession. Support for the independence movement has also come from former U.S. President Donald Trump.
Alberta, a province of about 5 million people, has about 3.1 million eligible voters, according to Elections Alberta, the province's election authority.
Polls open at 9 a.m. (3 p.m. GMT) and close at 6 p.m., though advance postal and in-person voting has already taken place.
Voters will decide 10 questions. The secession question will be counted first. Results could be available as early as Tuesday, according to election officials.
Calgary, with about 1.68 million residents, is Alberta's largest city, followed by the capital, Edmonton, with about 1.28 million. Its national parks in the Rocky Mountains attract tourists worldwide.
Alberta has some of Canada's most conservative voters. A movement advocating independence on cultural and economic grounds has existed for years.
Some oil industry representatives feel environmental regulations restrict them, while many protesters who opposed coronavirus restrictions and vaccine mandates later joined the independence movement.
Although the movement has long represented a minority of Albertans, it persuaded Smith, the province's conservative premier, to call the referendum. Smith herself has consistently advocated remaining part of Canada.

WFP cuts Gaza aid for 500,000 people as Israeli restrictions strain food supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:52:53 UTC
18:52:53 KST

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) announced on Monday that funding shortages have forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza by around one-third, leaving half a million people without critical support as winter approaches.
In a statement, the agency said it is now assisting 1.1 million vulnerable people in Gaza, down from 1.6 million last month, while food rations have been halved.
Families receiving assistance will now get one food parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour, it said.
The number of daily hot meals has also dropped from 250,000 to 150,000, while families in hard-to-reach areas, including near the Israeli army-controlled "yellow line," will receive meals every other day instead of daily.
The agency has also reduced the value of cash assistance for 75,000 families.
According to WFP, an estimated 1.4 million people, or 67 percent of Gaza's population, face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, including around 200,000 experiencing emergency conditions requiring immediate food assistance to prevent deaths from hunger.
Only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet, while unemployment exceeds 80 percent, leaving many families unable to afford nutritious food.
Israeli restrictions further strain food supplies
Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries and commercial imports have further strained food supplies in Gaza, compounding the impact of WFP’s funding shortfall.
In July, the UN humanitarian office, OCHA, reported that only 42 percent of aid arriving via Egypt and 65 percent of shipments from Ashdod port could be offloaded at Kerem Shalom in one week.
WFP has also said more than 70 percent of Gaza’s cropland is inaccessible, with only about 3 percent currently usable, limiting local food production.
The suspension of commercial shipments last week has added to the pressure.
On October 14, COGAT, the Israeli military body overseeing humanitarian affairs, announced that commercial goods would no longer enter Gaza, cutting off a major source of perishable foods, including fruit and meat, which aid agencies typically do not supply.
WFP warned that "modest" improvements in food security since the October 2025 ceasefire remain "fragile" and could quickly be reversed by further reductions in humanitarian assistance.
Funding shortages have also forced the agency to halve its assistance in the occupied West Bank, from 400,000 to 200,000 people.
The agency said it urgently needs $450 million to sustain critical operations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, through March 2027.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:49:31 UTC
18:49:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Kaohsiung has completed preparations and tests for its flood control facilities ahead of Typhoon Champi, which could bring strong winds and heavy rain later this week, the city’s Water Resources Bureau said Monday.
The Central Weather Administration forecast the storm will move northwest over waters east of Taiwan, with its greatest impact on Kaohsiung expected on Friday and Saturday, per CNA. Its outer circulation could bring intense short-duration rainfall, increasing flood risks.
All 100 pumping stations, 148 mobile pumps, and 29 detention ponds have completed operational tests, the bureau said. Emergency supplies and emergency personnel are ready for deployment, while staff monitor the typhoon’s path and debris flow risks in mountainous areas, it added.
The bureau has intensified inspections and clearing of drainage channels and stormwater sewers. Additional desilting has been completed at sites affected by sediment buildup during August’s heavy rains, including Houjing Creek in Renwu District.
The city’s 29 detention ponds have a combined capacity of 5.59 million metric tons, per CNA. Depending on forecasts and real-time water levels, the bureau will lower pond levels in advance to make room for incoming rainwater.
The bureau will use its smart water management system to monitor rainfall and water levels. It urged residents to follow typhoon updates and prepare flood barriers or sandbags in low-lying areas.

The train will return to Taipei Main Station on Saturday, Oct. 24. A public science fair at the station that day will feature interactive activities for visitors of all ages.

Taipei mayor faces opposition over Songshan Airport relocation plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:48:42 UTC
18:48:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) faces opposition to his proposal to relocate Songshan Airport and redevelop the site as an AI park, with a recent poll showing more residents oppose the plan than support it.
A TVBS poll released Saturday found that 41% of Taipei residents opposed the proposal, compared with 31% who supported it, while 28% expressed no opinion. The survey interviewed 1,131 Taipei adults from Monday to Thursday and had a reported margin of error of plus or minus 2.9%, per TVBS.
At the opening of the Lihu Childcare Center on Monday, Chiang said he was willing to listen to views from all sectors and work with the central government to resolve difficulties associated with relocating the airport, per CNA.
Chiang said Terminal 3 at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, scheduled to open in 2027, and its third runway, planned for 2033, could help accommodate flights currently handled by Songshan Airport. He said the period between 2027 and 2033 could be used to review the necessary arrangements and prepare for future industrial development.
The proposal has drawn scrutiny from the central government. Cabinet Secretary-General Chang Tun-han (張惇涵) said relocating Songshan Airport could not be decided by a few people looking at PowerPoint presentations, underscoring the need for a more detailed review.
Chiang responded that the Taipei City Government had informed the central government in 2023 that relocating the airport would benefit the city’s long-term development. He added that the city began coordinating with the Ministry of National Defense in 2024 over the recovery of land at Songnan Military Camp to develop an AI industrial cluster.
The mayor has proposed transforming about 300 hectares of airport land and surrounding areas into an AI park incorporating technology businesses, residential communities, and green space.
Transportation is a point of contention. Chiang said Sunday that business travelers could reach Taipei from Taoyuan Airport in about 36 minutes using the airport MRT or elevated highways, per CNA.
DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) said the proposal did not yet provide a complete alternative to Songshan Airport. Opposition has also come from outside politics. Pegatron Chair Tung Tzu-hsien (童子賢) said relocating the airport was inadvisable, arguing that a capital should retain a regional air transport hub, per UDN.
