17:42:00 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The southern Chinese province of Guangdong, a manufacturing hub and trade powerhouse, saw its quarterly foreign trade exceed 3 trillion yuan (about 446 billion U.S. dollars) for the first time in the third quarter of 2026, underscoring the resilience of China's foreign trade amid global headwinds.
In the third quarter, Guangdong's trade value hit a record high of 3.23 trillion yuan, accelerating to 31.3 percent year-on-year growth from 19.3 percent in the first quarter and 22 percent in the second, marking a steady quarterly pickup, according to the data released on Monday by the Guangdong Sub-administration of the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
It also marked the 13th consecutive quarter of year-on-year growth in the province.
Foreign trade in September reached 1.18 trillion yuan, soaring 45.7 percent and marking the largest single-month increase in five years. Monthly trade, meanwhile, has remained above the 1-trillion-yuan mark for four straight months since June.
In the first nine months of this year, Guangdong's imports and exports rose 24.5 percent year on year to 8.72 trillion yuan.
The province's trade diversification deepened, with imports and exports expanding to more than 160 countries and regions. Trade with Belt and Road partners reached 3.2 trillion yuan, up 18.2 percent, while trade with other APEC economies climbed 26.4 percent to 5.74 trillion yuan.
Trade composition improved as imports outpaced exports in growth by 28.3 percentage points, pointing to a more balanced trade structure. High-tech exports emerged as a key growth engine in the province, with advanced manufacturing products totaling 1.1 trillion yuan in outbound shipments, surging 33 percent. Exports of specialized equipment, integrated circuits, computer parts, lithium batteries and electric vehicles all posted strong gains. Imports of integrated circuits and computer components also surged.
An official with the GAC Guangdong Sub-administration said that the scale, structure and quality of Guangdong's foreign trade have all improved this year, reflecting sound development momentum.
The 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, is currently underway in Guangzhou, the capital city of Guangdong, and has drawn exhibitors and buyers from around the world. The event is expected to inject fresh impetus into Guangdong's trade innovation and sustain the province's strong outbound momentum into the fourth quarter, the official added.
The data came as China's foreign trade maintained solid momentum in the first three quarters of 2026. The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan in the January-September period, the GAC noted. ■

Tiger Shroff assassination bid: Why Mumbai Police can't get custody of Lawrence, Anmol Bishnoi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:38:06 UTC
17:38:06 KST

NEW DELHI: Mumbai on Sunday witnessed another assassination bid linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, this time targeting actor Tiger Shroff. Yet, Mumbai Police cannot secure the custody of either Lawrence Bishnoi or his younger brother and close associate Anmol Bishnoi.A day after the firing incident targeting Jackie Shroff’s son, actor Tiger Shroff, Mumbai Police and Rajasthan Police have arrested three accused in the case. Mumbai Police are now expecting to secure their custody for further interrogation.The city has witnessed several high-profile incidents linked to the gang, including the assassination of NCP leader Baba Siddique, firing outside superstar Salman Khan’s residence and an attack outside filmmaker Rohit Shetty’s home in Juhu.Despite these incidents, Mumbai Police face hurdles in securing the brothers’ physical custody for interrogation in cases registered in the city. Lawrence is currently lodged at Sabarmati Central Jail in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, while Anmol, who was deported from the US in 2025, remains lodged at Delhi’s Tihar Jail.
The latest firing incident has again brought the brothers into focus and raised questions over why Mumbai Police cannot take them into custody for interrogation.
The primary hurdle is a ministry of home affairs(MHA) order restricting the brothers’ movement from their respective prisons.
Why Mumbai Police can’t get Lawrence Bishnoi’s custody
In August 2023, the MHA issued an order under Section 268 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), preventing Lawrence from being taken out of prison for any purpose. The order was initially valid for a year and was subsequently extended. The restriction was renewed under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which replaced the CrPC.Section 268 of the CrPC empowered the government to prevent a prisoner from being removed from jail, overriding orders requiring the prisoner’s production before a court under Section 267. Section 303 of the BNSS provides a similar power to the state or central government, subject to the conditions specified in the law.The restriction has posed a hurdle for Mumbai Police, which has sought Lawrence’s custody in connection with cases registered in the city. In 2024, the crime branch approached the Union home ministry seeking permission to take his custody in connection with the firing outside Salman Khan’s residence.Police later sought his custodial interrogation in the Baba Siddique murder case as well.Lawrence faces multiple cases, including those involving murder, attempted murder, extortion and alleged drug and weapons smuggling, across states including Punjab, Delhi, Gujarat and Maharashtra. He is also in the NIA’s custody-related legal framework in connection with a case probing alleged terror funding to Khalistan supporters.The MHA restriction means that Mumbai Police cannot simply transfer Lawrence from Sabarmati Jail to Mumbai for questioning. Any access to him has to comply with the restrictions in force.
Similar MHA order for Anmol Bishnoi
The MHA issued a similar order for Anmol on December 5, 2025, barring police and investigating agencies from taking his physical custody for one year. The order requires agencies seeking to interrogate him to do so at Tihar Jail.Anmol was deported from the US in November 2025 and arrested by the NIA. He is a key accused in the Baba Siddique murder case and has also been linked to the firing outside Salman Khan’s residence.
The restriction has created a similar hurdle for Mumbai Police in securing his custody for investigations in Maharashtra. Although agencies can seek to question him, they must do so within the limits imposed by the MHA order.
Security concerns and court appearances
Lawrence’s court proceedings have also involved security concerns. After his counsel moved an application citing a threat to his life, a special NIA judge shifted hearings from the regular courthouse to the NIA headquarters.Lawrence has also frequently appeared before the court through videoconferencing.With both brothers lodged in different prisons and subject to MHA restrictions, Mumbai Police face a legal and procedural barrier to bringing them to the city for custodial interrogation.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

undulating plywood layers form stratum parametric public seating sculpture
the installation bridges the gap between commercial furniture and architectural sculpture, utilizing computational design to create an undulating public seating landscape.
prefer designboom on google
COMPUTATIONAL DESIGN YIELDS Stratum PARAMETRIC TIMBER BENCH
STRATUM is a monumental parametric wooden bench designed and manufactured by Zorka Furniture for Haywood Mall in Greenville, South Carolina. Spanning nearly 29 feet and featuring over 600 individually CNC-cut components, this sculptural installation transforms traditional seating into an interactive architectural landmark, combining innovative design, precision craftsmanship, and functionality in a contemporary public space.
600 CNC-CUT PLYWOOD COMPONENTS FORM MODULAR ASSEMBLY
The structure by design and manufacturing studio Zorka Furniture comprises over 600 individually CNC-cut wooden components milled from roughly 100 plywood sheets. Assembled into a three-dimensional, layered mass, the varying profiles produce a rhythmic sequence of curves, integrated seating niches, and arched pass-throughs designed for visitor interaction. Weighing over 5,500 pounds (2,500 kilograms), the bench was fabricated into modular sections, shipped on five pallets, and assembled overnight to accommodate the mall’s operating hours.

Every layer is precisely engineered to create a flowing architectural form that invites people to sit, explore, interact, and take photos. Hezbollah funding plan indicates a new challenge to Lebanon’s government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:34:56 UTC
17:34:56 KST

Hezbollah funding plan indicates a new challenge to Lebanon’s government
The reported $200m in aid from Iran to Hezbollah has put the Lebanese government under increased pressure from the US.
Beirut, Lebanon – Last week, Hezbollah announced it would provide financial support to families in Lebanon who had lost their homes in the latest war with Israel.
Hezbollah has a long history of providing financial and other support for constituents and compensating those who have lost their homes to Israeli bombing. And while the group has historically received Iranian funding, it also has independent funding pathways allowing it to support members of its base, who are predominantly Lebanese Shia.
But analysts said Hezbollah’s latest distribution drive, announced on October 13, is increasing pressure on the Lebanese government, which has sought to counter the group’s influence in the country.
Last week, the government seized hundreds of kilogrammes of explosives linked to Hezbollah. Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah said the stockpile belongs to the axis of resistance against Israel and demanded that it be handed back and those arrested be released.
Meanwhile, Ali Damoush, the group’s executive council chairman, said on Tuesday Hezbollah would continue to support its constituents who have been on the front lines of the war with Israel.
“At Hezbollah, and out of our religious and moral responsibility, we will continue to serve our people and make every possible effort to preserve their dignity and honour,” he said.
Damoush said the payments were aimed at “displaced people and those whose homes had been destroyed or severely damaged to the point of becoming uninhabitable”.
This follows a report by the Reuters news agency claiming that Iran had provided Hezbollah with $200m in an effort to ease the burden on Lebanon’s Shia population, after three years of devastating war with Israel.
At the height of the war, which began on October 8, 2023, there were as many as 1.2 million people displaced, with about 9,000 Lebanese killed.
A United States Department of State official denied that Iran, under stringent economic pressure, was able to transfer the funds to its Lebanese ally.
Nicholas Blanford, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera that the funds would be a huge boon to the group.
“In general, this will help. Hezbollah is very sensitive towards the needs of their support base, the Shia community, and I think that’s one of the reasons why they haven’t gone back to fighting the Israelis,” he said. “The Iranians call the shots ultimately, but for Hezbollah I think there’s an awareness that they need to let their people breathe a little bit.”
Hezbollah paying out for the displaced
Israel intensified its war on Lebanon on March 2 this year, the second such escalation in less than two years.
Hours earlier, Hezbollah had attacked Israel for the first time in more than a year after joint US-Israeli strikes on Tehran killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, an ally of the group. It also said Israel’s repeated violations of a 2024 ceasefire in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has traditionally had a strong presence, were another factor in opening up the war.
In the following days, Israel reinvaded southern Lebanon, displacing more than a million people from their homes and killing about 4,300 since then. Israeli forces began their widespread aerial attacks on Lebanese villages and towns, which they claimed contained Hezbollah positions, with growing intensity.
In June, a US-brokered trilateral framework was agreed between Israel and Lebanon. The goal was to have Israel withdraw from parts of southern Lebanon and have the Lebanese army deployed to disarm Hezbollah. Israel is yet to enter two of the first three pilot zone areas, where this programme was set to be unveiled.
Since then, Israel has largely not withdrawn from the Lebanese territory but has entrenched what analysts believe is likely to become a long-term occupation, with more than 50 front-line villages and towns completely eradicated. Israel continues to demolish houses south of the so-called “Yellow Line”, in a tactic that has mirrored Israeli genocidal actions in Gaza.
Tens of thousands of people remain displaced, staying with relatives, renting apartments, or staying in hotels. Many had their livelihoods disrupted. In this context, Hezbollah has tried to step in and provide support for the displaced, most of whom are Shia Muslims and make up Hezbollah’s support base.
Continued funding
This is where the money from Iran reportedly comes in. However, analysts point out that Hezbollah has its own funding schemes, including financial support from the diaspora. Despite being heavily sanctioned, it is able to access money via domestic financial institutions or cryptocurrency.
“It has access to funds from the state, wealthy individuals, various entities, companies and hospitals,” Marcel Baloukji, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Hezbollah says its members have conducted surveys in Beirut’s southern suburbs and in southern Lebanon to assess the damage caused by the war. Families in Beirut and its suburbs whose homes were destroyed in the war will get $14,000 each; those outside the capital will receive $12,000. Financing will also be provided for furniture.
The group said “everyone who has suffered harm in our country, regardless of their political position” will receive support. This suggests that even families who openly criticised the group for plunging the country into a disastrous war with Israel will also be eligible for payments.
“Anyone who owns another home should, in solidarity with us, forgo the housing allowance, but will still receive the furniture allowance,” the group added.
Hezbollah is widely acknowledged as Lebanon’s strongest political and military actor, but the group grew overconfident in the run-up to the October 7, 2023 attacks by Palestinian groups on Israel, analysts say.
The political reality in Lebanon from that point changed, particularly after the 2024 Israeli intensification of its campaign against Hezbollah, which saw much of the group’s military leadership killed, including General Secretary Hassan Nasrallah.
Such a blow has been difficult for the group and its constituents, who have borne much of the brunt of Israel’s assault on Lebanon.
“It’s been a rough three years for them,” Atlantic Council’s Blanford said. “[The funding] will alleviate, to an extent, some people’s suffering.”
Hezbollah’s announcement of support for those affected in the war is viewed by many as an attempt to maintain support on the ground.
“Hezbollah knows that providing financial support and compensation to its on-the-ground population is one way to maintain its mass support,” Dania Arayssi, assistant director at New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, told Al Jazeera. “This is especially important because Hezbollah has seen a decline in mass support for it and a rise in mass frustration against this ongoing war.”
Challenge for Beirut
But the group’s efforts to pay off those who have suffered do not guarantee loyalty. Many in the Shia community have praised Hezbollah for the support they have received, but most say it is not enough to cover their expenses.
“I’ve been hearing that there may be a problem between those that get compensation for destroyed homes and those with badly damaged homes who are going to get nothing,” Blanford said.
Arayssi said Hezbollah’s latest move will also be a challenge for the Lebanese government, which has come under increasing Israeli and US pressure to take action against Hezbollah’s influence.
Last Thursday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio phoned Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun to press him on the issue of the Hezbollah explosives Lebanese forces had confiscated.
“The Lebanese government is facing a real test and challenge to build and win the trust of the international community, and particularly the United States, against Hezbollah’s signalling attempts of rebuilding itself,” Arayssi said.
“This funding and support for Hezbollah will likely make it harder to negotiate with Israel on the verification plan and even on the withdrawal from remaining territories, claiming that the government is failing to control its financial system.”

'My hopes are high': No Kings weekend demonstrations across US rally for early 2026 midterm voting
Demonstrators across the US took to the streets over the weekend for a fourth round of No Kings demonstrations to urge Americans to cast their ballots early for the 2026 midterm elections.
The aim was to increase early voter turnout to ensure that every ballot is counted in what many consider to be one of the most important midterms in US history—and possibly the last chance to save the country's democracy.
"Our democracy is really at stake right now. It should be 'We the People' controlling the country," Connie Jeung Mills, an organiser with the anti-Trump protest group Indivisible, told The New Arab.
"Voting early will help if there’s any sort of sabotage, and to instill the idea that you don’t have to wait until election day to vote," she said.
In around 3,000 locations in towns and cities across the country (with some cities hosting multiple events), demonstrators gathered for get-out-the-vote drives. The events began in the morning and continued late into the day with block parties and performances by local musicians.
In a public display of voter participation, some smaller groups splintered off from the mass gatherings to march together to the ballot drop boxes.
Two days earlier, on Thursday, more than a hundred students from two universities in in North Carolina marched from their campus, where their voting site had been closed, to their next closest voting station 45 minutes away.
Since Trump took office for a second term nearly two years ago, at least 29 states have passed restrictive voting laws, according to the Brennan Centre for Justice.
Many demonstrators on Saturday experienced their own hindrance when the No Kings Instagram account was suspended for several hours during the protests, preventing people from using the app to share protest route maps and live locations. The app’s parent company Meta said suspension protest account was an error.
On Sunda, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone further elaborated with a post on X (formerly Twitter), saying, “Our engineering team discovered that the spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s ‘reading’ behaviour.”
He suggested the high volume of engagement appeared similar to bots. "These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than ordinary human browsing in our systems," Stone wrote.
Jay Lyon, a retiree who was trying to find the the main march in San Francisco (while the livestream of the event was suspended by Meta), told TNA, "I don’t like the Trump administration, and I'm also concerned about the upcoming race for Congress."
The latest gatherings come after a months-long lull in pro-democracy mass demonstrations, in part due to internal debates among organisers over whether or not to focus on demonstrations or voter drives. On Saturday, they did both.
Mirvette Judeh, president of the Arab American Caucus of California, says her hopes are high for the midterms, including for the voter turnout of Arabs and young people, who historically do not have high turnouts.
"My hopes are high," Judeh told TNA. "I see a lot of voter engagement and creative ways of getting people to vote. The youth are making sure their vote counts, and I know Arab Americans are coming out to vote. These groups are invested in making sure their voices are heard."
"People are angry. People are over it. People want change. They want it badly. And it looks like they’re willing to fight for it," she added.

Opinion
China’s export boom creates a difficult bargain for Southeast Asia
The issue is whether the region can become more capable through trade with China or if it is simply a larger outlet for China’s production
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Ronny P. Sasmita is a senior analyst at the Indonesia Strategic and Economics Action Institution. 
China’s export machine is accelerating as its domestic economy remains under strain. This comes amid growing trade friction as China’s partners question whether persistent surpluses can coexist with balanced and resilient regional growth.
Last month, China’s exports rose 36.3 per cent year on year, while shipments to Southeast Asia jumped 52.3 per cent. The trade surplus reached US$133.5 billion, taking the nine-month total to US$938.1 billion.
In contrast, retail sales grew just 0.4 per cent in August, according to the latest official figures. For the first eight months, fixed-asset investment dropped 7.2 per cent while property investment plunged 19.9 per cent. Yet industrial production for August rose 5.2 per cent.
These figures do not prove that exports alone explain China’s resilience or that every factory is overproducing. But they reveal how external demand sustains production while domestic demand remains uneven.

17:26:30 KST

Syria has strongly condemned escalating Israeli incursions into Quneitra province and the countryside of Daraa in recent days, alongside increased helicopter, reconnaissance, and military aircraft activity over southern Syria, according to Syrian state media SANA.
Israel has operated in this buffer zone and in Syrian villages near the Golan since the fall of the Assad regime. Jerusalem and the new Syrian government have increased tensions over these IDF operations.
Israeli leaders say that Israel will not withdraw from areas it seized along the border in December 2024, including the peak of Mount Hermon. The Syrian government was initially relatively quiet on this issue.
There have been other tensions.
Israel has backed the Druze in Sweida. This has raised questions about whether the Druze may seek an autonomous region or an independent state.
Other countries in the region have recently joined Syria’s condemnation of Israel’s role in the border area.
SANA noted that “in a statement issued on Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates said the Israeli actions constitute a flagrant violation of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and pose a threat to the security and safety of its citizens.” The ministry went on to note that there had been continued violations and that this undermines prospects for security and stability in the region.
The power vacuum near the border has led to concerns that threats could emerge that may destabilize southern Syria and threaten the Golan. These could include Hezbollah cells or even ISIS and other extremists.
Syria has tried to crack down on these threats. It has limited resources, and because Israel wants the area near the border demilitarized, Damascus has to rely on Interior Ministry forces to carry out police operations against threats.
Syria calls on international community to put an end to Israeli incursions
Syria has “called on the international community to assume its responsibilities, put an end to the violations, and force Israel to comply with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions in a way that helps prevent further regional tensions and create conditions for lasting security and stability,” SANA noted.
Syria is now critiquing Jerusalem’s actions more often. It likely hopes that the United States or others may persuade Israel to reduce its raids along the border. Syrian villagers complain that the raids affect their daily lives.
The IDF does not comment on these operations.
Its last statement on an operation in Syria was on October 10: “The IDF struck a Syrian terrorist who advanced terrorist attacks in Syria under the direction of the Iranian regime.” It added that the suspect “advanced terrorist attacks targeting Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers operating in southern Syria.”
The military added that it will “continue to operate to eliminate immediate threats on all fronts.”
On September 23, the IDF said that “following three months of operational activity, IDF soldiers of the 228th Brigade under the command of the 210th Division completed their mission in the Security Zone in Syria to remove threats to the State of Israel.”
Turkey a regional rival for Israel
The recent Syrian condemnation followed statements by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani on Saturday calling for Israeli forces to withdraw to the positions they held before December 8, 2024, and respect the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
In August, Israel also reportedly struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib province, prompting condemnation from Damascus. That strike was a message to Turkey.
Despite these tensions, Israel and Syria held US-mediated talks in August, aimed at reducing military friction and exploring a security agreement. However, disagreements over Israeli deployments and Syria’s sovereignty continue to complicate diplomatic progress.
In a new article at The Moshe Dayan Center, titled “The Israel-Turkey Rivalry after Abu Al-Duhur: Business as Usual or a Drift toward Escalation?” the author, Alex Grinberg, noted that “the Israeli strike on the Abu Al-Duhur airbase in Syria prompted fears that it would escalate a military confrontation with Ankara.
“Likewise, most think tanks and media argued that the strike was counterproductive and that it would not help Israel drive Turkey out of Syria.”
Grinberg added that “Turkish reactions best explain the strike. The Turkish military intended to install radars at Abu Al-Duhur that could compromise Israel’s freedom of action. Official statements and various informal media outlets offered several explanations, placing the onus exclusively on Israel’s behavior.”
“Overall,” he said, “Turkish reactions were measured and limited. This Turkish behavior itself debunks the fears that the Israeli attack would lead to an undesired miscalculation.”
Israel’s role in Syria is part of its security doctrine today.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu laid out some key components of the policy in a speech on Sunday. He spoke about the need to maintain overwhelming military dominance over regional adversaries, including deterrence by means of preemptive strikes, strengthening borders, and establishing buffer zones. Syria is one of those buffer zones.

Victims of sexual, violent crimes gain right to address parole boards in new regulations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:26:04 UTC
17:26:04 KST

Victims of sexual and violent offenses will be entitled to address parole boards directly before a prisoner’s early release is decided, under regulations signed by Justice Minister Yariv Levin and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir that are due to take effect in December.
The rules, announced Sunday, allow victims to choose whether to explain in person or in writing how an offender’s release could threaten their safety. They also set deadlines and procedures for delivering those statements to the boards.
The change is significant, but it does not create victims’ participation in parole proceedings from scratch.
Under the 2001 Crime Victims’ Rights Law, victims of sexual or violent offenses have long been entitled to submit written views on the risks posed by early release. Speaking directly to a parole board, however, was not a guaranteed right.
The new regulations put into practice legislation approved by the Knesset in June 2025, following a bill initiated by MK Chili Tropper and other lawmakers. That law gave victims the option to appear before a parole board and explicitly added their views about threats to their safety to the considerations the board must weigh.
Parole boards decide whether eligible prisoners can serve the final portion of their sentences outside prison under supervision and conditions. Prisoners are generally eligible to seek such release after serving two-thirds of their sentences.
The board must consider factors including their conduct in prison, prospects for rehabilitation and the dangers posed by release.
Victims given deadline to request role at hearing
Under the new procedure, a victim wishing to speak at a hearing must notify the parole board’s secretariat in writing at least 21 days in advance. The rules also allow for cases in which a victim learns of the hearing after that deadline, provided the hearing has not yet taken place.
A victim who prefers to submit a written statement must generally do so no later than seven days before the hearing. Such statements will go to the parole board’s secretariat within the Courts Administration, rather than initially being submitted through the Israel Prison Service, as under the previous regulations.
The accompanying form allows victims to indicate which option they prefer. It also provides for oral statements to be delivered to board members without the prisoner present.
There are limits: the law does not permit a hearing to be postponed solely to accommodate oral testimony if the prisoner has already served two-thirds of the sentence, or would have done so by the postponed date.
Victims whose cases are handled by the separate administrative unit dealing with shorter prison sentences retain a right to submit their views in writing rather than to speak in person.
Years of complaints from victims struggling to be heard
The legislation followed years of complaints from victims who said they struggled to make themselves heard. During Knesset deliberations, a survivor of convicted sex offender Alon Kastiel described difficulties obtaining permission to speak at his parole hearings and receiving adequate notice of proceedings.
Those accounts helped illustrate the difference between being permitted to send a letter and having an enforceable right to appear before the people making the decision.
Levin called strengthening victims’ rights a moral obligation of the justice system and said the regulations would make their participation more accessible while protecting their safety and privacy.
Ben-Gvir said the move would ensure that victims’ voices were heard before an offender was released, describing his policy as “less rights for criminals, more protection for victims.”
The right to speak does not give victims the power to block parole, nor does it make their statements automatically confidential: existing official guidance says written submissions may be shown to prisoners, although the new form provides for victims’ identifying contact details to be withheld.
The regulations are scheduled to come into force on December 1, when the 2025 law takes effect, or on their official publication date if that is later. Their practical impact will depend on whether victims receive timely notice of hearings and can use the new procedures.

France’s Macron declines minister’s resignation after violent protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:25:27 UTC
17:25:27 KST

France’s PM calls for curfews in aftermath of violent protests
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez acknowledges that police ‘lost control’ during weekend protests.
France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has called for “partial” curfews in some cities following the violent unrest that gripped the country over the weekend.
Lecornu said on Monday that he had asked regional authorities to impose “partial” and “localised” curfews in some cities to protect businesses after weekend demonstrations spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
The call came as calm returned, allowing the government to review the response of authorities to the riots, and strategies to prevent a reoccurrence.
President Emmanuel Macron on Monday morning declined an offer from Interior Minister Laurent Nunez to resign in the wake of the unrest, which grew out of nationwide demonstrations by students protesting educational conditions, the Elysee Palace’s presidential office said.
Macron said Nunez should stay in his position to ensure the chain of command is maintained within the police and security forces and asked the interior minister to establish new methods to deal with looters, the Elysee said in a statement.
The president also asked Nunez to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence”, the statement added.
Lecornu later said he had asked local authorities to impose partial curfews starting on Monday evening.
“It is out of the question to put all of Paris under curfew,” he said, but insisted that he was “fully resolved to restoring public order”.
A state of emergency could be declared if necessary, though partial curfews seemed “more appropriate” at this stage, he said, according to the Reuters news agency.
“I’ve asked the prefects to implement a number of curfews for this evening,” Lecornu said, adding that “the key issues” include both “the protection of people, but also of property and businesses”.
The government announced that curfews would run from 8 pm local time (1800GMT) to 6 am local time (0400GMT) in Lille in northeastern France and three nearby communes on Monday and Tuesday night.
Authorities also issued a curfew for Place de la Republique and the streets around Les Halles in Paris from 11 pm (2100GMT) on Monday night until to 6 am (0400GMT) on Tuesday.
Labour and Solidarity Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou and Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-sized enterprises and trade, were due to meet shopkeepers in Paris’s 10th arrondissement on Monday afternoon, the government said.
Increased arrests
The Ministry of the Interior said more than 2,300 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes were injured in protests on Saturday. Injuries were also reported among protesters, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
The nationwide demonstrations brought together students demanding better conditions in the French education system and residents protesting against the high cost of living and faltering public services.
More than half a million people took part in the protests on Saturday. Looting, arson and damage to property occurred in many cities, with masked rioters attacking town halls, police stations and other government buildings.
Nunez acknowledged that police “lost control” during the protests.
“On Saturday in some major cities, you couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn’t lost control,” he said.
Nunez acknowledged a “lack of anticipation” in the deployment of security forces, saying their numbers were insufficient to deal with the large crowds of rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.
The mayors of France’s biggest cities have demanded answers from the government over what they called a lack of preparation by security forces.
Nunez estimated that 60,000 law enforcement personnel were deployed across the country that day, and reported about 350 people were arrested in Paris on Sunday and overnight.
Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 percent of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
Looting continued on Sunday, and Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, describing the scenes as “unbearable”.
The violent weekend demonstrations were led by the yellow vest movement, which held weeks of violent populist protests over fuel prices in 2018-2020.
The unrest followed weeks of protests by high school students against overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and underinvestment in education, the biggest youth-led protest movement in the country in recent memory.
The unrest comes six months before France’s next presidential election, as pressure grows over a weak economy and surging national debt. The yellow vest movement has called for a new round of protests on Saturday, according to France24.

Türkiye’s Trade Ministry has fined 152 real estate agencies and car dealerships a total of 15.2 million Turkish Liras ($307,000) for publishing advertisements that violate regulations on social media, as part of efforts to combat fake listings and protect consumers.
The ministry said inspections were continuing under the Electronic Advertisement Verification System (EİDS), which requires identity and authorization checks for property and vehicle listings published online.
Businesses posting advertisements on platforms including Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and TikTok must share links to verified listings, ensure that photos and descriptions match the advertised property or vehicle, and include price information.
The ministry said 70 businesses were recently fined a combined 7 million liras, bringing the cumulative total to 152 businesses and 15.2 million liras in penalties.
Social media companies have also faced sanctions. Meta’s Turkish subsidiary was fined 20 million liras for failing to integrate with the verification system and meet identity and authorization requirements, while TikTok’s Turkish subsidiary received a 4 million-lira fine. Meta’s cumulative penalties under the measures reached 36.2 million liras, the ministry said.

The drone that entered Lithuanian airspace on October 18 and crashed in Pasvalys District was Ukrainian.
Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi reported this on X.
According to him, Russian EW systems may have diverted the UAV from its intended route.
“We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace and may have been caused by Russian electronic warfare systems that diverted the drones off course during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” Tykhyi noted.
He also emphasized Ukraine’s readiness to provide its Lithuanian partners with all the information needed to establish the circumstances of the incident and continue cooperation to prevent similar situations in the future.
On October 18, an unidentified drone violated Lithuanian airspace, prompting the country to issue an air raid alert.
To determine the type of aerial target, NATO fighter jets assigned to the Baltic Air Policing mission were scrambled, but the pilots were unable to visually identify the object due to poor weather conditions.
According to the Lithuanian military, the unidentified aircraft was moving north from Poland. Authorities later found possible drone debris near the village of Juodoniai in Pasvalys District.
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center, told LRT that the debris damaged a civilian car traveling along the road. The driver was unharmed.
Russian EW systems deployed in the Kaliningrad Region may affect the flight paths of Ukrainian long-range drones, diverting them toward Finland and the Baltic states.
Similar incidents have been reported before. In May, for example, debris from a possibly Ukrainian drone was found in Lithuania after it crashed in a field near the village of Samane in Utena District.
In August, Militarnyi reported on a warning from Lithuanian intelligence about the possibility of Russia using captured Ukrainian drones to stage provocations against the Baltic states.
The exact cause of the October 18 incident has not yet been established, and the theory that Russian electronic warfare systems were involved remains preliminary.

He urged Australians to approach differences with respectful debate.
"We can have differences. They should be debated out in a democracy, but they shouldn't be the subject of personal rancour," he said.
Haines has represented the seat of Indi as the federal member since 2019.
'Shocking day for our nation'
Opposition leader Angus Taylor said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the news and would be praying for Haines and her loved ones.
"This is a shocking day for our nation. No one should be targeted in this way," he said in a statement.
Taylor said he had spoken with Albanese and "we are united in our view that political violence must never be accepted as part of public life".
"I hope Helen, her family and her community across north-east Victoria know that Australians right across the country are thinking of them and holding them in their thoughts during this incredibly difficult time," he added.
David Shoebridge, leader of the Greens, said he was "horrified to hear" of the alleged attack, describing Haines as both a friend and a colleague.
"Helen is an extraordinary human being and brings people together like few others. In grief and solidarity wishing her a complete recovery," he wrote on X.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said she was "horrified and saddened" by the incident, and wished Haines a "full and speedy recovery".
"Violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia. Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety," she posted on X.
Earlier, Haines' family released a statement confirming the mother of three was receiving medical care following an "incident" outside her electorate office.
"We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response," the statement said.
"Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media."
"Please keep Helen in your thoughts."

It added that the system was cost-effective because it reduces reliance on expensive air defence missiles to intercept low-cost targets, helping preserve stocks of conventional ammunition.

Iran freestyle win team title of U23 World Championships
TEHRAN – Iran freestyle team won the team title of the U23 World Wrestling Championships held in the Las Vegas.
Ahora Khateri in 65kg and Mahdi Yousefi in 79kg won two gold medals for Iran to seal the title for the Persians.
Khateri's final against Kaiji OGINO (JPN) was spectacular bout with the Japanese leading, 6-1 with 40 seconds left in the bout. But Khateri began the comeback as he used an arm drag to go-behind Ogino and then scored a takedown and turn. The second two points were only awarded after a challenge from Iran.
With 10 seconds left in the match and down 6-5, Khateri snapped Ogino down and tried to go-behind. Ogino managed to remove the grip but Khateri pulled him down on the mat and eventually scored the takedown with 7-6 left.
Khateri burst into instant celebrations as he captured his first world title since 2023, when he won the U17 world title at 45kg. The gold medal will come as a relief after he finished with a bronze medal at the U20 World Championships in August.
"I was able to enter these competitions with a positive mindset," Khateri said. "I’ve changed weight classes, moving up from 60kg to 65kg. Even though I found myself trailing in every match, I managed to turn things around during the second period."
The two gold medals sealed the team title for Iran which also won the Greco-Roman team title. Iran won a total of nine medals, including four gold medals, in Las Vegas.
Yousefi's gold medal over Said Saidulov (RUS), 3-1, clinched the team title for Iran as any slip up there would have cost them the title.
Yousefi managed a takedown in the second period to lead 3-1. Saidulov got on Yousefi's leg in the final 20 seconds but the Iranian defend the position till time expired.
Iran finished with 180 points and Russia was second with 171 points. The United States, which had a underwhelming tournament, finished third with 104 points. Turkey finished a surprise fourth with 99 points and Japan was fifth with 74 points.

Belgian diplomat: ‘West Bank attack is a new escalation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:13:09 UTC
17:13:09 KST

Saturday was meant to be a day of solidarity and peaceful support, in the olive groves of the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied territories. An international diplomatic delegation, comprising Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, a French mayor, the Archbishop of Cambrai and a local priest, joined farmers for the annual olive harvest.
Belgian diplomat: ‘West Bank attack is a new escalation’
Their presence served a specific purpose: what is known in diplomatic circles as a protective presence.
“That means we go with the Palestinians to their olive groves and help with the harvest,” explains Anick Van Calster, the Belgian consul-general in Jerusalem, who was part of the delegation. “We hope that violent settlers will be deterred by our diplomatic presence.”
However, the atmosphere quickly turned. “It was a very violent morning,” Van Calster told VRT. “We’d already heard that the settlers were committing acts of violence elsewhere, but when we heard they were heading our way, we decided to get into the cars. We are diplomats and we do not seek confrontation.”
Before everyone had got safely into the vehicles, a group of attackers appeared. They were young, masked men armed with wooden and metal sticks.
“You could only see their eyes,” says Van Calster. “That didn’t bode well.”
The first vehicle, in which Van Calster was travelling, managed to drive off quickly. The second attempted to pick up members of the French delegation, including Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of the northern municipality of Aulnoye-Aymeries. It was unable to leave before the attackers reached them.
“Mayor Baudoux was physically attacked and thrown to the ground before he could even get in,” Van Calster says. “When the car finally managed to escape, the settlers pelted it with rocks, shattering the rear window.”
The violence has truly reached new heights
Consul-general Anick Van Calster
Once back in the village, the diplomats found a group of Israeli activists in a state of deep shock. “They had also been attacked by the settlers, who had told them: ‘We’re going to kill you’,” says Van Calster.
She stresses that this direct attack on diplomats crosses a dangerous line. “Attacking diplomats is a new escalation,” she says. “Since the start of the olive harvest, there have already been more incidents than there were throughout the whole of last year’s season. The violence has truly reached new heights.”
Many Palestinian farmers no longer dare to go on their own land for fear of their lives, creating economic hardship for many families.
An investigation by Israeli newspaper Haaretz reveals that the army ignored repeated warnings about the impending attack. Urgent calls for help were received at around 13.00, including the exact location and video footage of “at least seven masked settlers, armed with clubs”.
An activist sent the reports to a military helpline, but soldiers ignored the unknown number and did not pass on the information. It was not until around 15.00 that the information reached the army, by which time settlers had already smashed a window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian delegation.
The army has launched an investigation. It says the helpline was not intended for civilians and that the visit should have been coordinated in advance. According to Van Calster, the latter is not true.
Under the Oslo Accords, diplomats are not required to coordinate their visits in advance, she says. According to reports, the authorities had been aware of their presence and of the threat in the area for hours.
“We must not be blamed for a deterioration in the security situation, the effects of which we are feeling but which have absolutely nothing to do with us,” she says. “Our peaceful presence serves to show just how dire the situation there really is.”
In the wake of the incident, Foreign minister Maxime Prévot of Les Engagés is calling for joint international action. Belgium will continue to press for European sanctions against those responsible for the violence and those who support them, he says.
The European Union, too, has condemned the violence against European diplomats.

‘We believe in peaceful protest’: Tharoor rejects BJP’s India-Bangladesh comparison
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Monday rejected comparisons between India and Bangladesh or France amid the political row over the opposition's use of the phrase “regime change”, asserting that the demand was for free and fair elections and not an attempt to topple the government.Responding to Union minister Kiren Rijiju's remarks, Tharoor said India did not support violence and that protests should remain peaceful. He also questioned the relevance of comparisons with unrest in other countries."I think that India is not Bangladesh and India is not France. I don't see these analogies as particularly relevant... We would never condone any of the violence, setting alight buses and police stations and so on, that has occurred in France. We only believe in peaceful protest... that's the kind of protest that I have participated in, and that I believe the opposition in general supports... As far as the larger issues are concerned, there's no point distorting a phrase like 'regime change' and so on... What we are calling for is free and fair elections... What is troubling today is that large numbers of people have been cut from the electoral rolls as the result of a completely troublesome, irregular, and partially illegal process.
This is why we are calling for all this to be undone... It's a constitutional issue. It's not an issue of trying to topple a regime or anything like that..."
Tharoor also defended citizens' right to protect democratic institutions, while clarifying that his criticism was directed at their functioning and not their existence."...Democracy is not a gift of anybody... we, the ordinary citizens of India, are the custodians of it... Every Indian citizen has the right to protect our democracy... All I'm saying is we are asking institutions like the Election Commission to behave themselves, to perform as they are required to by the democratic Constitution of India. That's all it is. I'm not in any way challenging these institutions as institutions. I'm challenging the way they are behaving, the way they are conducting themselves, and that is something that honestly all of us in India should be concerned about..."
Political row over ‘regime change’
The remarks came amid a political exchange over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.On Sunday, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju alleged that “anti-India groups” and some politicians had colluded to provoke young people and spread violence, claiming that a conspiracy similar to the unrest in Bangladesh and France had been planned in India.“The violent incident that occurred in Bangladesh and the riots, arson, and looting that took place in France, a similar conspiracy was hatched for India as well,” Rijiju said in a post on X.He further asserted that a change of government in India could take place only through elections.“Regime change in India is absolutely possible, but only through elections, not through Soros,” he said.The row intensified after senior advocate Prashant Bhushan described the agitation against Kumar as a “fight for regime change”. All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora also referred to the Gen Z-led movement in Bangladesh.Rijiju had earlier accused political rivals and activists of using street protests to create unrest and destabilise constitutional institutions. He said India's youth were focused on nation-building rather than political upheaval.
Separately, Tharoor responded to Elon Musk's recent remarks regarding Starlink, saying the government had maintained that all companies bidding for the service were going through the same process and facing similar delays."I've heard the government's explanation on this issue, which is that there is a process and that all the companies bidding for this are in the same process and are facing the same delays. If that position of the government is taken literally, that means Musk is no further behind in the queue, and Ambani is no further ahead. I think we just have to wait for the process to play itself out... There are several factors. There are questions of the technology, certain security concerns, various kinds of details to do with the uplinking and finally cost.
The last one, the ordinary public will decide. If you are giving me a service and he's giving it to me for 10 times the price, I may take it from you. Or if I really feel that what he's doing is worth 10 times the money, I'll give it to him. Each subscriber will have to decide. Personally, I'm quite happy with my regular connections. I'm not looking for a Starlink myself. But if there are people who feel these things are useful, in a free country, let them have the opportunity."

Mali’s military and armed groups committing abuses against civilians: HRW
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:06:22 UTC
17:06:22 KST

Mali’s military and armed groups committing abuses against civilians: HRW
Soldiers, fighters and separatists in West African country committing grave laws-of-war violations, rights group finds.
Mali’s military and its Russian paramilitary allies have killed civilians in breach of international law, and opposition armed groups have done likewise, Human Rights Watch (HRW) says.
Soldiers and fighters “are committing grave laws-of-war violations while international organisations and governments largely stand by”, the United States-based rights watchdog said in a report released on Monday.
It urged the African Union’s Peace and Security Council to “urgently take action to prevent further atrocities” in Mali.
The West African country has been mired in fighting and attacks since 2012 as the military and its allies have battled an array of armed groups, including Tuareg separatists, and criminal gangs.
The military government that has ruled Mali since back-to-back coups in 2020 and 2021 has turned to Russia for support, enlisting the services initially of fighters from the private Wagner Group, which became the state-controlled paramilitary group Africa Corps in 2025.
‘Scores of civilians’ killed
The rights group said its report was based on interviews with 30 people – witnesses, human rights defenders, community leaders, journalists and a Malian soldier – conducted from late July to mid-September.
“Mali’s military and the allied Russia-controlled Africa Corps … have killed and wounded scores of civilians in attacks and in custody in violation of international humanitarian law,” HRW said.
Armed groups “have also violated the laws-of-war, including torturing and executing captured Malian soldiers”, it added.
HRW said it documented two “apparently indiscriminate” drone attacks by the Malian military.
According to the report, a July 29 attack in the Kidal region of northeastern Mali destroyed part of a health facility, and a second on August 19 hit a market in the central region of Bandiagara, killing six civilians and wounding at least 20.
HRW said it also documented an operation against armed groups in the Segou region in the south, where Malian soldiers shot and killed five girls, and another in the central region of Mopti, where members of the military-allied Dozo militia killed three civilians, “all with impunity”.
Fighters ‘execute’ soldiers
HRW also cited an attack on a military convoy in the Gao region on July 18 by Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and allied separatist fighters in the Azawad Liberation Front.
It said the two groups “tortured and executed at least 19 Malian troops” they had taken prisoner.
The JNIM acknowledged that prisoners were killed in the event but denied having ordered the deaths, HRW said.
The Azawad Liberation Front, HRW added, acknowledged fighting with the army and Russian forces in the northeastern region on the day but denied executing soldiers.
The HRW report also drew on research by Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a nongovernmentsl group that gathers conflict data from around the world.
It said its data show 49 air strikes by Malian forces and the Africa Corps from April to August that killed 89 civilians, “more than double the 22 strikes and 44 civilian deaths reported during the same period last year”.
HRW said it sent a letter to Mali’s defence minister on August 5 with its findings and questions but received no response.

Ho said the unions want Article 29 of the Labor Standards Act to clearly specify how companies should share profits and distribute the value created by their workers. The government should give equal attention to the technology sector and traditional industries to help generate better economic outcomes, he said.
Ho added that raising the minimum wage would benefit some service-sector workers, but companies should not use it as the benchmark for employee compensation. With prices continuing to rise, failing to raise wages effectively amounts to a pay cut, he said.

Prosecutions of Israeli settlers, however, are rare.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on X that the arrests were "a very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat" Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine.
A video released by the police of the predawn operation appeared to show at least one arrested suspect, whose face is not seen, wearing ritual tassels known as tzitzit, which are often worn by religious Jewish men.
The video also appeared to show two slingshots, which can be used to hurl stones, being found at one property. On Friday, when the Washington Post journalist was attacked, dozens of masked settlers, some armed, descended on a Palestinian olive harvest, with some settlers hurling stones with slingshots.
Police, military forces and the Shin Bet domestic security service took part in the operation.
Referring to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, Israeli Police Commissioner Daniel Levy said the law applied to everyone, "regardless of identity or affiliation."
"The Israel Police is committed to professional, equal, and impartial law enforcement, based on evidence and in accordance with the law," he said in a statement announcing the arrests.
Masked Israeli settlers were filmed Friday assaulting Levine, a U.S. citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank. Levine was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.
On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats.
However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose far-right coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the Oct. 27 election, has been more circumspect.
He has claimed the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations" and without coordinating with the military. He has also said that the facts of the attack on Levine were "unclear."
Levine has said she was attacked by masked men wearing tzitzit tassels. Israel's President Isaac Herzog has apologized, saying the "violent rioters" who "brutally attacked" her did not represent the values of Israel.
Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since Sept. 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

Türkiye to Receive Russian Diesel Under Moscow – Trump Deal

2026-10-19
08:00:45 UTC
17:00:45 KST

Türkiye will receive a share of the diesel fuel that Russia will supply to the global market under an agreement between Moscow and US President Donald Trump’s administration.
Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar announced this, Reuters reported.
According to the minister, the agreement is important for Türkiye’s energy security.
Bayraktar noted that Russia had restricted diesel fuel exports in recent months due to supply issues, but Ankara will now be able to receive part of the Russian fuel.
“Thanks to the negotiations we have held, we will receive part of this fuel for Türkiye,” Bayraktar said.
However, the minister did not specify how much diesel fuel Türkiye would receive or the terms of delivery.
On October 9, US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply 4.8million tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
According to Trump, Russia was to immediately deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of fuel, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November, 1 million tonnes shortly thereafter, and an additional 3 million tonnes within a short timeframe, depending on the capacity of Russian oil refineries.
On the same day, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued a temporary authorization for transactions involving Russian diesel fuel previously subject to US sanctions restrictions.
The document allows the sale, delivery, unloading, and import of such fuel until April 7, 2027.
Following Trump’s announcement, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said that Moscow was beginning to lift its own restrictions on diesel fuel exports ahead of schedule.

Chinese discovery of doughnut-like topology at tipping points breaks physics convention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:00:11 UTC
17:00:11 KST

Chinese discovery of doughnut-like topology at tipping points breaks physics convention
Study bridges critical phenomena and topology, opening new pathways for fundamental science research
Chinese physicists have discovered that a tipping point – a threshold where a physical system rapidly shifts states – can possess a smooth mathematical structure resembling a doughnut’s hole, challenging a belief that the two phenomena must be studied separately.
For decades, mainstream physicists have mostly treated critical phenomena, which describe how physical systems change at critical points, and topology, which studies the properties of geometry, as separate areas of research.
A classic illustration of topology is the difference between a sphere and a doughnut. The two cannot be transformed into each other by stretching or bending alone because they have a different number of holes, unless the surface is cut or glued.
The study by researchers at Singaporean and Chinese institutions was published in Nature on October 7, with Cheng Zheyu and Zhang Xiuhai, both affiliated with Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, as co-first authors.
Cheng and his colleagues set out to investigate whether doughnut-like topological properties could exist at critical points – the thresholds at which physical systems change their behaviour.

European delegation including Belgian diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:59:26 UTC
16:59:26 KST

A diplomatic delegation including the Belgian consul-general was attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Saturday. Violence in the area has escalated since the start of the olive harvest in late September.
European delegation including Belgian diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
The group of Belgian, French and Polish diplomats was taking part in the olive harvest in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, a spokesperson for Foreign minister Maxime Prévot confirmed. Their participation was a “symbolic gesture of support for the local population”.
During the visit, the convoy was surrounded by masked settlers armed with sticks, who pelted the vehicles with rocks, breaking a window.
Consul-general Anick Van Calster and a second Belgian diplomat were present at the incident. They were unharmed. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the French municipality of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was injured.
Prévot condemned the attack on X. “I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank,” he posted. “Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats ... As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.”
He said Belgium would continue to press for European sanctions “against those responsible for this violence and those who support them” and that “the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end”.
I was violently attacked and thrown to the ground. I was quite shaken
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries
Baudoux was in the West Bank because Aulnoye-Aymeries is twinned with the Christian municipality of Taybeh. He was visiting to pick olives with locals as a symbolic gesture.
“Suddenly, masked people arrived in cars and started attacking the group,” he said. “I had put on my sash, in the colours of the French flag, in an attempt to protect the people around me. But it was to no avail. I was violently attacked and thrown to the ground. I was quite shaken.”
The Israeli army said in a statement on X that “no Israeli soldiers were present” at the time of the attack. It also stated that the visit had not been coordinated with the army. According to the army, such coordination is “important to prevent incidents such as this”.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu describes the incident as a smear campaign against Israel. The army has, however, stated that it is launching an investigation. The Israeli police are also reported to have launched an investigation.
In the nearby village of Abu Fallah, around 80 Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers at the weekend. Wearing masks and dressed in black, they threw rocks and set fire to trees and vehicles.
The situation escalated when the Israeli army intervened. According to the Palestinian news agency Wafa, both Israeli soldiers and settlers opened fire. Several Palestinian farmers were injured.
Human rights organisations have again reported an increase in violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank in recent weeks. According to the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din, settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the olive harvest. The Palestinian Authority reports that at least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured.
Human rights organisations document a rise in violence almost every year during the harvest, which is a crucial source of income for many Palestinian families. This year, however, it appears to be escalating further in the run-up to the Israeli elections at the end of October.

Philippines summons Chinese ambassador over ‘use of force’ remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:58:04 UTC
16:58:04 KST

The Philippines has summoned China’s ambassador to Manila after he said Beijing could “easily win” a conflict between the two countries, prompting calls from Philippine lawmakers for his expulsion.
Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro conveyed Manila’s “serious concern and strong objection” to Ambassador Jing Quan over his public remarks on October 15, which the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs said amounted to a threat to use force.
The dispute follows a series of incidents involving the two countries’ militaries and coast guards in contested areas of the South China Sea.
China claims most of the strategic waterway, despite an international ruling that found no legal basis for its expansive claims.
Jing made the remarks last week after Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro described Beijing as a regional “troublemaker”.
Speaking to reporters after a speech at a school in Manila, the Chinese envoy said the Philippines should “feel fortunate” to have China as a neighbour.
“If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace,” he said.
The comments prompted calls from politicians, including at least two sitting senators, for Manila to expel the ambassador.
In its statement on Monday, the Philippine foreign ministry described Jing’s remarks as “provocative and unacceptable”.
“The Department reserves the right to take further diplomatic action as it deems necessary,” it added.
Jing called for peaceful resolution
Earlier, speaking at the Second Diliman Dialogue in Manila, Jing called for a peaceful approach to maritime disputes, urging both sides to maintain a safe distance, avoid deliberate provocations and prevent incidents from escalating tensions.
He said China and the Philippines should manage their differences through dialogue and consultation, warning against a cycle of reciprocal countermeasures.
Jing also argued that maritime disputes should not define the entirety of bilateral relations, pointing to continued trade, people-to-people exchanges and cooperation in other areas.
“We must not allow a small group of people, backed by forces from outside the region, to steer bilateral relations into a dangerous and uncertain course, or even toward confrontation and conflict,” he said at the dialogue.

Daycare prices outpace benefit cap, hitting low earners hardest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:57:09 UTC
16:57:09 KST

Daycare prices outpace benefit cap, hitting low earners hardest
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Seven in 10 daycare centres now charge more than the hourly rate covered by childcare benefit (kinderopvangtoeslag), and parents have to make up the shortfall, parents’ association BOinK reported.
The average hourly rate at the 400 organisations BOinK surveyed is €11.82, while the government only subsidises up to €11.23. The cap goes up to €11.60 in January, which is still less than most centres are already charging, and prices are set to rise again next year.
Low earners will get hit hardest, NU.nl reported on Monday. The state covers 96% of the capped rate for the lowest incomes, leaving them with a bill of a few cents an hour – until the surcharge above the cap is added.
A family on a low income with a child in daycare two days a week could be paying €80 a month next year, up from €70.
“For many parents, this means their own contribution keeps rising,” BOinK chairman Gjalt Jellesma said in a statement.
A social affairs ministry spokesperson told NU.nl that childcare is becoming more affordable overall and that the gap between the cap and actual prices has narrowed since 2023.

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages
- WFP says funding shortages are forcing Gaza aid cuts, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support and halving rations for many others.
- The agency says 1.4 million people in Gaza face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, while 200,000 are in emergency conditions.
- WFP needs US$450 million over six months and warns life in Gaza remains “brutal” as winter nears and basic services stay scarce.
AI generated
CAIRO/GAZA – The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid programme in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.
In addition, food rations have also been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza’s population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions.
The US-brokered Gaza ceasefire in 2025 calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
Life is still brutal in Gaza, says acting head of WFP
“It’s a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no basic services. There is no safety, no security,” acting executive director of the WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
“These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I’ve been through the winters here, absolutely brutal,” he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs US$450 million (S$575 million) over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
“We tell the world now is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery,” said Skau.
Israeli forces still hold more than 60% of the territory and conduct almost daily air strikes, while Hamas controls most of the area where more than two million Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with what aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies.
The Hamas-run Gaza government media office described the WFP announcement as “catastrophic” and said it might accelerate famine in the enclave, calling for more fund to aid agencies to prevent it.
“On top of the circumstances and the difficult life, you want to make it even harder on us,” said Palestinian woman Sabrine Kuhail, standing by a tent shelter at a displacement site in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza Strip.
“You made us hungry for three years with war, destruction, siege, and the bloodshed that is not stopping. What do you want from us? Enough, enough, we are tired.” REUTERS

Singapore sets aside 92 mln USD for bio-based chemicals research
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:55:19 CST
16:55:19 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Singapore has set aside 118 million Singapore dollars (about 92.23 million U.S. dollars) for research into producing chemicals from biological materials, the largest public funding commitment of its kind to date, the Economic Development Board (EDB) said on Monday.
The Bioeconomy Funding Initiative, launched under the 37-billion-Singapore-dollar Research, Innovation, Enterprise 2030 plan, aims to address industry challenges and support the transformation of Singapore's energy and chemicals sector, which accounts for one-fifth of domestic manufacturing output, the EDB said in a statement.
The initiative will target chemicals made from biological alternatives to petroleum-based feedstocks, such as yeast and oil palm, the EDB said.
Initial research will focus on converting industrial by-products, or "sidestreams," into usable materials, developing microbe- and enzyme-based production methods, and improving processing efficiency.
Research and development projects will also explore combinations of biological and chemical processes to produce commercially viable goods, including high-grade synthetic rubber.
"There are opportunities for Singapore to grow our capabilities in innovation and production of higher-value specialty chemicals and advanced materials, while supporting the transformation of our existing industrial base towards more sustainable production," said Jermaine Loy, managing director of the EDB.
The latest initiative builds on previous funding commitments and will bring government spending on bioeconomy-related initiatives to about 200 million Singapore dollars over the next five years. ■

ATHENS, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- An infant was among six people killed after a speedboat carrying migrants collided with a Greek coast guard patrol vessel off the eastern Aegean island of Lesvos on Monday, Greek authorities said.
