NAZARETH, Israel – Israel’s Palestinian leaders are urging people in the minority Arab community to vote in big numbers in next week’s election as they seek to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and topple the most right-wing government in the country’s history.
High turnout by the 21% Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by citizenship, could nudge Israel’s complex coalition arithmetic in favour of an anti-Netanyahu bloc led by a former military chief, Gadi Eisenkot.
“We can ensure the formation of a new government of change,” Mansour Abbas, an Islamist dentist-turned-politician who heads the United Arab List party, told Reuters in his office in Nazareth, Israel’s most populous Arab city.
Polls show Eisenkot short of majority without Arab support
Abbas and other Arab leaders face one big obstacle to their goal of playing a role in any future administration without Netanyahu.
Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties that most Palestinian Israelis will vote for, citing a lack of shared values.
But Abbas thinks there will be room for manoeuvre, perhaps after the vote, largely thanks to the cold, hard realities of electoral maths.
Opinion polls suggest Eisenkot’s patchwork bloc of centrist, right- and left-wing parties will get the most votes, but fall short of a majority, and will need Arab support, either as coalition partners or from outside, to prop up a minority government.
“We want to replace the right-wing government... to end the wars and these policies, to stop the expansion of settlements and to address the failure to stop settler attacks,” Abbas said.
“We also want a government that brings shared security and peace for Palestinians and Israelis.”
For now, Eisenkot is sticking to his position. “I will not align myself with any Arab party,” Eisenkot said in a podcast in October, citing among other issues their refusal to label Hamas a terrorist organisation.
If any bloc fails to form a workable government, that could lead to a period of political deadlock, then fresh elections in 2027, with Netanyahu left in charge in the meantime.
But Netanyahu, for one, appears to be taking the threat of some sort of Eisenkot-Arab alliance seriously, or at least sees it as an opportunity to rile up his base. His campaign has used doctored images and AI-generated videos to depict his rivals embracing Arab leaders.
One fake video, released over the summer, shows Eisenkot running through a meadow into the outstretched arms of Abbas.
Abbas’ own career shows such alliances can be made. In 2021 he became the first Arab Muslim to join an Israeli coalition as a minister, in a government led by Naftali Bennett, now a right-wing member of Eisenkot’s bloc.
That government collapsed after 18 months, partly over disagreements between the two men on the occupied West Bank.
This time round, Abbas said he could paper over those differences. To win over Jewish parties, he has taken the unprecedented step of giving the number two spot on his slate to a Jewish former police official, Yoav Segalovitz.
“It sends a message of partnership with the Jewish community and with Jewish citizens,” Abbas said.
Arabs frustrated with demonisation by Israel right, crime
Israel’s election will be the first since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack, and is being viewed as a referendum on the leadership of Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader.
Polls show Eisenkot’s bloc would win 52 of the Knesset’s 120 seats if elections were held today. Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist bloc would win 50 seats.
Abbas’ party is projected to win five seats, with a further eight going to the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab parties.
Ahead of the vote, Bezalel Smotrich, Netanyahu’s far-right finance minister, proposed a plan to “Judaize” areas around Nazareth in the north and in southern Israel where most Arabs live, describing it as similar to settler expansionism in the West Bank.
Party organisers in Nazareth are hoping to capitalize on Arab anger with Netanyahu, Smotrich and far-right police minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, as well as frustration with rising crime in their communities.
Last week, canvassers with Abbas’ party handed out flyers near Nazareth’s massive Church of the Annunciation.
“There is a greater need this time than ever before to go out and vote in large numbers,” said one of the people they approached, 74-year-old Gassan Bsoul. “The danger is greater than in the past,” he added.
Arab turnout expected to be high
Israeli pollsters expect Arab voter turnout to be higher than in previous rounds of elections in 2022 and 2020. The Stat-Net Research Institute, based in an Arab Druze town near Haifa, projects turnout of 63%, compared with 56% in 2022.
While Abbas has tried to position his party to potentially join government, leaders of the Joint List have said they could wield just as much influence by staying in opposition.

Spain's rush to clear Ceuta migrant backlog raises rights concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:05:55 UTC
16:05:55 KST

Spain's rush to clear Ceuta migrant backlog raises rights concerns
CEUTA/MADRID, Oct 19 - When heavily pregnant Fatna and her disabled son arrived in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta during a chaotic mass border crossing on July 30, she hoped to be high on authorities' list for help.
Nearly three months later, with her newborn baby girl suffering from kidney problems, Fatna, 21, and her family urgently need to reach mainland Spain for specialist hospital treatment.
However, travelling while her asylum claim is under review requires a permit that Spain's socialist government – ordinarily a staunch advocate of immigration – has been reluctant to grant to any of the thousands of migrants remaining in Ceuta.
Some are still scattered on the streets or hiding in the rolling hills of the tiny 20-sq-km port city on Morocco's northeast border.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's government is under pressure from the EU and an increasingly frustrated populace to sort out the crisis and faces a snap election on November 29.
It is working on shortcuts for asylum applications with the intention of sending most people home, mainly to Morocco, on the basis of being economic migrants not real asylum-seekers.
That, NGOs fear, risks violating migrants' rights.
Sanchez, one of Europe's few remaining left-leaning leaders, said this week that Spain was managing the flood of cases "responsibly, with a sense of solidarity and respecting migrants' human rights".
But more than 20 interviews by Reuters with migrants, lawyers, NGOs, and security forces revealed that many of those who remain have clear grounds for asylum or humanitarian protection: from unaccompanied minors to LGBT Moroccans fearing imprisonment if deported and families like Fatna's classified as vulnerable under EU law.
Last week, eight charities including Oxfam and Amnesty International filed a complaint with Spain's ombudsman seen by Reuters alleging "grave rights violations" in the tiny Ceuta enclave. They included the forced return of migrants from conflict-hit countries and denial of interpreters and legal assistance.
Spokespeople for Spain's central government, interior ministry, territorial policy ministry and migration ministry did not respond to Reuters requests for comment on the mistreatment accusations.
"There are people who will truly be in enormous danger if they are returned to Morocco," said Wendell Soares, coordinator of the Catholic migrant reception centre San Antonio which has taken in Fatna's family and dozens more vulnerable people, far beyond its usual capacity of seven.
"When the word ‘immigrant’ is used, it creates a collective image, as if they were all the same. Every person has their own story."
DEPORTED WITHOUT EXPLANATION
Spanish right-wing and far-right parties were already angry with Sanchez's government for providing legal status to nearly 1 million irregular migrants earlier this year. They have cast July's crossing as a deliberate invasion by Morocco – an accusation Morocco denies – and demanded that all migrants be returned.
But despite plans for a new EU-wide procedure enabling accelerated deportations in future emergency scenarios, current rules require that migrants be assessed case-by-case.
While most are from Morocco, the government estimated in August that more than 1,000 of the migrants remaining were from sub-Saharan countries whose nationals are granted asylum in over 90% of cases in Spain, according to government statistics.
The EU's new pact requires that cases be processed in border zones to permit faster deportations. But it does not require applicants to stay where they arrived, allowing for transfers to other border zones in Spain that would alleviate pressure on the 84,000-person enclave of Ceuta, Europe's only land border with Africa.
If vulnerable migrants' cases are to be properly assessed, such transfers are the "only option", said Juan Miguel Morales, director-general of NGO Sur Acoge.
While 262 minors have been transferred to the Spanish mainland since the July crossing, the government's strategy for the remaining adults has been to convince as many as possible to return of their own volition.
The government said this week that 12,000 had chosen to cross back since mid-August.
"There are no covert deportations under any circumstances," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said, describing the returns as voluntary and adding that up to 1,200 asylum applications had been received and 700 of them resolved.
However, at least nine NGOs have in public communication or interviews with Reuters claimed that migrants they support were coerced to return.
Asociación Elin said migrants from Sudan and Chad were summoned by police on September 24 and 25 and deported without warning, according to the complaint to the ombudsman.
In text messages reviewed by Reuters, Moroccan migrant Azhaar Chaouni told volunteers at German NGO Mission Lifeline that he and other migrants faced the same fate, after being picked up in buses by police from their makeshift camps on the beach and told they were being taken to reception centres.
"They deported us without explanation," Chaouni wrote, saying he was in Morocco.
Morocco's designation as a "safe country of origin" under EU rules does not strip its citizens of the right to apply for asylum, said Andrea de Petris, immigration expert at the think tank CEP, based in Freiburg, Germany.
"Each individual must be guaranteed a specific assessment of their personal circumstances," added De Petris who estimates the procedure would inevitably be "lengthy and costly".
Stories of others disappearing have instilled fear in Rayane, a 19-year-old gay Moroccan awaiting news on his asylum application in the San Antonio reception centre. Rejected by his family and unable to live openly in Morocco where same-sex sexual acts are prosecuted, he is desperate to get to mainland Europe.
"I can’t even imagine myself going back to Morocco. I’d kill myself before even crossing the border," he said.
PACT EXPOSED
Frontline workers and NGOs on the ground say the situation in Ceuta has proven that the 12-week limit set in the EU’s migrant pact for processing asylum applications is unrealistic, with seven stating they expect the process to drag on for months.
A lack of resources from staff to functioning computers meant that only around 100 migrants' cases were being registered daily by October 14, according to police union representative Raul Piera.
The union estimates roughly 7,000-8,000 more migrants are still scattered across the city, sleeping rough or squeezed into facilities provided by charities and civil society groups filling the gap left by Ceuta's overwhelmed social services.
"Looking at the remaining workload, this will last well into next summer," said Piera.
Spain's government has declined to comment on estimates of unregistered migrants, with Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres telling reporters on October 14 that it was impossible to know how many were hiding.
Doctors in Ceuta's only hospital are treating migrants for scabies, tuberculosis and gastrointestinal infections caused by long periods outdoors, said Enrique Robiralta, head of the doctors' union. At least seven women have given birth.
Fatna and her husband Mohamed are desperate to stay in Spain, fearing for the new baby and convinced their 3-year-old disabled son will die in Morocco. "We are doing everything for our son," said Mohamed. REUTERS

Losing Cuba, the global trickster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:02:58 UTC
16:02:58 KST

Losing Cuba, the global trickster
The Cuban Revolution, with all its contradictions, has given plenty to the world. Its fall will be a major loss.
Cuba is once again in the United States’s crosshairs. Washington’s operation in Venezuela at the start of the year is largely seen to have paved the way for a similar undertaking on the Caribbean island. Recent media reports have revealed US military activity nearby while US officials have repeatedly said they want “Cuba to be free”.
When and how the US may strike is still unclear. But indications are that the Cuban Revolution may be nearing its end. That is reason enough to pause and reflect on the outsized role this nation of 10 million has played on the world stage.
When thinking of the Cuban presence on the global geopolitical scene, the figure of Eshu, the most powerful spirit in Cuban Santeria comes to mind. Derived from the beliefs of the Yoruba people, Eshu is a divine messenger, the guardian of the crossroads and mediator between the past and the future.
In stories, Eshu is often portrayed as a mischievous elder, one whose antics are used to teach humility and morality. As a character, Eshu is a classic trickster, an archetype commonplace to many traditions that functions to challenge established norms, subvert power structures and reveal hidden truths.
It’s hard to imagine a more apt analogy for Cuba than Eshu, the trickster, foil to US hegemony. At its best, trickster Cuba forced an open debate on what kind of world we might aspire to and held the empire to account, at times even pushing the US towards its better angels, however begrudgingly. At its worst, it held up an uncomfortable mirror to US power.
It is a potent formula, one struck upon from the very earliest days of the revolution. In September 1960, just a year after taking Havana, Cuban leader Fidel Castro found himself visiting New York to address the United Nations General Assembly. Wary of his anti-imperialist rhetoric, a Cold War-obsessed US government put pressure on several prominent hotels to refuse service to Castro and his entourage. But the Cubans were not to be deterred. Instead, they went uptown to Harlem and found a place at the Hotel Theresa.
Photographers and TV camera people flocked there. A media sensation ensued. And Castro used the opportunity to draw comparisons between the plight of the Cuban delegation and that of Black Americans being refused service in the segregated South.
This landed like a bomb in the middle of the burgeoning civil rights movement. It was an awkward contrast, not just because of the optics but because of the location, not in the heart of Jim Crow, but in a liberal northern city, New York, the cradle of American civilisation. This was the first, but not the last time that Cuba, the trickster, would strike.
In the following years, the revolutionary government developed its programme of Cuban Internationalism, which inevitably stood as a counter to US soft power efforts in the developing world through organisations like the Peace Corps and USAID.
Cuba would send as many as 400,000 doctors, not to mention engineers, agricultural technicians and other professionals, to 164 countries across the world. This material solidarity garnered great affection for Cuba among many countries in the Global South, countries as disparate as Venezuela, South Africa and Vietnam, where characters like Castro and Che Guevara are as recognisable as national heroes like Simon Bolivar, Nelson Mandela and Ho Chi Minh. In these same countries, American leaders are remembered too, often in far less flattering terms.
Other examples of Cuba’s trickster antics abound. Perhaps most notable is the Cuban armed forces’ sound military defeat of the Bay of Pigs invasion, which, while carried out by Cuban exiles, was supported and funded directly by the CIA.
There is also the revolution’s support for the Palestinian liberation movement and the antiapartheid struggle even as the US provided diplomatic cover and military aid to Israel and the apartheid regime in South Africa.
From 1975 to 1991, more than 300,000 Cuban soldiers fought alongside forces in Angola, eventually emerging victorious in a proxy conflict with the US. Operation Carlota, as it was called, would not only liberate Angola and neighbouring Namibia, but it would precipitate the downfall of South African apartheid as well. According to former South African President Nelson Mandela, Cuba’s intervention in Angola “destroyed the myth of the invincibility of the white oppressor”.
Castro himself has carried the spirit of Eshu. The Cuban leader reportedly survived more than 600 assassination attempts and died of natural causes at the age of 90.
And there are the many ways that Cuba has defied the “third world” label so often foisted upon it by beating the US in literacy rates, infant mortality and life expectancy at various points in its revolutionary history.
But beyond all of this, there is the sheer fact of the revolution’s survival. For more than 60 years, the US has imposed a severe economic embargo against the island. The embargo – the world’s longest – has been intensified at various points, specifically after the fall of the Soviet Union as Cuba reeled from a profound economic crisis.
Despite this regime of maximum pressure from the world’s largest superpower, the revolution nevertheless persevered through the crisis of the 1990s by diversifying and liberalising the economy and by drawing upon its well-established programme of internationalism in the Global South. Not only that, but it managed a nationwide sustainable agricultural revolution in the process, a feat for any nation, but perhaps unsurprising for Cuba, given its trickster nature.
But tricksters also work in unexpected, even contradictory ways. Despite these accomplishments, the denial of political rights and the repression of the freedoms of expression and assembly have been the Cuban Revolution’s greatest failings.
Speech is not free in Cuba. Access to information and the internet is heavily restricted, and recent popular protests have been violently extinguished.
Such dynamics have long been pointed to by detractors as evidence of Cuba’s inherent authoritarian nature. But in this regard, Cuba is not the US’s opposite, but rather its peer.
The US in 2026 is a country facing its own rash of unfreedoms: comical levels of corruption; the erosion of democratic institutions; the embrace of AI and the panopticon surveillance it enables; continual attacks on free speech, voting rights and the media; extrajudicial killings of US citizens by masked agents of the state; and an increasingly monarchical presidency. All of which is to say nothing about the spectre of the infamous detention facility at Guantanamo Bay, still home to 15 detainees from the “global war on terror”, raised once more in relation to President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown.
One cannot help but be struck by the ways that the Trump administration appears to emulate countries like Cuba or Russia or Iran that it rhetorically maligns.
But in this way, Cuba carries on in its role as the foil to American power. In its repression, it reflects the creeping authoritarian inclinations that characterise the Trump administration. Tricksters, after all, are themselves morally ambiguous. And if the greatest flaw of the US has always been that it fails consistently to live up to its most laudable ideals, then in this sense, it is no different to Cuba and its revolution.
With the US poised and ready and with the conditions in Cuba deteriorating rapidly, we may be witnessing the final days of the revolution. That begs the question: When the day comes that Eshu no longer guards the crossroads, what then? What becomes of the world when there is nothing but unquestioned empires and techno-feudal overlords? Without tricksters to confound their power, will we revert to the revanchist past or tumble into some kind of dystopian future?
If and when the revolution finally falls, there will no doubt be cheering on the streets of Miami. But there will be tears elsewhere – tears not just for the revolution, but for the alternative that it represented, however flawed. Perhaps if the US had listened more or differently, they would have heard the lesson that Eshu was trying to teach.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Ukraine now gets only 12 Patriot interceptors a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:00:16 UTC
16:00:16 KST

- Zelenskyy said the U.S. now supplies Ukraine 12 Patriot interceptors a month, about a quarter of the Biden-era level.
- He said Washington has approved only part of the deliveries Ukraine paid for through NATO’s PURL mechanism, calling the delay not technical.
The United States is now sending Ukraine only 12 Patriot air defense interceptors a month, about a quarter of what Kyiv received under President Joe Biden, and is holding back some missiles Ukraine has already paid for, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy made the comments in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv published on Oct. 18. Under the Biden administration, Patriot missiles reached Ukraine as U.S. military aid, while under President Donald Trump, Washington sells them, with the purchases funded by Ukraine and its European allies.
Ukraine paid for weapons, including interceptors for ballistic missiles, through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL, a NATO-coordinated mechanism under which allies finance American weapons for Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. The U.S. side approved some of those deliveries but not the rest, and he said the holdup was not a technical issue.
The Patriot is one of only two Western systems in Ukraine’s arsenal that can shoot down Russian ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-M and the air-launched Kinzhal, alongside the Franco-Italian SAMP/T, which Ukraine operates in much smaller numbers. Each Patriot battery depends on a steady supply of interceptors, and Ukrainian officials have repeatedly said missile shortages force them to choose which cities and facilities to protect.
Zelenskyy said he had offered Washington a trade: Ukraine would stop striking Russian diesel fuel facilities if the United States supplied Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian infrastructure. Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has become a point of tension with the Trump administration, which has pressed Kyiv to halt the attacks.
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said recent U.S. steps appeared aimed at pushing Ukraine toward capitulation, while saying he was not claiming that was the goal of Ukraine’s allies. He also pointed to restrictions on the speed of Starlink satellite internet terminals used by Ukrainian forces.
Ukrainian drone units lost reliable Starshield service, the military version of Starlink, overnight on Oct. 13-14, when terminals stopped holding a connection above about 160 km/h (100 mph). Zelenskyy said earlier this month that the cap left Ukraine unable to intercept some of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, which fly at more than 400 km/h, before speeds were later partly restored.
Washington has not publicly given a reason for the pace of Patriot approvals. U.S. production of the PAC-3 MSE interceptor is rising under a multiyear contract with Lockheed Martin, but the missiles are in heavy demand from the U.S. military and allies in Europe, the Middle East and Asia.
Zelenskyy said he remains in contact with U.S. officials and hopes Washington will approve the remaining paid-for deliveries.

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.6 percent year on year in the first three quarters of this year, official data showed Monday.
The retail sales of services increased by 5 percent in the period from a year ago, and those of goods increased by 1 percent, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
In terms of services consumption, the categories of communication and information services, tourism consulting and leasing services, and cultural, sports and leisure services saw fast growth, the NBS data showed.
In the first three quarters of this year, the total retail sales of consumer goods, which include the sales of physical consumer goods plus the income generated from the catering services, exceeded 37 trillion yuan (about 5.51 trillion U.S. dollars), up by 1.1 percent year on year, the data showed.
In September alone, the total retail sales of consumer goods grew at the fastest pace in six months, rising 1.1 percent year on year and up 0.7 percentage points from the previous month, according to the NBS.
Retail sales of consumer goods in urban areas rose 0.9 percent while those in rural areas increased 2.3 percent.
Online retail sales of goods and services surpassed 15.1 trillion yuan, up 4.4 percent year on year. Of the total, online goods sales rose 3.8 percent year on year, while online service sales increased 5.3 percent year on year. ■

WELLINGTON, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's services sector continued to expand in September for a fourth consecutive month, although growth remained weak amid ongoing cost pressures and election uncertainty, a business survey showed on Monday.
The Bank of New Zealand (BNZ)-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index edged down to 50.9 in September from 51 in August, but remained above the 50-point level separating expansion from contraction.

BNZ Senior Economist Doug Steel said the fourth consecutive month of expansion was notable following two years of contraction. However, services sector growth remained weak, particularly compared with manufacturing, whose Performance of Manufacturing Index had remained well above the 50-point threshold for some time. ■

Chinese central authorities have recently issued a set of guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces to bolster high-quality development.
The guidelines outlined multiple key sectors for advancing the deep integration of the digital economy and the real economy, including building a national integrated computing power network and a nationwide blockchain network, among other initiatives.
Coordinated computing power development in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region is a good example of China's comprehensive advancement in building a national network.
By now, 36 data centers have been established in Langfang City, north China's Hebei Province, roughly a one-hour drive from Beijing.
These data centers are serving China's tech giants like Huawei and JD.com, as well as other companies. Computing resources here also meet the real-time computing demands of Beijing's sci-tech innovation industries, internet sector, and other sectors.
Building on the coordinated layout and construction of the national integrated computing power network, regions across the country are stepping up efforts to build and optimize computing hubs, data centers, and computing network nodes, while accelerating computing-electricity coordination and computing-network integration.
Other regions are also capitalizing on their strengths to gain a foothold in niche markets and pursue differentiated development.
The Lichuan AI Computing Center is nestled in the Wuling Mountains of Lichuan City, central China's Hubei Province. Its services cover culture and tourism, government affairs, and aerospace information.
This city is not endowed with abundant scientific or educational resources, but its mountainous location, cool climate and rich hydropower resources make it an ideal place for a computing center with relatively low electricity costs.
In Liangwu Township of Lichuan, a satellite ground receiving station has been built by GEOVIS Raywin Technology Co., Ltd. It allows instant access to computing power from the adjacent AI computing center when receiving and processing satellite data.
"The station's proximity to the computing center enhances the operational efficiency, convenience, and cost-effectiveness," said Gao Kui, the company's general manager of operations.
By the end of June this year, China's intelligent computing capacity had risen 177 percent year on year to reach 2,185 EFLOPS. EFLOPS refers to a unit measuring computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
By then, more than 70 computing transmission channels connecting computing hubs and key regions had been built, according to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
China is accelerating the construction of an integrated national computing power platform, aiming to enhance the quality and efficiency of computing resources and strengthen the country's capabilities in core technologies such as AI chips.
The China computing power platform has now achieved integrated nationwide computing power monitoring and coordination. It has listed over 2,000 computing products and connected to more than 300 large models, providing AI developers with on-demand access to computing power.
"A national integrated computing power network is not a simple pile-up of computing resources, but is connecting computing power, electricity, data, models, and scenarios into an infrastructure network for the intelligent economy," said Li Mingyan, an analyst at the industrial research institute of consulting firm CIO Manage.
This platform can meet the diverse needs of application scenarios such as large AI model training, autonomous driving, smart finance, and low-altitude economy.
Also, through the "East Data, West Computing" project and cross-regional computing power scheduling, it better matches the green electricity resources in the country's western regions with the computing power demand in the eastern regions, lowering the cost of computing use and promoting the consumption of green energy, according to Li.
As a national strategy, China's "East Data, West Computing" project operates similarly to a power grid, shifting the heavy data processing demands of the country's economically bustling eastern coast to resource-rich western regions. It utilizes the west's abundant green energy such as wind and hydropower, making it a major milestone in green technology and carbon reduction.
Industry experts said that industrial opportunities will gradually emerge along the upstream, midstream and downstream of the national computing network.
For example, the large-scale construction of computing clusters will drive demand for AI chips, high-speed optical modules, and green energy facilities. In addition, services ranging from computing power scheduling and model inference optimization to token-based metering and billing are expected to spur the growth of new platform companies.
"At the application level, the network will sustain intelligent upgrading across industries and help innovate businesses in areas of the token economy, cloud computers, and cloud phones," said Li Wei, a researcher at the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology.
The network also helps lower the barriers to digitalization and AI adoption for small and medium-sized enterprises, and improve quality and performance of traditional industries, she added. ■

From waste to wonder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:55:59 UTC
15:55:59 KST

Can a material that is thought to have served its original purpose become the starting point for a new work of art? Can an object regarded as waste regain value and become part of an aesthetic narrative? “Residui: From Waste to Wonder” is an exhibition that explores the creative potential of materials that are often overlooked in everyday life. The original title of the exhibition in Italian is “Residui: Dall’Informe alla Forma,” and it recently opened in Ankara at CerModern on Oct. 16, organized by the Italian Embassy in Türkiye as part of the IDEHA26 program. The exhibition, which is being presented to the public for the first time worldwide in Ankara, highlights the creative potential of agricultural and food waste through art and design.
Agricultural and food waste are addressed in the exhibition not merely as an environmental problem, but as resources that can be reevaluated, transformed and imbued with aesthetic value. Recycling food waste has long been on the agenda, and the aim of the exhibition is to offer viewers an approach that invites us to rethink our production and consumption habits, while also offering a fresh perspective on the relationship among sustainability, art and design.
Organized with the support of the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the exhibition aims to reevaluate agricultural and food waste through art and design, and to draw attention to the concept of the circular economy. Curated by Valentina Croci alongside Patrizia Catalano and Martina Barberis Casagrande from HoperAperta, and designed by Studio Gisto and Nolostand, the exhibition features nine works of art and design, a specially curated exhibition route and a materials library. In line with the Ministry’s commitment to promoting sustainability — both in content and implementation — the exhibition was designed according to the principle of efficient resource use. The installation itself is an integral part of this approach, designed to be reconfigured as a modular exhibition system before returning to its intended cycle of use.
Agricultural and food waste
Italy is a leading country when it comes to food. Italian food is always a crowd-pleaser, and any food product that bears an Italian name tag sells worldwide even if not produced in Italy. Italy has succeeded in becoming a trusted brand reference due to its commitment to producing the best products and enjoying the best taste, but also being serious about design. The “Residui” exhibition presents Italian design as a language capable of anticipating and addressing contemporary challenges. It focuses on innovative materials and processes, stimulating reflection on the value of research, experimentation and sustainable creativity as essential elements throughout the design and production process. Agricultural waste is a big problem in Türkiye, and food waste is a global problem for which countries are seeking solutions. Our own First Lady, Emine Erdoğan, has long been promoting the concept of the No Waste Kitchen and creating awareness around preventing food waste. However, it is not always easy to prevent waste. In household kitchens, we can try to minimize waste with thoughtful cooking and home economy planning, but the agri-food industry is on another scale. This is where design steps in.
‘Materioteca’
At the heart of the project is a “Materioteca,” which stands for a “Materials Library,” curated by Valentina Croci, containing surprising shapes, colors and textures — the sometimes-unpredictable result of transforming waste from various sectors of the agri-food industry. The Materioteca immediately communicates the design potential of these new materials. The selection includes innovative materials obtained from agricultural and agro-industrial waste, such as grape pomace, citrus peels, rice husks, coffee grounds, vegetable fibers and mycelium cultivated from agricultural by-products. Transformed through processes similar to those used in the wood-furniture sector, these materials find application in construction and design, representing one of the most promising developments in the Italian circular economy and contributing to the creation of replicable and sustainable production models.
The exhibition explores the creative potential of Italian agri-food waste, portraying the metamorphosis of waste from a peripheral material to a productive resource, eventually becoming the medium and language for new forms of creative expression.
Libraries are ideal places to study and think. That is where new ideas emerge. This materials library, Materioteca, is presented as a study space and physical archive that clarifies the origin of the materials—in this case, the “waste”—and their potential for the transformation process, which is the “wonder.” This transformation cannot merely be described as recycling; it is much more. Waste transforms into art, and art is always inspirational. The library is the starting point; the rest is for designers and artists to explore and find ways to create something new for the future.

Denmark orders more Norwegian anti-ship missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:53:04 UTC
15:53:04 KST

- Kongsberg signed a contract worth about NOK 400 million ($42.4 million) to supply more Naval Strike Missiles for Denmark’s coastal defense system.
- Denmark became the fifth NATO coastal NSM user in 2025 and has separately ordered the missiles for its frigates.
Denmark is buying more Naval Strike Missiles from Norway’s Kongsberg to arm the coastal defense system it acquired last year, under a contract worth about 400 million Norwegian kroner ($42.4 million).
Kongsberg announced the deal on Oct. 19, 2026, without saying how many missiles Denmark is getting. The sale is structured as a government-to-government agreement between Norway’s defense materiel agency and its Danish counterpart, the procurement agencies that also handled Denmark’s earlier purchase.
The Naval Strike Missile, or NSM, is a stealthy, subsonic anti-ship missile that flies low over the sea and uses an imaging infrared seeker to pick out its target, with a range of more than 185 km (115 miles). It can also strike targets on land.
Denmark bought the ground-based coastal version in 2025, becoming the fifth NATO country to operate it after Poland, the United States, Romania and Latvia. The system combines Kongsberg’s fire control system, the NSM missile and truck-mounted launchers that can be moved and hidden along the coast, letting a small force threaten enemy warships from shore.
Copenhagen has separately ordered NSMs for its navy’s frigates.
The United States is the largest user of the missile. The U.S. Navy carries NSM on its ships, and the U.S. Marine Corps fields it on the NMESIS launcher, an uncrewed vehicle carrying two missiles. The U.S. Marine Corps stood up its first medium-range missile battalion with NMESIS at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, this month.

In pro-Palestine hub of Athens, Israeli buyers increase local resentment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:51:10 UTC
15:51:10 KST

In pro-Palestine hub of Athens, Israeli buyers increase local resentment
Exarchia residents say short-term rentals are driving up rents and eroding its character.
Athens, Greece – Tonia Katerini, a 69-year-old architect, leaned into her computer, scrolling through the property contracts that she said are remaking her neighbourhood.
Across Exarchia, the Athens district long known for its radical left-wing politics, flats are being bought up and turned into short-term rentals, pushing out the people who live there.
For months, Katerini and a group of neighbours have been digitally mapping foreign purchases using public records, marking them with red dots.
She zoomed out from her street on the map; it was a sea of red.
The balcony doors of her flat, where she has lived since 1986, were open and noise from the cafes below drifted in past the plants and stacks of architectural plans.
Her group says much of the money behind the rentals is Israeli; by their count, more than half of the area’s new company-run hotels and rentals .
In a neighbourhood where Palestinian flags hang from balconies and solidarity slogans cover the walls, that has caused friction.
On her own cobbled street, where the noise of arriving tourists rolling their suitcases wakes her in the morning, Israeli investors have bought two buildings, she said. The flat below hers belongs to one such company.
A few streets away, a residential building is streaked with black paint.
“Airbnbs leave us homeless,” reads one slogan across its facade. “Zionists not welcome,” reads another.
Such buildings are easy to spot. Instead of residents’ names, the buzzer panels show only numbers and a keypad by the door releases keys for Airbnb guests.
Across the neighbourhood, activists have splattered keypads and facades with red paint.
They say short-term rentals are driving an aggressive gentrification that is pricing out locals and erasing the area’s identity.
Foreign money has poured into Greek property in recent years: non-residents invested a record 2.75 billion euros ($3.2bn) in Greek real estate in 2024, according to the Bank of Greece, before easing last year.
No official figures break down foreign buyers in Athens by nationality. But an annual survey of completed sales by the agency network RE/MAX Hellas found that Israelis were the largest group of foreign buyers in Attica, the region around the capital, ahead of buyers from Turkiye and Lebanon, reported the Greek weekly To Vima.
Exarchia’s political activism runs deep. In 1973, students at the nearby Athens Polytechnic rose up against the US-backed military government, which fell the following year.
In 2008, police shot dead Alexandros Grigoropoulos, a 15-year-old Greek student, in Exarchia, provoking protests that spread across the country. It came, Katerini said, like “fire on dry land”.
As Greece’s debt crisis deepened, that anger on the streets helped propel the left-wing Syriza party to power in 2015.
‘Tenants displaced, apartment blocks emptied’
Chrysoulla Papageorgiou, a schoolteacher who has lived in Exarchia for 24 years, is a familiar face on its streets. Earnest and straight-talking, the 46-year-old remembers it as “a neighbourhood of solidarity”.
The change came slowly, then quickened. At first, small owners rented out a spare room. After the COVID-19 pandemic, companies began buying entire blocks.
“Overnight, tenants were displaced and apartment blocks emptied,” she said.
Bars opened, spilling tables and chairs across pavements on streets that had once been quiet.
Rents rose and migrants and low-income families, many living in basements and on the lower floors, were the first to go. Schools lost pupils and old bookshops, traditional cafes and grocers closed.
For years, Exarchia residents sheltered refugees in occupied buildings. Sitting on prime real estate, they were among the first buildings police emptied and then sold, Papageorgiou said.
“Half were squats,” she said. “Now we have only one.”
That last building is draped in painted sheets declaring solidarity with the families inside. Neighbours help make sure the children get to school.
Since 2022, Exarchia Square, long the heart of the neighbourhood’s protests, has been a fenced-off construction site for a new metro station that many residents fought against. Riot police, Papageorgiou added, are now a daily presence.
The aim, she believed, is to turn central Athens into somewhere “purely touristic”.
In recent years, buyers have been “almost only Israeli”.
Near the square hangs a large Palestinian flag. Tourists sometimes scrawl anti-Palestinian messages on its white stripe, and activists paint it white again.
Foreign buyers, Katerini said, see Greece as a safer place for their money than Israel itself, and in Athens “the government is very friendly with Israel”. In August, Athens signed a missile deal with Israel worth $3.5bn.
‘A very good opportunity’ for investors
Vagelis Lazaridis, a stocky real estate agent who heads a branch of the Athens-Attica Real Estate Agents’ Association, talks about his trade with passion. He said the reasons for the investments were purely practical.
Exarchia “was a run-down area” which made it “a very good opportunity”, he said.
It is beside the centre, close to the metro and to universities full of students from abroad. Unlike Plaka, beneath the Acropolis, it has few building restrictions.
Once a handful of buyers arrive, he said, others follow.
Greece to become ‘far less appealing’ for Israeli buyers
The government is now trying to cool the market.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced last month that the transfer tax for homebuyers from outside the European Union would rise from 3 percent to 15 percent from next July.
“The party is over in Greece,” The Jerusalem Post wrote in a recent report. “The country, which in recent years has become a preferred destination for Israelis seeking real estate investments at reasonable prices and with attractive yields, is about to become far less appealing.”
Lazaridis said agents’ associations oppose the plan, which has yet to become law. It “may not take effect, or may be postponed”, he said.
Agents expect some non-EU buyers to speed up purchases before the deadline, reported the Greek news site in.gr.
‘Fewer Airbnbs’
Not everyone in the trade sees an unstoppable tide.
Iryna Rondyak, who is originally from Ukraine, runs her own estate agency near Exarchia. She said that when Israeli buyers began arriving about a decade ago, they made up about 60 percent of her foreign clients, many buying whole office buildings to turn into hotels.
Until around 2024, foreigners accounted for about 70 percent of her sales, she said.
This year, it is about 30 percent, as state-backed mortgages for young Greeks, under a scheme called “Spiti mou” (My Home), attract local buyers back.
She credits new rules for the turnaround.
No new short-term rental licences are being issued in central Athens, including Exarchia, and in September the freeze was extended to the end of 2027, reported To Vima.
Properties bought under Greece’s “golden visa” residency scheme can now only be let long-term. While a cheaper route into the scheme, at 250,000 euros ($280,000), rewards investors who convert empty office buildings into flats.
“Anyone living in Greece couldn’t find a home in the centre. Everything was on Airbnb,” she said. “Now there are far fewer.”
It is “a little better,” she said, but “the problem still exists”.
Rents remain high, at 10 to 15 euros ($12 to $17) per square metre, even in the southern suburbs, she said. Many flats sit empty because owners find renting them out is not worth the tax bill.
Residents are less convinced.
The rental freeze is temporary, they say, and investors with enough money can still find ways in. Nor does it undo what has already happened: many of the neighbourhood’s buildings are already short-term rentals.
Back in Exarchia, Papageorgiou counts herself lucky.
Her landlady, whose family has lived in the area for generations, refuses to raise the rent as an “act of resistance”.
Papageorgiou said jokingly that her landlady’s accountant has told her she is ruining the market.

No ‘turmoil’ at the White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:50:43 UTC
15:50:43 KST

No ‘turmoil’ at the White House
The media had a field day with Katie Zacharia’s short tenure, but claims of chaos in the Trump administration are exaggerated.
In the months leading up to the disastrous 2006 election, President George W Bush fired his press secretary, Scott McClellan, and withdrew the Supreme Court nomination of his close confidante, Harriet Miers.
He waited until after the midterms, in which the Republicans lost control of the United States Congress, to fire Donald Rumsfeld as his secretary of defence, who had led the increasingly unpopular war against Iraq.
History repeats itself imperfectly.
Last week, President Donald Trump abruptly pulled the plug on Katie Zacharia after she had served just five short days as the White House spokesperson. Aside from her own dismissal, the biggest news Zacharia delivered was Kimberly Guilfoyle’s ouster from her position as the ambassador to Greece.
It is rumoured that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is now on the chopping block, especially after the president rejected his plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a terrorist who shot 13 people at Fort Hood military base in 2009.
Obviously, there are differences between the two presidencies.
McClellan had been the press secretary for three years, not five days. Miers was not embroiled in scandal when her nomination was pulled. The media and the Senate just questioned her qualifications. And the war with Iran is not as bloody or as costly as the US invasion of Iraq turned out to be.
But the second half of the second term of all US presidents can be rocky.
In President Ronald Reagan’s second term, his press team dealt with the fallout of the Iran-Contra scandal. In President Bill Clinton’s second term, the Monica Lewinsky affair drove the news. President Richard Nixon faced impeachment in his second term. President Barack Obama had to deal with the scandal surrounding the Benghazi consulate attack in Libya throughout his second term, which also embroiled Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
Staff turmoil is also not unusual in the White House under any president, especially in the second term and especially when the voters are angry and the polls look dire.
Every midterm election is a referendum on the president, and it is not uncommon for the president’s party to be punished at the ballot box. In fact, in 18 of the 20 midterms held over the past 80 years, the governing party has lost seats in Congress.
The Trump administration is indeed facing troubles with the continuing US-Israel war on Iran and high energy prices. But a press secretary’s dismissal is hardly a sign of a serious crisis in the administration.
It is unclear how Zacharia got the job. She did not work on Trump’s re-election campaign, and while she has done media appearances in the past, she is by no means a working journalist. She briefly served in the press shop of the Department of Homeland Security when Kristi Noem was secretary. But given Noem’s short-lived tenure, rocked by various controversies and her own dismissal in March, that was hardly a positive experience.
Press reports have hinted that the president himself made the decision to hire Zacharia and that the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, was not an essential part of the process.
Trump saw that there was a problem with Zacharia and moved swiftly to deal with it to cut his losses. He has demonstrated he is clearly in control and his administration is not “falling apart” or “in turmoil” as media headlines have declared.
Not all presidents have moved as decisively as he has.
President Joe Biden, for example, should have done the same thing with his last spokesperson, Karine Jean-Pierre. She was every bit as incompetent as Zacharia, but Biden allowed her to stay in the job for three years, about the same tenure as McClellan.
Hopefully, Trump and his team will learn a valuable lesson about this sorry episode. Hiring incompetent people and putting them out for the press to destroy is not good for the White House, nor for the people they hire and are then forced to fire.
Trump deserves credit for moving quickly to remove Zacharia before she became more of an embarrassment. He also deserves credit for firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, a personal friend, for her alleged corruption in Europe.
But what the president really needs is a better process for hiring more competent people in the first place. Maybe next time he should check with his chief of staff first.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

“Since we are playing a match every three days, we are resting some of our players. We need to determine the load distribution well,” he added.

The Turkish club will definitely be without star attacker Marco Asensio. Team doctor Ahmet Kulduk announced that an MRI revealed a cartilage lesion in Asensio’s knee. He is scheduled for surgery next week and is expected to be sidelined for at least two months.
Despite the injury setback, squad morale remains high following recent domestic success. Striker Romelu Lukaku, who scored his first goal for the club in a 3-0 home win against Alanyaspor over the weekend, emphasized the importance of carrying that momentum into European play.
“The victory we got was important for our self-confidence,” Lukaku said. “We want to get our first win in the Champions League match we are going to play.”

From Paper to Space: Matter as Sensory Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Selecting a material during the design process involves more than defining an appearance. Its behavior in response to light, sound, touch, and the passage of time can transform how a space is perceived and used. At the same time, factors such as durability, strength, recyclability, and the environmental impact associated with its production introduce new variables into architectural decision-making. For Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen, cofounders of Vancouver-based design and production studio molo, these considerations have led to an exploration of paper and its potential to shape flexible, sensory spaces.
Lightweight, malleable, and visually delicate, paper is often associated with small objects, two-dimensional surfaces, or temporary applications. However, its possibilities change when it is understood as a material capable of acquiring volume, structure, and scale. Through folds, cellular geometries, and modular systems, paper can become an architectural element that defines boundaries, organizes circulation, and alters the perceptual conditions of an interior.
Forsythe and MacAllen have explored paper as a medium for creating spaces, questioning what happens when a material is no longer defined by its conventional uses and is instead explored for its spatial capabilities. With backgrounds in architecture and experience working with more traditional building materials, they have discovered a sculptural purity, freedom, and surprising strength in creating functional objects from this humble material.
This exploration led Forsythe and MacAllen to develop the soft collection, a family of space dividers, building blocks, furniture, and lighting made from paper or textile. Rather than treating these elements as isolated objects, the collection proposes using them as tools for transforming entire interiors. A panel can be opened, folded, extended, or reconfigured to create different degrees of privacy and varying scales of occupation.
Architecture can thus move beyond relying exclusively on permanent elements and begin to incorporate components that can change alongside the needs of their users. Here, geometry is as important as the material itself. Paper gains strength through its configuration, while its folds and internal cavities create a lightweight structure designed to stand and extend through space. The material's apparent fragility becomes a design quality: its lightness allows for the creation of boundaries that do not behave like conventional walls, but instead act as surfaces that encourage interaction with light, sound, and movement.
The collaboration between molo and Gmund Paper deepens this exploration by engaging with new sensory qualities, while still meeting stringent technical requirements. The first papers developed for the collection are deep blue and glacier blue. Custom-made, fire-retardant, long-fiber papers, they are free of harmful components. They are also lightfast, resist ink migration, and are recyclable. FSC® certification, along with the use of sustainable sources and production processes, adds another dimension to the material, extending the focus beyond its appearance to consider its performance throughout its life cycle.
Located along the Mangfall River in Germany, Gmund produces paper using hydroelectric power: approximately 75 percent comes from its own turbines, while the remaining 25 percent is supplied by certified plants in the region. The new blue papers developed for molo are produced on a machine with more than 140 years of history, updated with contemporary technologies such as lasers, robotics, and advanced water treatment systems. Wastewater is treated locally until it reaches drinking-water quality, while solid waste generated through the production of the papers for this collaboration is not sent to landfills.
Innovation, therefore, does not always mean replacing what already exists. It can also involve updating, adapting, and extending the life of systems that are part of an established manufacturing tradition. This relationship between material, technology, and perception becomes particularly evident in the sloped softwall, a sculptural version of molo's space-divider system that expands the possibilities for shaping space both visually and acoustically.
Its geometry changes the way the panel interacts with its surroundings. While one side retains vertical folds that emphasize its structure, the other is cut diagonally to reveal the internal cells. The result is a three-dimensional surface that interacts with light and alters the perceived dimensions of a space. The sloped side can also define rooms or circulation paths that visually expand upward, creating a sense of comfort and embrace. Its geometry establishes a shifting relationship between the body, the boundary, and the field of vision, while the internal structure transforms the way light passes through the material.
The two new tones further enhance this experience. Deep blue creates a more intense interplay between light absorption and reflection, evoking the shifting surface of the ocean and the deep hues of twilight. Glacier blue, by contrast, introduces a lighter and more translucent quality. When exposed to direct sunlight, the paper fibers take on an almost ethereal appearance, transmitting light rather than simply reflecting it. In both cases, color becomes more than a surface treatment; it becomes part of the material's spatial performance. Light, shadow, texture, transparency, and geometry come together to create atmospheres that shift according to the viewer's position and changing light conditions.
Presented at the 2026 International Contemporary Furniture Fair (ICFF) in New York, the collaboration between molo and Gmund Paper offers a reading of paper that extends beyond its traditional condition. The material can be strong without losing its lightness, structural without appearing heavy, and technically sophisticated without giving up its poetic dimension. By approaching materiality as a process in which physical properties, environmental conditions, and sensory experiences all contribute to the construction of space, new atmospheres and spatial configurations emerge through the interplay of light, color, and texture.
If a sheet of paper can become a wall, a piece of furniture, or a structure capable of organizing an interior, why couldn't architecture also emerge from what, at first glance, seems too fragile to build with?

Defence to find ten billion in savings by decade’s end
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:40:36 BST
15:40:36 KST

The Ministry of Defence must deliver £10.7 billion of efficiencies over four years, with the annual target rising from £1.4 billion this year to £3.5 billion by 2028-29, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked how the department’s Total Efficiency Commitment was split across the financial years to 2029-30.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “As set out in Table 21 of the Annex to the Defence Investment Plan, the Department’s total efficiency commitment of £10.7 billion is profiled across the four-year period as follows.”
The figures he gave run £1.4 billion in 2026-27, £2.6 billion in 2027-28, £3.5 billion in 2028-29 and £3.2 billion in 2029-30.
The shape of that profile is back-loaded, with more than three fifths of the total falling in the final two years. Departments commonly set targets that way because savings from reorganisation, estate rationalisation and contract renegotiation take time to land, but it also means the heaviest lifting sits beyond the current spending review period and will be inherited by whoever is in post when it arrives.
Efficiency commitments are counted against what the department would otherwise have spent, so they are a mix of cash released for reinvestment and cost growth avoided. In defence they have historically been delivered through headcount reduction in the civilian workforce, renegotiated support contracts, disposal of land and buildings, and changes to how equipment is maintained, with the Defence Equipment and Support organisation and the Defence Infrastructure Organisation carrying much of that load.
The Public Accounts Committee and the National Audit Office have both questioned the department’s record on turning stated efficiencies into real reductions, and the equipment plan has repeatedly relied on savings that were assumed and not yet banked. A commitment of this size sitting inside the Defence Investment Plan means the plan’s affordability depends on them being found. The department has separately committed to growing defence spending to 2.6 per cent of GDP by 2027 and set an ambition of 3 per cent in the next parliament, and the efficiency target is the internal counterpart to that external growth.

The Russian shipyards Britain has placed under sanctions
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:40:22 BST
15:40:22 KST

Britain has designated Russia’s largest shipbuilding corporation on the grounds that it supplied frigates and other warship classes deployed in Crimea, and the sanctions list now names 645 individual ships under the Russia regulations, according to the UK Sanctions List published by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.
Public Joint Stock Company United Shipbuilding Corporation was designated on 24 February 2022, the day Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The statement of reasons sets out the naval case against it.
It reads: “Public Joint Stock Company (PJSC) United Shipbuilding Corporation (USC) is a Russian state-owned enterprise. USC is the largest shipbuilding corporation in Russia, uniting shipbuilding, repair and maintenance subsidiaries. This includes the supply of several frigates and other warship classes that have been deployed in Crimea since Russia illegally annexed the region in 2014, and have conducted drills in the Black Sea in 2021. Therefore USC has been involved in destabilising Ukraine or undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty or independence of Ukraine. USC also operates in a sector of strategic significance, specifically, the Russian defence sector.”
USC carries an asset freeze, trust services sanctions and the director disqualification sanction imposed in April 2025. It is the holding company that owns most of Russia’s major yards, including Sevmash at Severodvinsk where the ballistic missile and cruise missile submarines are built, the Admiralty Shipyards and Severnaya Verf in St Petersburg, and Yantar at Kaliningrad.
Two individual yards carry designations of their own, the first of them JSC Zelenodolsk Shipyard in Tatarstan, designated on 15 March 2022, with the department recording that it “is a Russian shipbuilding enterprise that has constructed more than 1500 sea- and river-going ships and vessels” and that it therefore carries on business in sectors of strategic significance to the Russian government. The yard builds the Buyan-M class corvettes that have fired Kalibr cruise missiles into Ukraine, and the Gepard class frigates.
JSC Zaliv Shipyard at Kerch in occupied Crimea was designated earlier, on 31 December 2020, and for a different reason. The statement of reasons says it “actively participated in the construction of new railway approaches to the Kerch Bridge, connecting Russian to the illegally annexed Crimean peninsula. Therefore, it is supporting the consolidation of the illegally annexed Crimean peninsula into the Russian Federation.” The yard has since taken on the two Ivan Rogov class amphibious assault ships, the largest warships Russia has laid down in decades.
The list reaches down into the supply chain that serves those yards. Forss Technology Ltd of St Petersburg was designated on 4 May 2022 as a company “providing engineering services in shipbuilding, machine building, electrical technology, instruments manufacturing and high-tech products development”. Kranark LLC went the same day, on the grounds that it “has provided equipment for the construction of the Zvezda shipbuilding complex, a strategically important project for the Government of Russia”, the Far Eastern yard built to produce ice-class tankers and gas carriers for the Arctic routes.
On the commercial side, Sovcomflot, the Russian state shipping company, was designated on 18 May 2023. The 645 named vessels sit alongside it under shipping and transport sanctions, which bar a specified ship from entering a British port, allow it to be detained or given a movement direction, and permit its registration on the UK Ship Register to be terminated. Most of those listings carry the same wording, that the vessel “is involved in carrying oil or oil products that originated in Russia from Russia to a third country”.
Naval officers appear alongside the companies and the hulls, among them Rear Admiral Denis Berezovskiy, designated on 31 December 2020, who was appointed commander of the Ukrainian Navy on 1 March 2014 and swore an oath to the Crimean armed forces, breaking his oath to the Ukrainian Navy, before becoming Deputy Commander of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet and later of the Pacific Fleet. Rear Admiral Valery Kulikov, a former Deputy Commander of the Black Sea Fleet, is listed as responsible for commanding forces that occupied Ukrainian sovereign territory.

‘Protocol, not power’: Ex-IMF director rebuts Pakistan’s 'historic milestone' claim over 2027 leadership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:40:07 UTC
15:40:07 KST

This chair is purely ceremonial & rotates annually, Krishnamurthy on X.
NEW DELHI: Former International Monetary Fund (IMF) executive director Krishnamurthy V Subramanian has challenged Pakistan’s claim that its appointment to chair the IMF and World Bank Boards of Governors in 2027 marks a return to global financial leadership, calling the role “protocol, not power”.In a post on X, Subramanian said the chairmanship was ceremonial and rotated annually, arguing that it should not be equated with leadership of a major global economic forum.
“Claim: ‘Pakistan is heading back to the top table of global finance after 74 years!’ Reality: Pakistan will chair the IMF-World Bank Annual Plenary in 2027. This chair is purely ceremonial & rotates annually: Paraguay this year, Cabo Verde in 2025. It's protocol, not power,” he wrote.
Pakistan was recently named chair of the Boards of Governors of the IMF and the World Bank Group for 2027. The country will take up the position for the first time since 1953, with Pakistan’s Minister for Economic Affairs and World Bank governor, Ahad Khan Cheema, set to assume the role, according to an Islamabad statement.Pakistan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs described the appointment as a “historic milestone”, saying it would give the country an opportunity to contribute to global economic and development discussions and facilitate dialogue among member nations.
What Krishnamurthy Subramanian said
In another post, Subramanian rejected comparisons between India’s presidencies of the G20 and BRICS and Pakistan’s rotating chairmanship of the IMF-World Bank Annual Plenary, calling them a false equivalence.
“India's G20 presidency set the agenda for a major forum of global economic cooperation; its BRICS presidency drove an emerging-economies platform... Pakistan's role is to preside over an annual meeting,” he said.
Pakistan’s dependence on IMF support
Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a $1.4 billion Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).The EFF is intended to address the country’s balance-of-payments needs and support economic reforms, while the RSF provides longer-term financing to help tackle climate-related risks and strengthen economic resilience.Pakistan is also expected to receive around $1.2 billion from the IMF, subject to approval by the fund’s Executive Board. The expected disbursement follows an agreement between IMF staff and Pakistani authorities on the latest reviews of the two loan programmes.

Automakers warn against excluding Türkiye from ‘Made in EU’ plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:33:43 UTC
15:33:43 KST

Türkiye has been a destination for investment by European automakers for 55 years. Total investment over the past 55 years has reached 21 billion euros.
Excluding Türkiye from stricter “Made in EU” auto rules, backed by France and Germany to counter Chinese competition, could raise costs, disrupt supply chains and erode Europe’s competitive edge, industry representatives have warned.
French President Emmanuel Macron’s plan to protect the European automotive industry against China has sparked debate. Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz agreed to lower the 2035 emissions target from 100 percent to 90 percent and tighten “Made in EU” measures. Under the plan, internal combustion vehicles would still be allowed to be sold after 2035, while EU production requirements in public procurement would be strengthened and vehicles would be required to contain 70 percent European-origin parts.
However, manufacturers such as Toyota, Ford and Hyundai warn that excluding trade partners such as Türkiye would raise costs and weaken both supply chains and Europe’s competitiveness.
Yoshihiro Nakata, President and CEO of Toyota Motor Europe, said in Brussels that Europe should adopt a “Made with Europe” approach rather than “Made in Europe.” Nakata said that including reliable trade partners such as Türkiye, the U.K. and Japan would expand Europe’s production and market scale to around 31 million vehicles, which is necessary for global competitiveness.
Toyota also proposed increasing the European-origin content requirement to 70 percent after a three-year transition period and called for Customs Union partners such as Türkiye to remain within the framework.
Jim Baumbick, President of Ford Europe, also objected to the proposed rules. Baumbick said production in Türkiye and the U.K. should be evaluated together with factories inside the EU.
“Made in Europe should be measured by where value is created, not where the last bolt is tightened,” he said. Using the electric Ford Transit Custom produced in Türkiye as an example, Baumbick noted that the vehicle is engineered in the U.K. and Germany, its electric motor is produced in the U.K. and its battery in the EU. More than half of the vehicle’s component value originates from EU countries, he said.
“By any economic measure, this is a European vehicle,” Baumbick said, warning that excluding Türkiye would also weaken manufacturing inside the EU.
Xavier Martinet, CEO of Hyundai Europe, previously said Türkiye should be treated fairly and included in the “Made in EU” process.
“If Türkiye is not included, we may have to look at alternative scenarios. But I think that would create a lose-lose situation for everyone. If some vehicles that can be produced in Türkiye have to be produced in Europe, they will certainly become more expensive. In the end, if customers can no longer afford to buy certain vehicles because they have become too expensive, then Europe also loses,” Martinet said.
The compromise between France and Germany marked a turning point in discussions over Europe’s protectionist legislation. However, there is still no final European Union decision. If Türkiye is left outside the framework, industry representatives say the cost of the protective wall Europe wants to build against China could ultimately be borne by European consumers.
Kâzım Eryılmaz, board member of the Automotive Suppliers Association of Türkiye (TAYSAD), said Europe has a legitimate interest in protecting its industry from China but warned that excluding Türkiye would also hurt Europe.
“Europe’s automotive industry does not consist only of EU countries. Türkiye has been an important part of this ecosystem for half a century. A regulation aimed at improving Europe’s competitiveness should not weaken the existing production ecosystem,” he said.
“Türkiye offers not only geographic proximity but also cost advantages, quality, engineering capability, flexible production and logistics benefits. If Europe seeks to strengthen its competitiveness against China while disadvantaging integrated production partners such as Türkiye, it could increase costs and supply risks for its own industry. While trying to escape China, they will be hit by hail if they exclude Türkiye,” Eryılmaz said.
Last year, the EU exported 812,000 cars worth 18.8 billion euros to Türkiye, while Türkiye exported 798,000 vehicles worth 18.2 billion euros to the EU. Total two-way automotive trade reached 37 billion euros. Europe accounts for 73.7 percent of Türkiye’s automotive exports, while EU-origin vehicles represent 73 percent of Türkiye’s imported car market. Automotive products account for 26 percent of total Türkiye-EU trade.

6 in 10 men over 45 unaware of their prostate cancer screening status: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:33:12 UTC
15:33:12 KST

69% unable to name a single risk factor; only 1 in 6 report ever being screened
NEW DELHI: Nearly six in 10 Indian men aged 45 and above do not know whether they have ever been screened for prostate cancer, while only around one in six report having undergone screening, a survey by NGO Heal Foundation has found.The survey of 1,036 men across Delhi-NCR, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Maharashtra points to significant gaps in awareness of prostate cancer risk factors, screening and when to seek medical advice. Nearly 69% of respondents could not name a single risk factor, while only 13.2% recognised family history as one. Around three-fourths believed prostate cancer monitoring should begin only at age 50 or later.The findings highlight a disconnect between routine healthcare and prostate-specific awareness. Although 62% of respondents said they underwent annual health check-ups, 60.8% did not know their prostate cancer screening status and only about 16% reported having ever been screened.Awareness of the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test was also limited. Only around 31% had heard of PSA as a marker, and just 14% had specifically requested the test.
“These findings point to a fundamental awareness gap around prostate cancer,” said Dr Devavrat Arya, vice-chairman, medical oncology, Max Healthcare, Delhi. He said awareness of risk factors, screening and when to consult a doctor needed to become a more visible part of routine health conversations among men over 45.The survey found that 59.5% of men were uncomfortable discussing screening or treatment with doctors, while only 18% would initiate the conversation themselves. Although 67% trusted doctors and hospitals, just 36% identified a urologist as the appropriate specialist. Meanwhile, 84% searched online or on social media for health information.The biggest barriers to screening were believing it was unnecessary (34%), having no symptoms (28%) and not receiving a doctor's recommendation (22%). Cost (19%), embarrassment or privacy concerns (17%), fear of diagnosis (14%) and not knowing where to go (11%) were other reasons.Gaps widened with age: around 72% of men aged 65 and above were unsure of their screening status, while 80% reported low treatment knowledge. Overall, 71.2% had limited knowledge of treatment options, only 10% felt confident across the treatment pathway, and 44% wanted a second opinion before treatment.
Dr Nitesh Rohatgi, principal director of medical oncology at fortis memorial research institute, said symptoms in older men were often dismissed as ageing, delaying diagnosis, while awareness of advanced treatments such as radioligand therapy remained limited even after diagnosis.The findings highlight the need for greater risk awareness and informed discussions with doctors. However, the survey reflects self-reported awareness and screening experiences, not prostate cancer prevalence or screening rates among all Indian men.

Five men and one woman died after a speedboat carrying migrants from Turkey made a sudden manoeuvre and overturned roughly four nautical miles north of Samos, the Greek coast guard said.
Fourteen men survived and a search-and-rescue operation was under way. Authorities arrested one of the survivors, an Iranian national, on suspicion of migrant smuggling.

Authorities arrested a 37-year-old Turkish national who was among the eight survivors and identified him as the suspected smuggler and operator of the boat.
The government vowed "zero tolerance" towards migrant smugglers, whom it blamed for the deaths.
On the incident off Lesbos, Greece's shipping minister Vassilis Kikilias said evidence so far indicated the speedboat struck the left side of a coast guard vessel with its bow, adding that the exact circumstances were under investigation.
"Our position is non-negotiable: zero tolerance for smugglers," he said in a post on X.
Greece, for years a favoured gateway to Europe for migrants and refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia, was at the front line of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-2016 and nearly 1 million people landed on its islands, mainly from Turkey.
It has since toughened its stance and has been accused by human rights groups of forcibly returning migrants and asylum-seekers on its sea and land borders, a practice it denies, saying its coast guard acts with full respect for human lives and rights. REUTERS
