Nakshabid Architects’ Alternative Factory Model in Bangladesh Receives the RIBA International Prize 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The Green Field Factory of Karupannya Rangpur Limited, designed by Nakshabid Architects, has been named the recipient of the RIBA International Prize 2026. Since 2016, the RIBA International Prize has been awarded to "a building that demonstrates visionary thinking, originality, excellence of execution, and makes a distinct contribution to its users, surrounding environment and communities." This year, the Green Field Factory was recognized for offering an alternative model for factory design and operation, challenging traditional workplace environments and creating new opportunities for women workers. The shortlist included three other projects: the Royale Belge renovation in Brussels, Belgium, by Caruso St John Architects in collaboration with Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+; Z33 House for Contemporary Art in Hasselt, Belgium, by Francesca Torzo Architetto; and BRAC University in Dhaka, Bangladesh, by WOHA.
Nakshabid Architects' design challenges the conventions of industrial architecture in Bangladesh, a context long scrutinized internationally for poor working conditions and unsafe environments. The building, a rug factory designed for 5,000 employees, proposes an alternative vision of what a contemporary factory can be and questions deeply rooted social hierarchies of the workplace. The main front door serves as the only entrance for everyone, unlike a typical industrial facility, where workers and management use different entrances. At the entrance, workers face a Bonolota sculpture, a traditional Bengali representation of female strength and empowerment, which begins an interior route of artworks depicting women's multifaceted roles in work, family and community. Two grand ceremonial staircases, inspired by spaces traditionally associated with royalty and privilege, welcome all employees to ascend the seven-story building through a system of multiple routes and stairways.
The 13,450 m² building is located in Robertsongonj, Rangpur, an area surrounded by open fields, informal settlements and roadside development. Based on a biophilic concept of well-being rooted in the traditional Bengali homestead, the workplace is designed to take advantage of natural ventilation and maximize daylight, rainwater, and wind, reducing reliance on mechanical systems. The facilities are organized around courtyards, deep verandahs, gardens, and a green facade. The factory includes water reservoirs, rainwater harvesting systems, and passive cooling systems that regulate temperature naturally. Abundant planting creates an ecosystem for insects and birds and provides a setting for workers' breaks. Additional amenities include a rooftop daycare center, an on-site medical clinic, a grocery store, a prayer room, and a shared canteen. Outside working hours, a dedicated stage is available for performances and events for workers' families and the wider community.
Related Article
Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFFARCHITECTS Wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
 We asked a simple question: what if a factory were designed first as a home for the people who work in it? Every courtyard, garden, water body and shaded verandah grew from that question. A factory should not be a machine that consumes human energy. It should be a living place that restores it. At Green Field, we wanted to prove that industry can breathe, nurture and inspire. — Bayejid M. Khondoker from Nakshabid Architects
The RIBA International Prize Grand Jury was chaired by Bijoy Jain, founder of Studio Mumbai, and also included José Toral, co-founder of Peris + Toral Arquitectes and recipient of the RIBA International Prize 2024; and Dr. Sofie De Caigny, head of collections at the New Institute in Rotterdam. On Friday, October 16, RIBA announced Lion Green Road, a housing development in South London designed by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFFARCHITECTS for Croydon Council, as the recipient of the 2026 Stirling Prize. Another housing initiative, the Balearic Social Housing Model, was recently recognized with the 2026 OBEL Award for transforming social housing administration in the Balearic Islands between 2019 and 2023. The ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards honorees were announced in mid-September, recognizing 20 emerging and forward-thinking practices expanding the possibilities of architecture today.

Lula and Bolsonaro trade insults in heated Brazil election debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:19:48 UTC
14:19:48 KST

Firing off personal attacks, Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro held an acrimonious first debate on Sunday, a week before a tight presidential election runoff.
A chaotic exchange between the two men, who called each other liars on multiple occasions, accusing each other of corruption and dragging up various scandals, encapsulated the tone of a bitter election campaign in the deeply polarised nation.
Bolsonaro, 45, son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, secured a shock first-round lead over Lula earlier this month and polls predict a close battle for the runoff on October 25.
The two men sparred over the economy, public security, healthcare, corruption, and Brazil's ties to the United States.
"Brazil is going to retire you," fired off Bolsonaro, seeking to unnerve his adversary by pacing up and down behind him throughout the debate in view of the camera, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing while his adversary spoke.
Lula called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar, a thug," and said he did not want to stand close to a "militiaman," alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups.
Bolsonaro, who made several jabs about Lula's time jailed for corruption on charges that were later annulled, retorted that it was better he stay at a distance "because my wallet could be stolen."
Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in power, battled to control his irritation at times and repeatedly asked viewers to "look it up on Google" to prove his adversary was lying.
While Bolsonaro has led in polls since the first round, his edge slightly narrowed in two polls this week which showed him with 51 percent of voting intentions compared to 49 percent for Lula.
'Subservient' to US interests
Bolsonaro hammered away at the primary concerns of Brazilians -- such as the cost of living and insecurity -- and accused Lula of "reckless spending to get re-elected" due to various social measures he has announced while campaigning.
Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic "chainsaw" cuts to public spending implemented by Argentina's libertarian President Javier Milei, which led to higher unemployment and cuts to benefits.
Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro dodged the question and pivoted to different topics.
Lula questioned the right winger's his ties to US President Donald Trump -- an ally of the Bolsonaro family -- and plans to "hand over" Brazil's rare earth minerals.
"It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests," said Lula.
Former president Jair Bolsonaro came up several times, including when his son asked Lula why so many prisoners had supported him in the election.
Lula said he wanted all of their votes, including that of Jair Bolsonaro -- who is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for a botched coup bid after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
"Vote for me, Bolsonaro, you know your son, you know I'm better than him."
'A state of calamity'
Ahead of the showdown, tens of thousands of supporters of Lula and Bolsonaro gathered in cities around the country.
In Sao Paulo, a sea of people dressed in the yellow and green of the Brazilian flag rallied for Flavio Bolsonaro, who made his way down Paulista Avenue on the back of a truck.
"The country is in a state of calamity. To make ends meet or buy anything, you have to work two or three jobs just to pay the bills," said Sara Machado, 36, wearing a T-shirt with the slogan: "Right-wing. With pride."
The rally drew about 71,000 people, according to monitors at the University of Sao Paulo (USP).
Swimmers and singers for Lula
In Rio de Janeiro, swimmers at Praia Vermelha beach synchronised in the water to spell out Lula's name with their bodies.
Later, on Copacabana Beach, iconic octogenarian singer Caetano Veloso led a "rally for democracy" in favor of the president, which USP monitors said drew some 56,000 people.
Fabiana Leite, a 51-year-old nurse and social worker, said Lula's social welfare programs saved her after she was wrongly incarcerated, lost custody of her daughters, and had to rebuild her life after being freed.
"You might have the desire to fight and to grow, but without the means, without social programs, it's just not possible. That is why I am here, continuing the fight," she told AFP.

AIIMS removes uterus of 98-cm-tall woman through keyhole surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:11:13 UTC
14:11:13 KST

A 44-year-old woman endured extreme menstrual cramps attributed to deep pelvic endometriosis and adenomyosis. (Pic Credit: ANI)
NEW DELHI: A 44-year-old woman, just 98 cm tall and weighing 22 kg, has undergone laparoscopic hysterectomy at AIIMS, with doctors adapting the surgical approach to minimise fracture risks from severe osteoporosis and address anaesthesia challenges linked to her exceptionally small stature.The woman, who has been living with osteoporosis, or fragile bones, since 2019, had suffered from extremely painful menstrual periods for nearly a year. The pain disrupted her daily life, forcing her to rely frequently on painkillers. Investigations revealed deep pelvic endometriosis and adenomyosis, a condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus or within its muscular wall.Prof Neena Malhotra, head of Obstetrics and gynaecology said that the patient recovered well and was discharged on the third day after surgery.Given her age, bone fragility and high blood pressure, hormonal treatment was not considered feasible.Doctors recommended removing the uterus to relieve her symptoms. Teams from gynaecology, endocrinology and anaesthesia jointly assessed the risks before proceeding with minimally invasive surgery.
“Minimally invasive surgery is now routine for most hysterectomies, but operating on an adult woman of this size, with severe bone weakness and hypertension, poses unusual challenges,” said Prof K Aparna Sharma from the department of obstetric and gynaecology.A major concern was positioning the patient. The conventional lithotomy position, in which the legs are raised and supported, could have exposed her lower back and thigh bones to fractures.“Due to short stature along with severely fragile bones, standard lithotomy position for hysterectomy could have put her at risk of lower back and thigh bone fractures. There was a need for utmost care in proper positioning and cushioning during surgery,” said Prof Rajesh Khadgawat of the endocrinology department.
At the request of the patient and her family, the team opted to perform the procedure with her lying flat on her back, taking precautions to minimise injury.“The uterus was enlarged due to adenomyosis, and the uterus and ovaries were stuck to the adjacent intestines, while the space in her abdomen was very limited. We were able to complete the hysterectomy successfully through the laparoscopic route in around 90 minutes,” said Prof Reeta Mahey, who performed the surgery.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

====================================================================================================

Israeli company weaponised online advertising to track millions of devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:04:46 UTC
14:04:46 KST

Australia's nuclear agency targeted with ads linked to spyware that infect devices without a click
In short:
Highly sensitive government agencies have been targeted by a sophisticated, foreign bad actor.
Online ads were used to install spyware on some systems, researchers say.
What's next?
An Australian spyware researcher said it shows the need for more oversight of the online advertising industry.
Australia's nuclear science agency and other highly sensitive government and critical infrastructure organisations have been targeted by a sophisticated, foreign bad actor that secretly weaponised online advertising to track millions of devices and install spyware on some systems, according to researchers.
Research group, The Citizen Lab, said it found proof that an Israel-based company exploited digital advertising technology to install back doors onto devices, merely by the victim viewing an advertisement on a website or in an app.
It said millions of devices were targeted in the unprecedented attack, including those on networks belonging to Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO) and a number of other Australian government agencies, critical infrastructure and major media organisations.
A spokesperson for ANSTO said it had not identified any impact to its systems as a result of the techniques identified by The Citizen Lab.
Deakin University associate professor Diarmaid Harkin, who has researched the spyware industry, said it was a novel case revealing how bad actors were using online infrastructure to compromise their opponents.
"This is a demonstration of how the online advertising industry is not only being used to surveil, but also is being exploited for what looks like espionage,"
he said.
A 'little bit' of code in an online ad enough to install back door
The Citizen Lab is a University of Toronto research lab that has uncovered numerous high-profile examples of cyber espionage targeting governments, businesses, non-for-profits, media outlets and political organisations.
Last week, it published a report, Exposing AdFection: How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware, that identified what it said were bad actors using online advertising to infect devices using spyware.
Dr Harkin said normal online advertising technology runs a "little bit" of code in browsers and apps to show an ad.
"That's normally something innocent, but this time, it wasn't the case," he said.
Instead, this exploit — called ''zero-click mercenary spyware" — allowed bad actors to run code on devices that installed software that acted as a back door to the device, allowing them to access things like passwords, emails and details of internal systems.
The Citizen Lab claims that a company, Discover-Tech, acted as the go-between for online advertising platforms like Google and spyware and hacking companies. At least one of those, Candiru, has been placed under US export controls because of its "malicious cyber activities".
As part of normal online advertising practices, Discover-Tech "bid" against other prospective advertisers to show ads on websites and apps like Duolingo, the BBC and New York Times.
When they won the online auctions, they showed seemingly benign ads to users that secretly included code that could infect their devices.
"This report shows that this ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware," the report said.
The Citizen Lab verified that bad actors were able to use these advertisements to infect devices belonging to international news network Al Jazeera.
The research group traced the moment from Al Jazeera devices first seeing the infected ad, to the initial contact between its devices and servers spyware maker Candiru, to files being installed on the Al Jazeera computers that would hijack the device.
Merely viewing the ad didn't guarantee the devices were successfully infected, only that it had been exposed to the exploit.
However, researchers said the company was also able to exploit the online advertising technology to profile devices so it could identify them, track their web activity and find their geographical location.
This information would be enough to reveal a person's name or suggest where they worked, and was used to help target the subsequent spyware attacks, researchers claim.
Public records from online advertising show that Discover-Tech carried this out against millions of devices.
Australian critical infrastructure and nuclear-linked organisations targeted
Among numerous international defence forces, cyber agencies, and international organisations including NATO, The Citizen Lab highlighted a "substantial cluster" of impressions in Australian critical infrastructure, government, university and media networks.
The report does not specify most of these, however it does say many Australian targets were working on nuclear research, and named the ANSTO and its Australian Synchrotron research campus.
A spokesperson for ANTSO said it was aware of the reports but said its systems had not been breached.
"We are following standard response processes and have not identified any impact to our facilities, systems, and information from the techniques described in the reports," they said.
The Department for Home Affairs directed the ABC's inquiries to Australia's cyber intelligence agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, which declined to comment.
The Citizen Lab report said Google removed Discover-Tech from its platform once the researchers had shared their findings.
Dr Harkin said the report showed how the size and ubiquity of online advertising offered a unique opportunity for bad actors
"What this demonstrates is how zero-click exploits need to find information about who to target with that particular exploit and vulnerability. And what allows them is using the ad tech," he said.
Dr Harkin said it raised questions about how a company was able to gain the trust of major advertising players, like Google, and use them to distribute their exploit without being caught.
"If these ads are being delivered to our devices, our browsers, are they going to do anything malicious once they reach the user? That's the question that needs to be handled upstream by those who are running these ecosystem and by who's regulating them," he said.
"Who's acting as a watchdog for these digital advertising systems?"
Google was approached for comment.

8 arrested after West Bank attacks on US journalist, European diplomats

2026-10-19
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

The Israel police arrested eight Jewish suspects in the West Bank early Monday as part of a new operation launched following violent attacks on American photojournalist Heidi Levine and European diplomats over the weekend, incidents that sparked international condemnation, including from senior U.S. officials.
Police said the operation, codenamed "Olive Leaf," began before dawn and was continuing Monday morning. The eight suspects were detained on suspicion of involvement in the assaults, which took place in the Benjamin region north of Jerusalem.
Several vehicles were also seized during the raids. At the same time, Israeli military and Border Police forces were conducting enforcement operations targeting illegal construction, violations of military orders and the unauthorized occupation of a Palestinian home.
The arrests follow a weekend of violence during the annual olive harvest in the West Bank, which has drawn extensive international attention after masked Jewish extremists attacked Palestinian farmers, a Washington Post photographer and visiting diplomats from several European countries.
On Friday, dozens of masked Jewish attackers descended on Palestinian olive harvesters near the village of Abu Falah, in the Ramallah area, injuring two people, including veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was covering the harvest for The Washington Post.
Levine was evacuated to a hospital in Ramallah in moderate condition following the assault. Images and accounts of the attack triggered widespread condemnation, including from senior officials in the U.S. administration.
A day later, on Saturday, Jewish extremists attacked diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland, along with Israeli activists, who were visiting an olive harvest near the Palestinian village of Taybeh, widely considered the West Bank's last entirely Christian village.
Video footage from the scene showed masked men approaching a vehicle carrying the diplomats, armed with clubs and stones, before pursuing the delegation on an all-terrain vehicle.
Another video showed Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, sitting on the ground with his back against a vehicle. He was wearing the French tricolor sash identifying his official position. According to members of the diplomatic delegation, Baudoux was pushed during the attack.
The incidents are part of a broader pattern of violence involving residents of unauthorized settler outposts and agricultural farms in the West Bank. Attacks on Palestinians have been reported almost daily for years, with a marked escalation since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Much of the violence has traditionally occurred in Area C, which is under full Israeli security and administrative control, but incidents have increasingly spread into Area B, where Palestinian authorities exercise civil jurisdiction while Israel retains overriding security powers.
Despite repeated incidents, law enforcement authorities have struggled to contain the violence. Few indictments have been filed, and suspects arrested in connection with attacks have frequently been released shortly afterward.
Violence typically intensifies during the autumn olive harvest, when Palestinian farmers travel to their groves, often near Israeli settlements and unauthorized outposts. This year's harvest has attracted particularly extensive international coverage following the attacks on journalists and foreign diplomatic representatives.
Monday's arrests mark a new enforcement operation following the weekend's incidents, with police continuing to search for suspects while military and Border Police forces carry out additional enforcement measures in the area.

Georgia Merritt stages contemporary design show at London antiques dealer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

Georgia Merritt stages contemporary design show at London antiques dealer
Emerging designer Georgia Merritt has unveiled Refrain, an east London exhibition of sculptural furniture pieces informed by 18th-century architectural mouldings and musical staves.
Refrain is the second solo show for Merritt, who was featured in our London Design Festival Dezeen Dispatch lineup of London's rising stars.
The exhibition brings together five of Merritt's pieces arranged across M Kardana, a 20th-century antiques shop on Hackney Road that was stripped back to form a gallery setting to accommodate the works.
"My pieces can be read as furniture, but equally as sculptures, or propositions for an interior," Merritt told Dezeen. "Showing them at M Kardana, within the context of an antiques dealer, plays on that ambiguity."
The design of each of Merritt's pieces was rooted in the inspiration she finds in the precision of both musical notation and architecture.
Among them is a slim, wall-mounted mirror flanked by a duo of black lacquered doors that open out on full-length piano hinges.
Although made of birchwood, the doors look as if they are solid stone thanks to Merritt's distinctive painting technique, which involves hand-painting timber to create trompe l'œil faux marble furniture.
The designer developed the granular process during a gilding apprenticeship that she completed when struggling to find work as a fine art graduate in 2020.
Also on display is a delicate, hand-formed wire lamp encased in an ellipsoid shade made of silk organza overlaid with gazar.
The lamp and its shade were positioned atop a stainless steel frame fitted with a central, rectilinear tray.
Underscore is a sweeping bench supported by a single leg at one end, and resting against a wall at the other.
The curved seating was carved from smooth sapele wood. Merritt wanted to visually interpret a glissando, the musical term for sliding from one note to the next.
"The bench's profile recalls both Georgian architectural mouldings and the parallel lines of a musical stave," said the designer.
A glass tablet was fitted atop the furniture's single leg, which was selected to echo a magnifying glass or other "apparatus for observation or examination".
Merritt's fourth piece is a low-slung glass table, topped with an elongated canopy made of ivory silk that was clamped to the upper panes of glass with stainless-steel arms.
The final piece in the exhibition is another wall-mounted mirror fastened with piano hinges, but this one is full length and finished entirely in black lacquer.
"When closed, the mirror's doors form a monolithic, modernist silhouette," said Merritt.
Refrain marks the second show that the designer has presented at M Kardana, following her Vague Precision exhibition in 2023.
The designer considered how her practice, which she defines as art as much as design, has developed in recent years.
"I think I'm continually working towards expressing something that I can sense quite clearly but can't necessarily define," she said. "With this exhibition, I feel a little closer to it."
Merritt is interested in making pieces with an "ability to move between different contexts, whether that's a gallery, a domestic interior, or somewhere else".
"I like the idea that their identity might shift slightly depending on where they're placed," she said.
The designer was among the creatives showing in the Max Radford Gallery presentation at London's Collect fair in February.
The photography is by Tazy Jessett Nash.
Refrain is on display at M Kardana, 188A Hackney Road, London E2 7QL, United Kingdom, from 9 to 31 October 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

The protesters, including opposition parties, the CJP and several student groups have claimed that the exercise led to the deletion of lakhs of voters’ names and raised questions over changes to Form 6, which is used to register as a voter. These allegations, however, remain subject to verification.The counter-outfit called for questions about political organisations, their funding and alleged links to unlawful activities to be examined through verified documents, lawful investigations and official findings.

Moscow pursues three-power talks on Ukraine without Kyiv - report
Putin’s proposal would bring Trump and Xi into negotiations next month, but Washington has yet to commit and the scope of any meeting remains unresolved, the Wall Street Journal reports
Ukraine would have no seat at a proposed meeting where the leaders of Russia, the United States and China could discuss how to end the war, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
The diplomatic initiative, put forward by Russian President Vladimir Putin, would shift discussions toward a forum dominated by three major powers. For Kyiv and its European partners, the central concern would be their exclusion from deliberations over a settlement affecting Ukraine’s territory and security.
No summit has been agreed. The Journal cited a senior US official as saying President Donald Trump had made no commitment, while Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the newspaper that the arrangements and subjects for discussion remained undecided.
Moscow has suggested using November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen as the setting, according to people familiar with the exchanges cited by the Journal. Russian representatives have approached China, and Beijing has signaled openness provided Trump participates, the report said.
For Putin, the proposed format offers both a negotiating opportunity and a symbolic gain. The Journal described a Russian effort to secure an outcome favorable to Moscow while presenting Russia as an equal partner in decisions involving Washington and Beijing. European governments, which have supported Ukraine throughout the conflict, would also be absent.
The overture comes as Trump has taken steps toward closer economic dealings with Russia while increasing pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. According to the newspaper, Putin broached the meeting during an October 9 call with Trump that also produced an arrangement involving Russian diesel purchases.
Trump has since held back major sanctions measures against Moscow and criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Journal reported. His administration has defended its fuel decisions as an attempt to bring down prices, although energy specialists cited by the newspaper questioned how much additional Russian supply would help.
The Journal reported that officials in Beijing are concerned the meeting could distract from their plans for APEC and complicate economic relations with Europe.

Pope greeted by crowds in first major appearance since lung cancer surgery
Pope Leo pledges a gradual return to duties in an address to the Catholic faithful in St Peter’s Square at the Vatican.
Pope Leo XIV has thanked some 15,000 Catholic faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square during his Sunday address, his first major public appearance since lung cancer surgery.
“Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers,” Leo said.
The 71-year-old pontiff addressed the crowd from a window overlooking the square at the Vatican, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing, he revealed that a nodule had been found in his lung and would be surgically removed.
The operation confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
Leo said the experience of the past week “has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity”.
He told the crowd that he had “truly felt your support” and expressed “particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli Hospital” in Rome, where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa, in Rome for a Catholic meeting, danced and ululated after the pope’s blessing.
“He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of the Congo said. “This is an expression of our joy.”
Meanwhile, Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, United States, said she felt “very blessed” to be present for the pope’s return to his flock.
There had been doubts that a planned papal voyage to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November would go ahead.
The Vatican’s secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told journalists on Friday that the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule “according to the condition of his health”.
But Leo’s surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were “no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead”.
Latin Americans in the crowd in St Peter’s Square welcomed the news.
“We are all hoping for his recovery, and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is OK, and we’re pleased,” Soledad Espinosa from Ecuador said.

Taiwanese trips to China up 20% through August as overall travel grows

13:40:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese trips to China rose 19.6% year on year in the first eight months of 2026, outpacing the 15.2% growth in overall overseas travel, according to Tourism Administration data.
Huang Cheng-tsung (黃正聰), an associate professor of tourism at Providence University in Taichung, told CNA that the rise in trips to China was in line with broader growth in overseas travel.
Huang said business trips could be contributing to the increase, adding that some companies now hire travel agencies to help organize business and visiting groups to China. This arrangement falls outside the ban since early 2024 on local agencies actively soliciting package tours to China.
China remains the second most popular destination for Taiwanese travelers, according to the data. Trips there have exceeded 300,000 a month since earlier this year.
Since June, however, Taiwan has placed China, Hong Kong, and Macau under its second highest travel warning, urging the public to avoid nonessential trips to those areas.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), a professor at the University of Taipei who heads the Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience, said the warning was unlikely to discourage people who need to travel to China. He urged the government to provide risk information tailored to travelers’ identities and reasons for travel, along with guidance on seeking help if they are questioned or detained at the border.
The Mainland Affairs Council warned of the risks of traveling to China, citing entry and exit rules that took effect there in September. Experts said Chinese border officials can demand to inspect travelers’ personal devices and social media accounts if they suspect activity that threatens national security.
The council advised travelers to weigh the risks carefully and monitor official safety notices.

Taiwan, Philippines seek closer coordination amid Chinese maritime pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
04:39:32 UTC
13:39:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan and the Philippines are gradually deepening security ties amid increasing Chinese aggression, Nikkei Asia reported.
A senior Taiwan government official involved in cooperation with the Philippines told Nikkei Asia that “as close neighbors in the first island chain, both nations face China’s expansionist, coercive and aggressive behavior.”
“As China attempts to assert its false maritime claims through the use of both military and non-military assets, such as coast guard or research vessels, it’s important for Taiwan and the Philippines to engage in closer coordination and exchange relevant experiences on maritime security,” the official added.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA) fired water cannons at a Chinese fishing boat near Dongsha Island in the South China Sea on Oct. 1. Last Tuesday, it used close-range maneuvers to drive away four Chinese coast guard ships near Kinmen.
On Sunday, the CGA monitored and drove away 16 Chinese coast guard, research, and fishing vessels conducting maritime harassment operations around Taiwan proper and Dongsha Island.
In the past two weeks, the Philippines has also driven away Chinese maritime militia and research vessels, per Nikkei Asia.
Amid this common threat, the CGA plans to send a ship carrying 100 officers and students to the Philippines in October 2027. It would be the first such visit in 53 years. In September, the CGA also confirmed that it had donated a retired patrol vessel to the Philippines.
National Security Council Deputy Secretary-General Lii Wen (李問) previously said that “Taiwan has been learning from the Philippines’ success on assertive transparency,” according to Nikkei Asia.
The Philippines publicizes information about Chinese ship activities in the South China Sea. “Many countries in the region are increasingly recognizing the importance of disclosing China’s coercive maritime behavior in a clear and timely way,” Lii said. “It is important for more countries to adopt transparency initiatives together, so that China cannot pressure and bully the few countries that speak up.”
Oriana Skylar Mastro, a fellow at Stanford University’s Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, stressed the importance of Taiwan’s efforts to deepen ties with the Philippines.
“From a military operational perspective, the only two places within combat radius of Taiwan are the northern Philippines and the southwest islands of Japan,” Mastro said, according to Nikkei Asia.
“The more connectivity there is between Taiwan and the Philippines, [the more likely] the Philippines will allow operations off their soil in the defense of Taiwan,” Mastro said.
Dan Blumenthal, a former senior Pentagon official, said the CGA’s planned visit and the ship donation are “small in material terms, but they matter as signals,” per Nikkei Asia. The priority is to ensure Taipei and Manila can communicate effectively when incidents occur, particularly those involving fishers in areas where their exclusive economic zones overlap, so that an incident does not escalate into a political crisis, Blumenthal said.
He also called for cooperation in search and rescue, disaster response, maritime domain awareness, and joint training.

After War of Words, China Says Relations With Philippines at ‘Critical Juncture’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
04:38:00 UTC
13:38:00 KST

China on Friday expressed willingness to improve its relationship with the Philippines, but admitted that relations were at “an extremely sensitive and critical juncture” due to the actions of unnamed “outside forces.”
The two governments have been engaged in a war of words since Friday, when Jing Quan, China’s ambassador to Manila, declared that China could “easily win” a war with the Philippines. Jing was responding to a remark by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who the day prior described China as the lone “troublemaker” in Southeast Asia, due to its aggressive actions in contested parts of the South China Sea.
Speaking to the press after a Diliman Dialogues organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City, Jing said that the remark was “nonsense.”
“We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region,” he said. “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace. In this region, we enjoy peace.”
Asked on Friday about Ambassador Jing’s remark, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said that it “sounds very much like a threat” and that he would summon the ambassador to provide an explanation. Jing, who began his posting last December, was previously summoned by Marcos in July, after a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with the China Coast Guard at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands and the subsequent publication of a video by the state-run China Daily depicting Filipinos as monkeys and U.S. puppets.
Yesterday, the Chinese embassy issued a statement in which it said it considered the Philippines a “close neighbor and friend with deep historical and cultural ties.” It also said the Philippines need not choose between China and the United States and that the two sides “should maintain dialogue, manage differences, and expand cooperation in trade, investment, people-to-people exchanges, and law enforcement.”
At the same time, it said that China-Philippines relations were “at an extremely sensitive and critical juncture and require prudent, careful handling” and lambasted “anti-China politicians” who it said, “deliberately ignore China’s clear and consistent position on China-Philippines relations, instead twisting its words out of context and maliciously distorting the facts for political gain.”
It concluded by saying that differences “should be managed through dialogue” and that “outside forces” – i.e., the United States and its allies – “should not be allowed to steer bilateral relations toward confrontation.”
“China is ready to work with all sectors of Philippine society to promote dialogue, deepen trust, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation,” it added.
Such exchanges have taken place periodically between the two governments over the past few years, often linked to events in the South China Sea, where the two nations have overlapping maritime claims. Besides, Chinese and Philippine coast guards have engaged in a string of confrontations, some involving the use of physical force, which have pushed relations to their worst point in years.
Jing’s comments were preceded by a chain of public comments and responses emanating from the Philippines’ fractious domestic politics, hinting at the apparent growing polarization of foreign relations along partisan lines.
This began on October 6 with the airing of allegations that Chinese entities had sent just over $5 million in remittances to a Philippine company linked to the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, a major rival of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The claims, which came to light during Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial in the Senate, prompted Marcos to state that the involvement of Chinese money made the issue “a national security issue.”
“If it is true, it is a threat – a threat at the highest level to the republic,” Marcos said on October 12.
Duterte responded the same day by stating that the Philippines was becoming the main “troublemaker of Southeast Asia” by treating business ties with China as a national security concern. Teodoro’s comment about China being the main “troublemaker” in the region was a direct response to Duterte. At this point, Jing made his incautious entry into the “debate,” turning the domestic war of words into a potential diplomatic incident.
The incident is notable for what it says about how bitter political rivalries in the Philippines have the potential to impact Manila’s delicate balancing of relations with China and the United States. In late 2016, the administration of President Rodrigo Duterte, Sara’s father, initiated a bold turn toward China, downplaying maritime disputes in order to gain Chinese financial support for major infrastructure projects. The needle swung back under Marcos, who, after coming to office in 2022, strengthened the Philippines’ relationship with the United States and became much more forceful in his condemnations of Chinese behavior in the South China Sea.
There is now some danger that as the country moves toward the next presidential election in 2028, the two rival camps will come to see benefits in depicting each other as agents of foreign forces (the U.S. and China, respectively). The impacts of this could stretch beyond the periodic diplomatic incident. Indeed, they could begin to impact Manila’s ability to maintain a stable and predictable approach toward the challenges posed by China’s aggressive actions in the South China Sea.

Imprisoned Australian activist Hiep Tran tells family he did not cross border into Vietnam
In short:
Imprisoned Australian pro-democracy activist Hiep Tran has told his family that he "never crossed the border" into Vietnam.
His message contradicts the account of Vietnamese authorities, who said that Mr Tran tried to illegally enter Vietnam to engage in "terrorist and sabotage activities".
Mr Tran's wife says she was told by Australian officials that he is "in a fragile mental state, gripped by fear, and experiencing erratic blood pressure".
Imprisoned Australian pro-democracy activist Hiep Tran has told his family he never crossed the border into Vietnam, with supporters alleging it is more evidence he was abducted by Vietnamese authorities a month ago.
Australian officials were able to meet Mr Tran last Thursday at the B34 detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City, where he is being held after disappearing in Cambodia on September 18.
His wife, Chloe Dang, said Australian officials passed her a brief message from her husband which read: "Hi, how are you all going? I want you to know that I never entered Vietnam on my own."
"I never crossed the border. I am struggling mentally — traumatised and terrified by the situation."
That contradicts the account of Vietnamese authorities, who said that Mr Tran and another human rights activist, Norwegian citizen Duc Thuan Nguyen, tried to illegally enter Vietnam to engage in "terrorist and sabotage activities".
Mr Tran is a member of Viet Tran, an overseas Vietnamese opposition group that Vietnam's ruling party has labelled a terrorist organisation. However, most scholars say it has evolved from its armed anti-Communist roots into a political party committed to peaceful change.
The group alleged the message showed that Hiep Tran and Duc Thuan Nguyen — along with a third activist — were "abducted in Cambodia by the Vietnamese authorities and forcibly taken to Vietnam, where they are being detained".
Ms Dang said in a statement that she had "received a few fragmented details" about her husband's condition from Australian officials after the visit.
"I was told that he is in a fragile mental state, gripped by fear, and experiencing erratic blood pressure, none of which he had ever experienced before," she said.
Ms Dang told the ABC that Australian consular officials were able to hand over fresh clothes to her husband, as well as verbally conveying messages from both her and Mr Tran's mother.
They were also able to show Mr Tran a family photo — although he was not allowed to keep it.
She also said Vietnamese prison officials kept strict limits on the discussion, saying they warned Australian consular officials would be kicked out if they discussed topics outside those approved by Vietnamese authorities.
And she said Vietnamese authorities were still yet to provide Mr Tran with the details of the charges against him.
Small groups of Vietnamese community members and activists gathered in Sydney on Saturday night to hold a candlelight vigil for Mr Tran and the two other activists who disappeared in Cambodia. A similar event is also being organised in Melbourne.
Ms Dang said Sunday marked "exactly one month since this terrible ordeal began for my husband".
"Over the past month, the Australian Government has provided tremendous support to me and my family, and I am deeply grateful," she said.
"However, I sincerely hope that the Australian government, along with people around the world, will continue to speak up and do everything possible to help bring my husband home safely and as soon as possible.
"No-one, whether an Australian citizen or anyone else, should ever have to endure the terrible ordeal that my husband and our family are going through."
Vietnam's embassy did not respond immediately to questions from the ABC about the latest developments in Mr Tran's case.
But it said in a statement last week that the kidnapping allegations were "unfounded and misleading" and that "arrests and prosecutions are carried out in accordance with the law" in Vietnam.

Eisenkot's plan to beat Netanyahu: Win Likud voters and sink his smaller allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
04:32:34 UTC
13:32:34 KST

Gadi Eisenkot is pursuing an election strategy designed not only to make his Yashar party Israel's largest, but also to weaken Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political bloc by pushing smaller right-wing parties below the electoral threshold, according to people close to the opposition leader.
Facing criticism from other opposition leaders, particularly Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Lieberman, Eisenkot has defended his campaign to become the country's largest party, arguing that it offers the opposition its best chance of winning the October 27 election and forming a government with broad public and political legitimacy.
In private conversations, Eisenkot rejected claims that his strategy was coming at the expense of other parties opposed to Netanyahu. "On the contrary. The campaign to become the largest party doesn't hurt the bloc, it helps the bloc. A large party can move Likud voters," he said.
According to Eisenkot, undecided voters and Israelis disillusioned with Netanyahu are more inclined to support Yashar because it is emerging as the largest opposition party and a credible alternative to Likud.
Associates of the former IDF chief of staff say the strategy is already proving effective in drawing voters away from Netanyahu's coalition and into the opposition camp.
"We are the only party bringing in a substantial number of disillusioned coalition and right-wing voters," an Eisenkot associate said. "He attracts votes from the right, and people who vote for him acknowledge that he can be trusted. He's Mizrahi, he served in the Golani Brigade, and he's popular. There are no negative feelings toward him. The Palestine campaign doesn't work on them."
The associate was referring to Eisenkot's appeal among right-wing voters, including his Mizrahi Jewish background and military service in the Golani infantry brigade.
"Our findings show that the most popular politician among Netanyahu bloc voters, after Netanyahu himself, is Eisenkot," the associate continued. "They don't hate him. Voters disappointed with Netanyahu see a party larger than Likud and understand that it's a safe place to move to. That definitely affects our bloc."
Eisenkot's campaign also believes that a racist remark by Channel 14 commentator Yinon Magal, who described the Yashar leader as "a monkey with elitist Ashkenazi Jews behind him," has damaged Netanyahu's camp. According to Eisenkot aides, some supporters of the prime minister and his coalition regarded the remark as "deranged."
The campaign points to Netanyahu's own response as further evidence that its strategy is working. The prime minister has increasingly emphasized the importance of Likud emerging as Israel's largest party, warning that if Eisenkot wins more seats, President Isaac Herzog could choose him to form the next government.
"If we are not the largest party in Israel, it would be a major disaster, because the president could task Eisenkot with forming the government," Netanyahu said. Coalition chairman Ofir Katz has made similar remarks.
But Eisenkot's strategy has another objective: forcing Netanyahu to compete for votes with smaller parties in his own bloc. By drawing the prime minister into a battle over which party will emerge as the largest, Yashar hopes Likud will attract voters who might otherwise support smaller right-wing factions.
That could hurt parties such as Amcha Yisrael, led by former IDF brigadier general Ofer Winter. If such parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, their votes would not translate into Knesset seats, potentially reducing the overall strength of Netanyahu's bloc.
Eisenkot's associates insist that the same risk does not apply to the opposition. "The bloc led by Eisenkot is organized, and there is no concern that any of its parties will fall below the electoral threshold," one associate said.
The Yashar leader is also signaling to his opposition partners that they have a shared interest in fielding one particularly strong candidate against Netanyahu, rather than several smaller parties competing for leadership.
"Being the largest party will give the president the legitimacy to task us with forming a government from a position of strength," a senior Eisenkot campaign official said. "We're not talking about six seats or 12 seats. We're talking about genuinely becoming the largest party."
According to the official, the strategy is also supported by opinion polls published by various Israeli television networks, which have consistently shown Eisenkot ahead of Netanyahu in head-to-head surveys asking voters who is better suited to serve as prime minister.
For Eisenkot, the calculation is that a dominant Yashar party could achieve two goals at once: draw voters directly from Likud while prompting Netanyahu to consolidate right-wing support at the expense of his smaller allies, potentially leaving the prime minister with fewer seats across his bloc even if Likud itself grows.

"It is no coincidence that the letter arrived at the Leader's Office the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection," Senator Steele-John wrote.
"It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party preselections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself."
The senator claimed the document's history showed only one person had accessed it since 2019, a former employee to him, who had done so in July of this year.
'Like succession, but more amateur and boring'
The WA senator's open letter has burst open long-simmering hostilities within the western branch of the party.
Senator Steele-John was re-elected for a six-year term in 2025, and does not face pre-selection for years.
But the West Australian Greens branch will soon decide on a replacement on its Senate ticket for Dorinda Cox, who defected to Labor in 2025.
Senator Steele-John's ally and chief-of-staff Sophie Greer and WA Legislative Council member Sophie McNeill are two of the prominent names expected to contest for the spot.
One Greens insider rubbished Senator Steele-John's claim that allegations of his misconduct would be weaponised for a coming pre-selection contest, saying the incident was a "binfire" that had damaged anyone's chances of winning a seat.
The WA Greens branch is widely considered among party members to be a "cowboy" branch known to campaign more aggressively.
A former Greens staffer told the ABC there was still "bad blood" inside parts of the branch since former senators Rachel Siewert and Scott Ludlam moved to secure Senator Steele-John's preselection for the senate more than a decade ago.
They said the branch was small and while there were not formal factions, there were groupings around "old-school" environmentalists and social justice advocates, and personal allegiances could weigh heavily on party decision-making.
"WA Greens factionalism is actually more like a family dynasty. Like Succession, but more amateur and boring," they said.
They also said some members in the branch had "a chip on their shoulder" about being distant from east coast Greens and that insularity led to the branch often seeking to resolve conflicts its own way.
Mr Ludlam and Ms Siewert were contacted for comment.

SEOUL, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's automotive exports fell last month, weighed down by weak demand from Asia and the Middle East, industry ministry data showed Monday.
The outbound car shipment dipped 5.5 percent from a year earlier to 6.05 billion U.S. dollars in September, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
Shipments to core markets expanded, with North America rising 9.2 percent to 3.07 billion dollars and the European Union (EU) gaining 15.3 percent to 1.11 billion dollars.
They were dragged down by a 60 percent plunge in Asia to 329 million dollars and a 7.1 percent reduction in the Middle East to 354 million dollars.
Despite the overall downturn, eco-friendly vehicles showed relative resilience, with their exports growing 5.9 percent to 2.89 billion dollars.
The eco-friendly vehicles included electric vehicles, fuel cell electric vehicles, hybrid electric vehicles, and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.
The number of exported vehicles totaled 237,443 in September, up 4.1 percent from the same month last year. Auto parts shipments fell 7.2 percent to 1.77 billion dollars.
The number of vehicles manufactured in local factories increased 3.7 percent to 346,618 last month.
It was boosted by local carmakers ramping up operations to make up for earlier production losses after concluding annual wage negotiations.
The number of cars sold inside the country, including locally-made and imported vehicles, was 135,396 in September, down 14.3 percent from a year earlier.
The slump was attributed to fewer working days as the Chuseok holiday, the South Korean version of Thanksgiving Day, shifted from October last year to September this year. ■

Airlines are also struggling to get their hands on new jets, leaving few spare aircraft to send to start-ups like Western Sydney International where passenger demand is unproven.

Lula and Bolsonaro spar in Brazil’s fiery first presidential run-off debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
04:27:00 UTC
13:27:00 KST

Lula and Bolsonaro spar in Brazil’s fiery first presidential run-off debate
Brazil’s president and his opponent lob a barrage of attacks on each other in debate a week before the October 25 vote.
Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro fired off a barrage of personal attacks during their first debate a week before a tight presidential run-off.
In a chaotic exchange on Sunday, the two men called each other “liar” multiple times, accused each other of corruption, dragged up various scandals, and clashed on issues from public security to healthcare.
Lula said Bolsonaro was “a habitual liar” and a “thug”, and physically distanced himself on stage from the candidate he called a “militiaman”, alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro’s paramilitary groups.
Bolsonaro, who led the first-round election with 47 percent to Lula’s 45 percent, said it was better to keep Lula at a distance “because my wallet could be stolen”.
Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, paced behind Lula, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing as his adversary spoke.
The 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth term, demanded an explanation regarding a corruption investigation involving the older Bolsonaro, a question his opponent dodged.
The younger Bolsonaro responded by calling Lula a “clown”, and then parried by bringing up a potential corruption case involving one of the president’s sons.
Jair Bolsonaro has been under house arrest while serving a 27-year sentence connected to efforts to overturn the 2022 election, which he lost to Lula.
Cost of living, public spending in focus
Flavio Bolsonaro hammered away at the top concerns of Brazilians, such as the cost of living and crime, and accused Lula of “reckless spending” to get re-elected, referring to various social measures the president has announced during the campaign.
Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic public spending cuts implemented by Argentina’s right-wing president, Javier Milei.
Bolsonaro dodged the question throughout the debate and pivoted to different topics.
When his father’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic came up, Bolsonaro admitted that this “wasn’t an area where we saw the best results during Bolsonaro’s presidency. I’ll offer a mea culpa here.”
Lula also sought to portray his opponent as out of touch with poor Brazilians, saying Bolsonaro had never used the country’s public healthcare system or taken a bus.
“My opponent only knows about buses from books. He has never even stepped foot on one. He has no idea what the world of work is like,” Lula said.
Voters show their colours
Ahead of Sunday’s debate, supporters of each candidate gathered en masse in public to show their allegiance.
Pro-Bolsonaro crowds wearing Brazil’s national colours of yellow, green and blue packed Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo’s financial centre, where the candidate addressed the crowd.
Lula supporters wearing red, symbolic of his Workers’ Party, filled Brasilia’s plaza of government buildings, while students backing the president protested against Bolsonaro in Rio de Janeiro.
“We need the current government to remain in power. If another government comes in, we’re, excuse my language, screwed,” said Lula supporter Sonia Maria at the Brasilia rally.
“I don’t like bandits. Out with Lula!” said Bolsonaro backer Vera de Sousa in Sao Paulo.
Also on Sunday, Brazil’s federal police asked the country’s Supreme Court to open an investigation into Bolsonaro over a money laundering accusation involving a lawyer close to him.
The presidential candidate is already under investigation for his links to Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced former banker who financed a movie about Jair Bolsonaro’s life.
Lula spent 580 days in prison in 2018 and 2019 on a corruption conviction that was later annulled over flaws in the investigation and legal proceedings.
Polls suggest a close race for the October 25 run-off, with Flavio Bolsonaro holding a slight advantage after finishing nearly 2 percentage points ahead of Lula in the first round on October 4.
Both candidates hope to engage the 33 million voters who stayed home in the first round, equal to about one in five eligible voters.
Sunday’s debate was the first between Lula and Bolsonaro after the candidates both declined previous opportunities. A second debate is scheduled for October 23, just ahead of the run-off.

Emily Chancellor announces retirement ahead of Wallaroos Test against Scotland
In short:
Former Wallaroos captain Emily Chancellor has announced her retirement from international rugby union.
Chancellor says she still feels physically capable of playing but is "ready for the next chapter".
What's next?
Chancellor will run out for her 42nd and final Test on Friday night against Scotland in Canberra.
An emotional Emily Chancellor admits that if she were told she would feature in two Women's Rugby World Cups, earn 41 caps for the Wallaroos and spend eight years with the national team, she would have laughed.
Even after announcing her retirement from international rugby on Monday, the 35-year-old still cannot fathom what has really unfolded over her glittering career.
"Rugby wasn't an option for me growing up. I didn't know that it [the women's game] existed," Chancellor said as tears welled up in her eyes.
"Having found the game when I was at uni, playing sevens, dabbling in that, and then finding 15s in 2015. I knew from the start that this was a game that I wanted to be involved in.
"It [retirement is] a hard one because I'm still here, physically, and feel capable. But I also think I'm ready for the next chapter.
"But if you told me then that I would have been playing internationally for eight years, I would have probably laughed at you."
Chancellor is set to play her final game for the Wallaroos when she runs out against Scotland on Friday at Canberra Stadium.
The back-rower's potential 42nd Test comes after she made her debut against New Zealand in 2018 aged 26, when she was awarded the player of the game.
"I was so terrified. I remember sitting in the change room, thinking, 'Oh my goodness, I'm playing against another country. I'm not good enough for this,'" she said.
"Then [I was] like, 'Well, of course I'm good enough. I've been picked to play for my country'.
"I'd been a rugby fan for a long time, gone to games with my dad and mum all the way through growing up. I just didn't realise that you could do it as a girl.
"As a curious person, someone who had always watched the game, [I wanted] to actually nail the detail, the intricacies of such a complex game."
The 35-year-old featured in her first World Cup in 2021 before suffering an ACL injury in 2024.
But the best was yet to come for the back-rower as she would become the Wallaroos' 19th captain last year before featuring in the World Cup campaign in England.
"If I can drive a standard and keep pushing a program to be better than we are, then I have done my job. And I think back to the years of being in this team, and I'm pretty proud of how I have tried to do that," Chancellor said.
"It's a really special team. I've played with 108 players across my [Wallaroos] career.
"We've seen the growth. We've been part of some crazy experiences … I wouldn't have pushed myself and my body and made the choices to choose this lifestyle for so many years if it wasn't worth it."

Ramaswamy Facing Tougher Fight Than Republicans Had Expected in Ohio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
04:06:00 UTC
13:06:00 KST

On the day Vivek Ramaswamy made official his run for Ohio Governor, President Donald Trump did not dally.
“He will be a GREAT Governor of Ohio, will never let you down, and has my COMPLETE AND TOTAL ENDORSEMENT!” the President wrote on Truth Social on Feb. 24 of last year, within hours of Ramaswamy kicking off his campaign.
Trump’s post essentially cleared what had been expected to be a crowded GOP field, boxing out the likes of state Attorney General Dave Yost, state Treasurer Robert Sprague, and Lieutenant Governor Jim Tressel in a state where Republicans felt dominant. It also effectively gave Ramaswamy almost two years to focus on keeping the Governor’s mansion in GOP hands. But the very connections to Trumpism that fueled Ramaswamy’s fast political rise are now giving his party reason to worry, as polls show him trailing Democrat Amy Acton, a former state health chief and a first-time candidate.
“Something is happening here. I just can’t tell you what,” says one Ohio Democratic strategist, reflecting the apprehension pervasive in both parties right now.
On the campaign trail, Ramaswamy occasionally moderates his image as the brash MAGA warrior railing against “the woke left,” pitching tax cuts and economic development when he’s with suburban crowds and chamber of commerce types. But he can still come off at times as a pugilistic troll. He has promised to be "the most conservative Governor in Ohio's history,” defying Ohio’s history of moderate conservatives who have governed the Heartland homebase. He has embraced AI data centers in a state where they are far from popular. And he has not shrunk from Trumpian hardline immigration policies, especially when he appears with Trump.
"As Americans, we believe in merit, that the best person gets the job, regardless of their skin color, that you are judged not on the color of your skin, but on the content of your character and your contributions,” Ramaswamy said during an Oct. 12 rally with Trump in Youngstown, where Acton grew up. “That is who we are as Americans."
Ramaswamy has not developed a thicker skin than when he ran for the White House just two years ago. In July, when confronted by hecklers at Xavier University in Cincinnati, he simply walked off stage: “Peace out, see you guys.”
The polls still show a close-range contest, but in the increasingly nasty ad war, the spending suggests a far more lopsided fight. Ramaswamy and his supporters have now run $101 million in ads against Acton, with $36 million of that coming from Ramaswamy himself.
Acton and groups supporting her have spent about one-third of the Ramaswamy media wave, much of it describing Ramaswamy as a “swindler” who conned his way to a fortune and harnessing anti-billionaire sentiment.
“This is a guy who has been flying around the state on his corporate jet. Ohio is not a huge state geographically. It’s a state that’s incredibly driveable,” says David Cohen, the director of the Applied Politics Program at the University of Akron. “He was the worst possible choice for Republicans, not that they really had a choice.”
A loss for Ramaswamy would be a stunning reversal of fortunes for Ohio Republicans. Once seen as a quintessential swing state, Trump won Ohio during all three of his presidential bids with margins between eight and 11 points.
If Democrats can show a rebound in Ohio, the state may actually wind up back on the must-visit list for 2028 contenders from both parties. After all, states like Georgia and Arizona were also once solidly red until break-out candidates—backed by party spending—upended those assumptions.
“Calm down,” says a consultant who has worked with Ohio candidates in past cycles, when asked about Democrats’ optimism. “It’s still Ohio.”
Ramaswamy’s rise via Trump
For a while there two years ago, Ramaswamy seemed like the most obvious heir to Trumpism. When he launched his presidential bid in 2025, he couched it in effusive praise for the then-former President, to the point that he sometimes sounded like a Trump surrogate in the GOP debates that Trump refused to attend.
After a weak showing in Iowa, Ramaswamy ended his campaign and quickly folded into the broader MAGA-verse. He was chosen by Trump to help Elon Musk upend the federal government at the Department of Government Efficiency, before dropping out of that partnership.
But the talent for going viral that helped Ramaswamy gain a national profile has proved less successful this election cycle in Ohio. Social media videos of him hitting tennis balls and baseballs while listing his policy proposals have provided a font of online mockery. He hastily left Ohio State’s season opener after being booed and heckled. Later, he faced criticism for having worn a knock-off Ohio State jersey to the game.
Ramaswamy has also struggled to navigate his identity as a Hindu and the son of immigrants from India in the modern GOP. In the gubernatorial primary, auto entrepreneur Casey Putsch ignored Trump’s endorsement of Ramaswamy and vied for the nomination, pitching himself as an “America First” alternative to Ramaswamy. In one YouTube spot, Putsch hoisted a rifle and challenged Ramaswamy to a game of “cowboys and Indians.”
While Ramaswamy easily won his party’s nomination, almost one-in-five votes in the primary were for Putsch, a hint that Ramaswamy’s appeal had its limits even within his own party. “One of the storylines here is a man who is Indian American and whose religion is Hindu,” says Christopher Devine, a political science professor at the University of Dayton, says. “There are a lot of members of the Republican base who may have difficulty voting someone of his demographic profile.”
Amid efforts by both campaigns to push policy ideas like tax cuts and education reform, the ad war has boiled down to attacks portraying Ramaswamy as a conman and Acton as a drunk. The latter is based on an August 2019 incident in which police responded to an incident in Acton’s home that Acton has accused Ramaswamy of dramatically mischaracterizing, to the point that she refused to share a debate stage with him. Ramaswamy has also refuted allegations his fortune came from misleading investors.
Devine says the tone of the attacks is a shift from the Senate race, where former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown and current Republican Sen. Jon Husted both have extensive records for each side to focus on. “In the Governor’s race, there’s no record to pick apart. Without much of a track record in politics to run on, they’re focusing on personal attacks against the other,” Devine says.
Ohio polling raises questions
As polling consistently shows an advantage for Acton, Republicans are increasingly arguing that the polls may be wrong by just enough to give Ramaswamy the win. One proof point is 2018, when some polls showed Brown winning re-election by double digits. By the time votes were cast, Brown won by less than seven points
Republicans, heading into a make-or-break stretch of voting, are repeating those statistics to make the case that the polling once again is under-counting Republican voters.
Cohen, the political science professor, doesn’t share that view of skewed polling: “I’m not skeptical at all. All of the polls are trending in the right direction for Acton.”
Democrats, for their part, are viewing the race as a tie, at best. Among their reasons for concern is Ohio’s poor track record when women are on the ballot. The state’s voters have never elected a woman as Governor and rejected both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris as presidential contenders.
Yet given the strong headwinds against Republicans’ national brand, they can’t hide their bullishness toward the races for Governor and Senate, where polls show Brown up over Husted. “I haven’t felt this good, like we have a chance, in a while,” says a second Ohio Democratic strategist. But, he adds, given how tight both races may be, no one should expect an early race call once the polls close.

Mali forces, Russian backers kill scores of civilians in drone strikes, report says

Mali forces, Russian backers kill scores of civilians in drone strikes, report says
DAKAR, Oct 19 - Mali's armed forces and their Russian backers utilized some "apparent indiscriminate" drone strikes and other abuses as part of an ramped-up offensive against insurgents in recent months that has killed scores of civilians, Human Rights Watch said in a report on Monday.
The drone strikes and resulting civilian casualties more than doubled between April and August, compared to the same period a year ago, the report said citing ACLED data, in response to nationwide attacks by the regional al-Qaeda affiliate, known as JNIM, and by Tuareg-led separatists.
The insurgent attacks launched on April 25 killed Mali's defence minister and hit multiple towns and cities as well as the main airport in Bamako, underscoring the government's struggle to improve security in the landlocked West African country.
Mali's military leaders, who seized power in coups in 2020 and 2021, have turned to Russia for support in their fight against insurgents, and they enlisted the Russian paramilitary group Africa Corps in their response to the April attacks.
The data from US-based conflict monitor ACLED showed Malian forces and Africa Corps carried out 47 drone strikes resulting in 94 civilian deaths from April-August, up from 22 strikes resulting in 44 civilian deaths a year earlier.
STRIKES HIT CATTLE MARKET, HEALTH CENTRE, REPORT SAYS
Some of the incidents in the report were "apparent indiscriminate drone strikes," including an August 19 strike on a cattle market in the Bandiagara region of central Mali that killed six men, and a pre-dawn strike on July 29 on a health centre in the northern region of Kidal, near the Algerian border, Human Rights Watch said.
The report also documented abuses that did not involve drones, including an incident on July 12 in the Segou region in which it said soldiers shot and killed five young girls they mistook for attackers.
A Malian army spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Human Rights Watch said it received no response to a letter sent on August 5 to Mali's new defence minister that detailed the group's findings.
Mali has previously denied killing civilians in counterinsurgency operations.
The Russian embassy in Bamako did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Africa Corps's involvement.
The Human Rights Watch report also documented abuses by JNIM and the Tuareg-led separatists, including the execution of 19 soldiers in the northern Gao region in July.
JNIM's Sharia Committee told HRW that the killings "did in fact take place" but denied ordering them and said "it is not our policy to do such things".
The Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front denied executing soldiers. REUTERS

World faces nature reality check at UN biodiversity conference
- World leaders meet at COP17 in Armenia to review the Kunming-Montreal biodiversity plan. Countries are off track on 22 of 23 goals, though 27.5% land protection may be reached by 2030.
- Talks are stalled over funding, including how to raise US$30 billion (S$38.39 billion) in public finance and US$200 billion a year by 2030. A draft UN report says 144 countries have made action plans.
- A major focus is reforming US$500 billion in harmful subsidies and boosting private sector support through the Cali Fund. Businesses say clearer rules could improve investment and help stop species loss.
AI generated
LONDON – World leaders, diplomats and nature experts gather in Armenia this week to assess lagging efforts to halt biodiversity loss, with countries off track on most global targets and divisions over funding still unresolved.
The 17th United Nations Conference of the Parties, dubbed COP17, is the first major review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the landmark 2022 agreement that aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
The climate-focused COP31 begins on Nov 9 in Antalya, Turkey.
While the world is likely to reach an estimated 27.5% of land protection by 2030, scientists say many of the broader goals needed to halt biodiversity loss remain well off track.
From pesticide use to unsustainable fishing and subsidies for a host of damaging activities, the deterioration of ecosystems threatens food production, water security and economic stability across the planet.
Countries are not on track to meet 22 of the 23 goals set out in the Kunming-Montreal framework, a draft UN report showed.
While the UN says that 144 countries including Brazil and China have so far created action plans, who pays and how much towards a US$30 billion (S$38.4 billion) public finance goal is less clear and will be central to two weeks of talks in Armenia’s capital Yerevan.
The broader goal is to mobilise at least US$200 billion annually by 2030.
Subsidy reform
Another major focus is reforming US$500 billion a year of subsidies for activities that damage nature, with governments urged to set a two-year timeline to identify and redirect the most damaging ones.
That could, for example, include those that encourage farmers to cut down rainforest or the offer of state discounts on synthetic fertilisers and chemical pesticides which damage soil and water.
Doing so would help governments address nature loss and related issues like food and energy security without committing more public money at a time of war, energy crises and other inflationary pressures.
“This isn’t primarily a story about conservation,” said Eva Zabey, chief executive of the non-profit Business for Nature, at a media briefing.
“It’s an economic, fiscal, political and competitiveness story, which is grounded in resilience and resource security.”
More than 130 businesses including retailer H&M and consumer goods company Nestle issued an open letter ahead of the talks urging governments to set clearer policies and a plan to reform incentives over the next 12 months, arguing that it would help make it more attractive to invest.
Subsidies ultimately cost governments between US$11 trillion and US$24.7 trillion a year, non-profit Conservation International estimates, as they often pay twice – once for the subsidies and again to patch up the damage that follows, including cleaning up pollution, treating illness and repairing infrastructure.
Bigger role for private sector
With public money tight, many are looking to the private sector to play a bigger role, including through the Cali Fund.
That fund was set up in 2025 to get companies which rely on digital databases of biological samples for their products, such as in the pharmaceutical, cosmetic and commercial agriculture industries, to help pay to preserve nature.
Details still to be ironed out include how funds should be shared between countries and indigenous communities, and whether companies should contribute based on total revenue when only part of their business relies on these genetic resources.
For Cristian Samper, managing director and leader of Nature Solutions at the Bezos Earth Fund, the talks are also an opportunity for governments to do more to halt the extinction of species.
“We know recovery is possible. The decisions we make in Armenia should give more conservation teams the backing to make it happen,” he said. REUTERS
