Zelenskiy says Ukraine got no warning as Russian missiles rain in
KYIV, Oct 19 - Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed.
Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones in attacks stretching from Kharkiv and Dnipro in the east to Odesa in the south and Volyn and Rivne in the west.
The strikes killed two people in Kyiv and the nearby region and two more people in the industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, officials said.
Tensions are running high between Zelenskiy and President Donald Trump's administration over US support for Ukraine and Washington's approach to Russia.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app.
"When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners."
Zelenskiy said that the United States had slowed some vital supplies for Ukraine, adding that the delays were at the US Defense Department level. He provided no other details. Kyiv has previously said it has struggled to get interceptors critical to repelling Russian missile attacks.
For several months, Ukraine has suffered from critical shortages of US-made Patriot missiles.
Zelenskiy said that some political agreements on air defence were not implemented at a working level.
Throughout the nearly five-year war, Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to detect Russian ballistic missile launches and provide early warning of incoming strikes.
Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian air force, said Kyiv received no warning ahead of the first ballistic missile strike overnight but did receive information ahead of a second attack.
"For some reason, no information was received the first time, a matter our experts are investigating together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred," Ihnat told Ukrainian television.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the United States had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
ROLLING BLACKOUTS
Ukrainian air defences downed 247 targets - four cruise missiles and 243 drones, the air force said.
Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces carried out a "massive strike" using precision weapons and attack drones against Ukrainian defence industry facilities, drone and cruise missile storage sites, and a data centre.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said the energy sector was the main target of the attacks, with damage reported across the country. Ukraine's energy ministry said rolling blackouts were introduced for households and businesses as crews worked to restore supplies.
Koretskyi said Russia has hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure more than 2,000 times since mid-July, intensifying its attacks from previous years of the war.
Railway and metro stations, pharmaceutical warehouses, commercial properties and residential buildings were also damaged, Koretskyi said. Ukrainian businesses have already lost $7.7 billion due to wartime damage so far this year, he said.
"The aim is obvious — to wear people down," Koretskyi said. REUTERS

US warns EU of 'devastating' retaliation over satellite spectrum plan

The United States Ambassador to the European Union has warned that European firms could face "devastating" commercial retaliation in the US market if the bloc moves forward with plans to reserve key satellite-to-smartphone spectrum bands for EU operators, potentially curbing access for American companies such as SpaceX and Amazon.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Sunday, Ambassador Andrew Puzder warned that European enterprises "should be wary" of potential countermeasures, cautioning that the fallout could prove "very devastating" given the sheer scale of the American market.
The regulatory dispute centres on a European Commission proposal to ring-fence portions of the radio spectrum utilised by mobile devices to connect directly with orbiting satellites exclusively for European providers.
The measure would directly limit market entry for overseas companies, including Elon Musk's SpaceX, which operates the Starlink constellation.
SpaceX has criticised the planned restrictions, warning they could undermine connectivity in Ukraine, where Starlink provides critical communication infrastructure for civilian and military operations.
Technology rivalry
Puzder acknowledged Europe's sovereign right to shield sensitive government data but insisted that regulation must not serve as a tool to handicap American industry.
"If the purpose is to make the United States less competitive, I think that that's not a legitimate goal of this kind of legislation," Puzder stated.
"You don't make European companies more competitive by making US companies less competitive."
The ambassador also questioned the European Commission's enforcement of its Digital Markets Act, querying whether regulatory penalties are genuinely designed to foster fair competition or simply generate state revenue from US tech firms.
Puzder urged Brussels and Washington to align their strategies rather than engage in regulatory disputes, pointing to mounting global competition from China in artificial intelligence and quantum computing.
"It'd be a lot easier if we were working with Europe instead of fighting Europe," he said.

Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case amid widening regional outbreak
Kenyan health authorities say latest patient was likely exposed to the country’s first Ebola case.
Kenyan health authorities say an eighth Ebola case has been detected in the East African nation.
Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth told Kenya’s Citizen TV that of the 38 people tested on Sunday, one had returned a positive result.
“He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain,” he said.
Amoth said the man, who worked as a patient attendant cleaning utensils and linens, was likely exposed to Kenya’s first Ebola case, discovered earlier this month.
He developed symptoms on Saturday, was quarantined and tested for the virus, a Ministry of Health source said.
The ministry reported four new cases on Saturday, three of whom were health workers who treated the country’s first Ebola patient, a man who travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to Nairobi and died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
In a post on X, the ministry said the fourth person was related to the deceased patient.
Kenya has been on heightened alert, as the Ebola outbreak has spilled across the border from the DRC. The current outbreak is of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no vaccine or specific treatment.
The DRC has recorded at least 9,400 cases, including more than 4,500 deaths, in the deadliest outbreak in the country’s history, which started in May.
Ituri province in eastern DRC remains the disease’s epicentre, accounting for almost three quarters of confirmed cases, according to the government’s most recent data. It announced on Sunday that the virus has reached an eighth province, North Ubangi.
State-run news agency ACP reported on Sunday that authorities in North Kivu province, where the World Health Organization said substantial transmission continues, are introducing a one-week ban from Monday on people entering the province from Ituri in an effort to slow the spread.
Other measures set to be introduced include restrictions on passenger numbers in cars and on motorbikes and suspension of large public gatherings.
Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases, including 15 imported from the DRC, and two deaths, before it was declared Ebola-free in August.

Meta says Claude AI tool triggered No Kings Instagram suspension
- Meta said an automated security system wrongly suspended the No Kings Coalition’s Instagram account after Claude AI tool activity looked like bot traffic during a major protest push.
- The account was down for about 90 minutes on Oct 17, and full access returned at 5.33pm New York time, though organisers said they were still locked out for longer.
- No Kings criticised Meta for disrupting its election turnout work, while Meta apologised and said the error came from “high-volume” requests that triggered its systems.
AI generated
Meta Platforms said an automated security system mistakenly suspended the Instagram account of the No Kings Coalition at the height of a nationwide series of demonstrations.
The technology company offered an apology and a more detailed explanation for the disruption, which came during the group’s early-voting push ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Instagram’s engineering team found that the accounts’ “reading” activity triggered the security system. A tool from Anthropic PBC’s Claude was accessing profiles, posts and hashtags at roughly four times the normal rate in intense bursts on Oct 17, Meta’s vice-president of communications Andy Stone wrote in a social media post on Oct 18.
“These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems,” Stone said.
Meta said an automated review about an hour later determined the account should not have been removed and restored it, though it took longer to return administrative access.
“We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error,” Stone said.
The No Kings Coalition, an anti-Trump group, said on Oct 17 that its Instagram page was unavailable for about 90 minutes and that organisers remained locked out of the account even after it became publicly visible again.
Full access was restored at 5.33pm New York time on Oct 17 (5.33am Singapore time on Oct 18), according to the coalition.
Organisers criticised Meta for restricting the account during the demonstrations, saying Instagram was a crucial platform for communicating with supporters.
The coalition said millions of people participated in nearly 3,000 events in all 50 states and Washington in an effort to expand early vote access and defend election integrity.
Stone’s statement on Oct 18 did not specify which Claude tool was involved, who was operating it or what activity it had been carrying out in connection with the account. No Kings did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The explanation clarified Meta’s initial account of the incident. Stone said on Oct 17 that unusually high rates of posting, sharing or commenting had triggered the company’s automated systems and that such activity had caused the No Kings account to be suspended. He called the action “clearly” an error.
No Kings, which has organised several anti-Trump protests since he was inaugurated, said it plans a national organising call on Oct 21 focused on turnout ahead of Election Day. BLOOMBERG

It is said that often truth is the first casualty of war. This is increasingly becoming true of political contests as well, where post-truth politics is emerging as an important dimension of public discourse.In the post-truth scenario, false propaganda, distorted narratives, and emotional appeals devoid of logic often take precedence over objective facts and verifiable evidence. And, reasoned debate gives way to demagoguery.
Once largely a subject of academic debates, post-truth has now become a feature of everyday politics. Misinformation campaigns designed to gaslight are increasingly used to not only sway public opinion but also discredit democratic institutions.Allegations are repeated and amplified even when the evidence to substantiate them is conspicuously absent. In this, truth seems to be not merely the first casualty, but it risks becoming the final casualty as well.India’s political discourse is not immune to this post-truth phenomenon. Increasingly, sections of the opposition parties appear to be manufacturing outrage, peddling propaganda and weaponising misinformation to spread anarchy, placing avaricious political goals above national interests.
The article does not aim a jeremiad against the opposition nor a claim that constitutional institutions are beyond criticism. Dissent is the lifeblood of democracy. What it is not is a licence to peddle falsehoods. Disagreement is necessary for better policymaking. What it is not is a pass for vindictive and sustained assault on public trust through allegations that crumble under factual scrutiny.The purpose, therefore, is to challenge these falsehoods and restore public trust in constitutional institutions, which has been eroded by the cynical politics of manufactured distrust.This becomes particularly significant when we examine how electoral institutions and processes have been attacked by certain sections of opposition to hide the fact that people are rejecting them again and again.Three issues, in particular, stand out: the recurring allegations of manipulation of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), the controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and unscrupulous attempts to discredit the Election Commission of India (ECI).First things first, EVMs have repeatedly been subjected to allegations of manipulation by the opposition. The Supreme Court has examined such challenges on multiple occasions. Finally, in 2024, in its ‘Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India’, the Supreme Court put to rest all doubts and rejected demands for a return to paper ballots. The Supreme Court observed that repeated challenges based on suspicion and doubt, without cogent material or data, were “execrable and undesirable”. But this could not stop the opposition from repeating the same lies again and again.The controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls is another example of how a legally right and administratively justified exercise has been impugned for narrow political interests by some in this post-truth era.In 2025, the Supreme Court in its ‘Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India’ judgment, affirmed that the integrity of electoral rolls is foundational to free and fair elections. It described the objective of ensuring the “accuracy, completeness, and integrity of the electoral roll” as “not only legitimate but is integral to the constitutional mandate” entrusted to the Commission.The Court also found that the reasons advanced for the revision bore a “direct and rational nexus” to maintaining a credible electoral process. These observations reinforced a fundamental principle: protecting the right to vote requires not only safeguarding every eligible voter, but also ensuring that electoral rolls remain accurate, complete and reliable.Beyond EVMs and SIR, a sustained campaign has been run to discredit the office of the Chief Election Commissioner, and by extension the institution of the Election Commission of India (ECI).For nearly seven decades, Congress governments retained executive control over the appointment of Chief Election Commissioner. Our government changed this by institutionalising the appointment process through a multi-member Selection Committee that includes the Leader of the Opposition.The record of Congress has been far from inspiring when it comes to respecting the independence of other constitutional institutions as well.In 1951, the then government introduced the First Constitutional Amendment to reverse Supreme Court judgment and curtailed freedom of speech and expression.During the Emergency, constitutional amendments were weaponised to serve the interests of the government. The amendments made the proclamation of Emergency non-justiciable and placed the Prime Minister’s election beyond judicial scrutiny. It also granted sweeping immunity to high constitutional functionaries and curtailed judicial review. The amendment power was turned from an instrument of constitutional reform into a tool for executive aggrandisement.Not only institutions were trampled but human rights of citizens were also violated. Attorney General Niren De, representing the then Union Government, argued in the Supreme Court that even if an innocent person was killed by a police officer acting out of personal enmity, the victim’s family could not seek judicial relief.Now, compare this with how the Constitution has been honoured in the last 12 years under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, passed by a special majority of Parliament, was struck down by the Supreme Court. The verdict was not only respected, but no attempt was made to overturn it through backdoor legislation. This respect for the Constitution and its principles has also guided our approach to some of the most consequential issues facing the nation.The construction of the Ram Mandir began only after the Supreme Court’s judgment. When Article 370 was abrogated and the Supreme Court upheld the decision, many in the opposition still disagreed with the judgment.Even legislative processes and offices have not been spared by the Congress. A no-confidence motion was moved against the Lok Sabha Speaker when he simply asked the Leader of opposition to follow the rules.Post-truth politics has also extended to matters of national security. In 2019, the Congress leader wrongly attributed a slogan to the Supreme Court’s Rafale judgment and later tendered an unconditional apology in contempt proceedings. In August 2025, the Supreme Court again questioned the basis of claims made by Rahul Gandhi regarding the occupation of Indian territory, asking what credible evidence supported them.Respecting differences of opinion has always been an integral part of our democratic ethos. When people raised concerns over the three farm laws passed by Parliament, we not only listened to those concerns but also repealed the laws in the larger public interest.In a democracy, one is free to disagree with a decision. But such disagreements cannot be founded on falsehoods, nor can their purpose be to create disorder and anarchy. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, in his famous speech in the Constituent Assembly, often referred to as the “Grammar of Anarchy,” warned against the dangers of resorting to unconstitutional methods.His message remains profoundly relevant today. Opposition leaders would do well to read this historic speech and understand the crucial distinction between dissent and anarchy in a democracy.
We believe that the foundation of a vibrant democracy lies not merely in political equality, but also in economic and social justice. This principle underpins the decisions taken by our government.At the same time, for a stable and mature democracy it is important that dissent and concerns be expressed through legitimate and democratic channels, and resolved through dialogue and mutual understanding rather than by resorting to disorder.The need of the hour is to ensure that neither our democratic institutions nor India’s rise are held hostage to the frustration arising from political defeats. And, at no cost will the nation's progress be allowed to be undermined by those who would rather discredit the system than confront the reasons for their own setbacks.Rajnath Singh is the minister of defence, Government of India.

====================================================================================================

What It Took to Deliver a Legendary F-117A Stealth Aircraft to the Smithsonian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
00:58:33 UTC
09:58:33 KST

EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Ca.—The flat-black fuselage rolled forward on its landing gear, pulled from its hanger at Lockheed Martin’s secretive Skunk Works compound by an aircraft tug.
More than a mile away, a giant C-5M Super Galaxy waited, its nose cone open and waiting for its unique cargo. Against a desert backdrop, the dramatic angles of the wingless airframe cut an unmistakable silhouette, a shining example of America’s first stealth aircraft, this one dubbed “the Overachiever” because it was the only Nighthawk to fly in all four major conflicts in which the jets participated.
More than 40 years after the original YF-117 operational prototype flew test runs from the shadowy Lockheed facility, the Overachiever returned to its Palmdale birthplace for a $1 million refurbishment to look its best when it assumes its place in history alongside other iconic aircraft on permanent exhibit at the National Air and Space Museum’s Stephen F. Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Va., beside Washington Dulles International Airport.
Air & Space Forces Magazine was on hand to witness the F-117’s 2,254-mile journey across the United States as a passenger aboard the C-5M from Air Force Reserve Command’s 512th Airlift Wing.
Conceived to give the Air Force an edge against the Soviet Union in the 1970s, the radar-evading F-117 was developed to sneak past the Russian-made, radar-guided antiaircraft missiles that had so vexed the U.S. Air Force in Vietnam.
The aircraft’s faceted exterior design radically reduced the F-117’s radar cross section, allowing it to evade radar detection during testing. While their first use in combat, in 1989’s Operation Just Cause in Panama, had been a disappointment, the Nighthawks’ performance in Operation Desert Storm proved stunning: On Jan. 17, 1991, the Nighthawks flew unobserved into heavily defended Iraqi airspace and destroyed their targets to mark the opening salvo of the Gulf War.
“This aircraft was specifically designed to be able to penetrate heavily defended areas that have radar-based defenses … which gave it a huge tactical advantage on the battlefield,” Michael Hankins, curator of modern military aviation at the Udvar-Hazy Center, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “This will be the [museum’s] first example of the earliest generation of stealth aircraft. A lot of new aircraft that are in service today—like the F-22 Raptor, the F-35 lightning—really built on the foundation that was set by the F-117.”
The Air Force officially retired its F-117 fleet in 2008 after the F-22 Raptor achieved initial operating capability in 2005. But Nighthawks remained in “flyable storage,”and since around 2020 have participated in exercises such as Red Flag and in undisclosed activities.
Securing The Overachiever for the Air and Space Museum was the result of months of coordination between the Air Force, the Smithsonian, and Lockheed. Jeffrey Corbets, who oversaw the plane’s restoration at the Skunk Works Special Systems department, said preparing Tail No. 818 to become a museum showpiece required months of tedious restoration work by a dedicated team of more than a dozen Skunk Works employees.
The specialists who did the work aren’t standard-issue aircraft technicians. “They’re kind of different people,” Corbets said. “The team that’s actually working the bulk of this also supports our U-2 program, so they’re really familiar with supporting some of our longer-term, historical legacy products.”
Because of its highly classified status, the F-117 could not fly into Dulles and taxi over to the Udvar-Hazy Center as some other historical aircraft have done. It had to be completely de-militarized, which involved stripping away its most guarded secrets, Corbets said. From late January to early August, the Skunk Works team bead-blasted off the jet’s radar absorbing coating, known as RAM, leaving bare metal. The unique edges on the wings and rudders were replaced with “all new fake edges,” Corbets added.
“It’s a lot of manual labor,” he explained. “The first thing you have to do is actually get access to all the connectors, the bolts, and whatnot that hold edges on” These were hidden beneath the stealth coating. “You have to very carefully dig out the RAM, so you can get to those to take them off. And then once you have all the edges removed, then we can actually go into a bead blasting type operation to get the rest of the coatings off.”
The de-mil process also involved removing classified technical “components” in the cockpit, said Corbets, who would not elaborate on the systems that were removed.
“The cockpit is mostly intact, so they have, I’d say, 95 percent of the avionics are still in there—the screens and the displays are still in there, the hub system is still in there, the ejection seat, etc., etc. To even the educated observer, it would look like an operational F-117,” Corbets said. “The museum wanted it to be as representative a configuration as we could leave it, so if it didn’t absolutely have to come out, we didn’t take it out.”
Other F-117s are already in museums, including at the Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. Lockheed’s Skunk Works performed a similar job in 2019 so a Nighthawk could go on display at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum in Simi Valley, Calif.
To fit the Nighthawk into the C-5 transport, the F-117’s wings had to be removed, secured to wheeled dollies and loaded separately onto the aircraft. Air Force loadmasters used an electric winch and cable to gently pull each dolly onto the ramp and back to the rear of the plane. Airmen completed the slow, tedious task in the desert heat without incident.
But loading The Overachiever’s freshly painted fuselage onto the plane, so it could be safely secured for flight, was not without surprises. The wings and fuselage together weighed about 24,000 pounds, an easy lift for the C-5, which has a maximum cargo capacity of 285,000 pounds—enough to carry not just one, but two M1A2 Abrams tanks.
But there’s more to moving a disabled plane than weight. A miscommunication during the restoration process meant the aircraft lacked the proper amount of bolt-on anchoring points when it was time to tie it down in the cargo bay. That meant special anchoring collars had to be attached to each of the three landing gear struts to keep the jet from shifting during flight.
“We decided to use the collars that we use on the struts to help secure it down, but in order for that to work, we had to raise the struts so we get the right angle to use the collar,” a maintenance technician said. Getting clearance to make raise each strut roughly four inches and mount the collars took time.
Air Force Reserve Senior Master Sgt. Vasean Townsend, a C-5 loadmaster for the past 13 years, said it was nothing he hadn’t seen before.
“Basically, one of the tie-down points was missing on each side,” said Townsend, who helped transport another F-117 some years earlier. “We as loadmasters have to find a way to create other tie-down points. “If something is missing … we’ve just got to be creative. That’s part of the job.”
With the problem solved, Lockheed staff and aircrew silently watched as The Overachiever was lashed down for its flight to Dulles.
For C-5 pilot Maj. Dean Mouritzen, the mission was “humbling.”
“This is my last flight in the military,” he said. “It’s my last mission, and doing something this—taking an F-117 to a museum and being able to tell my kids, my grandkids, that I was just one of the peons to take it some place where it’s going to sit forever—it’s pretty awesome.”
To Corbets and the Lockheed team, “it’s a little bit like watching a friend leave you, because obviously everyone’s been really excited to be part of the project, and now it’s going off to its new home.”
After hours in the air, the C-5 landed at Dulles and finally lowered its ramp at 8:38 p.m. local time, and the crew quickly offloaded The Overachiever’s fuselage and wings onto the chilly ramp by 9:16 p.m. From there, museum officials whisked it away to the nearby Mary Baker Engen Restoration Hangar, where it will be reassembled before going on exhibit.
The Overachiever was scheduled to be unveiled for public viewing at the Udvar-Hazy Center late this month.
“The current plan is to have this airplane on the floor next to all the other aircraft in our Cold War modern military section,” Hankins said. “It’ll be right next to the F-15 Eagle, which it flew with during Operation Desert Storm. There’s a lot of a lot of historical significance there to having those two together on the floor.”
“This is a really big step and a very historic and important aircraft in the history of U.S. aviation,” said Hankins, who said he had been working on the project for “several years.”
“We’re so excited to have this on the floor,” he said, “and be able to show the public why this airplane is so unique and special and important and iconic.”
Shaun Barrows, senior multimedia manager at Air & Space Forces Association, contributed to this story.

Kinship and surveillance: The return of Somali piracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
00:56:17 UTC
09:56:17 KST

Kinship and surveillance: The return of Somali piracy
Somalia’s piracy crackdown leaves coastal fishermen struggling to survive.
Mogadishu, Somalia – The fishing town of Bander Beyla, on Somalia’s Puntland coast, has become a focal point of the renewed piracy crisis. But beyond the hijackings and international security operations, residents are struggling to protect their livelihoods as fishing restrictions, arrests and surveillance reshape daily life.
Abdifatah Mohamed has spent 20 years fishing off Somalia’s coast. He began at 15, but says declining catches and foreign trawlers have made it increasingly difficult to support his family.
“I don’t catch as much fish anymore, and the prospects for catching lobsters have become rare,” the 35-year-old said.
“Foreign trawlers are emptying out the seas,” he added.
Somalia’s central government collapsed in 1991, weakening maritime oversight and leaving its waters vulnerable to illegal fishing. Some fishermen, angered by foreign vessels exploiting the country’s resources, have turned to piracy.
“We’re [fishermen] no match for the foreign trawlers, who possess capabilities far greater than us, which impacts the livelihoods of our families on land,” Mohamed said.
He added, “Some from our community have taken up arms at sea, but deep down I know it’s hurting our community.”
A community caught in the crackdown
Piracy has surged off Somalia since late April 2026. The reported number of hijackings varies according to whether counts include commercial ships, fishing vessels and dhows. Several seized vessels have been held near Bander Beyla, bringing the crisis close to the town’s fishing community.
In late August, local authorities restricted fishermen from going to sea amid concerns that pirates were disguising themselves as fishermen.
“The local authorities gave an order the last week of August preventing us from going out at sea, which would remain in effect for two months,” Mohamed said.
“Our families depend on what we catch at sea. Even though our catches [of fish] have gone down in recent years, it helped provide for our families at home. But it’s like we were being punished for crimes we have nothing to do with, and our families have suffered for it.”
For fishermen, Mohamed said, going to sea has become a risk whether they obey the restrictions or defy them.
“It’s a two-way risk, because if the authorities know you went out to sea, they could accuse you of piracy or even transporting supplies to the ships that were hijacked,” he noted.
“While out at sea, you could face arrest or violence from international navies, and get mistaken for pirates, and taken away to a jail in a foreign land. It’s happened to a lot of men from this town.”
Abdirizak Said, who has fished in Bander Beyla for 15 years, said the crackdown has deepened the hardship faced by residents.
“Dozens have been arrested, most of them after they brought food or khat to the pirates, when the ships were anchored near Bander Bayla,” he said.
“Businesses and stores were even ordered by the [local] government not to sell anything to pirates, and if they do, they’ll be viewed as pirates themselves.”
The networks behind piracy
Some of the people involved in the hijackings come from the same town now bearing the consequences.
“Some of the pirates involved in the hijackings are from Bander Bayla and hail from this community,” Said added.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said that piracy cannot be understood solely as a criminal activity at sea. It also depends on networks on land that can provide money, equipment, manpower and protection.
“Kinship networks can effectively function as a form of financial and social infrastructure, and for piracy, this is no different,” he said. “Pirate groups have historically been able to mobilise credit, and get equipment, manpower and protection.”
“In other words, clan relationships can underwrite the practical resources and act of mobilising that make piracy possible. This is precisely why effective counter piracy requires understanding the land-based networks that make those operations possible,” Norman added.
These networks also help explain why efforts to disrupt piracy reach into ordinary commercial life. Said noted that the consequences extend beyond fishing: boats carrying supplies from Yemen to Somalia have stopped arriving, for instance.
“The boats that used to bring supplies from Yemen have also ceased, because of these [pirate] attacks,” he said.
Residents push back
Despite the disruption, Mohamed said that some residents have tried to prevent young men from joining the attacks.
“Recently there was an attempt by local youth with guns trying to go out at sea, but the residents told them not to do it and that they would be harming their community even more,” Mohamed said.
“It was civilians that took the initiative to stop them and not the government because it’s the civilians in this town that will suffer the blowback if they launch attacks from here,” he added.
Two local government officials, speaking anonymously because they were not authorised to talk to the press, confirmed that restrictions had been imposed to weaken the local support networks supplying pirates.
“The security restrictions were lifted on October 1 after successful anti-piracy operations led to the release of three ships,” the first local official said.
The International Maritime Organization confirmed on October 2 that three hijacked vessels, Honour 25, Seamull (also known as Sibu 1) and Eureka, had been freed. It said 44 seafarers were released and reported that five crew members died during the rescue operation involving Honour 25.
The lifting of restrictions has not ended the visible security presence around Bander Beyla, according to the officials.
“Military helicopters flying inland from the sea routinely hover over the town, and these flyovers are more frequent in the nearby remote coastal areas,” one local government official added.
“They’re looking for any movements of armed individuals on the coast,” a second local government official said.
Both officials said the helicopters belonged to the European Union Naval Force, which has conducted counter-piracy operations in the region for years.
Security forces stretched thin
The renewed attacks have emerged amid wider regional instability and competing demands on maritime security forces. Abdinur Abdella, a Somali political and security analyst, said international naval attention shifted after Houthi attacks began in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in late 2023.
“When Houthis began carrying out attacks in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in late 2023 in response to the conflict in Gaza, it saw international navies change their focus and efforts to the Houthi threat, which allowed armed groups active on the Somali coast to take advantage of the lax in security,” Abdella said.
Norman said Puntland’s maritime forces have also been diverted by other security challenges.
“The PMPF [Puntland Maritime Police Force] has been stretched thin by its fight against ISIS in the Al-Miskad mountains. It also lost some personnel to the 2023 anti-Somaliland rebellion in Las Anod,” he told Al Jazeera. “Some Dhulbahante fighters from Puntland’s forces, including the PMPF, joined the uprising, which wrested roughly a third of Somaliland’s claimed territory from its control.”
“Again, this links back to the clan dimension, and the strength of kinship ties and obligations as essential to understanding contemporary piracy networks and counter piracy initiatives,” Norman added.
For residents of Bander Beyla, these overlapping security pressures are not abstract geopolitical developments. They determine whether fishermen can work, whether supplies arrive and whether people risk being mistaken for pirates.
Said noted that the presence of aircraft remains a reminder that even after restrictions were lifted, fishermen are still being watched.
“We can hear the sound of aircraft and the louder it gets, the closer they are, so we know they’re watching,” he said. “I just want to make a living without worrying whether I’ll make it back to shore safely.”

Deepavali vs Diwali Sparks New Political Row in Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
00:56:00 UTC
09:56:00 KST

In India, religious sentiment has become such a fragile commodity that it can be hurt by almost anything: a joke, a film song, a movie title, or even a slogan printed on a T-shirt.
Far from India, a slight change in spelling and pronunciation has sparked a political maelstrom. In Malaysia, the Hindu festival of lights is celebrated as a public holiday. This time a controversy erupted because the traditional terminology, “Deepavali,” was not used in public greetings.
After Kuala Lumpur City Hall erected festive arches wishing the public a “Happy Diwali,” M. Saravanan, deputy president of the Malaysian Indian Congress (MIC), accused the authorities of erasing the traditional terminology. For him, the change in spelling has become a question of cultural identity and religious sentiment.
Saravanan subsequently wrote to Hannah Yeoh, minister in the Prime Minister’s Department responsible for Federal Territories, asking her to restore the legally gazetted name. He said that the choice of name was not merely a matter of semantics but one of respect for the linguistic and cultural heritage of Malaysian Hindus.
Saravanan’s objection is linked to the fact that he, like the majority of Malaysian Hindus, traces his ancestry to southern India, particularly Tamil Nadu. He says the term “Diwali” is typically associated with North India, while most southern states in India continue to use “Deepavali.”
The controversy highlights the apprehension that minorities face in any country, where tinkering with religious or cultural symbols can be seen as an attempt to dilute their identity, particularly given Malaysia’s history of ethnic tensions.
However, there is a political dimension to this debate. Critics see Saravanan’s objection as an attempt to bring back MIC in political discourse, as the party, after being drubbed in the 2018 general election, lost the sobriquet of sole representative of the country’s 2 million Hindus. Even the party’s supreme leader Samy Vellu could not retain his parliamentary seat, which he had held since 1974.
The historic 2018 election completely reshaped the political landscape. For the first time, Indian voters moved away from the MIC, in favor of Pakatan Harapan and its two main parties, the Democratic Action Party and People’s Justice Party.
Critics and political commentators argue that the MIC’s focus on semantic issues is a calculated effort to regain its relevance amid its declining influence in Malaysian politics. The “Deepavali versus Diwali” debate may generate headlines, they say, adding that the party needs to address deeper socioeconomic challenges, such as the forced relocation of Hindu temples and the long-standing economic disparities facing Malaysian Indians.

Millions risk fines as key tax deadline nears. Here's what to do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
00:48:44 UTC
09:48:44 KST

Time is running out for millions of Australians yet to lodge their 2025-26 tax return.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has already received 9 million income tax returns, but it says around 2 million people are yet to submit theirs ahead of the deadline, with late lodgers potentially facing fines.
When is the 2026 tax return deadline?
This year's deadline is Monday 2 November.
The last day of October is traditionally the due date for self-prepared tax returns, but when the 31st falls on a Saturday, the deadline moves to the next business day.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
If you are using a tax agent to file your return, the ATO says you must be on their books by 31 October.
ATO assistant commissioner Anita Challen warns taxpayers using this option should also ensure their tax profession is registered with the Tax Practitioners Board.
"Taxpayers should be sceptical of anyone making promises that sound too good to be true," she said.
"No reputable tax professional will encourage you to inflate your deductions, guarantee a refund amount, or claim they can fast-track ATO processing."
What happens if you lodge your tax return late?
If you fail to lodge your return before the due date, the ATO will first try to warn you over the phone or in writing before issuing a penalty.
For taxpayers struggling to file on time or experiencing extenuating circumstances, the ATO says to call and talk to an ATO officer who may be able to offer additional support, including extra time to lodge or pay.
If you are given a fine, you'll receive a notice in writing with the amount and the due date for payment. The payment will be due at least 14 days after the notice is given.
How much is the ATO late lodgement fine?
The fine is calculated based on one penalty unit for every 28 days (or part of that period) that the document is overdue. The maximum for an individual is five penalty units.
A penalty unit for a federal organisation like the ATO is currently valued at $364. So, an individual may be fined up to $1,820.
The range is multiplied for medium and larger entities.

The talks would not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, an unprecedented move which would be expected to alarm many European countries, WSJ wrote.
According to the report, the Kremlin suggested the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which takes place Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, southern China.
Putin first suggested the meeting while speaking to Trump on October 9, in the same conversation in which the two leaders agreed that the US would buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale, a former Russian intelligence officer told WSJ.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions over a potential meeting were ongoing.
“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told WSJ.
A senior US official told WSJ that Trump hadn't agreed to the meeting but may be receptive to the idea due to his desire to end the war.
Trump, Zelensky clash over Ukrainian attacks, US sanctions
This comes as Trump and Zelensky publicly criticize the other's decisions, with Zelensky saying on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, and Trump suggesting that Ukraine needs a new president.
Trump claimed that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," in a post on Truth Social earlier on Sunday, calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
Neither the White House nor the Chinese Embassy in Washington has commented on the report, but analysts told WSJ that a meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could advance Xi's ambitions for China's place in global diplomacy.
“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the US and Russia,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank, told WSJ.
However, Chinese officials have expressed concern that the meeting could overshadow China's role in the region at APEC, according to the report.
People familiar with the discussions told WSJ that Xi is also trying to balance support for Putin and economic ties with Europe. A meeting with Putin and Trump to discuss Ukraine could raise the risk of European backlash.

A wave of unrest that erupted across France over the weekend was accompanied by antisemitic incitement and conspiracy theories on X/Twitter, accusing Israel, Mossad, and Jews of responsibility for the violence and destruction in the streets, according to a report published Sunday by the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM).
The study, conducted by CAM's Antisemitism Research Center (ARC), examined activity on X between October 16 and 18 and identified 1,384 posts linking the riots to Jews or Israel. According to the organization, the posts included conspiracy theories alongside calls for physical violence, expulsion, and extermination.
Antisemitic conspiracy theories blame Israel and Mossad for France riots
According to the findings, influential social media accounts spread claims that "Mossad is burning France right now" and described the unrest as a "civil war orchestrated by Jewish elites."
Other accounts linked French President Emmanuel Macron to the Rothschild family, while far-right activists with hundreds of thousands of followers circulated the message: "The Jews did this to France. Don't let them do it to America."
CAM said this was the fourth time in less than three months that its research center had identified a similar pattern of antisemitic conspiracy theories spreading in response to major news events. The report cited the migrant crisis in Ceuta, the anniversary of the September 11 attacks, and an attempted hijacking of a plane bound for Ben-Gurion Airport.
Verified X accounts accused of amplifying antisemitic incitement
The study also found that accounts subscribed to X Premium, identified by blue verification checkmarks, were among those spreading some of the most extreme messages.
According to CAM, the content received millions of views, with the organization arguing that the platform's amplification mechanisms helped spread the messages.
CAM CEO Sacha Roytman warned of the connection between online incitement and violence in public spaces.
"Once again, we are witnessing the same distorted pattern in which hatred of Jews and Israel becomes the automatic explanation for every national crisis," Roytman said. "Worse still, social media platforms are incentivizing those who spread hatred instead of stopping them."
CAM calls on French authorities and social media platforms to act
Roytman called on French authorities and social media companies to take action against violence and incitement.
"French law enforcement authorities must take firm action against the rioters, and platform executives must put an end to this lawlessness before lives are lost," he said.
The Combat Antisemitism Movement is an international, nonpartisan coalition dedicated to combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish communities. Its work includes researching and monitoring antisemitic content online, conducting public awareness campaigns, and promoting policy initiatives with governments and international institutions.

====================================================================================================

Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
00:32:07 UTC
09:32:07 KST

Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oslo
- Summary:
- Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders.
- Share:
What if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago? A new scientific analysis suggests that some of his ideas about the mind share surprising similarities with one of the most influential theories in modern neuroscience.
Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.
This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine. Rather than simply responding to information from the outside world, the brain is constantly anticipating what will happen next. It then compares those expectations with incoming information from the senses and works to reduce any differences between what it predicted and what actually occurred.
Scientists believe this ongoing process plays a central role in how people perceive their surroundings, make decisions, behave, and regulate emotions.
Researchers Erik Stänicke, Bendik Hovet, and Line Indrevoll Stänicke, together with colleagues, argue that this modern understanding of brain function has important parallels with ideas that psychoanalysts have been developing for more than a century.
"For over 130 years, psychoanalysis has developed psychological theories about how predictions take place at a subjective level, which cognitive neuropsychology is now studying at a physiological level."
How Freud's Ideas Connect to the Predictive Brain
Although neuroscience and psychoanalysis approach the mind differently, the researchers suggest that both may be describing related processes.
Neuroscience examines the physical mechanisms behind thought and behavior, often using mathematical models to explain how the brain processes information. Psychoanalysis, which grew out of Freud's work, focuses more on unconscious mental processes, emotional experiences, and the ways past relationships influence present behavior.
In other words, one field investigates what happens inside the brain, while the other explores how those processes are experienced by the individual.
A particularly interesting connection involves the psychoanalytic concept of projection and the neuroscientific concept of prediction.
In psychoanalysis, projection involves attributing feelings, intentions, or qualities to someone else. The researchers suggest that this resembles how the brain uses previously learned expectations to interpret new experiences.
"When we attribute qualities, intentions or feelings to other people, our brain shapes our experience of the world in line with established expectations," says Stänicke.
For instance, someone who has repeatedly experienced rejection may become especially sensitive to signs that other people are rejecting them. Even an ambiguous remark or facial expression might be interpreted negatively because past experiences have shaped what the person expects.
Over time, these expectations can influence how someone approaches unfamiliar situations and forms new relationships.
"This corresponds to the neuroscientific distinction between changing one's own predictions, perceptual inference, and the attempt to make the world conform to them, namely active inference."
Perceptual inference refers to the way the brain interprets sensory information and updates its expectations in response. Active inference, by contrast, involves taking actions that help bring experiences into line with predictions or reduce uncertainty.
Together, these concepts help explain why people do not always experience the world as it objectively is. Their expectations can influence what they notice, how they interpret events, and how they respond.
Why the Brain Holds On to Negative Expectations
The researchers believe the similarities between Freud's ideas and modern neuroscience could offer valuable insights into mental health disorders, particularly those involving deeply established patterns of thinking and behavior.
Both approaches portray the mind as constantly seeking stability and predictability. This tendency is related to homeostasis, the process through which a system maintains a relatively stable internal state.
In the predictive brain model, reducing uncertainty is an important part of maintaining that stability. The brain relies on familiar expectations to make the world easier to understand, even when those expectations are inaccurate or no longer helpful.
"Psychoanalysts refer to the tendency in the mind to recreate familiar relational patterns, even when these are poorly adapted," says Stänicke.
This could help explain why people sometimes repeat harmful patterns in relationships or continue interpreting situations negatively despite evidence that challenges their assumptions.
"Rigid and persistent symptoms, such as paranoid ideas or an internalized critical voice, may be stable but not very flexible prediction models," says Stänicke.
"For example, there may be people who automatically expect criticism, rejection or hostility from others, and therefore interpret situations through this filter despite the fact that reality does not warrant it."
Such expectations can become deeply entrenched because they make experiences feel familiar and predictable. Even when the resulting interpretation is distorted, maintaining an established mental model may feel less uncertain than changing it.
According to Stänicke, this offers a possible explanation for why some psychological symptoms can persist for years and why changing longstanding patterns of thought and behavior often requires considerable time.
The connection is particularly interesting because it suggests that some mental health difficulties may involve more than consciously held beliefs. They may also reflect deeply learned expectations that automatically shape emotional responses and interactions with others.
How Psychotherapy Could Help Change Deeply Rooted Patterns
The researchers also highlight an important distinction between what people consciously believe and what they have learned through experience.
"In addition, both models give us insight into how parts of our expectations of the outside world are not only anchored cognitively, but in procedural memory that is expressed in relational ways of being," he says.
Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory involved in learned habits and skills. It allows people to perform familiar actions without consciously thinking through every step.
In the context of relationships, the researchers suggest that a similar form of learning may help explain why certain emotional reactions and patterns of interaction become automatic.
Someone might intellectually understand that other people are not necessarily hostile or critical, for example, yet still instinctively respond as though rejection is inevitable.
These expectations are not simply thoughts that can be changed through reasoning. They can also be embedded in habitual ways of reacting to people and navigating relationships.
This distinction may help explain why psychotherapy sometimes needs to address personal relationships and emotional experiences rather than focusing only on conscious thoughts.
"Therefore, psychotherapy sometimes has to work relationally. For example, new experiences in the relationship between therapist and patient can gradually help to change entrenched relational patterns."
Through repeated experiences that challenge familiar expectations, patients may gradually develop different ways of interpreting situations and relating to other people.
Bringing Freud's Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Together
The researchers argue that connecting psychoanalysis with modern predictive brain theory could benefit both fields.
Neuroscience may provide a biological framework for understanding processes that psychoanalysts have long described through subjective experience. At the same time, psychoanalytic theories may offer more detailed explanations of how expectations are experienced emotionally, interpreted personally, and expressed through relationships.
The proposed similarities do not establish that Freud's broader theories were correct. Instead, they suggest that two very different traditions of studying the mind may offer complementary ways of understanding some of the same psychological processes.
By examining both the brain's physical mechanisms and the individual's inner experience, researchers hope to develop a more complete understanding of human behavior and mental health.
"Bringing these two fields together can open up for a more holistic psychology, in which both neurological mechanisms and subjective experience are included. In this way, we can understand subjectivity in a more scientific manner."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oslo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Erik Stänicke, Bendik Sparre Hovet, Line Indrevoll Stänicke. Freud’s Model of the Mind Within a Predictive Processing Neuroscientific Paradigm. Entropy, 2026; 28 (3): 318 DOI: 10.3390/e28030318

Indonesian Stock Exchange Plunges After Fresh MSCI Downgrade Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
00:16:00 UTC
09:16:00 KST

Indonesia’s stock market fell more than 11 percent on Friday, the steepest one-day drop since 1998, after the global index provider MSCI proposed the country’s removal from its global stock indexes.
In a statement on Friday, MSCI said that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.”
The proposal is more serious than MSCI’s earlier threat, announced in January to downgrade Indonesia from “emerging market” to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market. Chief among these were the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
On Friday, MSCI again cited “significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market, including persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behavior.”
MSCI said it would procure feedback from market participants until the end of April 2027, and then announce its decision by June 30.
MSCI’s role as the primary benchmark for institutional investors gives it considerable power over emerging economies. As Reuters explains, a downgrade to “standalone” status “would exclude Indonesian stocks from indexes tracked by global funds, potentially triggering billions of dollars in capital outflows.”
Markets responded to the news as one would expect, with the Jakarta Composite Index falling by 11.6 percent, losing $65 of value. It was the largest single-day drop since the Asian financial crisis.
After MSCI’s January announcement, which also caused a hemorrhage in Indonesian equity markets, Indonesia announced a long list of reforms to address MSCI’s concerns, including a doubling of the minimum free float for listed companies to 15 percent. Top executives of the exchange and regulatory body also stepped down.
However, in its statement on Friday, MSCI said that “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market.”
“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.”
MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”
If downgraded, Indonesia would join Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe in the standalone category, becoming both the largest economy and the only Asia-Pacific market in the grouping. MSCI has said that reclassification to “standalone” status is typically done in cases of “severe deterioration in market accessibility or size and liquidity.”
The announcement, which came ahead of MSCI’s expected verdict on Indonesia’s reclassification to “frontier” status next month, came as a shock to many observers. Rully Arya Wisnubroto, head of research at Mirae Asset Sekuritas in Jakarta, told Reuters that the proposal “goes well beyond what we had considered our worst-case scenario.” Another analyst described it as “a wake-up call for Indonesia.”
Reza Priyambada, an analyst and director at Reliance Sekuritas, told the Jakarta Globe that given the reputational impact a downgrade to “standalone” status would have, the government had to act urgently to show it was serious about reform.
“Reforms should not focus solely on market development and the enforcement of sanctions,” he told the paper. “Authorities also need to ensure a level playing field in market mechanisms and address other issues that shape international investors’ assessments of the quality of Indonesia’s capital market.”
If the government fails to stave off a downgrade, it would severely impact Indonesia’s attractiveness as a destination for foreign investment and put significant pressure on President Prabowo Subianto, whose administration has marked a break with the conservative financial stewardship of its predecessors.
Coming to office in late 2024, the former general set an ambitious goal of 8 percent annual GDP growth for the rest of his term, and has introduced a number of high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, that, along with the global spike in fuel prices, have widened the fiscal deficit. Prabowo has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s returns from natural resources and international trade.
The president’s pugnacious and highly personalized style of governance, which has affected everything from fiscal policy to foreign relations, is at the root of much investor concern. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for the country, with the latter citing the “increasing policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”
Perceptions have also been shaped by the growing sense of volatility and unpredictability in how Indonesian institutions as a whole operate. A good example is the jailing in June of Gojek co-founder Nadiem Makarim, previously a leading member of Indonesia’s tech scene, on flimsy corruption charges related to the procurement of Google Chromebooks during his time as education minister.
As one observer noted at the time, the Nadiem case confirmed many investors’ perception of Indonesia as a country where “the line between a business decision, a policy misjudgment, and a prosecutable offense is drawn after the fact by whoever holds power at the time.”
As a reflection of the general economic malaise, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June.
In addition to the aforementioned reforms, the Prabowo administration has reshuffled its economic team in a bid to restore investor confidence. In July, the governor of the central bank stepped down, followed by Prabowo’s replacement of his finance minister in September. It will no doubt also announce a host of new reforms in the days and weeks to come.
Whether all of this has much effect on MSCI’s verdict remains to be seen. Judging by the wording of its latest announcement, some kind of downgrade for Indonesia is certain; it is now merely a question of how severe the shock will be.

2026-10-19
00:02:20 UTC
09:02:20 KST

Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman has met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi to review regional security developments and explore avenues for enhanced Gulf cooperation.
In a statement on the X platform, the Saudi defence minister confirmed that the two sides "affirmed the depth of the fraternal and historical relations between our two brotherly countries" and held detailed discussions on "developments in the regional situation and ways to enhance cooperation and joint Gulf action."
Prince Khalid also met UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
The discussions addressed the critical importance of sustained bilateral coordination "on issues of mutual concern and ways to support efforts aimed at consolidating regional and international security and stability," the minister said.
Yemen conflict
The UAE's official state news agency WAM reported that both sides "exchanged views on regional developments with the aim of contributing to strengthening security and stability and achieving lasting peace in the region."
The diplomatic meetings take place against a backdrop of heightened instability across the wider Middle East, driven by the ongoing Us war on Iran and resumed fighting in Yemen.
In recent weeks, Yemen's Houthi militia have launched repeated attacks targeting Saudi civil aviation infrastructure, including airports, as well as critical energy installations.
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab military coalition in Yemen since March 2015 against the Houthi militia, who seized control of the capital, Sanaa, and several other northern provinces in September 2014.
The UAE, which officially withdrew its main combat forces from Yemen in 2020, announced in December 2025 that it would end its remaining military presence in the country.

India needs more fighter jets. It cannot build them fast enough
Delayed engines and assembly bottlenecks leave India’s domestic output falling behind the pace of fleet retirements
On October 11 at an airbase in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh strapped into a Tejas jet for the last time. It was his final fighter sortie before retiring later this month and he flew it in an Indian-built jet to show support for the country’s domestic defence industry.
A week earlier, he had warned that the Indian Air Force (IAF) faced a critical shortage of fighter squadrons. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year,” Singh said on October 3, noting that “between 36 and 40 aircraft” would need to be produced annually to meet India’s target of having 42 fighter squadrons in service.
“Actually, we need even more than that,” he said.

Flight from Israel makes emergency landing in Bulgaria after bomb threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:58:05 UTC
08:58:05 KST

Flight from Israel makes emergency landing in Bulgaria after bomb threat
Crew of Austrian Airlines flight OS82 decides to land in Sofia after receiving bomb threat, Bulgarian authorities say.
An Airbus A320 flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna has made an emergency landing in Bulgaria following a reported bomb threat, according to the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport.
Austrian Airlines flight OS82 was near the border with Romania when the crew received a bomb threat and decided to land in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, the Transport Ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
Bulgaria’s Ministry of Defence said an air force MiG-29 fighter jet escorted the plane to Sofia airport.
Initial information showed the aircraft carried six crew members and 51 passengers, all of whom have all since disembarked, according to the Transport Ministry’s statement.
The airline told the AFP news agency that a security search of the aircraft was conducted.
“Once the search of the aircraft is complete, the passengers will be rebooked onto alternative flights as quickly as possible,” the airline said.
A crisis response team has been set up, and relevant authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, the Bulgarian Transport Ministry said.
According to aviation and flight tracking site FlightAware, Austrian Airlines 82 left the Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday at 6:46pm local time (15:46 GMT) and landed about three hours later at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia at 9:43pm (18:43 GMT).
Flightradar24 data showed it entered Romanian airspace at about 9:10pm (18:10 GMT) before turning south and heading back towards Bulgaria.
Information from the flight-tracking platform ADS-B Exchange indicates the aircraft was transmitting squawk code 7700 – a signal for a general emergency – at around the same time.
Flydubai incident
Last month, a Flydubai plane carrying 174 passengers was on its way from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv when a co-pilot allegedly attacked the pilot with an axe in an attempt to crash the plane.
The aircraft plunged about 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control by other Flydubai pilots after passengers and other crew subdued the alleged attacker.
The flight was diverted and forced to make an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia.
Authorities in the UAE said the co-pilot was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.
The co-pilot, Hamam Al-Hammami, an Omani national, has since been charged with terrorism offences in the UAE.
The Israeli government responded to the incident by ordering checks on the identities of all pilots flying into the country.

Phone on speaker in train? You may be fined, jailed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:54:30 UTC
08:54:30 KST

As per law, creating a nuisance in Metro rail also attracts a penalty and such persons can be removed from coaches (AI image)
NEW DELHI: In a move that could bring relief to railway passengers disturbed by people playing music or watching videos on their phones in speaker mode and check the growing menace, Southern Railway has warned that such behaviour could attract a penalty of Rs 1,000 and lead to removal from railway premises, including coaches. People persisting with such an act could even face up to six months of jail and up to Rs 5,000 penalty.Southern Railway has invoked Section 142 of the Railways Act, as amended under the Jan Vishwas Act, to enforce provisions dealing with causing a nuisance.Officials said that the provision can be invoked by other railway zones and even by Metro systems to check such behaviour, which adversely affects the comfort of other passengers. As per law, creating a nuisance in Metro rail also attracts a penalty and such persons can be removed from coaches.Section 270 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) defines public nuisance as an act that causes common injury, danger, obstruction or annoyance to people using a public right and hence amounts to an offence.In a circular issued to all its divisions this month and marked to Railway Board, Southern Railway flagged the problem of passengers playing music or audio through speakers at railway stations and inside trains, describing it as a “nuisance”.
The circular also referred to a Railway Board communication issued in July 2012 on the use of mobile phones. The board had flagged issues such as “loud talking, lengthy conversations” and sound of objectionable ringtones inside coaches and asked all zones to create awareness against such practices.
Official communication from Southern Zone stated, “In recent times, with the advent of widespread mobile internet access, the playing of videos and other content in speaker mode is highly prevalent in public spaces. ln the present scenario, there is urgent need to put in place arrangements in order to ensure that travelling passengers are not inconvenienced.”It has directed its divisions to educate passengers on the relevant legal provisions and discourage them from playing music or videos in speaker mode or engaging in loud conversations while travelling or on railway premises. Awareness campaigns are to be conducted through public address systems in regional languages, Hindi and English. It has said that ticket examiners and other senior officials from commercial division can impose the Rs 1,000 penalty on offenders.

Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:36:11 UTC
08:36:11 KST

Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."
The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.
An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.
The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported.
The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.
Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.
"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.
Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.
In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

Anthropic plans 5% stake pledge to tackle AI's impact on workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:27:44 UTC
08:27:44 KST

US artificial intelligence company Anthropic has said that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a newly established public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
The initial commitment to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund is subject to stockholder approval, while an additional 2% of shares may be allocated at the board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value above a predetermined baseline.
The fund will support initiatives addressing the broader societal effects of AI, including potential labour market disruptions, an issue Anthropic has already committed $200 million to researching and addressing.
The fund will operate as a wholly owned limited liability company (LLC), allowing flexibility in distributing resources through donations to nonprofits or direct financial support to specific populations.
The initiative builds on existing commitments from Anthropic's co-founders, who pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and an employee donation programme involving approximately half its workforce.
Combined with the new commitment, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares will be dedicated to public benefit initiatives, including existing pledges, with potential increases tied to future valuation milestones.
Elon Musk, who runs Anthropic rival xAI, on X said he recommended "giving the shares directly to the public."
Anthropic cited the potential impact of AI on workers as one area of focus for the new fund, building on a previously announced $200 million commitment to study and address labour-market disruption.
Global companies have cut thousands of jobs after investing heavily in AI, with many, primarily tech firms, pointing to higher efficiencies from the technology's rapid adoption.
IMF research shows that some 40% of jobs will be either augmented, downgraded or eliminated by AI, with the number as high as 60% in advanced economies, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said last week
