In brief
- The Greens party leader has said it was the "understanding of Senator Shoebridge that leave was agreed".
- Steele-John has denied that and said allegations of inappropriate behaviour against him had been weaponised.
Greens leader David Shoebridge has said it was his "understanding" that it had been "agreed" fellow party senator Jordon Steele-John would take leave, after the latter said he wouldn't step back from his role and accused party factions of weaponising allegations of inappropriate behaviour and comments towards women.
"Senator Shoebridge remains of the opinion that leave is appropriate under the circumstances and reiterates that this in no way prejudges any of the matters being referred to an inquiry commissioned by the WA Greens," a spokesperson for Shoebridge said on Monday afternoon.
"It was the understanding of Senator Shoebridge that leave was agreed."
Shoebridge announced the Western Australian senator had sought leave from the party last week, after media reports emerged of a letter reportedly sent by seven Greens members to Shoebridge detailing allegations made about Steele-John between 2017 and 2025.
However, in a statement published on social media on Sunday night, Steele-John said he was not on leave, adding that he had repeatedly asked Shoebridge not to announce he was as that would appear to validate the allegations against him.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It was a bad call from David. We've all made those in politics," he said.
"So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David's statement."
In the statement, Steele-John also denied any wrongdoing and said he would take part in the inquiry — the key findings of which must be made public, Shoebridge said in his statement on Monday afternoon.
"Because these references have been widely reported as allegations in their own right, I want to address each one fully and directly," Steele-John wrote in his 2,400-word social media statement.
"And I will explain how my experience of family violence collided with nasty political games, and why, despite what you've heard, I'm not on leave."
Steele-John, who uses a wheelchair, responded to three matters raised in the letter, the first about a nickname applied to him: "feels on wheels".
He said the nickname did exist and was used after he became emotional while giving speeches about the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability.
"Over the years, this nickname would periodically resurface like strategic clockwork, growing in lore each time," he said.
"Eventually, I was informed that this phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately.
"And now, in this letter, the existence of the nickname itself is the allegation."
The second matter referred to an alleged Greens event in 2024 that the letter writers claimed had not been reported because of fears the alleged victim would not be believed.
"I'm really concerned to read this. No details were provided in the letter, so unfortunately, at this point, I don’t know how I could respond, or how anyone would begin to investigate it," Steele-John wrote.
The third matter in his response was about allegations of a "serious sexual misconduct" made about him by a woman he had previously dated.
"This is true. There was a complaint of this nature made about me," he said.
"I briefly dated someone in 2025. This person was abusive towards me. With the support of people close to me, I came to recognise that abuse and stopped seeing her."
He said the complaint was made to the Greens leader's office at the time, Greens WA, and to WA Police. He said he cooperated with a police investigation but no adverse findings were made against him.
Steele-John also responded to the creation of a 47-page dossier detailing how the WA Greens would manage media coverage of the allegations.
He claimed his election to the Senate in 2016 had come from a "highly unwinnable spot" and resulted in some party members feeling "that their personal political ambitions had been upended".
"They pressured me to resign the Senate seat immediately and make way for their preferred candidate, and when I refused, they were determined to stop me from being preselected for the next election," he said.
Over the years, Steele-John said the group recruited more members to become an "unofficial faction" within the state party. He said they deployed a "smear campaign" against him by trying to tip off the media about "half-heard" rumours concerning a personal conflict between him and two other friends in 2017.
In 2019, after the rumours resurfaced, Steele-John said a Google document was created so that the party had access to the same information and to formulate a response.
"So why has this been pushed to the media now? It is no coincidence that the letter arrived at the Leader's Office the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection," he said.
"It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party preselections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself."
Shoebridge also said on Monday that he "firmly believes this matter must be resolved with a fair, timely and independent process as is being commissioned by the WA Greens, and he has worked to ensure this occurs".
"This process must include procedural fairness for all involved, with the key findings made public."

mirrored acrylic skin dissolves cube pavilion into its surroundings in mexico
Unknown

mirrored acrylic skin dissolves cube pavilion into its surroundings in mexico
by blurring the boundaries between object and surroundings, the reflective pavilion shifts attention away from its own form and toward the landscape and the people that inhabit it.
prefer designboom on google
MIRROR-FINISH ACRYLIC PANELS CONCEAL pavilion IN GUADALAJARA
Designed by errre taller, Sfumato is a temporary reflective pavilion that reinterprets the Cubo MEM, a prominent sculptural landmark at the ITESO architecture complex in Guadalajara, Mexico. Selected as the winning proposal for the inaugural Pabellón MEM competition, the project investigates how an existing architectural structure can become visually imperceptible while maintaining its physical footprint.
CONCEALED STEEL FRAMING FORMS MONOLITHIC SKYWARD PAVILION
The intervention by studio errre taller wraps the 6.40 × 6.40-meter cube in a reflective envelope composed of 3 mm mirror-finish acrylic panels. The standard 1.22 × 2.44-meter sheets are combined with 76 cm cut sections to maximize material efficiency while maintaining surface continuity. The panels are attached using double-sided tape and silicone to a light-gauge metal stud-and-track framing system supported by an interior wooden sub-structure fixed to the original PTR steel frame.
To preserve the illusion of a monolithic volume, a single access portal is positioned discreetly on the less prominent west face. Inside, the pavilion functions as an open-air chamber for skyward observation, where shifting solar angles track the passage of time through changing internal shadow patterns. Sfumato explores the paradox of architectural presence through disappearance.
project info:
name: Sfumato
designer: errre taller
design team: Humberto Espinoza, Jessica Corona, Fernando Hernández
location: Guadalajara, Mexico

Trump's Netanyahu U-turn comes as Israel fears losing US support and faces European sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:34:24 UTC
05:34:24 KST

Just two days ago, US President Donald Trump was asked whether he trusted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and replied, "I don't trust anybody." But on Sunday evening, in a striking reversal, Trump issued an unequivocal endorsement of Netanyahu, just nine days before Israel's October 27 election. What prompted the sudden change? Until now, all indications suggested Trump had no intention of intervening in the Israeli election. He even avoided meeting Netanyahu on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly last month, apparently to avoid accusations of electoral interference.
Behind the scenes, several figures had urged Trump to distance himself from Netanyahu, arguing that the Israeli prime minister was an obstacle to his plans, particularly the reconstruction of the Gaza Strip. Nevertheless, Trump abruptly abandoned his previous reluctance to intervene and threw his support behind Netanyahu.
Relations between Trump and Netanyahu have experienced their share of ups and downs, but throughout both of Trump's presidential terms, he has generally been careful to demonstrate support for the Israeli leader. Even so, opposition figures in Israel claim Netanyahu had pleaded with Trump and his advisers to secure a public endorsement. According to those claims, Trump's statement was a form of compensation for his refusal to allow Israel to launch an attack on Iran before the election.
Asked whether the endorsement would help Netanyahu, a senior opposition figure said: "It's a question of how it is framed. If the public understands that this is compensation at the expense of security, and that Trump is not allowing Bibi to attack Iran, it could actually hurt him."
In any case, an endorsement from Trump does not necessarily guarantee electoral success. The US president backed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and even sent Vice President JD Vance to Budapest to demonstrate his support. Despite the White House's intervention, Orbán lost the election.
Democratic Rep. Daniel Goldman sharply criticized Trump's decision to campaign on Netanyahu's behalf, while also attacking the prime minister himself.
"Trump should not be expressing his opinion about democratic elections in another country, but it is not surprising that he is doing so for the anti-democratic, pro-authoritarian candidate," Goldman wrote on X. "Make no mistake: The US-Israel relationship depends on bipartisan support, and this alliance will suffer irreparable damage if the Israeli government remains in power after the October 27 election."
Trump and the risks of backing losing candidates
Trump's support for Orbán, including Vance's public appearance in Budapest, ultimately failed to secure victory for the Hungarian leader, who suffered a decisive defeat. By contrast, Trump also supported Argentine President Javier Milei, who went on to achieve a major electoral victory. Trump's approach to political endorsements, including his relationships with allies such as Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, provides another possible explanation for his decision to back Netanyahu.
One assessment is that Netanyahu conveyed a message to Trump that Israel's election was extremely close and convinced him that a presidential endorsement could prove decisive. Trump also consulted John McLaughlin, Likud's American pollster, who worked on two of Trump's presidential campaigns. However, at least two Trump advisers reportedly urged the president not to publicly endorse Netanyahu.
Would Trump's endorsement have any significance if another candidate wins Israel's election and forms the next government? Probably not. Despite the forceful language of his endorsement, it is difficult to imagine Trump being unable to work with another Israeli prime minister.
Could Israel lose the United States?
Meanwhile, an attack by Jewish extremists on European diplomats Saturday in the West Bank village of Taybeh, following an assault on an American photojournalist the previous day, has triggered a diplomatic uproar. Senior Israeli officials warn that the incidents are accelerating European pressure for sanctions while also fueling anger in the United States, both among Democrats and within the Trump administration, which is already grappling with increasingly vocal anti-Israel sentiment among some Republicans.
The attacks have brought renewed urgency to a broader question about the future of relations between Jerusalem and Washington. Netanyahu himself acknowledged Sunday that Israel could lose American support after Trump's presidency ends.
According to a senior Israeli official, the responses from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to the West Bank attacks were unequivocal. The official said American representatives regarded the assault on the diplomats as an act of terrorism and were particularly troubled by the fact that it occurred in a Christian Palestinian village.
Another Israeli source assessed that the attack on the diplomats had reached the attention of the White House, noting that Pope Leo XIV is American-born. Israeli officials also believe Vice President JD Vance, a devout Catholic, may contact Netanyahu about the incident.
The assault on American photojournalist Heidi Levine has provoked particularly strong anger in the United States. Senior Israeli officials note that candidates in the approaching US midterm elections have already issued sharp condemnations of Israel, while some congressional candidates have pledged to promote sanctions and block funding if elected.
A senior official familiar with US-Israel relations expressed concern that the Democrats could gain control of the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate as well. Regardless of the outcome, the official warned that Congress could become far more difficult for Israel beginning in January, even if the Trump administration continues to support the country.
The official pointed to Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, who has been ahead in some recent polls and whose political platform includes strong criticism of Israel.
There are still many supporters of Israel within the Democratic Party, the official said, but the question is how effectively they will withstand pressure from the party's more progressive factions.
Trouble in Europe
At the same time, the West Bank attacks are further complicating Israel's already strained relations with Europe.
The European Union issued a statement condemning the attacks by violent settlers, including those targeting European diplomats, while acknowledging condemnations issued by Israeli officials. The bloc demanded accountability and effective measures to prevent further violence, and called on Israel to halt settlement expansion.
Pro-Palestinian demonstrations and public displays have continued across Europe. On Sunday, an installation in Utrecht, the Netherlands, displayed the names of 26,000 children whom organizers said had been killed in Gaza.
"Anyone who thinks they are protecting the settlements this way is actually endangering their future," a senior Israeli official said of the attacks.
The official described decisive enforcement against the perpetrators as "a moral and legal obligation, as well as a clear Israeli interest."
"European governments are currently under enormous pressure to take action against Israel and the settlements. The day is not far off when those governments will no longer be able to withstand that pressure," the official warned.
"People need to understand that these Jewish rioters, with their own hands, will cause countries that have not yet imposed restrictions on settlement products to do so. There is genuine public and political pressure to impose sanctions because people are seeing the images from yesterday. Decision-makers are under pressure to accelerate legislation and its implementation, and that would cause enormous damage to the Israeli economy."
Another Israeli official familiar with relations between Israel and Europe said that certain EU sanctions would require unanimous agreement among the bloc's 27 member states, meaning Germany would have to retreat from its traditional defense of Israel and abandon its veto.
"The Germans might actually do it," the official warned. "They are already hinting that they have reached the limit of their ability to defend us. We also need to see what other countries friendly to Israel, including the Czechs, Slovaks and others, will do."
The official predicted that if violence by Jewish extremists continues, sanctions will follow, with the measures primarily targeting the West Bank.
"They will try to distinguish between Israel and the territories, but we know there is no such thing as a real distinction," the official argued. "If you impose sanctions on an Israeli bank that provides regular banking services to a settler from Ariel, that bank becomes subject to sanctions, including in the United States. That will affect all of us, including trade, flights and, of course, academia."

Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case as regional outbreak spreads

“Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola,” Amoth said in an interview on Kenya’s Citizen TV.

The latest case developed symptoms on Oct 17, was separated from other people in quarantine, and was tested for the virus with the result returning positive on Oct 18, a health ministry source said.

‘Anger and shame’: Macron denounces France’s nationwide rioting, looting
President Macron promises to increase security, but stops short of announcing a state of emergency or curfew.
French President Emmanuel Macron has expressed “anger and shame” over what he described as violent protesters’ attempts “to bring down the republic”.
In a televised address to the nation on Sunday, Macron promised that rioters and looters would “pay for their crimes”, after Saturday saw some of the worst urban violence in France in years.
The country’s Interior Ministry said that nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Saturday, with about 1,000 police and gendarmes injured.
Macron said there must be a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”.
The president pledged to launch a “crisis unit” to provide “urgent aid … for those who are going through difficult moments”. He added that “lessons will be learned” after the destructive violence erupted this weekend.
“We need to be clear: yesterday, our law enforcement officers and officials, despite their professionalism, were subjected to unprecedented violence in several cities,” he said.
“I’ve asked the government to provide all the lessons learned and to be able to anticipate it to make sure that this does not happen again,” Macron said, adding: “We need unity, we need calm and respect.”
Reporting from Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said Macron’s speech had “perhaps no surprises”.
“Whether it’s going to be enough to placate some people, I’m not really sure, because those who have been out protesting say they’re fed up of hearing these sorts of speeches by the French president,” Butler said.
The protests are quickly becoming a political football for parties vying for public support ahead of presidential elections next year.
Left-wing presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said the French government is “solely responsible” for the destruction during protests, and has “failed to organise the maintenance of public order”.
Far-right presidential hopeful Jordan Bardella called Macron’s Sunday speech “lamentable” and “cowardly”, saying the government has nothing left to offer the French people and “cannot even protect them”.

He passed checks for delayed concussion before returning.
Steve Smith has revealed his anxiety about another concussion after he was struck on the helmet in the first Test against South Africa.
Smith batted on after he was hit by Anrich Nortje in Durban, before staying off the field on day four once Australia declared.
The 37-year-old then passed checks for delayed concussions that evening and the next morning, before returning to the match on day five.
Smith has experienced concussions before, most notably when he was hit by Jofra Archer during the 2019 Ashes and missed the next Test.
"I was a little bit anxious to be honest after the hit," Smith said on Kayo Sports ahead of the start to the second Test.
"I've had a few in the past, and had a few concussions and I really don't like the way that makes me feel.
"The rest of that day I wasn't travelling too well. I think it was more to do with anxiety of hoping not to feel the way that I felt in the past, waking up the next morning and things like that.
"Fortunately I woke up well. I passed all the tests and things recovered pretty quickly."
Smith made scores of 25 and 27 in Australia's 214-run win in Durban, but his bigger contribution was his brilliant catching in the slips.
The right-hander's future has long been a talking point, with Smith often teasing that he could decide at any point he is ready to retire.

"A lot of people have a grand exit and plan it years ahead. But where he's at, and I totally get it, is 'I don't really want to think that far ahead'," Cummins said.
"That doesn't necessarily mean that something's imminent. I think it means he's in a really good place.
"You don't need to read into it any more than that … He's batting really well, catching really well. He seems to be enjoying himself around the group.
"Hopefully he's playing for a lot longer, but any conversation that I have isn't for a big grand exit that's very well planned ahead."

“Father, Father! Call an ambulance!” horrified parishioners could be heard shouting before the live broadcast abruptly cut out.

Vanuatu says it expects fall in China's police presence after signing Nakamal Agreement with Australia
The federal government has notched a potentially significant strategic win in the Pacific, with Vanuatu saying China's police presence there was "expected to reduce over time" following its signing of the Nakamal Agreement with Australia.
China has expanded policing ties with several Pacific nations in recent years, but this is only the second time a Pacific nation has made an on-the-record commitment, albeit with a caveat, to wind back Beijing's police presence on the ground.
Fiji's prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said in 2024 that Chinese officers in his country's police force had been "repatriated" because the two countries had different legal systems.
China has maintained a small police training team in Vanuatu since 2023, and its internal affairs minister, Andrew Napuat, travelled to Beijing last month to renew its policing cooperation pact with Beijing.

Australian activist imprisoned in Vietnam tells family he is 'terrified'
Imprisoned Australian pro-democracy activist Hiep Tran has told his family he never crossed the border into Vietnam, with supporters alleging it is more evidence he was abducted by Vietnamese authorities a month ago.
Australian officials were finally able to meet Tran last Thursday at the B34 detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City, just after a month after he disappeared from Cambodia, where he was meeting other activists opposed to the Vietnamese ruling party.
His wife, Chloe Dang, said Australian officials passed her a brief message from her husband which read: "Hi, how are you all going? I want you to know that I never entered Vietnam on my own."
"I never crossed the border. I am struggling mentally — traumatised and terrified by the situation."
That contradicts what Vietnamese authorities have said. They insist that Hiep Tran and another human rights activist, Norwegian citizen Duc Thuan Nguyen, tried to illegally enter Vietnam to engage in "terrorist and sabotage activities".
Tran is a member of Viet Tran, an overseas Vietnamese opposition group that Vietnam's ruling party has labelled a terrorist organisation. However, most scholars say it has evolved from its armed anti-Communist roots into a political party committed to peaceful change.
Viet Tran says his message is more proof that he was in fact abducted in Cambodia by the Vietnamese authorities and forcibly taken across the border.
Dang said in a statement that she had "received a few fragmented details" about her husband.

Analysis: Without a careful plan, winning the next election could be Labor's undoing
What if the worst thing that can happen to a political party is to win an election?
History is littered with unexpected wins — sweet victories — but are they really that sweet if they let a party overstay its welcome and trash its political capital and brand?
Scott Morrison's unexpected win in 2019 is an example. The Coalition cycled through three prime ministers and went to the election with a thin agenda. Morrison declared the result a miracle. Three years later, the party had trashed its political capital and lost the 2022 election.
John Howard's victory in 2004 is another example. An aging government secured a thumping win and with it, control of the Senate. The extraordinary power it had been handed gave it the freedom to introduce WorkChoices, an industrial relations overhaul that became a political millstone, leading to Kevin Rudd's win in 2007, an election that also cost Howard his own seat.
Read the full story from Patricia Karvelas in the link below.

Macron denounces 'unbridled' violence as France hit by new clashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

Breadcrumb
Macron denounces 'unbridled' violence as France hit by new clashes
President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday slammed the "unbridled" violence that erupted in cost-of-living protests across France, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested Saturday in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, the interior ministry said.
In an address to the nation, Macron said authorities would increase security and vowed lessons would be learned over the police response. But he stopped short of announcing any drastic measure, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
"Tonight, we all feel anger and shame," Macron said, adding that there must be a distinction between protesters with "legitimate demands" with "those who destroyed, smashed, and looted".
"Those who have destroyed must pay," he said, vowing the government would be "uncompromising" towards the "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups, joined by numerous delinquents" who "unleashed unbridled violence in our cities".
AFP journalists said police Sunday fired tear gas and stun grenades at hundreds of people gathered in a Paris square following social media calls for a gathering that authorities said had not been approved.
Bottles and rocks were hurled at police who made several arrests. Shops were also looted around Republique square with specialist anti-riot police deployed for the second day.
Violence also erupted Sunday in the southeastern city of Lyon where a police thwarted youths who attempted to smash the windows of a luxury clothing store.
'Lamentable' address
The unrest came just months from a presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls.
Le Pen said the troubles showed that Macron's administration was "running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented". Her top lieutenant Jordan Bardella described Macron's speech as a "lamentable" address that showed the authorities had "nothing more to say" to France.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, head of the hard-left France Unbowed party, also running for president, urged Macron to respond to the protesters' demands, saying young people "need this episode to reach a positive conclusion".
Macron said "our country deserves a fine presidential election", marked by debates "with the parties, rather than in the streets with violence".
Saturday's protests had seen unions, the anti-Macron Yellow Vests movement that ruffled the early years of his presidency and school students, who had protested for the last weeks, join forces in a show of anger at the cost of living and prospects for young people.
With images of French town halls burning and shops being looted grabbing headlines around the world, US President Donald Trump waded into the debate, blaming immigration for the unrest.
"France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country," Trump said in a social media post.
'All necessary lessons'
Macron vowed that top officials would "make decisions in coordination with mayors to protect our cities, public buildings, and businesses."
"Seeing the streets of our cities ransacked in this way is unbearable," he said, pledging "support" for businesses that suffered.
Macron vowed there would be "full transparency" over the response by security forces to the protests, after criticism that police preparations had been inadequate.
Some opposition politicians have already called for the sacking of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.
Macron said he had asked Nunez to "draw all necessary lessons", particularly with regard to intelligence gathering and anticipation, adding he expected "clear answers".
"It's like we had a war," a 78-year-old Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told AFP amid burnt street barricades from Saturday's protests.
The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire that local prefect, Maurice Barate, told news channel LCI had been deliberately set by "a wild horde".
In Lyon, a tourist office in the city centre was set ablaze during the protests amid multiple clashes and looting.
A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne. In Mulhouse a 17-year-old girl lost an eye, according to prosecutors.

Wages can't rise until productivity does. But what if it already has?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:01:08 UTC
05:01:08 KST

Wages can't rise until productivity increases, but what if it already has?
Workers have been tarred as lazy or inefficient and warned that wages will not rise until there is a lift in Australia's low productivity rate.
But an increasing body of research suggests our shift from a manufacturing-based economy to one dominated by human-delivered services means we are not capturing the full impact of productivity created by jobs in health, education and caring.
"I think we've done a really bad job of talking about how we measure what productivity looks like," says Emeline Gaske, national secretary of the Australian Services Union, whose members work in community services.
"For our members, say, providing support to women escaping family violence: What does productivity look like, in that environment?" she asks.
"Is it how many women they talk to in a day? Or is it whether they're able to find a safe place for even one of those to spend the night with their children?"
Measuring the outcomes of complex questions like these is an increasingly important challenge for our economy.
What is productivity and why is it important?
Productivity is about how much the economy can produce with a certain amount of "inputs": human working hours, capital (like money and technology) or both.
It increases when you get more results — output — with the same amount of inputs, or you get the same amount with fewer inputs.
Australia's productivity rate has been falling as our economy has become increasingly focused on producing services, such as health and education.
That has been a problem in many economies, as Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock observed recently:
"It's just much harder to find productivity improvements … Australia is in that situation as well. We're not alone. But it doesn't mean that we shouldn't be trying to do something about it."
More than 60 per cent of our annual gross domestic product (GDP) is created by services.
We are now locked in a key economic argument: Can a system that's proven precise at measuring how many toasters a factory worker can assemble in a day, measure an economy based on care-giving and teaching?
'Soft outcomes' harder to measure
Georgia Harraway-Jones works with people often experiencing overlapping issues of addiction, mental health and poverty.
"Nobody accesses homelessness services for fun; people are in the worst, dire situations," she says. "Really tough circumstances."
At a motel in Melbourne where she helps people find temporary accommodation, Ms Harraway-Jones reflects on the impact she has been able to have for some clients.
"Where they moved from being homeless, living in a van, to being housed, to being supported to complete some training, to then being able to work and contribute back," she says.
She is concerned that blunt measures of outcomes don't take into account what workers like her are trying to achieve.
"Looking at productivity and looking at the inputs and the outputs and the soft outcomes, we really need to find ways to measure just the social impact that these social and community services have on people's lives."
Productivity gains to 'look very different' in future
The Productivity Commission is the government's think tank and has been vocal about the need to boost productivity so workers can earn more and enjoy higher living standards.
Reports have blamed weak business investment, called for increases in taxes on powerful firms that dominate sectors so that other more competitive businesses might see tax cuts, and to reduce regulation on business.
Australia is not unique, says deputy chair Alex Robson.
Because our economy has shifted from making things to intellectual labour and human services, we need to change how we measure.
"It's not a matter of replacing people with equipment in factories, or better ways of farming, or more efficient ways of mining," he says.
"But what it means is that productivity gains are going to look very different in the future from what they have in the past."
It might be that, instead of lifting the number of patients a nurse deals with in an hour, we focus on care that lowers the risk of expensive re-admissions.
"We know that these costs are coming through the pipeline," he agrees.
"Is there a way that we can spend a bit of money today and invest to avoid those future costs and get that prevention right?"
The growth in our care sector, things like the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) and aged care, means we will need to look at what Professor Robson calls the "difficult and controversial" way we measure productivity.
'Ultimately what we care about is outcomes'
About one in six workers are employed in health, social services or education, and Toby Phillips despairs that we simply count the cost of delivering those services and the amount they get used.
The Centre for Policy Development's (CPD) economic director and co-author of a report about this issue says we should count the things that really matter.
"If our patients are living healthier lives, if our students are getting a better education, and if we're doing all of that for the same dollars, that should represent a productivity improvement," he says.
"The way that we measure productivity and the way the statistics are reported is that doesn't show up at when we get better outcomes and better social value from these sectors."
Mr Phillips says research suggests altering how we measure to capture that value vastly changes what we think about productivity:
- A Productivity Commission report that adjusted to include "patient outcomes" suggests productivity is growing at 3 per cent annually;
- Another looking at education found productivity was 1.3 per cent higher than estimated, once learning outcomes were included;
- Mr Phillips says the Australian Bureau of Statistics found that in education "the public sector is actually getting more efficient per dollar spent". A recent ABS report detailed that "productivity in the underlying [private] market segment fell 16.8 per cent whereas the underlying [mostly public] non-market segment rose 3.9 per cent."
It sounds small. But, in the context of trying to boost our productivity, these numbers are huge.
"The problem is in the very next breath, these same publications that shape government decision-making go on to say part of the reason the productivity slowdown is happening nationally is because of the growth of these sectors," he observes.
"And that just isn't true."
Productivity not as simple as working harder
If community services worker Georgia Harraway-Jones doubled her caseload of 19 clients (and some dependent children), it would theoretically improve her productivity.
But she is blunt about the outcome.
"I wouldn't be able to do it," she says. "The work I do is really quite complex; it's very involved, there's a lot of nuance."
Describing clients with alcohol and drug dependence, mental health issues and complex trauma, she says a bigger caseload would not allow time to address the factors that contribute to people being homeless.
"Frankly, they would receive worse outcomes."
Helping people lead more stable lives is not easy.
And it is not easy to quantify, either.

China facing an investment cliff: ANZ
ANZ's Greater China economic team, led by Raymond Yeung, has done a deeper dive into the NBS economic releases today, including Q3 GDP and key domestic figures centring on the domestic economy including retail sales and fixed asset investment (aka infrastructure and property spending).
As Mr Yeung points out, China's economy expanded 4.5% y/y in Q3, higher than 4.3% in Q2, but year-to-date growth slowed down to 4.6% y/y in Q2 from 4.7 in Q3.
"This underscores the continued loss of growth momentum despite a resilient external sector" Mr Yeung said.
"Weak domestic demand, persistent deflationary pressure and an ongoing property downturn continue to constrain activity.
"While exports have provided an important buffer, they are unlikely to fully offset softness elsewhere in the economy.
"Growth has stabilised, but it has not yet entered a self- sustaining recovery.
Here is some more of the ANZ team's key commentary.
"Investment cliff"
"Property sector: Fixed asset investment growth stayed subdued (-7.2% y/y ytd).
"The property sector remains firmly in contraction, with real estate investment down almost one-fifth year-to-date (-20.6% y/y ytd).
"The property downturn has now evolved from a cyclical adjustment into a structural drag on growth.
"Given property's extensive links to local government revenue, household wealth and financial conditions, its weakness weighs heavily on broader economic activity.
Structural imbalances
"This year's growth figures highlight a deeper rebalancing challenge for the medium term.
"Growth has become increasingly dependent on exports, while domestic demand remains weak.
"While this has supported industrial production (5.5%y/y), it increases China's vulnerability to external shocks.
"Rising trade tensions, protectionist measures and geopolitical frictions pose significant risks to future growth."
"Another imbalance is that technology-led growth has not generated a broad-based recovery.
"China's success in sectors such as semiconductors, AI-related hardware, electric vehiclesand advanced manufacturing has boosted exports and industrial output.
"Their rapid expansion does not automatically translate into any significant improvement in household wealth and earnings, higher consumption or improved confidence.
"Growth has therefore become increasingly concentrated in select sectors rather than spreading across the broader economy."
Balance sheet recession
"China increasingly exhibits characteristics associated with a Japan-style balance- sheet recession, where households and businesses focus on reducing debt rather than increasing expenditure despite accommodative monetary conditions.
"Under such circumstances, stronger public-sector demand may be necessary to offset weak private-sector spending."
Key Event
China's economy accelerates, driven by exports
China's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as a surge in exports and strong factory activity offset persistent weakness in domestic demand, easing pressure on policymakers to roll out more forceful stimulus measures.
The 4.5% growth rate, released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) beat the consensus forecast for 4.4% growth, and improved from the more-than-three-year low of 4.3% in the April-to-June period.
The stronger headline growth was underpinned by a surge in exports, with China's trade surplus widening more than expected in September and keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record $1.2 trillion surplus.
September activity data also showed signs of improvement.
- Retail sales rose a better-than-expected 1.1% from a year earlier, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase and marking the fastest growth since March. Consumer spending remained subdued overall, however, highlighting the uneven nature of the recovery.
- Industrial output grew 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August and marking the strongest pace in six months, underscoring the continued resilience of the manufacturing sector.
- Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2% in the first nine months, dropping at the same pace as in the January-to-August period.
Policymakers have held back from rolling out broad-based stimulus, betting that robust exports, boosted by the global AI-driven tech boom, will keep growth on track to meet the annual target of 4.5%-5.0%.
For January-September, the economy grew 4.6%, within the range of the government's growth.
"The key macroeconomic message is that China's economy is still supply- and production-side driven," said Yuhan Zhang, principal economist at The Conference Board's China Center.
"This supports near-term growth and industrial upgrading, while continued efforts to strengthen household consumption, services demand, and consumer confidence would make the recovery more balanced and sustainable."
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate. A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.
China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.
On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2% in the third quarter, surpassing expectations for a 1.1% rise and accelerating from 0.9% in April-June.
According to Mao Shengyong, deputy head of the NBS, new growth drivers, including high-end manufacturing, the digital economy and modern services, contributed more than 40% to economic growth in the first three quarters.
Beijing has recently expanded support for home buyers, unveiled measures to steer cheaper credit into sectors including infrastructure and technology and allocated 550 billion yuan ($US82.28 billion) in unused government debt quotas to ease local governments' financial strain and expand infrastructure investment.
Authorities also stepped-up fiscal support, including expanding loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers and tapping an 800-billion yuan policy-based financing tool to spur infrastructure investment.
Still, infrastructure investment shrank 4.2%.
"Improved government investment helped arrest the consistent worsening in fixed asset investment," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
Investment in property, however, remained weak, falling 20.6% in the first nine months of the year.

Are you saying 'No' now that you know how much 'Yes' costs?
Hi team,
I was at some auctions on the weekend because a change in Victorian law has injected some fairly radical transparency in the buying and selling of homes.
The reserve price, which is the "Yes, I will sell at that price" number, must now be published a week in advance.
From December 2027 the sale price must be published for 18 months after its sale. (At the moment they are sometimes listed, or you have to pay for that knowledge from companies like Domain or REA)
The auction of the property I attended, and another we got vision of for the TV report, both sold for exactly the published reserve amount.
I'm not suggesting that's what happened, or will happen, more broadly.
But I'm keen to know, for a future report I'm doing, if you've decided not to go and bid on a property because you now know the reserve price.
Are you saving time by not going to places where you wouldn't have enough to buy it? And are they reaching that amount?
I'm on ziffer.daniel@abc.net.au

Key Event
Cleanaway accepts Swedish takeover bid, shares jump
Cleanaway Waste Management has agreed to be bought by Swedish private equity group EQT in a deal valuing Cleanaway at about $9.3 billion.
The announcement prompted an almost 20% jump in the share price of the integrated waste management and environmental services company.
Under the terms of the deal, Cleanaway shareholders will receive $3.095 in cash for each share held, less the cash amount of any dividends paid before completion of the transaction.
The deal reflects EQT's indicative offer of $3.13 per share, adjusted for Cleanaway's final dividend paid on October 8
Cleanaway said the $3.13 offer values the company at about $9.3 billion, including debt, and represents a 32% premium to its closing share price on August 12, the last trading day before EQT's approach was disclosed.
In a statement to the ASX, Cleanaway's board unanimously recommended that shareholders vote in favour of the scheme implementation deed, in the absence of a superior proposal.
Cleanaway said it may pay aggregate cash dividends of up to $0.19 per share before implementation, including a fully franked special dividend. Any dividends paid will be deducted from the scheme consideration.

Separately, in an earnings update, Challenger reported a 5% rise in its assets under management to $31.9 billion for the first quarter of FY 2027, citing strong sales momentum across both domestic and offshore annuities.

Key Event
Bendigo Bank profit, lending slip
Bendigo and Adelaide Bank has posted a lower (unaudited) Q1 net profit of $66 million, down 8.6% from its quarterly average for the second half of FY26.
However, on a cash-earnings basis, the bank's preferred measure that strips out on-off gains and losses, Bendigo reported an 18.5% lift to $112.7 million over the quarter.
Residential lending at $66.2 billion was marginally higher over the quarter, while net interest margins — the difference between the bank's borrowing and lending rates — barrowed 6bps to 1.94%.
The bank says the margin contraction was mostly due "to temporarily higher liquid assets, higher wholesale funding and an adverse change in deposit mix."
Customer deposits rose by 4.8% (annualised) to $74.3 billion over the quarter.
Key Event
Ampol's refining margins double
A bit earlier, we posted the Q3 profits being raked in by global oil giants from the impact of the US/Iran war. Well, you can add Ampol to the list, having just announced a doubling in refining margins in its Q3 earnings update.
Ampol said margins at its Brisbane-based refinery at Lytton more than doubled to $US23.92/barrel over the quarter — a 125% increase compared with the third quarter last year.
In a statement to the ASX, Ampol said "refining performance continued to benefit from elevated regional refining margins, partially offset by higher landed crude premiums".
Year-to-date, the refining margin stands at $US27.05/barrel, a 220% increase on the same period last year.
Ampol noted the impact rising tensions in the Middle East were having on its business and the ongoing constraints in the supply of fuel products.
"These conditions continue to be net favourable for Ampol's integrated supply chain, noting that the unique trading environment that supported the first half has not recurred," Ampol said.

Key Event
Oil producers reaping the benefits of soaring prices
To the surprise of no-one, quarterly reports from oil producers and refiners across the globe are pointing to an extremely profitable past three months.

AI vs AUD — friend or foe?
Sometime back in the mists of time (actually it was 7:24am this morning— but it feels much longer), we pointed out that the US dollar was becoming closely tied to the AI trade, and that while Friday's AI swoon hit the Greenback, it gave the Australian dollar a bit of a leg up in Friday trade.
The big UK bank Barclays has just posited another entirely different idea about the link between AI and the little Aussie battler.
According to Barclays FX team, Australia's role as a global commodities currency play looks likely to benefit from the AI boom's ongoing demand for our minerals.
Barclays's research on the Aussie dollar found "a positive commodity shock affects the RBA and AUD 2–3 times as much as the housing headwinds markets have focused on".
Barclays says while the AUD has lagged both the commodity move and recent RBA rate repricing, the fundamentals have not changed, and it remains "bullish" about the AUD's prospects.
"Australia remains a key beneficiary of the AI commodity supercycle, which is generating a terms-of-trade boost to the economy," Barclays said in a research note.
"Housing measures introduced in the latest budget are a modest headwind, but commodity tailwinds dominate those by a considerable margin."
Tech and AI stocks focus for the week's earnings reports
Stumbles in the market-leading AI trade are set to test investor confidence in the rally in the coming week as Wall Street focuses on quarterly results due from key players, including Meta Platforms.
AI-linked stocks, central to the bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary, struggled last week, with sharp declines in shares of semiconductor companies and tech hardware firms such as Dell Technologies.
Meta, among the hyperscalers spending massively to build AI data centers, highlights the upcoming week of quarterly reports, along with semiconductor firms Lam Research and Texas Instruments and Elon Musk-led companies SpaceX and Tesla.
Worries rippled through markets over risks tied to the financing of the AI build-out boom, which has lifted profits for a wide swath of companies and boosted economic growth.
In other recent signs of caution, strategists at Deutsche Bank and RBC Capital Markets separately pulled back on their recommendations of the tech sector.
Nonetheless, S&P 500 companies are expected to have increased earnings by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES.

What was behind Friday's AI sell-off?
Here's a bit more on Friday AI sell-off from NAB's Senior FX Strategist, Rodrigo Catril, in his morning note:
The US equity sell-off reflected a reassessment of the economics underpinning the AI investment boom rather than a simple downgrade to end-demand.
Investors are increasingly questioning whether future revenue can justify the capital and financing required for data centers, chips and power infrastructure.
CoreWeave sat at the center of the stress: its shares fell 12% on Friday and 25% over the week, while bonds tied to the company and other data-center borrowers weakened.
Pressure broadened from highly leveraged issuers into investment-grade data-center debt, reinforcing concern that tighter financial conditions could restrain the AI capex cycle.
Reports that Apple and Meta would collaborate on AI models able to run locally on laptops, rather than relying entirely on data centers, added another challenge to the prevailing infrastructure-heavy narrative.
The damage was broad across the AI supply chain.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 3.8% on Friday and extended its losing streak to eight sessions, the longest since 2008.
Nvidia declined 1.4% on Friday, while Dell fell 4.6% and lost more than 22% over the week.
The market is also becoming increasingly concerned over the level of concentration with Dow Jones indices noting that around 45 S&P 500 companies identified as having material AI exposure had contributed roughly 39% of the index's 14.1% return through 11 October.

Key Event
Wall Street stumbles on AI worries, ASX set to dip
Fear trumped greed on Wall Street's Friday session as tech and AI stocks were dumped.
All three key indices closed in the red, with the tech-centric Nasdaq sporting the deepest, darkest shade of red.
- S&P 500: -1.1%
- Dow: -0.3%
- Nasdaq: -2.1%
Australia's paucity of tech and AI related stocks looks likely to insulate the ASX from a savage sell-off today.
When the trading closed on Saturday morning (AEDT), ASX 200 futures pointed to a marginal 0.1% decline.
European markets, also largely underweight in AI, had a solid close to the week with the pan-continent Eurostoxx 600 gaining 0.7% across the session.
Wall Street was wobbly all week with investors rattled by concerns over higher interest rates and the debt-fuelled financing behind the AI boom, triggering a selloff in technology and chip stocks.
The S&P 500 shed almost 2% over the five sessions, the Nasdaq fared even worse down 4.5%. The ASX on the other hand gained 1% , Europe was up 2%.
Technology and communication services drove losses while the top gainers were utilities and energy stocks, buoyed by oil prices bubbling up again.
CoreWeave, a data centre operator often viewed as similar in structure to Australia's Firmis, saw its shares down another 12% on Friday having shed around 25% over the week amid increasing investor scrutiny of the financing for the massive AI infrastructure buildout.
"CoreWeave is absolutely the canary in the coal mine" for a market segment that is coming under more stress, Max Frumes, global head of distressed and leveraged finance at 9fin, a fintech corporate credit data and analytics company, told Reuters.
"This is going to be a turning point in the pricing and availability and structure of credit that's supporting the AI boom," Mr Frumes said.
Mr Frumes says other AI-linked debt will follow CoreWeave into distressed territory.
"It's going to get more expensive. There will be a lot more scrutiny and probably some pushback from investors."
The AI jitters spread to currency and bond markets with the US dollar slipping on fading expectations of another rate hike from the Fed any time soon.
StoneX head of market research Matt Weller said it was interesting that the US dollar was becoming closely tied to the AI trade.
"Usually if we see a selloff in tech stocks you would expect the greenback to get a safe-haven bid. We are seeing an element of that into bonds, but the dollar is actually falling," Mr Weller said.
The weaker Greenback supported the Aussie dollar which gained 0.4% to just under 69.50 US cents.
In commodity markets, the global oil benchmark Brent crude futures briefly touched $US110/barrel, its highest level since May as traders reflected on the ongoing drone and missile strikes in the Middle East and the fact that Russian diesel, even if it made to the global market, was unlikely to shift the fuel dial much.
Gold was largely steady on Friday but closed the week down around 0.7%.
Copper prices led other base metals higher on Friday as a weaker dollar offered support.
Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange rose 0.5% to $14,498/tonne, recovering from a near two-week low.
However, copper was lower over the week as the end of strike at big mine in Chile eased supply fears and the reassessment of AI investment weighed on industrial-demand expectations.

Quick hits: Boland's rain-soaked brilliance and a touching family moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:37:55 UTC
04:37:55 KST

Scott Boland makes a destructive return to the team and a South African debutant has a touching family moment as rain plays spoilsport in Gqeberha.
Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Boland's immediate impact
With a Test bowling average under 19 and with 82 wickets from his 19 matches before today, Scott Boland may well be the best bowler to have never nailed down a spot in his country's first-choice XI.
Of course, that's through no fault of his own — the four bowlers ahead of him just happen to be Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.
But the upside of being the team's fifth-choice bowler and fourth-choice seamer is that Boland is, injuries aside, usually only called upon when the conditions are apocalyptic enough to allow for an all-out pace attack.
And Boland would have been licking his lips as he arrived on day one.
Overcast skies, intermittent rain, and a pitch almost indistinguishable from the surrounding turf meant Boland would take Lyon's place in the team.
Surprisingly, however, the wicket didn't appear to be offering a whole lot during Starc and Hazlewood's rain-interrupted opening salvo.
But that all changed with Boland's introduction — the seamer managing to extract some movement during his first over and then wickets in his second.
First, he had Aiden Markram bowled through the gate to one that jagged back viciously off the pitch, then he had David Bedingham caught behind with the very next ball.
What else would you expect?
2. Chris Gaffaney goes down
A man conspicuously absent on day one was veteran Kiwi umpire Chris Gaffaney.
Originally down to stand in his 71st Test, Gaffaney was a late withdrawal after a battle with food poisoning, opening the door for hometown boy Arno Jacobs to make a fairytale Test debut less than a month after umpiring in his first ODI.
Jacobs spent much of his 144-game First Class career in the Eastern Cape, during which he averaged 38.08 as a versatile middle-order batter.
Gaffaney, for what it's worth, averaged 33.41 with the bat during his domestic red-ball career.
3. Ackerman's touching moment
If it weren't for all the rain, you'd call it a baptism by fire.
With inclement weather having delayed the start of play by two hours, 30-year-old South African debutant Marques Ackerman strode out to open the batting on what looked to be a seaming green top and against four of the very finest bowlers in the world.
It was nightmare-inducing stuff — but Ackerman was compact and composed to begin his innings, looking relatively unfazed by Australia's opening barrage.
The only thing missing was a run.
Loading Twitter content
And with drizzle setting in once again during the sixth over of the day, you could tell Ackerman was anxious to get off the mark before the covers returned to the field.
The South African proceeded to nudge a single through gully, receive a warm round of applause, and promptly leave the field as the rain grew heavier.
On his way from the middle, the broadcast cameras caught a lovely moment as a relieved Ackerman located his wife and young child in the crowd, with the three exchanging smiles and waves all the way back to the pavilion.
4. The band plays on
Day one was frustrating for those in attendance at St George's Park.
But through the rain, dreariness, and disappointment, the ground's famous brass band played on.
Loading Twitter content
Their spirited performance didn't quite make up for the frankly laughable 12.2 overs bowled on day one — but it provided a rather jaunty soundtrack to the Gqeberha malaise.

Almost a century after J&amp;K HC was set up, Ladakh gets bench
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:37:32 UTC
04:37:32 KST

CJI Surya Kant inaugurates the Ladakh HC bench in Leh Sunday
NEW DELHI: Almost a century after the establishment of Jammu & Kashmir HC, the Union Territory of Ladakh Sunday got a high court bench, which will sit in Leh, 3,500 metres above sea level — an altitude no other HC can ever match.Inaugurating the Ladakh bench of J&K HC, CJI Surya Kant said, “I am told no HC in our country has ever sat higher. Of course, what matters today is not how high this court sits. What is important is how close it now stands to the people it serves.”
J&K HC came into existence on March 26, 1928, with three judges, including Chief Justice Lala Kanwar Sein.Speaking on the evolution of the justice delivery system in Ladakh in the presence of HC Chief Justice Pushpendra Kumar Bhati and SC judges, CJI Kant said given the difficult terrain and harsh winter, approaching the court was more arduous than the cost of litigation for many. Only after Ladakh became a UT in 2019 was J&K HC rechristened HC of J&K and Ladakh.“But a name on a court’s letterhead is not the same as a court on one’s doorstep… The high court has today crossed the passes to reach Ladakh, instead of asking the people of Ladakh to cross the passes to reach it,” he said, appreciating the efforts of Union govt and Lt Governor V K Saxena, who was present at the ceremony along with attorney general R Venkataramani.
But even establishing an HC bench at Leh would not take justice to the doorstep of far-flung villages in the region, the CJI said, advocating liberal use of technology and legal aid services.“Access to justice, after all, begins not in the court’s compound, but at the litigant’s door. The law places this duty on the HC as well, through its legal services committee, and I am confident that, working... with the legal services authority, it will discharge that responsibility by reaching every door in Ladakh where justice is still awaited,” he said.
In an unprecedented gesture, the CJI said, “Once video-conferencing facilities are adequately available to the lawyers of the Ladakh bench, Supreme Court shall list all matters coming from Ladakh on a single day, and hear them on a day-to-day basis, also through videoconferencing.”“Somewhere in Ladakh today, in a classroom in Kargil or Nubra, there is a young child who will one day argue her first case in this court, and perhaps even sit on its bench as a judge. When that day comes, we will know that this bench has not merely arrived in Ladakh but taken root here,” the CJI said.

Albanian PM refuses to quit as violent protests enter sixth day
Albanian police fired water cannon and tear gas Sunday as violent anti-government protests entered a sixth day and Prime Minister Edi Rama rejected demonstrators' demands that he resign.
Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday, with protesters calling for action over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again at noon in front of the education ministry chanting "Rama, resign" amid a tense standoff with police.
After police bid to disperse the crowds, the protests scattered across the city centre, escalating into hours-long violent clashes.
Protesters set ablaze litter bins in the streets, smashed windows, including at the headquarters of the governing Socialist Party, and set fire to a police station and the entrance of the interior ministry.
Chaotic clashes extended to the main boulevard and square, with demonstrators throwing rocks, Molotov cocktails and charging pyrotechnic devices, as the police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas, according to an AFP journalist.
Ambulances were seen rushing in and out of the scenes of clashes to pick up the injured.
The ministry of Health told AFP that 16 police officers were injured -- 14 of them when protesters attacked the police station.
Before the protest, shops and offices in the city centre secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent them being thrown by protesters.
In a video broadcast lasting more than an hour, Rama ruled out resigning, stating that the protests are the "work of an outside hand".
According to Austrian federal press service, Rama's official visit to Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker scheduled for Monday, has been cancelled by the Albanian side.
Buildings on fire
Writer and activist Lura Elezi, 38, told AFP that she is protesting for "a better life, rule of law and against crime and corruption".
"I love my country, but my government does not respect us - it defies us. Every citizen must take responsibility for their country, taking on the duty to lead, to love, and not to destroy one's own nation", she said.
Tirana saw its harshest violence on Saturday when protesters threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins to use as barricades against advancing police.
Buildings including a court, banks and a post office were set on fire or severely damaged. Police used rubber bullets on demonstrators for the first time since the protests began, AFP journalists saw.
Albert Nushi, from the police public security department, said in a statement that because of "the unprecedented scale of attacks on the police", a "limited use of specialised crowd-control equipment was used".
He urged protesters to stay away from masked individuals behind the violence and "assemble in a peaceful manner".
He said police detained 54 individuals in Tirana on Saturday, and 27 face criminal proceedings.
According to a health ministry report issued Sunday, 65 people were injured, including 37 police, with 12 people hospitalised.
Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured in the clashes, including 169 police, the ministry said.
Albania's close ally, the United States, reacted late Saturday. Its embassy in Tirana urged "restraint and calm on all sides".
The European Commission in a written statement, "condemned the use of violence in Tirana and other cities", adding that the response to it "must remain proportionate".
"In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process... grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner," the statement said.
The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.

‘Wild West’ in southern Israel: illegal gun dealers turn Negev into a firing range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:35:24 UTC
04:35:24 KST

Gunfire during the day. Gunfire at night. In cities, Bedouin communities and the surrounding countryside. Across a vast stretch of southern Israel's Negev desert, residents say they are suffering from the same relentless problem, from Rahat, Tel Sheva and Omer to Retamim in the Ramat Negev Regional Council and the communities of Nevatim and Givot Bar in the Bnei Shimon Regional Council.
Rahat Mayor Talal al-Krenawi expressed confidence in the police but acknowledged that the gunfire could not be ignored. "There is no doubt that there has been scattered gunfire over the past week," he said. "These are not brawls. These are arms dealers testing weapons. This is a matter for the police, not the municipality or the community."
The practice of arms dealers taking weapons out for a "test drive" for prospective buyers is nothing new. Residents of Nevatim, among others, have long suffered from the phenomenon, with certain areas regularly used by dealers and buyers as makeshift firing ranges. After all, prospective buyers want to test the merchandise before purchasing it.
"There is constant gunfire at night," said a Nevatim resident. "By the time the police reach the more remote parts of the area, the criminals have already disappeared. Over the past year, the gunfire has become more intense and frequent, including shooting incidents in broad daylight. Despite police efforts and the recruitment of volunteers to help protect our homes, we feel as though we've gone backward. All these efforts are just a drop in the ocean."
A resident of one of the Bedouin communities described an atmosphere of fear and lawlessness. "It's the Wild West. It's not like it used to be. Today, you worry about every step your children take. You never know where the danger will come from. We think twice before going out because we're afraid. We used to let our children walk home from school, but now we make sure to drive them there and back because you never know what might happen. Young people do whatever they want, and nobody holds them accountable. They know it, and they don't care. It's a terrible feeling."
Al-Krenawi said local authorities were cooperating fully with the police but argued that more sustained enforcement was needed. "The amount of weapons out there justifies establishing a command center in Rahat for an extended period, not just two weeks or a month. In the meantime, we're purchasing drones through philanthropic donations. I must point out that shooting incidents in the city have fallen by more than 40% since the beginning of the year. But when police forces leave the city, the shooting returns."
Residents of Rahat themselves are increasingly desperate. Just last week, kindergarten and elementary school children had to make their way to school while gunfire could be heard in the background. In such circumstances, it is hardly surprising that many residents feel there is little point even calling the police.
In practice, complaints from residents of Jewish communities tend to attract greater attention, including from the media. Nir Zamir, head of the Bnei Shimon Regional Council, said: "We view the shooting incidents and the harm to our residents' personal security with the utmost seriousness, particularly in recent weeks. The reality in which Negev residents, Jews and Bedouins alike, suffer from the terror of gunfire, violence and a lack of law enforcement is intolerable and demands immediate, fundamental action."
Zamir said local authorities were working continuously to protect residents but stressed that they could not replace the state's law enforcement and judicial institutions. "We call on those responsible at the national level, the government, the National Security Ministry, the police and the justice system, to step up efforts on the ground to tackle gunfire and the breakdown of law and order in the Negev. Our residents' personal security is not a privilege. It is the state's most basic obligation to all its citizens," he said.
Omer Local Council head Erez Badash argued that the latest shooting incident reflected a much broader security threat. "The latest shooting incident in the Negev is not an isolated case. It is further evidence on the ground supporting the warning issued by the head of the Shin Bet during a Cabinet meeting," he claimed. "The processes of radicalization and 'Palestinization' in the Negev are no longer merely a local criminal problem but a strategic and national threat. 
Over the years, the increase in marriages to women from the Gaza Strip and the West Bank has brought extremist influences and ideologies into the Bedouin population. We have been seeing the consequences on the ground for years, from the events of Operation Guardian of the Walls in 2021 to the armed groups operating today."
"Even if this involves a minority of the population, when that minority is driven by a radical agenda and possesses hundreds of thousands of weapons, it dictates the reality and the balance of security on the ground," Badash continued. His claims about the scale of the weapons and the causes of radicalization were not substantiated in the report. 
"The events of October 7 showed us all the price of turning a blind eye. It is time for the Israeli government and the prime minister to move from words to action: determined enforcement, cutting off weapons smuggling and addressing nationalist radicalization at its roots before the next disaster occurs."
Israel Police said in response: "Calls received by the police emergency hotline, 100, were answered and handled immediately, and police forces operated on the ground to stop the gunfire. Israel Police continues determined and sustained operational activity in the area, during which arrests have been made and weapons seized. These operations have led to a reduction in shooting incidents in the region and will continue in order to strengthen residents' security and protect public safety."

The threat against an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna that was diverted to Sofia on Sunday was made in a telephone call to Vienna airport, Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said on Monday.
Authorities are investigating the threat, Karner said in a joint press conference with his Bulgarian counterpart, without giving details about the nature of the threat or the person who made it.
Following the alert, the captain declared an emergency by transmitting the international emergency transponder code, Squawk 7700, and diverted to Sofia Airport.
The aircraft landed safely in Sofia at approximately 7:42 p.m. local time. Emergency crews and security personnel were waiting at the airport, and passengers and crew were evacuated under the supervision of local security authorities.
All passengers and crew were safe and unharmed, an airport spokesperson said. The aircraft was moved to an isolated area, where bomb disposal teams and security personnel conducted searches in accordance with established procedures. No explosive device had been reported as found at that stage.
IAF emphasizes incident did not occur in or near Israeli airspace

Gaza flotilla postpones mission to 2027 after mechanical failures, migrant deaths at sea

19:33:36 UTC
04:33:36 KST

The international flotilla scheduled to reach the Gaza Strip in October will not complete its voyage this year, this time without being intercepted by the Israeli Navy, organizers from the Freedom Flotilla Coalition announced on Saturday.
The flotilla’s organizers cited a series of mechanical failures, prolonged repairs, and two distressing encounters with the bodies of migrants who died attempting to cross the Mediterranean Sea.
According to the organizers, the delays significantly narrowed the time remaining for the voyage, prompting a decision to postpone the attempt to reach Gaza until spring 2027.
The flotilla embarked on a tour of European ports aimed at mobilizing public and international support for the campaign against Israel's naval blockade of the Gaza Strip.
One of the main vessels in the campaign, the Kate, also known as the Tenacity, departed Bristol, UK, on August 17 and stopped at ports in Ireland, France, and Spain. It was scheduled to arrive in Sicily on October 14, from where it was expected to sail toward the Gaza coast.
However, the two encounters with the bodies of migrants in the open sea were described by participants as a "distressing experience." They emphasized, however, that the technical malfunctions and the need for extensive repairs were what ultimately reduced the time available to complete the voyage.
"We set out for Gaza, and it is painful to end this journey without reaching it," said Frank Romano, a volunteer aboard the Kate. "The commitment that brought us aboard the ship remains as strong as ever. We will carry the solidarity we encountered at every port in Europe into our preparations for the 2027 mission."
Governments worldwide have failed to protect Palestinians, activists say
Huwaida Arraf, a human rights lawyer and member of the flotilla's steering committee alongside Israeli activist Zohar Regev, criticized the international community, arguing that governments worldwide had failed to protect Palestinians.
The organizers stressed that postponing the voyage did not mean suspending their activities. They said they would continue campaigning against Israel and demanding that governments halt arms transfers and military cooperation with the country.
Meanwhile, in the Sicilian city of Catania, flotilla activists and supporters are holding an interfaith conference over the weekend under the title "Faith in a Time of Genocide."
Christian, Muslim, and Jewish religious figures are expected to participate, including Sandra-Laya Ruch of Canada, a former activist with the Isha L'Isha organization in Haifa who is described as a "Jewish priestess."
Participants will discuss the responsibilities of religious communities in light of the war in Gaza and possible courses of action against Israeli policies.
The flotilla organizers also announced their support for international activists traveling to the West Bank to participate in the olive harvest alongside Palestinian farmers. They condemned plans to deport foreign activists arriving in the area.
Next flotilla expected to depart in spring 2027
According to the organizers, they will continue their land activities and preparations for the next flotilla in the coming months.
The next flotilla is expected to depart in spring 2027, although no precise sailing date has been announced.
Israel, for its part, maintains that its naval blockade of the Gaza Strip is a necessary security measure intended to prevent weapons smuggling and remains determined to enforce it.
Separately, the Italian legal team representing the Gaza-bound Sumud flotilla welcomed progress in an investigation by the Rome Prosecutor's Office into senior Israeli officials on Saturday, over suspicions of their involvement in the interception of flotilla vessels in 2025 and 2026 and harm allegedly inflicted on participants.
The investigation, launched following complaints filed by 50 Italian citizens, concerns suspected acts of torture, kidnapping, physical assault, and other offenses.
Among those named on Saturday were Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, and other senior officials in the IDF, Israel Police, and Israel Prison Service.
In a statement, the legal team said the investigation was advancing in the direction it had advocated in its appeals to the authorities, describing the development as "a significant signal against the sense of impunity enjoyed by the chain of command responsible for these serious crimes."
The team said it would continue working to advance legal proceedings in other European countries.
