The cost of putting off an economic reckoning is looming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Australia has delayed economic reform and now a crisis is looming
Procrastination. As your correspondent can attest, it's an easy trap to fall into.
Prioritise another task to avoid something more difficult or unpleasant, even though you know you'll eventually need to do the thing you're putting off, and it will be all the more painful because of the delay.
The problem is that we're now doing it collectively, at least across much of the Western world, including Australia.
Take budget repair, with related implications for long-term fiscal sustainability and intergenerational equity.
A new Grattan Institute report titled Budget reboot: How to fund Australia's future notes that state government debts have more than doubled since 2019.
"Outside of the COVID pandemic, the last time Australian governments owed this much, the country was still paying off debt from a world war," the report says.
The interest bill on state government debt has also doubled to 0.6 per cent of Australia's annual economic output, and is likely to soon double again as rising interest rates have pushed the cost of borrowing to fund deficits up roughly fourfold since immediately before COVID.
The federal government hasn't been nearly so profligate, at least since the pandemic stimulus period ended, but it too is stuck in a structural deficit, and may find itself on the hook as some states meander towards fiscal disaster.
The Grattan report argues that governments should be saving for a rainy day now, as global economic, climate and geopolitical shocks are set to become more frequent. But most aren't.
"Tomorrow's Australians will increasingly pay the price for today's deficits, whether through higher taxes or worse public services," the authors warn.
The price of past inaction
A separate survey-based report from AMP finds that today's young Australians are already paying a large personal price for policy inertia in the past decade, long after it became clear that a cocktail of tax breaks, planning restrictions, low interest rates and financial deregulation was pushing housing out of reach.
The study finds that more than half of adults under 30 have changed their intentions about having children due to cost-of-living pressures. Close to half have reconsidered having children altogether.
Almost two-thirds feel they need a foot on the property ownership ladder before starting a family, but AMP's calculations show most need more than a decade to save a 20 per cent deposit.
No wonder Australians are having children later, and fewer of them when they do.
One might consider this a form of enforced procrastination due to the social and economic conditions young people are facing.
Ironically, this seems likely to compound the budget problems already brewing, especially when smaller migration programs are in vogue.
"As Australia ages, the challenge is sustaining living standards and meeting growing demand for care without placing an ever-greater burden on working families," AMP deputy chief economist Diana Mousina writes.
A plan for GST reform
The Grattan Institute's plan isn't for swingeing budget cuts, although it does urge far greater spending discipline, especially at the state level.
"Too often, politicians approach 'budget repair' as if it merely requires cutting a few wasteful public spending programs," the Grattan report pointedly cautions.
"But given the size of the fiscal challenges Australia faces, the reality is that lasting repair will require both spending and revenue reform."
In fact, given it considers Australia "a relatively low-taxing country", at 29.4 per cent of GDP compared to the OECD average of about 34 per cent, the report argues there's room for a modest revenue increase.
But is there the will?
The single best means to raise that additional revenue, the Grattan report argues, is through an expanded goods and services tax (GST), with a higher rate of 15 per cent (up from 10) and fewer exemptions.
It wants fresh food taxed, with future consideration given to removing other current exemptions, such as health and education, which it argues favour higher income earners who spend more on these services.
The higher rate and taxation of all food would bring in an additional $76 billion in annual revenue.
Loading...
Grattan argues close to half of that ($33 billion) should go to cutting income tax, particularly for low- and middle-income earners.
It earmarks about $25 billion to boost welfare payments and rent assistance to compensate for the increased GST, with a bit extra to reduce poverty among this group.
The states would receive the remaining $18 billion to improve their fiscal sustainability in the face of soaring healthcare costs.
It also strongly recommends pulling the 2018 sweetheart GST allocation deal with Western Australia and using the $6 billion that saves to boost the federal budget bottom line.
Is a crisis necessary?
It's difficult to have much optimism that Grattan's vision is politically possible.
We've already seen Anthony Albanese run a mile from any hint of abandoning WA's favourable GST distribution, concocted by his Liberal predecessor Scott Morrison.
Loading
Even where the federal government is trying to claw back savings, it's on the back foot.
Look at the losing battle it's facing to remove an additional private health insurance subsidy from older Australians.
Politicians opposing the change have pointed to the number of pensioners who would be left worse off, portraying them as a universally disadvantaged group who cannot afford the extra cost.
But the modelling they have provided hasn't distinguished between the numbers of full and part pensioners affected. The reality is that relatively few full pensioners are likely to have private health insurance.
Most of those with health insurance are on part-pensions, often supplemented by income streams from substantial savings, and are typically owner-occupiers with very low housing costs because they aren't paying rent or a mortgage.
In fact, my GP's practice stopped blanket bulk-billing for pensioners a few years ago because they found many of these patients had more spare cash to spend than the doctors treating them. The clinic now bulk-bills on a discretionary basis to those in genuine need.
That's not to mention the heat the government is facing over its much bigger reforms to rein in NDIS spending, reduce tax minimisation via trusts, or to wind back the negative gearing and capital gains tax breaks that have done so much to pump up the housing market and reduce intergenerational equity in the first place.
As Treasurer Jim Chalmers recently said: "Power is much more effective right now in the distorting and blocking than the building or reforming."
The sense of hopelessness is spread across the political spectrum.
One of Chalmers's predecessors, Joe Hockey, with a very different vision of reform as expressed in his largely rejected austerity budget of 2014, recently told The Business things would need to get a lot worse before they might get better.
"There's going to have to be a crisis now. There's going to have to be a financial crisis," the Abbott government treasurer warned.
"And people will only take the medicine when they feel really ill about it. And I think this is coming right across the world."
As debt balloons around the globe and interest rates start soaring with it, it seems the time for procrastination is finally approaching its end.

Women allege pregnancy discrimination inside government departments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Pregnant women and parents allege discrimination inside Australia's public service
In short:
Twenty-four women working in the public sector tell Four Corners they have faced pregnancy discrimination at work.
A former high-ranking counterterrorism official alleges she was denied flexible working arrangements after her second child.
A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson says her role evolved after the Bondi terrorist attack and required attendance five days a week.
Australia's public sector is meant to set the national standard for promoting gender equality in the workplace.
But inside government departments, Four Corners has uncovered accusations of discrimination against mothers and pregnant women who work in public sector roles.
These women describe being demoted, denied flexibility, turned down for promotions and refused a comfortable place to breastfeed.
Some were made redundant or let go after they fell pregnant or took parental leave.
And it is not just a handful of cases.
They were among more than 100 women who told Four Corners they had experienced discrimination at work after becoming pregnant or having children as part of a wider investigation.
Former counterterrorism official denied flexible work
Until June, Alisha Warner was a counterterrorism senior executive in the Department of Home Affairs, one of Australia's most powerful government departments.
For nine months, before going on leave for her second baby, Ms Warner had a flexible arrangement in which she worked full-time hours over four days.
"When I mentioned that I was looking to come back on the same arrangement … I was surprised to be met with an immediate response that senior executives cannot work flexibly," Ms Warner told Four Corners.
"I was really shocked and a bit concerned immediately about what that was going to mean."
Documents obtained under Freedom of Information laws show Ms Warner's managers asked Human Resources for advice about Ms Warner's request to return on compressed working hours.
The department had "reasonable business grounds" to reject Ms Warner's flexible request, the advice said. However, it acknowledged it was "arguable" that Ms Warner's four-day arrangement "remains in place".
When asking for a response to be prepared to send to Ms Warner, a department official said: "Confirming the intention is not to support the request, so I'd be grateful for a response on that basis."
The department offered Ms Warner a short transition period but, after that, required her to work five days a week.
"Going back full-time [over five days] is not always an option. In my case, I can't get another day of child care for my children," she said.
"I was very strongly given a message that flexible work was not going to be supported anywhere."
Ms Warner's managers said they needed someone in her role five days a week, because the counterterrorism space had changed.
"The scope, complexity and sensitivity of the responsibilities assigned to the relevant role under consideration evolved post the Bondi terrorist attack, and now require sustained senior executive level oversight, leadership and decision-making," a Home Affairs spokesman told Four Corners.
"Accordingly, the department was not in a position to approve compressed hours."
Ms Warner said she was surprised to hear this response.
"In my previous arrangement, I was available whenever needed on that day off for anything critical," she said.
"There [were] lots of assertions made about how busy the role was, but to be honest, not a lot of real tangible evidence or information about why it couldn't be performed under the same arrangement."
Ms Warner eventually took a voluntary redundancy and was asked to sign a confidentiality agreement, which she refused.
"A lot of people are forced into signing non-disclosure agreements, and that has led to a complete dark hole of people feeling like they're alone in what has happened to them," she said.
Looking back, Ms Warner said she did not want to leave her job.
"It's not a real choice when you don't feel like you have any other choices," she said.
"The thought of leaving a full-time, secure, senior executive role that I worked so incredibly hard to get filled me with absolute dread."
Former senior government official supports increased flexibility
In a rare interview, former assistant commissioner of the Australian Border Force, Kylie Rendina, said some managers in the public service viewed flexible work arrangements as too costly.
However, she said it was often a greater financial loss for an agency to lose a staff member who needed flexibility.
"Sometimes, the people who are making the decisions at all levels don't really have a good understanding of the costs of losing a resource and retaining a resource," she said.
Analysis showed replacing an experienced staff member in an organisation could cost 50 to 200 per cent of an annual salary, Ms Rendina said.
Now working as a consultant in the public sector, she called on agencies to change their attitudes toward flexible work arrangements to keep up with the demands of raising a family.
"We didn't need the flexibility that we want today, probably largely based on one parent being at home a lot of the time,"
Ms Rendina said.
"That's just not reality anymore."
A Home Affairs spokesman denied there was a culture of denying flexible work arrangements due to cost but acknowledged it was a factor.
"Any expenditure of resources, including the engagement of staff, must be considered within the department's budget and in accordance with its obligations under the Public Governance Performance and Accountability Act," he said.
Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth said the Australian public service, including the federal government, aimed to be a "model employer".
"We've got to make sure that we're not suggesting just because you're taking flexible work, that somehow you're less productive or not contributing," she told Four Corners.
"That's a bit of an outdated stereotype.
"We've got to make sure that everyone is promoting those conversations, but there is a right for flexible work."
Ms Warner took action against the Department of Home Affairs in the Fair Work Commission, alleging a breach of the flexible work provisions.
The mediation ended without agreement, and she decided not to escalate her claim to the Federal Court.
"I strongly believe in my case, but I also know how much lawyers cost," Ms Warner said.
"The biggest disappointment for me is the message that [my story] sends to all the other women coming up through the ranks in the public service, who are already thinking, 'I have to hold myself back if I want to have kids.'"

Houthi missile strike kills 53 Yemeni soldiers, wounds 200 as Saudi Arabia cancels major summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

02:52:59 KST

At least 53 Yemeni soldiers were killed and 200 others wounded Monday when Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles at a military training camp in southern Yemen, in one of the deadliest attacks since fighting intensified earlier this year, Yemeni military officials said. The strike came as Saudi Arabia canceled a major international investment conference following repeated Houthi attacks on its territory.
The missiles struck a camp in Shabwa province operated by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. According to a Yemeni military official, the attack occurred as newly recruited soldiers were lining up for a training session. The provincial government warned that the death toll could rise as authorities assessed the casualties.
The Shabwa authorities condemned the strike as a major escalation, saying it had targeted recruits undergoing training and preparation. They called on Yemen's presidential leadership and the Saudi-led coalition to accelerate the deployment of air defense and early warning systems to protect the province against further attacks.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, promised a "firm response," accusing the Houthis of resorting to terrorist attacks when facing military pressure. The rebels acknowledged carrying out the strike, claiming that the camp was operated by Saudi officers and that some had been killed. They provided no evidence to support that assertion, and Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The attack marks another escalation in Yemen's civil war, which has intensified since the broader conflict involving Iran began in February. The renewed fighting shattered a ceasefire established in 2022 that had largely halted major hostilities between the Houthis and government forces.
The Houthis, who control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north, have expanded their military operations in recent weeks, targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities while also capturing territory along the Red Sea coast near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
On Monday, the rebels claimed to have conducted six additional attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting oil facilities, military installations and Riyadh's international airport. They did not specify when the operations occurred. Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued danger alerts, although there were no immediate reports of casualties or damage from those latest claims.
The continuing attacks have begun disrupting major economic events in the kingdom. Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it was canceling an international investment conference scheduled for the following week, which had been expected to attract senior executives from Wall Street and other international financial institutions. The decision underscored the growing consequences of the Houthi campaign for Saudi Arabia's economy and international business activities.
The latest escalation follows a series of deadly incidents inside Yemen. On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry accused Saudi-led forces of carrying out an airstrike in the rebel-held northern province of Saada that killed at least nine people, including five children and two women. The rebels said additional strikes over the weekend had left more than 30 people dead or wounded. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to those allegations.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large areas of northern Yemen. Riyadh has long viewed the movement's military capabilities and its ties to Iran as a threat to its security. According to U.N. experts, Iran and allied groups in Lebanon and Iraq have provided the Houthis with military expertise, training and advanced weapons, although Tehran denies supplying arms to the rebels.
The conflict has taken on renewed strategic importance as Houthi forces advance near Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major offensive aimed at removing the rebels from recently captured territory along the coast.
Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department renewed its demand Monday for the release of more than 20 Yemeni employees of the American Embassy in Sanaa, marking five years since their detention by the Houthis. The embassy suspended operations in 2015, but local employees continued providing security and maintenance services. Washington called for their immediate and unconditional release.

“Eventually, I believe, current attempts to understand the mind by analogy with…

“Eventually, I believe, current attempts to understand the mind by analogy with man-made computers that can perform superbly some of the same external tasks as conscious beings will be recognized as a gigantic waste of time.”
— Thomas Nagel, The View from Nowhere

Ukraine war latest: Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says

Ukraine war latest: Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
Key developments on Oct. 19:
- Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
- Ukraine brings home 23 children from Russian occupation
- Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
- 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
- 'Absolute atrocity' — Russian drone strike on park in Kharkiv Oblast kills children
- Russia strikes 28 critical energy facilities across Ukraine in latest wave of attacks, Zelensky says
Ukrainian forces have carried out what they describe as a "first-of-its-kind" aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier directly from a front-line position by drone, the Ukrainian military and defense company Gurzuf Defense announced on Oct. 19.
The operation involved Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, and 10th Army Corps, along with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Gurzuf Defense.
The Ukrainian military did not disclose the date of the operation or the section of the front line where it took place.
The wounded soldier, serving with the 30th Brigade, had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position "under constant threat of death." His fellow soldiers maintained contact with him and delivered food, water, ammunition, and medicine by drone, Gurzuf Defense said.
After the soldier suffered a severe injury, evacuating him by ground became impossible because of Russian drone activity in the area and mined terrain. Attempting to reach him on foot or with a ground robotic vehicle, the usual way of evacuating the wounded, would have put the rescue team at risk.
Ukrainian troops used a heavy-lift hexacopter drone, the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6.
The team first delivered special equipment with carabiners to the wounded soldier, then sent the drone equipped with a winch. Guided remotely by fellow soldiers who remained in contact with him, the soldier secured himself to the evacuation system, Gurzuf Defense said, calling the operation an "unprecedented mission."
The drone then transported him to a safer position, where other soldiers met him and arranged further evacuation to a hospital. The mission lasted 1 hour, 14 minutes, and 36 seconds, covering a distance of 62 kilometers (39 miles).
The company said the operation required close monitoring of the airspace and electronic warfare protection throughout the flight. The soldier is now receiving treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger, according to the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade.
"An extremely complex operation, but a successful one. This is a historic event," "Napalm," a 92nd Brigade programmer who was involved in preparing the operation, said.
"It marks the next stage in the evacuation of the wounded, which we will all eventually reach. Now the serious, systematic work begins to ensure that such missions take place on a regular basis," Napalm added.
Gurzuf Defense co-founder Pavlo Feldblium warned that aerial evacuation should not be treated as a routine practice, citing the risks to wounded soldiers during flight. Each mission would need to be planned individually for the specific circumstances and location, he said.
"Air rescue is a last resort when there is no other way to save a person," Feldblium said.
According to the Ukrainian outlet Ukrainka Pravda, the hexacopter Heavy Shot Ayudag-6's platform has a flight range of up to 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) and an operational altitude of 150–300 meters (500 to 1,000 feet), while the aircraft itself weighs about 98 kilograms (215 pounds) and can carry 70–90 kilograms (150 to 200 pounds).

Ukraine brings home 23 children from Russian occupation
Ukraine has brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory over the past week, the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19.
The rescued children are now receiving psychological support and assistance in restoring their Ukrainian documents, Bring Kids Back UA said.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory is 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
Another child returned to Ukraine was 13-year-old Polina, who survived a Russian combat drone strike near her home and was later afraid to go outside, the statement said.
Russian troops also raided her home and destroyed communication devices to limit access to information, according to Bring Kids Back UA.
As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia.
Ukrainian human rights groups estimate that hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian children are under Russian control, including those who have been deported or forcibly transferred and those who remain in occupied territories and are at risk of deportation.
Ukrainian officials estimate the real figure of abducted children could be far higher. Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets puts the number at up to 150,000, while Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights Daria Herasymchuk has given a range of 200,000–300,000.
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.

Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
Ukraine and Russia are nearing an agreement on the final details of civilian evacuation from the front-line town of Oleshky and nearby settlements in the Russian-occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
The two sides are discussing a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, rather than having to travel first through Russian-occupied areas and then through Russia and Belarus, Lubinets said in an interview with Ukrainian broadcaster Espreso.
"We are making as much progress as possible. We are now moving toward agreeing on the final details to ensure a ceasefire and evacuate everyone ... directly to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government," Lubinets said.
Lubinets did not specify what direct evacuation to Ukrainian territory entails, but one possible option is to transfer civilians across the Dnipro River to the Ukrainian-controlled western bank.
He added that Kyiv has been holding daily negotiations to unblock the humanitarian evacuation and that Moscow has begun considering a proposal Kyiv put forward long ago.
"We still have some difficult issues to resolve, but I hope that in the near future we will all see concrete results from these negotiations," Lubinets said.
No final agreement has been publicly announced, and it remains unclear when an evacuation could begin.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people possibly remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.

3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
At least one person was killed and eight others injured after multiple waves of Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight on Oct. 19.
Several explosions rocked the capital just before 11 p.m., with further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m., Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported. Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said damage was reported in at least three districts.
One person was killed in the Desnianskyi District where a non-residential building caught fire and a metro station was damaged, DSNS said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko earlier reported a fatality was that of 21-year-old woman.
The above-ground Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were temporarily closed for repairs, city officials said.
Later on Oct. 19, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said more than 70 workers were repairing the damaged metro infrastructure, with the most difficult work involving power supply and train control systems. Repairs had continued since overnight but were being slowed by air raid alerts, which forced crews to take shelter.
Train service between Lisova and Akademmistechko stations was expected to resume that evening, with trains skipping Chernihivska until repairs were completed, Klitschko added.
Five people were injured in the Solomianskyi District when a 25-story residential building was damaged, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It is not yet clear where the other injuries occurred.
The Cosmo Multimall shopping and entertainment center sustained significant damage in the Solomianskyi District. Its administration said no employees were injured and that the mall was working to resume operations as soon as possible. The center did not disclose the extent of the damage or provide a timeline for repairs.

'Absolute atrocity' — Russian drone strike on park in Kharkiv Oblast kills children
Two children were among six people killed in a Russian drone strike on a park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv Oblast, on Oct. 19, according to updated casualty figures released by Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
The victims included two girls, aged eight and one, three women aged 28, 34, and 36, and a man around 40 years old, Syniehubov said, adding that at least 15 people were injured, including seven children.
The drone struck the town's central park while many people, including families with children, were there, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. He also pointed out that the attack made no militarey sense.
The governor initially said that at least 15 other people were injured, including seven children. He later raised the number of people killed to six, including three children.
The attack occurred at around 4:30 p.m. local time, the Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office said. According to preliminary findings, Russian forces used a Geran-3 drone for the attack.
"This cannot be treated as just another news story. The world must not get used to the killing of Ukrainian children and civilians," Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Telegram.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the attack an "absolute atrocity."
He said a girl called Angelina, a little over a year old, was killed in the park, and her mother Inna passed away in the hospital. He also identified another victim of the attack as a 14-year-old girl.
"These are horrific photos, but behind them lie shattered lives and the truth about this war. We must protect lives. Ukraine needs air defense," Zelensky said. "We ask that sanctions against Russia NOT be lifted until the killings stop."
Prosecutors have opened a pre-trial investigation into a possible war crime.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and 17 settlements in the surrounding region, injuring 11 people, over the past day, Syniehubov said.

Russia strikes 28 critical energy facilities across Ukraine in latest wave of attacks, Zelensky says
Russian attacks struck 28 substations and other critical energy facilities across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19, following another wave of missile and drone attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.
At least 550,000 households lost power overnight, Zelensky said, following a coordination meeting on the situation in Ukraine's regions.
Russian forces targeted energy infrastructure in 11 oblasts overnight and on the morning of Oct. 19, First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov reported. Additional power outages caused by Russian strikes and ongoing hostilities were reported in four other oblasts.
One energy worker was injured in an attack on an energy facility in Vinnytsia Oblast, Nekrasov said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity wherever security conditions allow, although prolonged air raid alerts and the threat of renewed Russian strikes are slowing restoration efforts, according to the Energy Ministry.
During the overnight attacks, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in several waves in what Zelensky described as a "targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast."
Zelensky said Ukraine had "once again" received no advance warning from its partners about the strikes.
Nekrasov said that over the past week, Russia carried out 87 targeted attacks on Ukraine's energy, oil, and gas sectors. Authorities recorded 224 incidents that caused damage to energy, oil, and gas infrastructure during that period.
Russia has carried out 2,147 attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since July 16, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian published on Oct. 19, citing figures as of Oct. 17.
"Not a single day has passed without attacks on energy infrastructure," Koretskyi said.

Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest

Unknown Publisher

Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest
Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European integration, spoke out in an Oct. 19 interview against the idea of an open contest for prosecutor general.
The EU has demanded a reform of Ukraine's notoriously corrupt and politicized prosecution service and called for making the procedure for picking the prosecutor general less political and more merit-based. Meanwhile, anti-corruption activists and pro-reform lawmakers have accused the Ukrainian authorities of sabotaging rule of law reforms and resisting the demand for depoliticizing the Prosecutor General's Office.
"I see experts arguing that there should be an open competition for the position of prosecutor general," Chentsov told the Ukrainian media outlet Yevropeiska Pravda. "But that is not something the EU requires, nor is it standard practice in Europe."
He argued that recommendations by Council of Europe experts "clearly emphasize the need to comply with Ukraine’s Constitution, which sets out the roles of the president and parliament in the appointment process."
"How to ensure transparency and select candidates based on their professional qualifications remains open for discussion," Chentsov said. "But personally, I see neither the need nor the possibility of holding an open competition for the position. A balance must be struck between political independence and professional competence."
According to a plan approved in December by Taras Kachka, Ukraine's former deputy prosecutor general for European integration, and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, Ukraine should "conduct a comprehensive review of the selection and dismissal procedure of the prosecutor general, with a view to aligning it with European best practice." The plan also envisages reinstating transparent contests for other top prosecutor jobs.
According to Ukraine's interim benchmarks for EU accession, Kyiv "needs to depoliticize the position of the prosecutor general, including by making the selection and dismissal procedures more objective, transparent and merit-based, taking into account European standards."
An EU official who spoke on condition of anonymity told the Kyiv Independent that the EU accession benchmarks "are not calling for it to be an elected position but the process should still change."
"For the EU, the gold standard is to have the involvement of independent, international vetters," the official said. "Separately, the EU and Ukraine launched a task force last week to implement Kachka-Kos and the EU's Rule of Law benchmarks. It serves to identify deficiencies in the current set-up, which would also include the prosecutor general's selection process."
In June, Anastasia Radina, head of parliament's anti-corruption committee from President Volodymyr Zelensky's party, submitted to parliament a bill seeking to select the prosecutor general in a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
Radina's opponents argue that the Kachka-Kos plan does not envisage a contest involving international experts and that a contest for the prosecutor general's job contradicts Ukraine's Constitution.
Radina has denied the claim that it contradicts the Constitution.
"There may be different interpretations of the benchmark, but I'm not aware of anyone having proposed an alternative approach so far," she told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine's prosecutor generals are appointed by the president with parliament's approval and have been seen as closely aligned to whoever is in power. Radina's bill seeks to depoliticize the prosecutor general's appointment.
The debate on selecting the prosecutor general intensified under the previous occupant of the job, Ruslan Kravchenko.
Kravchenko faced scrutiny due to his role in the crackdown on the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) in 2025.
He was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated.
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
As Kravchenko left Ukraine, he simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him. The charges were later dropped as unfounded.
Kravchenko later moved to Austria, the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 23.
